items.question: What If an earlier, more thorough modernization of Russia
human_answers: I would highly recommend you watch NojRant's NOT the Origins of Russian Authoritarianism . If you'd like a forum post, read my posts in another thread from here onward to here : they briefly go over parts of what you're interested in, and some of it is repeated below. If you want good detail, I'd recommend Robert K. Massie's book Peter the Great . tl;dr - clothes were only a small part of the reforms, there was major modernization of the economy, education and the legal system, and you seem to have a very, very stereotyped and caricaturish understanding of the topic to speak with such confidence. The problem with the reforms was not in their superficiality, but that most of them required follow-through by Peter's successors that, for reasons I'll get into, did not happen until Catherine II some 40 years later. A highly ideological statement if ever I've heard one. Define what it means to be 'European' in clear terms. Absolutism is actually a major benefit in this situation, mainly because it is not a parliament. Parliament is essentially a tool for the ruling class to give themselves endless privileges and benefits: a ruling class composed of rural nobility would see urbanization as a threat to their power over their tenants (and ultimately their wealth) and pursue policies that deurbanize the country, whereas one dominated by bourgeois interests would be enriched by urbanization. Urbanization ultimately leads to a richer, stronger, more industrialized nation overall, while deurbanization does not. As long as Russia has a strong nobility and a comparatively weak bourgeoisie, parliament is a nonstarter for your purposes because the default net effect of parliamentary actions will be to increase nobles' control over their tenants, hence limiting urbanization, hence limiting development of private capital for industrialization. A country with no strong king to keep the nobility in check will increasingly resemble basketcases like high medieval Hungary or early modern Poland, where the nobility could ignore the king as they pleased and even fight each other as warlords ( picrel ). Even in a lesser form, this can have severe consequences: for example, under the Dual Monarchy, the Hungarian half of the empire was granted wide-ranging autonomy, which the Magyar nobility used to systematically and shortsightedly block the development of industry. The result was that Hungary remained agrarian and economically backward, even failing to compete in agriculture - the thing the Magyar nobles had sought to protect - to the extent that Russian grain imported via the Adriatic was undercutting Hungarian grain on the Austrian market. In a strong monarchy, even if the king still has to appease the nobility somewhat, he has control over the spigot of privileges and benefits and only gives them out when he has to, and expects loyal service in return - and can even retract privileges if his position is strong enough, like Ivan the Terrible did in Russia or Charles XI did in Sweden (ref. the Great Reduction ). This is constitutionally impossible with a strong parliament, though the king can always try his luck with a coup or a civil war. Even strong monarchs who retained parliaments as vestigial organs of the state, like Louis XIV, actively avoided involving them in political decisions because they knew that weak parliaments were made strong by getting involved in decisions that could've been made by the king's bureaucrats instead. However, monarchies can be weakened by unexpected deaths, child kings / regencies, changes in dynasty, coups, successful riots by the urban population against taxes, and successful rebellions by uppity nobles. These events force the king to repeal unpopular laws and grant new privileges to the nobles in exchange for their support, because his normal ability to make himself obeyed by his subjects is drastically reduced and he needs to sweeten the pot for them to obey him again. This must be avoided to preserve the king's power and prevent the nobility from pressuring him to grant more privileges. 17th century Russian tsars were weakened by the Time of Troubles, which allowed the nobility to demand a host of new concessions in exchange for their support of Mikhail Romanov as the next tsar. The most notable concession was that their pomestie fiefdoms, which were previously non-hereditary and granted to them in exchange for service to the state, were made hereditary. Russian tsars spent the next century trying to repeal these various privileges with limited success, and were occasionally hampered by new setbacks, such as the 1648 salt riot , which led to tighter restrictions on serfs being introduced to satisfy the nobility. 18th century Russian tsars were weakened by chronic succession problems, which resulted in the new tsar/tsarina having to bribe the nobility as a class with extra privileges to get them to accept their rule. The reason was that Peter had revised the succession law from male primogeniture to "Whoever the tsar chooses," meaning that the tsar's will could be forged or denied by any member of the imperial family who could bribe the palace guards to support them in a coup. Catherine I, Elizabeth, Catherine II and Alexander I all rose to the throne this way. Doable - NojRants covers this succinctly in the Serfdom section of his video. If you can't avoid the Time of Troubles, then you need to avoid all further destabilizing events which allowed the nobility to wring additional concessions out of the tsar. If you want participation in European scientific exchange, look to the Russian Academy of Sciences. Its alumni included such giants as Lomonosov: they corresponded regularly with their peers in the rest of Europe, and many foreign luminaries visited to teach at the academy, such as Euler. Many advances in cartography, botany and geology came from the work of scientists who had been educated in the Academy or invited from abroad to work there. But given the list of names you chose, I suppose your chief interest in the Enlightenment is politics. Of which I frankly don't see the point. If you want to be welcomed at the salons of Paris and London, dressing in European fashion is a bonus, otherwise you might taken as a neat little foreign curiosity. What led you to this conclusion?

I would like to see that properly thought out! ... but: You'd probably need to address the "modernisation challenge" that any Eastern European polity would face and that stems from the divergent socio-economic foundations on which society rested in Western and Eastern Europe respectively. This hearkens back to the Middle Ages and the long-term demographic consequences of the Mongol devastations and the division of labour that only became more and more entrenched over the centuries: The High Middle Ages saw a trend towards slow re-urbanisation, communalism, development of crafts, revitalisation of trade, a new surge in scholarship and education, and while the epicentres of this were in Italy, France, along the Rhine and across the channel in England, this was, in the 11th and 12th centuries, a trend that spread everywhere, towards the North and towards the East. Kiev was a huge bustling urban centre of trade, learning... I know that the "Mongol explanation" is criticised for being overused in the history of Eastern Europe. But the Mongols did wipe out particularly the urban populations and, where their influence lingered, continued to be an important indirect factor working against urban communal independence, hemming the kind of social milieu from which early modern advances stemmed. And so, even before the conquest of the Americas by Western European powers, Eastern Europe became tendentially focused on exporting unprocessed raw materials while Western Europe developed proto-capitalist structures and more and more complex structures of value addition - and while the latter fomented the growth of a bourgeoisie, the latter could do with mostly just landowners and peasants. This is the situation you're still facing in a 17th century Russia, and every new world crop that was invented and massively increased agricultural productivity in Russia would, under these circumstances, only deepen the continental division of labour. The basic difference between Dutch society and Russian society was not clothes, you are right, but it also wasn't some political or religious agenda of its individual rulers. It was, I would argue, that the Netherlands had a sizable and growing bourgeois class where ideas which we consider "modern" grew and were pushed, while Russia had much less of that. Thus, in my eyes, the real challenge you're faced with is how to close or bridge this gap of bourgeois development.

This is more thinking aloud on possible developments that you'd need than dismissing this as impossible, but "the modernization didn't go deep enough" raises the question on what would be enough. Russia is rather removed from being comparable in some significant ways to England and France even in Ivan's (as in Ivan the Terrible) time for a multitude of reasons, and that's with quite a bit longer than a POD in Fyodor III's time. You'd probably need something where there's more capital (and that going into trade and industry) for Russia to meaningfully resemble the West in the sense you're aiming for, which is not something any tsar can simply make from sheer determination and energy or Peter would have managed it OTL. Saying this was OTL too much focused on clothing and beards is being rather unfair when he genuinely wanted a stronger and richer Russia and was trying to make one, not just imititate Western European fashions. I'm not saying someone else couldn't have done better than him (I'm very sure someone more familiar with economics than I can describe his failings much better than this post), but anyone in this position has a lot of work ahead of them.

Actually, modernization did start almost immediately after the ToT. However, it is rather difficult to expect some kind of a miracle from a poor country with very limited natural resources surrounded by the aggressive enemies. So obviously the progress was slow and not because of the Dutch clothing. The beards considerably shortened during Alexey’s reign and by time of FIII death the Hungarian dress became popular. FIII conducted a fundamental administrative reform when he abolished appointments by the pedigree. Formally, it was: the imperial status was recognized throughout Europe and after the GNW it became a dominating regional piwer. Serfdom in a form everybody is talking about only started during the reign of PI and reached its apogee during the “enlightened” reign of CII. BTW, a “popular perception” among the noble classes, merchants and manufacturers by the time of CII was that serfdom is beneficent for economy. How and why would it change? AFAIK, since mid-XVII the “enlightened absolutism” was a trade mark in what you are calling “Europe” (geographically, Russia was the biggest European country). Now, this is a truly interesting part. Can you please elaborate on how exactly it will get richer within social and economic framework reasonably well related to OTL? This is a genuine question and a meaningful answer will be greatly appreciated. How Enlightenment improved life of the French lower classes in the XVIII century? Well, some of these “giants” had been simply bought (reasonably cheap) by CII, which guaranteed acceptance of the Russian aristocrats in the salons Paris as welcomed equals regardless of their intellectual capacities. I’m sure that in London’s and Paris’ equivalents of the saloons they were even more welcomed. BTW, by mid-late 1700 Russia had a reasonably well developed literature. Unfortunately, Russian drama of that time was, as in the rest of Europe, under the French influence (eek) but this did not apply to the comedies. This is quite possible by the virtue of him not being Peter and a chance to avoid the GNW. However, the problem of the natural resources will not go away and neither would one of the fools and roads.
items.original_question:
AHC: an earlier, more thorough modernization of Russia

PoD: the 1600s. I mean a Russian modernization with less emphasis on shaving beards and adopting Dutch clothing but more on modernizing the economy, education and the legal system. The end state - Russia becomes an European country by the 1700s. Serfdom isn't abolished yet (albeit it's weakened), neither is absolutism, but Russia is genuinely richer and it participates fully in the Enlightenment - by the mid-late 1700s Russian thinkers stand alongside Montesquieu, Rousseau and Diderot (or their ATL equivalents) as the intellectual giants of the era, they aren't just curiosities, they're welcomed at the saloons in Paris and London as equals. I think a healthy Fyodor III might be a good starting, IOTL he died in 1682 aged just 20, if he lives until 1720s, things might be significantly different.

criteria.1-2: Ignores Russian structural conditions and assumes reforms succeed because a ruler wills them.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two constraints, such as serfdom or autocracy, but treats them simplistically or as easily removable.
criteria.5-6: Covers several major constraints and links them to modernization outcomes, though some mechanisms are shallow or uneven.
criteria.7-8: Explains how landed nobility, serfdom, limited urban bourgeois development, fiscal-military needs, and succession politics shape reform feasibility.
criteria.9-10: Integrates Russia's social, economic, institutional, and geopolitical constraints into a nuanced causal model showing why some reforms could succeed while others would resist change.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Modernization Pathways
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the concrete mechanisms through which earlier modernization could affect Russia's economy, state, military, education, science, law, urbanization, and integration with Europe.
criteria.1-2: Gives broad claims about Russia becoming more European or powerful without explaining mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Lists possible reforms but rarely explains how they alter institutions, incentives, or social groups.
criteria.5-6: Explains several pathways, such as army reform, schooling, bureaucracy, or industry, but omits important interactions or bottlenecks.
criteria.7-8: Covers multiple interacting pathways, including capital formation, urban growth, technical education, bureaucracy, military competition, and elite incentives.
criteria.9-10: Provides a rich, interconnected account of how reforms propagate through state capacity, class structure, markets, knowledge exchange, legal administration, and military-fiscal pressures.

criteria.name: Long-Range Chain Coherence and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces plausible medium- and long-term consequences of earlier modernization across Russian domestic development, European balance of power, expansion, reform cycles, and later crises.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly to sweeping outcomes such as liberal democracy, industrial superpower status, or no revolution without intermediate reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Offers some downstream effects but relies on linear, deterministic extrapolation and misses major feedback loops.
criteria.5-6: Traces a plausible sequence over decades, with some attention to feedback between reforms, elite resistance, war, and economic growth.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent long-range chain from the point of divergence through 18th- and 19th-century consequences, including tradeoffs and unintended effects.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a detailed, causally linked timeline showing how reforms reshape or fail to reshape Russian society, imperial expansion, European relations, industrialization, and revolutionary pressures.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids overclaiming, handles uncertainty, and maintains internal consistency with the chosen premise and known historical dynamics.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident, contradictory, or anachronistic claims with little regard for feasibility or uncertainty.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty superficially but still asserts implausible outcomes or contradicts its own assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Generally consistent and cautious, though some claims are underqualified or not fully reconciled with stated constraints.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes and flags major contingencies such as ruler death, noble backlash, war, and fiscal limits.
criteria.9-10: Maintains strong internal consistency, explicitly manages uncertainty, presents alternative plausible branches, and avoids deterministic or self-contradictory reasoning.

items.model_answer:
The question of what might have happened if Russia had undergone an earlier and more thorough modernization is one of the great counterfactuals of modern history. To answer it, we need to consider what "modernization" would have meant in the Russian context—typically a combination of industrialization, agrarian reform (especially the abolition of serfdom), legal and administrative rationalization, expansion of education, and the development of representative political institutions.

Had Russia pursued such reforms more vigorously in the late 18th or early-to-mid 19th century—say, under Catherine the Great following through on her Enlightenment correspondence, or under Alexander I acting on the constitutional drafts of Speransky, or under Nicholas I rather than retreating into reaction after the Decembrist revolt—several major consequences become plausible.

First, the abolition of serfdom decades before 1861 would have allowed a freer labor market, a more dynamic peasantry, and faster urbanization. Russia's chronic agricultural backwardness, which persisted even after emancipation because of the redemption payments and the commune (mir), might have been avoided if reform had been pursued in conditions less defensive and grudging.

Second, earlier industrialization would have meant Russia entering the late 19th century not as a catching-up power but as a genuine peer of Germany, France, and Britain. The Crimean War defeat of 1856, which exposed Russia's technological and logistical weakness, might never have happened—or would have gone differently—altering the entire balance of power in Europe.

Third, and most consequentially, a modernized Russia might have developed a stable constitutional order. The tragedy of late imperial Russia was that reform always lagged behind social pressure: the 1905 constitution came only after revolution, and even then the autocracy resisted genuine power-sharing. An earlier, organic development of representative institutions, civil society, and the rule of law could have produced something resembling a constitutional monarchy on the British or Scandinavian model. This would likely have prevented the radicalization of the intelligentsia, the appeal of revolutionary populism and Marxism, and ultimately the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917.

The global consequences of avoiding 1917 are staggering to contemplate: no Soviet Union, no Communist International, possibly a very different course for the interwar period, the Chinese Revolution, decolonization, and the Cold War. World War II itself might have unfolded quite differently if Germany faced a stable, industrialized constitutional Russia rather than perceiving the Bolshevik state as both a threat and an opportunity.

That said, one should be cautious. Russia's size, ethnic complexity, and geographic exposure created structural challenges that reform alone could not erase. Modernization in other empires (Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Qing) often destabilized rather than saved them, by raising expectations the regime could not meet. It is entirely possible that earlier modernization would have produced earlier revolution, simply on different terms. The Russian autocracy's dilemma was real: to reform was to risk losing control, but not to reform was to guarantee eventual collapse. The counterfactual is illuminating precisely because it forces us to see how narrow the window for successful reform actually was.

items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?

items.model_answer:
If Britain and France had made peace in 1811, the trajectory of the early nineteenth century would have shifted dramatically, though the durability of such a settlement is highly questionable.

By 1811, both powers were exhausted in different ways. Britain was straining under the costs of the Continental System, which damaged its export economy and triggered the financial crisis of 1810–11, while also being entangled in the brutal Peninsular War in Spain and Portugal. France, despite Napoleon's apparent dominance, was finding the Continental System impossible to enforce, particularly against Russia, which had begun openly trading with Britain again by late 1810. A peace would most plausibly have required Napoleon to abandon or relax the Continental blockade in exchange for British recognition of French hegemony in continental Europe, possibly including formal acceptance of Joseph Bonaparte in Spain and a settlement over colonial possessions.

The immediate consequences would have been significant. The Peninsular War would likely have wound down, as Wellington's army depended on British naval supply and political will; without that, Spanish and Portuguese resistance might have been crushed or forced into compromise, consolidating Bonapartist rule in Iberia. More importantly, Napoleon would no longer have had a strategic rationale for invading Russia in 1812. The catastrophic Russian campaign, which destroyed the Grande Armée and triggered the War of the Sixth Coalition, was driven largely by Tsar Alexander's defection from the Continental System. With the blockade lifted, that flashpoint disappears, and Napoleon retains his veteran army intact.

The War of 1812 between Britain and the United States, which was caused largely by British maritime practices stemming from the war with France (impressment, Orders in Council), would probably never have occurred, sparing North America considerable bloodshed and possibly altering Anglo-American relations for decades.

However, a lasting peace seems unlikely. The fundamental incompatibility remained: Britain could not tolerate a single power dominating the European coastline from Hamburg to Cadiz, and Napoleon could not abandon his ambition to reshape Europe. Previous peaces, like Amiens in 1802, had collapsed within fourteen months. A 1811 peace would probably have functioned as a truce, giving Napoleon time to consolidate his empire, train his son as heir, and perhaps stabilize his dynasty—conceivably allowing Bonapartist France to survive as a great power well into the nineteenth century. Conversely, if war resumed after a few years' breathing space, Napoleon would face Britain with a stronger continental base but without the moral and military catastrophe of Russia having weakened him first.

The most profound long-term effect might therefore be the survival of the Napoleonic dynasty and a continental Europe organized around French rather than Austro-Russian principles, delaying or preventing the conservative Restoration order established at Vienna in 1815.

edus.text: If Britain and France had made peace in 1811,
the trajectory of the early nineteenth century would have shifted dramatically,
though the durability of such a settlement is highly questionable.
By 1811, both powers were exhausted in different ways.
Britain was straining under the costs of the Continental System,
which damaged its export economy and triggered the financial crisis of 1810–11,
while also being entangled in the brutal Peninsular War in Spain and Portugal.
France, despite Napoleon's apparent dominance, was finding the Continental System impossible to enforce,
particularly against Russia,
which had begun openly trading with Britain again by late 1810.
A peace would most plausibly have required Napoleon to abandon or relax the Continental blockade in exchange for British recognition of French hegemony in continental Europe,
possibly including formal acceptance of Joseph Bonaparte in Spain and a settlement over colonial possessions.
The immediate consequences would have been significant.
The Peninsular War would likely have wound down,
as Wellington's army depended on British naval supply and political will;
without that, Spanish and Portuguese resistance might have been crushed or forced into compromise,
consolidating Bonapartist rule in Iberia.
More importantly, Napoleon would no longer have had a strategic rationale for invading Russia in 1812.
The catastrophic Russian campaign, which destroyed the Grande Armée and triggered the War of the Sixth Coalition,
was driven largely by Tsar Alexander's defection from the Continental System.
With the blockade lifted,
that flashpoint disappears,
and Napoleon retains his veteran army intact.
The War of 1812 between Britain and the United States,
which was caused largely by British maritime practices stemming from the war with France (impressment, Orders in Council),
would probably never have occurred,
sparing North America considerable bloodshed
and possibly altering Anglo-American relations for decades.
However, a lasting peace seems unlikely.
The fundamental incompatibility remained:
Britain could not tolerate a single power dominating the European coastline from Hamburg to Cadiz,
and Napoleon could not abandon his ambition to reshape Europe.
Previous peaces, like Amiens in 1802, had collapsed within fourteen months.
A 1811 peace would probably have functioned as a truce,
giving Napoleon time to consolidate his empire,
train his son as heir,
and perhaps stabilize his dynasty—
conceivably allowing Bonapartist France to survive as a great power well into the nineteenth century.
Conversely, if war resumed after a few years' breathing space,
Napoleon would face Britain with a stronger continental base
but without the moral and military catastrophe of Russia having weakened him first.
The most profound long-term effect might therefore be the survival of the Napoleonic dynasty and a continental Europe organized around French rather than Austro-Russian principles,
delaying or preventing the conservative Restoration order established at Vienna in 1815.

items.question: What If the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant?
human_answers: You are thinking of the Mongol's as a unified force which by this time is not exactly correct. Hulegu and the Ilkhanate were based in Iran (mostly) so the OTL force would not be interested in expanding in Eastern Europe. Batu / Berke and the Golden Horde started their drift towards Islam in this period but their control over the European fringe via their vassals in Kiev and Muscovy wasn't absolute and relied on the tolerance of their Orthodox faith. Any attack on Europe may well become religious in nature (which by itself is an interesting counterfactual) and I suspect any support from the Russian principalities would be lukewarm perhaps even moving towards outright rebellion. It would also be short lived given that the Mongol Civil War is coming. Biggest outcome if the Russian principalities do revolt could be a more Islamised Russia which would be a huge change for world history.

Is there any reason to assume that the forests of western europe were somehow “denser” than those of the eastern? Specifically, those of the Central Russia? BTW, it is not like the Mongols uniformly came from the open steppe: IIRC, Subotai came from Uryankay area which, AFAIK, mostly forests and mountains and he was doing quite well in the Russian forests and pretty much everywhere else. Of course, the Southern direction was much richer than the western one but #1 was the eastern one - China. AFAIK, the South ended up being problematic due to a limited feeding base for the horses but all theories about Mongolian conquest of the west are seemingly ignoring allocation of the resources. The western campaign (including Russia) presumably started with a big force but its second stage, Hungary and Poland, was on a much lesser scale. The map on the OP has “Ulus Jochi” and “Ulus Batu” as separate entities but this was not the case: Batu was a titular head of the Ulus of Jochi. Was there an interest in Mongolia in expanding Ulus Jochi even further at the expense of other endeavors (and other family members)? IMO, this is unlikely because China remained the main theater (BTW, Subotai was sent there after the european campaigns). Were there unlimited human resources? Hardly: part of Hulagu’s force were troops “lended” by Batu. So, with what would Batu conduct his european conquest and why would the Great Khan be interested in its continuation? Formally, the task as formulated by Genghis was fulfilled: the Kipchaks punished and subdued and “the last sea” (Adriatics would do) reached. Was Batu too interested? It does not look like this was a case because he had to create a brand new state from the scratch with the very limited resources (something like 5,000 Mongols).
items.original_question: What if the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant? https://www.reddit.com/r/imaginarymaps/comments/pkb97x/what_if_the_mongols_invaded_europe_the_old_world A sudden interesting thought came to mind. What if, unlike in OTL, the Mongol Empire had not expanded into the Levant and had instead resumed its campaign into Europe? In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. If this did happen, what changes would follow? - The Mongol Empire’s advance into Western Europe. - The survival of the Abbasid Caliphate.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise discipline and factional accuracy
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames which Mongol forces could plausibly redirect toward Western Europe instead of the Levant, accounting for mid-13th-century fragmentation among the Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, and Great Khanate rather than treating the Mongol Empire as a single unified actor.
criteria.1-2: Treats the Mongols as a fully unified empire and ignores the Levant-to-Europe substitution problem.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Mongol factions but misassigns motives, geography, or command structures in major ways.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some fragmentation, such as Batu/Berke versus Hulagu, but applies it inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes Mongol polities and explains which faction could plausibly attack Europe and why.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the scenario in Mongol succession politics, Jochid-Ilkhanid rivalry, and Great Khan priorities while preserving the counterfactual premise.

criteria.name: Logistical and military feasibility in Western Europe
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the practical constraints on a Mongol westward campaign, including manpower, horse fodder, distance from steppe bases, terrain, fortifications, and competing theaters such as China and Iran.
criteria.1-2: Assumes effortless conquest or impossible failure without discussing logistics or military conditions.
criteria.3-4: Gives generic claims about forests, castles, or cavalry but lacks connection to the actual Mongol operational situation.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several relevant constraints but underdevelops their causal effect on campaign scale and duration.
criteria.7-8: Explains how troop availability, remounts, fodder, fortifications, and distance would shape likely outcomes in Europe.
criteria.9-10: Integrates logistics with Mongol strategic allocation, showing why Western Europe might be raided, coerced, or partially conquered rather than uniformly overrun.

criteria.name: European and Rus' political-religious response
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the treatment of likely reactions by Russian principalities, Hungary, Poland, the Papacy, the Holy Roman Empire, and other European actors, especially whether a westward Mongol push becomes entangled with Orthodox, Catholic, and possibly Islamic alignments.
criteria.1-2: Ignores European and Rus' responses or portrays them as a single unified reaction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions resistance or crusading but with little attention to divisions among European powers or Rus' vassals.
criteria.5-6: Covers some actors, such as the Papacy or Russian princes, but misses key religious or vassalage dynamics.
criteria.7-8: Shows how Mongol demands could provoke Catholic coalitions, Orthodox ambivalence, Rus' rebellion, or opportunistic alliances.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced political-religious map, including Golden Horde Islamization pressures, Orthodox toleration, papal framing, and fragmented European incentives.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain and downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how coherently the answer traces second- and third-order effects of a Mongol turn toward Western Europe, such as altered Crusades, delayed or accelerated Muscovy, changes in Golden Horde authority, papal politics, trade routes, state formation, and possible Islamization of parts of Rus'.
criteria.1-2: Lists isolated outcomes without causal links or long-range implications.
criteria.3-4: Provides a short chain of effects but jumps abruptly or relies on unsupported historical determinism.
criteria.5-6: Develops plausible medium-term effects but gives limited attention to broader Eurasian consequences.
criteria.7-8: Connects campaign choices to regional power shifts, religious developments, and state formation over decades.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent multi-decade chain linking Mongol internal politics, European responses, Rus' trajectories, Crusader states, and Eurasian trade or religious transformations.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly distinguishes plausible, speculative, and unlikely outcomes while avoiding contradictions with known constraints such as the Mongol Civil War, limited Jochid manpower, Hulagu’s Iranian base, and the priority of China.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but contradictory claims and ignores major historical constraints.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but still contains major inconsistencies or anachronistic assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible but occasionally overstates certainty or leaves tensions unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language, flags uncertain branches, and maintains consistency with key Mongol and European constraints.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly compares plausible branches, explains why some outcomes are more likely than others, and avoids internal or historical contradictions throughout.

items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had turned its full attention to Western Europe in the mid-13th century instead of pivoting toward the Levant and the Mamluks, the trajectory of European history would likely have been dramatically altered.

The Mongols had already demonstrated their capability in Europe during the 1241–1242 campaign under Batu Khan and Subutai, when they crushed Polish and Hungarian armies at Legnica and Mohi. Their withdrawal was largely due to the death of Great Khan Ögedei, which forced the commanders to return to Karakorum for the succession. Had political circumstances kept them committed to the western front, Western Europe in the 1240s–1260s would have faced an enemy whose tactics, mobility, and siegecraft (enhanced by Chinese and Persian engineers) European feudal armies were poorly equipped to counter.

A sustained Mongol invasion would probably have devastated the Holy Roman Empire, which was politically fractured during the conflict between Emperor Frederick II and the Papacy. France under Louis IX was militarily strong but isolated, and the kingdoms of Iberia were preoccupied with the Reconquista. Cities like Vienna, Prague, and possibly the towns of the Rhineland could have suffered the fate of Kiev or Baghdad. The fragmented political landscape of Latin Christendom—lacking a unifying authority—would have made coordinated resistance very difficult.

The longer-term consequences are more speculative but profound. A Mongol-occupied Central or Western Europe would likely have been organized as a tributary extension of the Golden Horde, with Slavic and Germanic principalities reduced to vassal status much like the Rus' principalities. The Catholic Church's authority might have been severely weakened, and the cultural flowering we associate with the late medieval period—the rise of universities, Gothic architecture's spread, the early Renaissance in Italy—could have been delayed, redirected, or stunted. Conversely, the Pax Mongolica would have extended directly into Europe, potentially accelerating the transmission of gunpowder, paper, printing, and Eastern administrative practices by a century or more.

Geopolitically, the Levant would have been spared the Mongol invasions of 1260 and after, meaning the Mamluk Sultanate might never have risen to the prominence it achieved at Ain Jalut. The Crusader states could have survived longer, and Islamic civilization in Egypt and Syria would have retained the cultural and economic dominance that the Mongol incursions had partly disrupted. The Abbasid Caliphate's fate would depend on whether the Mongols still sacked Baghdad in 1258, but a westward focus might have spared it as well.

Ultimately, a sustained westward Mongol campaign would probably not have led to permanent occupation of all of Western Europe—logistics, terrain (dense forests, castles, fragmented polities), and the eventual fragmentation of the Mongol Empire itself would have imposed limits. But the shock would likely have reshaped European political structures, possibly accelerating the centralization of surviving monarchies, fundamentally altering the religious balance of the continent, and shifting the cultural center of gravity of medieval civilization eastward for generations.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. No one considers Ohio the birthplace of the AR. Semantics? maybe, but I don't think so.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.
items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?

items.model_answer:
If the American invasion of Quebec in 1775 had succeeded—if Montgomery had taken the city rather than dying beneath its walls, and Arnold's forces had consolidated the conquest—the cultural and social trajectory of Quebec would have diverged sharply from what we know.

In the immediate aftermath, the Continental Congress had already extended an open invitation to the Canadiens to join the rebellion as a "fourteenth colony," and Quebec would likely have been admitted as a state, perhaps with a French-speaking delegation in Philadelphia. The crucial question is whether the Americans would have honored the religious and legal guarantees the British had recently granted under the Quebec Act of 1774. Initially, pragmatism would probably have prevailed: keeping the Canadiens loyal required tolerating Catholicism and French civil law. However, the deep anti-Catholic sentiment among New England Protestants—visible in the Continental Congress's own earlier denunciations of the Quebec Act—would have created chronic friction. The Catholic Church, which in our timeline became the dominant institution shaping Quebec identity through the nineteenth century, would have faced a much more hostile political environment without the British Crown's protective umbrella, which the Church had traded loyalty for after the Conquest.

Socially, the seigneurial system would likely have been dismantled far earlier than 1854. American settlers, land speculators, and Protestant missionaries would have poured northward along the St. Lawrence, especially after the Revolution, and the demographic balance would have shifted faster than it did historically. Without the influx of 40,000 to 50,000 Loyalists who in reality fled north after 1783—people who created English Canada—the anglophone presence in Quebec might paradoxically have been more diffuse but also more aggressively assimilationist, modeled on the gradual erosion of French communities in Louisiana, Vermont, and Michigan.

Language is perhaps the most consequential variable. In our timeline, Quebec preserved French largely because the Catholic Church controlled education, because the British found accommodation politically convenient, and because Confederation in 1867 institutionalized linguistic duality. Under American rule, with no constitutional protection for French (the U.S. has never had an official language policy supportive of minorities), public schooling in English by the mid-nineteenth century would have steadily eroded French as a public language. Quebec might have come to resemble Louisiana: a region with a distinctive Francophone heritage, Creole-style cultural products, place names, cuisine, and folk traditions, but with French surviving mainly in rural pockets and among the elderly by 1900.

The Quiet Revolution, the FLQ crisis, sovereignty referendums, Bill 101—none of these would exist in recognizable form, because the political vehicle for francophone collective identity (a province with provincial powers within a federation that acknowledged two founding peoples) would never have come into being. Instead, Quebec would likely have a regional identity comparable to Cajun Louisiana or perhaps Hispanic New Mexico: proud, distinctive, gastronomically and musically influential, but politically integrated into a dominant Anglo-American culture and without serious separatist potential.

One important counter-current: a successful 1775 campaign would have meant no Loyalist migration, no British North America, and likely no Canada at all in its present form. The Maritimes and the West would have followed different paths, possibly absorbed into the United States over the nineteenth century. In that broader American polity, Quebec's Francophone heritage might actually have left a larger imprint on continental culture than it did historically, simply because it would have been part of a much bigger story rather than walled off behind a national border.

edus.text: If the American invasion of Quebec in 1775 had succeeded
if Montgomery had taken the city rather than dying beneath its walls
and Arnold's forces had consolidated the conquest
the cultural and social trajectory of Quebec would have diverged sharply from what we know.
In the immediate aftermath, the Continental Congress had already extended an open invitation to the Canadiens to join the rebellion as a "fourteenth colony,"
and Quebec would likely have been admitted as a state,
perhaps with a French-speaking delegation in Philadelphia.
The crucial question is whether the Americans would have honored the religious and legal guarantees the British had recently granted under the Quebec Act of 1774.
Initially, pragmatism would probably have prevailed:
keeping the Canadiens loyal required tolerating Catholicism and French civil law.
However, the deep anti-Catholic sentiment among New England Protestants
visible in the Continental Congress's own earlier denunciations of the Quebec Act
would have created chronic friction.
The Catholic Church
which in our timeline became the dominant institution shaping Quebec identity through the nineteenth century
would have faced a much more hostile political environment without the British Crown's protective umbrella,
which the Church had traded loyalty for after the Conquest.
Socially, the seigneurial system would likely have been dismantled far earlier than 1854.
American settlers, land speculators, and Protestant missionaries would have poured northward along the St. Lawrence,
especially after the Revolution,
and the demographic balance would have shifted faster than it did historically.
Without the influx of 40,000 to 50,000 Loyalists who in reality fled north after 1783
people who created English Canada
the anglophone presence in Quebec might paradoxically have been more diffuse but also more aggressively assimilationist,
modeled on the gradual erosion of French communities in Louisiana, Vermont, and Michigan.
Language is perhaps the most consequential variable.
In our timeline, Quebec preserved French largely because the Catholic Church controlled education,
because the British found accommodation politically convenient,
and because Confederation in 1867 institutionalized linguistic duality.
Under American rule,
with no constitutional protection for French
the U.S. has never had an official language policy supportive of minorities
public schooling in English by the mid-nineteenth century would have steadily eroded French as a public language.
Quebec might have come to resemble Louisiana:
a region with a distinctive Francophone heritage, Creole-style cultural products, place names, cuisine, and folk traditions,
but with French surviving mainly in rural pockets and among the elderly by 1900.

possibly absorbed into the United States over the nineteenth century.
In that broader American polity,

items.question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed?
human_answers: With this POD, Spain and, especially, France may have a very different trajectory from 1776. Both have been looking for a way to get back at Britain for the disastrous 7YW. ARW provided that way, OTL. That involvement did 2 things (more than that, but)...it waylaid the slow progress Spain was making up the Pacific Coast, and most importantly, helped set the stage for the French Revolution. There will be another war. Maybe the WoBavarian Succession spins out of control. Maybe Britain decides to assist Portugal in its struggles against Spain in mid-late 1770s, and this spins out of control. Maybe one or the other leaves the path to the French Revolution still on track. Or, maybe the wars are delayed, and FR as we know it is butterflied. That is beyond BIG. And, this all assumes that the colonies remain at peace, not rising up for round 2, or 3. During the Nootka Crisis, Spain looked to France for assistance, which it didn't get because of the FR. Plus, throughout the 18th century, France didn't go to Spain's aid, but, rather, expected it to be the other way around. I wouldn't count on France backing Spain in the Nootka Crisis, even if there was no FR. If left by its lonesome, Spain likely backs down as OTL. Or maybe Spain has used the decade or 2 of peace to continue settling the Pacific north coast.

I guess if England would have kept the economically important and more or less developed 13C it would have a smaller interest in Notka/Oregon/access to the pacific. If the ARW ends in 1775/1776 then yes, Spain would have had more time and resources to actually colonize Notka. To be honest, I never understood why so many people believe that with a failed ARW, the French R. simply never happens. France was still economically and politically and socially in a bad situation. So yeah, I think the FR still would have happened. Maybe sooner or later (most likely a bit later) and maybe less bloody, but IMO it still would have happened nonetheless. And yeah, France and Spain still would have tried to get revenge on England. How realistic is that if the ARW ends in 1775/1776? I mean the whole American mythos of Americans rising up against the british crown is not that true. A lot of American colonists were loyal to the crown. Its not that every peasant in the 13C rose up against George III and with that rebellion or uprising put down quickly, I think the motivation for another rebellion would be low. How realistic is a peaceful solution to the pacific question? So England keeps the 13C and let's say that that James Cook dies earlier so there is no English expedition at the pacific coast and England has less information and is less interested in these regions. And if Spain has more time, money to colonize Notka could England have decided to just let Spain have it?
items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies

items.model_answer:
If the United States had never come into existence—meaning the thirteen colonies remained part of the British Empire after the 1770s—the administration of Britain's North American holdings would likely have evolved along lines similar to what actually happened in Canada, Australia, and other settler colonies, though on a much grander scale and probably at an accelerated pace.

In the immediate aftermath of avoiding revolution, Britain would have had to address the grievances that sparked the actual rebellion. The most likely path would have involved granting the colonies greater representation in their own affairs while maintaining imperial oversight on matters of trade, defense, and foreign policy. The Coercive Acts would presumably have been repealed or never extended, and some form of colonial assembly with expanded taxation authority would have emerged. However, direct representation in the Westminster Parliament was unlikely; the British political establishment consistently rejected this option for all colonies throughout the 19th century.

By the mid-19th century, the colonies would almost certainly have followed the pattern established by Lord Durham's Report of 1839 and the subsequent grant of "responsible government" to Canada in the 1840s. This system gave colonies internal self-rule through cabinets responsible to elected legislatures, while reserving foreign affairs, defense, and constitutional matters for London. The various North American colonies—the original thirteen plus Quebec, Nova Scotia, and territories acquired later—would likely have been consolidated into one or more federations, much as the Canadian Confederation occurred in 1867. Given the population and economic weight of the former thirteen colonies, such a federation might have been established earlier and become the dominant Dominion within the Empire.

Westward expansion would still have occurred, but under imperial coordination rather than American manifest destiny. This might have produced different boundaries with Spanish (later Mexican) territories, possibly avoiding wars like that of 1846-48, and Indigenous policy might have followed the Royal Proclamation of 1763 model more consistently, with treaty-based dealings rather than the aggressive removal characteristic of US policy. Slavery presents a particularly significant divergence: the British abolition of 1833 would have applied to the southern colonies, fundamentally altering their economic and social development, though enforcement would have been politically explosive and might have triggered a different kind of civil conflict.

By the 20th century, the entity would likely have evolved into a Dominion comparable to Canada or Australia, with full self-government, its own parliament, and gradually achieving sovereignty in foreign affairs through processes like the Statute of Westminster (1931). Whether it would eventually have severed ties entirely or remained a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state is speculative, but the trajectory of peaceful constitutional evolution rather than revolutionary rupture would have produced a fundamentally different political culture—one likely more parliamentary, less suspicious of centralized authority, and without the distinctive American constitutional tradition built around written rights and separation of powers.

edus.text: If the United States had never come into existence
meaning the thirteen colonies remained part of the British Empire after the 1770s
the administration of Britain's North American holdings would likely have evolved along lines similar to what actually happened in Canada, Australia, and other settler colonies
though on a much grander scale
and probably at an accelerated pace
In the immediate aftermath of avoiding revolution
Britain would have had to address the grievances that sparked the actual rebellion
The most likely path would have involved granting the colonies greater representation in their own affairs
while maintaining imperial oversight on matters of trade, defense, and foreign policy
The Coercive Acts would presumably have been repealed or never extended
and some form of colonial assembly with expanded taxation authority would have emerged
However, direct representation in the Westminster Parliament was unlikely
the British political establishment consistently rejected this option for all colonies throughout the 19th century
By the mid-19th century
the colonies would almost certainly have followed the pattern established by Lord Durham's Report of 1839 and the subsequent grant of "responsible government" to Canada in the 1840s
This system gave colonies internal self-rule through cabinets responsible to elected legislatures
while reserving foreign affairs, defense, and constitutional matters for London
The various North American colonies—the original thirteen plus Quebec, Nova Scotia, and territories acquired later—would likely have been consolidated into one or more federations
much as the Canadian Confederation occurred in 1867
Given the population and economic weight of the former thirteen colonies
such a federation might have been established earlier
and become the dominant Dominion within the Empire
Westward expansion would still have occurred
but under imperial coordination rather than American manifest destiny
This might have produced different boundaries with Spanish (later Mexican) territories
possibly avoiding wars like that of 1846-48
and Indigenous policy might have followed the Royal Proclamation of 1763 model more consistently
with treaty-based dealings rather than the aggressive removal characteristic of US policy
Slavery presents a particularly significant divergence
the British abolition of 1833 would have applied to the southern colonies
fundamentally altering their economic and social development
though enforcement would have been politically explosive
and might have triggered a different kind of civil conflict
By the 20th century
the entity would likely have evolved into a Dominion comparable to Canada or Australia
with full self-government, its own parliament, and gradually achieving sovereignty in foreign affairs through processes like the Statute of Westminster (1931)
Whether it would eventually have severed ties entirely or remained a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state is speculative
but the trajectory of peaceful constitutional evolution rather than revolutionary rupture would have produced a fundamentally different political culture
one likely more parliamentary, less suspicious of centralized authority, and without the distinctive American constitutional tradition built around written rights and separation of powers
