items.question: What If Louis the Pious was able to successfully pass his reforms?
human_answers: Currently I cannot write a comment as it is yes it must on what Louis's successfully implemented reforms are like could upend the development not only of the Frankish Empire and the Papacy, but also of the rest of Europe ( in particular directly involving Al - Andalus, the Viking raids, the Slavic potentates and relations with Constantinople ) and how is all this it like that will influence the perception of Charlemagne's legacy, and the claim of political continuity with Rome in the Latin Christianity, so for now I will content myself with quoting some of my old comments on the era in general Yes I admit that they are a bunch of quotes, since in looking for them all I got a bad headache, but at least they cover in full the entire historical period and some hypotheses of evolution that can be generated by a different internal policy within the Carolingians

I don’t know if he’d be able to gain the loyalty of his siblings seen as Frankish traditions would still be pushed for. Even with some kind of alliance against Louis the Bald he’d need enough influence to assure that his brothers don’t turn against him afterwards but I do like the idea of him turning against his father. Another issue here is that the Frankish aristocrats would still be mostly opposed to Lothaire getting most of the empire and nominally inheriting it so he’d need to assure the aristocracy’s loyalty. I agree, the process of feudalism was already taking place and with how Charlemagne had organized his empire, it wouldn’t be far fetched to think that it’d be somewhat divided, especially with special status regions like Septimania and Bavaria existing in the empire. On the other hand if someone were to centralize power to himself, say Lothaire, I do imagine that it isn’t impossible that the Carolingian Empire is divided in subdivisions that maintain the Emperor’s loyalty and don’t solely pledge loyalty to their dukes. Charlemagne assassinated and killed those who wouldn’t integrate into his empire so it’s not that far fetched to think that the emperor would kill to maintain the empire’s loyalty.

It was never centralized though. It was extremely decentralized even back during Charlemagne's era, and he had to regularly travel around his empire as well as send his own emissaries, the Mayors of the Palace, to enforce his authority. Even in the days of the Holy Roman Empire, the position was more concentrated around the personality of an Emperor, as when Barbarossa took the throne in the 12th century, his authority was ephemeral as it existed on paper, having lapsed without a stronger monarch on the throne. Barbarossa was an extremely intelligent and energetic figure who also knew how to play the game well which was why his reforms largely endured (in Germany he was a pragmatist, but in Italy he was more of a romantic and pushed against the papacy when he didn't need to allowing Manuel Komnenos to undermine him heavily damaging Imperial rule in Italy). That was the issue with Louis the Pious, who played the game of prestige and power wrong. His blinding of his nephew Bernard while indeed a strong show of force, it came off as overly cruel to the nobility. At the same time his open display of supplication and show of piety made him seem weak. This was the issue with his sons, whom he simply failed to properly control. Funnily enough Louis the Pious was actually a very competent Emperor. He just had a lot of things going against him. And with his intellect, he often derived overly romantic solutions to certain problems he should have been more pragmatic about. His blinding of Bernard was extremely ruthless. So much so it caused quite a stir in Francia. His sons were scared of him at certain points and expected to be blinded at his hands for some of the actions they'd done. Instead of blinding, a firm punishment such as tonsuring his most rebellious sons for their pride (long hair was a cultural hallmark of the Franks) would have probably done the job. These rebellious sons being sent to a monastery close under his own influence and watch would have set a decent enough example for those who defied his will. As for the division of the Empire, if it were subdivided along reasonable lines it might have actually worked to some degree, as it would have accounted for the natural fragmentation of power and regionalism that would develop in a state like this without any sense of overarching national identity or even political capital. The fragmentation of these Kingdoms within the Empire would have unironically helped the Emperor maintain power over his kin who'd reign as subkings under his authority.
items.original_question: What if Louis the Pious was able to successfully pass his reforms? Louis the Pious had conceived the empire to never be divided. It was through this conception that he decided that power would only be relegated to his eldest son while to compensate for the lack of power, the younger sons would be gifted smaller kingdoms (like, for example, the kingdom of Italy). Nevertheless these smaller kings would still declare loyalty towards the emperor. He had also believed that imperial power came from the pope, hosting his coronation in Reims with the pope. These reforms were never truly put in place however, as the Frankish court had viewed them negatively as they did not follow Frankish tradition. In tandem, the younger brothers of Lothaire (who was meant to have the throne) played against their father. Coupled with Judith of Bavaria attempting to give her son, Charles the (eventual) Bald as much heritage as he could possibly get. Thus, progressively, until the day of Louis the Pious’ death his power was more and more fractured. Therefore, what would happen if he was more politically competent, if he was able to somehow circumvent of push back against the court politics that brought about his downfall and the division of the empire?

items.model_answer:
If Louis the Pious had successfully passed and maintained his reforms, the Carolingian Empire might have avoided its rapid fragmentation and the century of instability that followed his death in 840.

Louis's primary reform goal was the *Ordinatio Imperii* (817), which attempted to preserve imperial unity by designating his eldest son Lothair as co-emperor and sole successor, while giving his younger sons Pippin and Louis subordinate kingdoms. The plan collapsed when his second wife Judith bore Charles (later Charles the Bald), prompting Louis to repeatedly revise the succession, which triggered civil wars among his sons.

Had the original reform held, several consequences seem likely:

**Political consolidation**: A unified succession would have prevented the Treaty of Verdun (843), which divided the empire into three kingdoms and created the territorial basis for future France, Germany, and the contested middle kingdom. Imperial authority might have remained stronger and more centralized.

**Reduced Viking vulnerability**: The civil wars among Louis's sons left the empire fragmented and unable to mount coordinated defenses against Viking raids that intensified in the 840s-880s. A unified empire could have organized more effective resistance, potentially limiting Scandinavian settlement and influence.

**Different European state formation**: Without Verdun's division, the distinct French and German identities that emerged from West and East Francia might have developed differently or more slowly. The concept of a unified Christian empire under one ruler might have persisted longer.

**Ecclesiastical relations**: Louis's reforms also involved church governance and the relationship between imperial and papal authority. Success might have strengthened imperial control over the church, potentially altering the later investiture controversies.

However, deeper structural problems—overmighty regional aristocracies, inadequate administrative infrastructure for such a vast territory, and the fundamental tension between Frankish inheritance customs (which favored division among sons) and imperial unity—suggest that even successful initial reforms might only have delayed rather than prevented fragmentation.

nodes.text: If Louis the Pious had successfully passed and maintained his reforms,
the Carolingian Empire might have avoided its rapid fragmentation and the century of instability that followed his death in 840.
Louis's primary reform goal was the *Ordinatio Imperii* (817),
which attempted to preserve imperial unity by designating his eldest son Lothair as co-emperor and sole successor,
while giving his younger sons Pippin and Louis subordinate kingdoms.
The plan collapsed when his second wife Judith bore Charles (later Charles the Bald),
prompting Louis to repeatedly revise the succession,
which triggered civil wars among his sons.
Had the original reform held,
several consequences seem likely:
A unified succession would have prevented the Treaty of Verdun (843),
which divided the empire into three kingdoms
and created the territorial basis for future France, Germany, and the contested middle kingdom.
Imperial authority might have remained stronger and more centralized.
The civil wars among Louis's sons left the empire fragmented and unable to mount coordinated defenses against Viking raids
that intensified in the 840s-880s.
A unified empire could have organized more effective resistance,
potentially limiting Scandinavian settlement and influence.
Without Verdun's division,
the distinct French and German identities that emerged from West and East Francia might have developed differently or more slowly.
The concept of a unified Christian empire under one ruler might have persisted longer.
Louis's reforms also involved church governance and the relationship between imperial and papal authority.
Success might have strengthened imperial control over the church,
potentially altering the later investiture controversies.

However, deeper structural problems—overmighty regional aristocracies, inadequate administrative infrastructure for such a vast territory, and the fundamental tension between Frankish inheritance customs (which favored division among sons) and imperial unity—
suggest that even successful initial reforms might only have delayed rather than prevented fragmentation.

items.question: What If Japan had pursued a navy-centered national strategy?
human_answers: Your argument is intriguing. I wrote a post last year that made a similar argument to yours. Post in thread 'If Japan had not taken over Korea, where would they have expanded instead?' Feb 8, 2025 I feel like Korea keeping Japan from being too aggressive gives china a lot more breathing room to consolidate its own development- Seeing the modernisation happening in Korea probably strengthens reform factions in china- although if it means the Qing feel the need to reestablish control over this unpredictable vassal, could potentially lead to the sino Japanese war being replaced by a sino Korean War that also humiliates china and exposed its failure. Madhukar_Shah However, even back then, there were comments on that post saying that “even if Korea were to modernize, Japan would not abandon its ambitions toward Korea and the continent. One of the reasons for that is precisely the topic of this post. I once read a Korean alternate-history novel in which the Japanese Army and its internal factions acted as obstacles to cooperation between Korea and Japan. In the end, meaningful Korea–Japan cooperation only began to make real progress after Yamagata Aritomo fell from power following the Ōtsu Incident and was even subjected to an assassination attempt.

Huh? After the Sengoku Period Japan experienced one of the most peaceful and stable periods in its history under the Tokugawa Shogunate, which lasted lasted 250+ years. The only period in Japanese history that lasted longer was the Heian period. But that was hardly a stable regime, with regular infighting between retired emperors, the Fujiwara, and ultimately the Taira and Minamoto clans. And after the failed invasion of Korea at the end of the Azuchi-Momoyama period there were no serious Japanese attack against the mainland until the Meiji Period. ​ I am not sure why you think it was the army that uniquely pushed Japan to pursue expansionist policies? The navy was fully complicit in this as well, in fact the navy is the enabling factor in this because it's the only way for Japan to actually attack anybody outside the home islands in the first place. You use Britain and Venice as examples but how did these two powers not also use their navies for aggressive expansionism overseas? The bushi never rising in the first place, which takes you all the way back to the aforementioned Heian period. The utter failure of e.g. the Jokyu War or the Kenmu Restoration shows how powerless the court nobility became once the bakufu was established. Not to mention that the ultimate restoration of imperial power itself was enabled by the military power of the bushi, just the ones that opposed to bakufu.

I think the most interesting POD would be in the early 17th century during the first decades of the Togugawa shogunate. During the Senkaku period Japan had been relatively open to foreign trade due to the lack of central authority and when they first came to power the Togugawa tried to regulate but not stop this exchanges, including provisions such as the "Ted Seals" that allowed large Japanese merchantmen of the same name reach all the way down to Indonesia if not further. The shogunate and their allies also possessed a few European style galleons, most famously the San Juan Bautista . Now OTL the shogunate would end up halting this trade and impose the Sakoku policy which closed off Japan from almost all foreign trade, as well as starting the persecution of Christians. While the reasons behind this are still debated two of the primary reasons stated is that the Shogunate was increasingly worried about the threat that colonial European powers presented to Japan as well as the fact that a lot of this trade (including many of the Read Seal Ships) were controlled by southern houses that were not seen as loyal to the Togugawa. Now ponder a reality where the Shogunate decides a forward defense policy is better as an answer to European encroachment and that rather than cut off trade its better to let its own vassals control the Red Seals. Such a Japan would eventually have to develop the centralized naval infrastructure to protect that trade and fend of Europeans, resulting in a state for whom the navy is the central military concern (much like Britain). Edo era Japan was no economic slouch and could probably sustain a trade/semicolonial empire. Places like the Ryukyus and Hokkaido would fall under central Japanese control much earlier and sino-japanese relations would be very different. A Japanese naval empire could lead to similar responses from the Qing and the Joseon as well. Of course this would have big social ramifications within Japan: we probably wouldn't' see the same system for controlling samurai as OTL and merchants would end up much more influential much quicker. The rigid social hierarchy that the Togugawa tried to impose would fall apart before it was even properly enforced. Christianity might be more accepted but its equally possible that anti-Christianity could form the roots of an early form of Pan-Asianism.

Due to the influence of typhoons and unstable wind patterns in the East Asian seas, the region's "most strategic commercial sea lane" has historically been the trade route along the coastline, while the distant island chains have traditionally been uninhabited. Regarding the so-called "central place in trade," there were four key players in East Asian trade: mainland Japan, which produced precious metals; mainland China, which produced handicrafts (I don't believe that naval power alone could completely control trade along the Chinese coast, especially since excessive trade with China would only lead to all the precious metals flowing into China, destroying Japan's domestic industries); the Europeans; and the Spice Islands (which were within the Dutch sphere of influence, and required passing through the Philippines to reach Japan). It is clear that Japan could only control valuable trade centers if its navy surpassed the combined strength of Spain and the Netherlands; any navy less powerful than that would be meaningless. However, without any positive feedback or incentives, I don't believe it would be possible to build a navy in mainland Japan that could surpass the combined naval power of these two countries.
items.original_question: What if Japan had pursued a navy-centered national strategy? Unlike most island nations, Japan historically possessed an army with substantial political and social influence. With the emergence of the samurai class, Japan experienced prolonged periods of civil war and state formation led primarily by warrior elites. Particularly after the Sengoku period, cycles of civil war, the birth of new regimes, and expansion toward the continent were repeatedly observed. After the Toyotomi Hideyoshi regime emerged from the outcome of internal conflict, Hideyoshi employed the greatly expanded army to pursue continental ambitions, leading to the invasion of the Korean Peninsula. Following the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate and the wars that accompanied it, the Meiji government was established and Japan embarked on a program of modernization. However, unlike Britain and other island nations, Japan maintained an army with considerable autonomy and political influence despite its insular geography. Consequently, Japan’s expansionist trajectory once again focused on the Korean Peninsula, Manchuria, and the Asian continent. What I am curious about is the following. If Japan were to become a country in which the navy held complete primacy over the army, how would its history have needed to unfold differently? In this scenario, the army would be limited to roles such as suppression of internal rebellions, defense of the home islands, and naval infantry (marines), possessing only minimal status and political influence. The navy would constitute the principal military force, and national defense strategy and institutional design would likewise be shaped under naval leadership. Furthermore, the direction of external expansion would be determined from the perspective of a maritime power, rather than that of a continental state. If Japan had chosen the route of a maritime power like Britain or the Venetian Republic, or if its modernization had been deliberately oriented toward a completely navy-led military structure, how would Japanese history have unfolded differently? The Japan I'm referring to includes not only the Empire of Japan but also earlier periods of Japanese history. POD is not just in 1868 but extends to several centuries earlier.

items.model_answer:
If Japan had pursued a consistently navy-centered national strategy rather than the contested army-navy duality that actually shaped its modern history, the trajectory of East Asia in the late 19th and 20th centuries would likely have looked very different.

From the Meiji period onward, Japan's leadership was split between a continental, army-dominated school (influenced by Prussian models and figures like Yamagata Aritomo) that saw Korea, Manchuria, and China as Japan's strategic frontier, and a maritime school (drawing on British naval thought and figures like Yamamoto Gonnohyōe) that saw the seas of East Asia and the South Pacific as Japan's natural sphere. The army's vision generally prevailed in resource allocation and grand strategy after the 1930s, dragging Japan into the quagmire of the China War.

A navy-centered strategy would probably have emphasized several different priorities. First, securing maritime trade routes and a strong merchant marine, recognizing that Japan's prosperity depended on imports of raw materials and exports of manufactured goods. Second, deepening the Anglo-Japanese Alliance or a comparable maritime partnership rather than letting it lapse in 1922; a naval Japan had strong structural reasons to align with Britain and, later, possibly the United States, since all three were status-quo maritime powers dependent on open sea lanes. Third, treating Korea and Taiwan as defensive maritime perimeters rather than springboards for continental expansion, and avoiding the costly occupation of Manchuria and northern China.

Economically, such a Japan would likely have invested more in shipbuilding, commercial shipping, overseas finance, and resource diplomacy—buying oil, rubber, and ore rather than seizing them. The disastrous decision to invade Southeast Asia in 1941, which was driven largely by the army's prior commitment to the China War and the resulting U.S. oil embargo, might never have occurred. Without the Pacific War, Japan could have retained its empire in Taiwan, Korea, and the Pacific mandates well past 1945, though pressures from nationalism and decolonization would eventually have challenged it.

Geopolitically, the consequences would have rippled outward. China, spared a full-scale Japanese invasion, might have continued its uneven Nationalist modernization under Chiang Kai-shek, possibly preventing or delaying the Communist victory in 1949. The Soviet Union would have faced a different strategic picture in the Far East. The United States, lacking Pearl Harbor as a galvanizing event, might have remained more isolationist regarding Europe, with significant implications for World War II.

That said, a navy-first Japan would not have been free of risks. Naval strategies are expensive, technology-intensive, and vulnerable to arms races—as the Washington and London Naval Treaties demonstrated. Japan would still have faced the fundamental dilemma of being a resource-poor island nation in an era of great-power competition, and tensions with the United States over China and the Pacific could have produced conflict by other paths. Moreover, the political culture that empowered the army—rural poverty, ultranationalism, weak civilian control—would not automatically have disappeared simply because the navy held strategic primacy.

In short, a navy-centered Japan would most plausibly have been a wealthier, less overextended, more diplomatically integrated power, aligned with the Anglo-American maritime order and avoiding the catastrophic continental war that destroyed the empire in 1945—but it would still have been navigating the same harsh structural constraints that made Japanese grand strategy so difficult in the first place.

edus.text: If Japan had pursued a consistently navy-centered national strategy rather than the contested army-navy duality that actually shaped its modern history,
the trajectory of East Asia in the late 19th and 20th centuries would likely have looked very different.
From the Meiji period onward, Japan's leadership was split between a continental, army-dominated school
influenced by Prussian models and figures like Yamagata Aritomo
that saw Korea, Manchuria, and China as Japan's strategic frontier,
and a maritime school
drawing on British naval thought and figures like Yamamoto Gonnohyōe
that saw the seas of East Asia and the South Pacific as Japan's natural sphere.
The army's vision generally prevailed in resource allocation and grand strategy after the 1930s,
dragging Japan into the quagmire of the China War.
A navy-centered strategy would probably have emphasized several different priorities.
First, securing maritime trade routes and a strong merchant marine,
recognizing that Japan's prosperity depended on imports of raw materials and exports of manufactured goods.
Second, deepening the Anglo-Japanese Alliance or a comparable maritime partnership rather than letting it lapse in 1922;
a naval Japan had strong structural reasons to align with Britain and, later, possibly the United States,
since all three were status-quo maritime powers dependent on open sea lanes.
Third, treating Korea and Taiwan as defensive maritime perimeters rather than springboards for continental expansion,
and avoiding the costly occupation of Manchuria and northern China.
Economically, such a Japan would likely have invested more in shipbuilding, commercial shipping, overseas finance, and resource diplomacy
buying oil, rubber, and ore rather than seizing them.
The disastrous decision to invade Southeast Asia in 1941
which was driven largely by the army's prior commitment to the China War and the resulting U.S. oil embargo,
might never have occurred.
Without the Pacific War,
Japan could have retained its empire in Taiwan, Korea, and the Pacific mandates well past 1945,
though pressures from nationalism and decolonization would eventually have challenged it.
Geopolitically, the consequences would have rippled outward.
China, spared a full-scale Japanese invasion,
might have continued its uneven Nationalist modernization under Chiang Kai-shek,
possibly preventing or delaying the Communist victory in 1949.
The Soviet Union would have faced a different strategic picture in the Far East.
The United States, lacking Pearl Harbor as a galvanizing event,
might have remained more isolationist regarding Europe,
with significant implications for World War II.
That said, a navy-first Japan would not have been free of risks.
Naval strategies are expensive, technology-intensive, and vulnerable to arms races
as the Washington and London Naval Treaties demonstrated.
Japan would still have faced the fundamental dilemma of being a resource-poor island nation in an era of great-power competition,
and tensions with the United States over China and the Pacific could have produced conflict by other paths.
Moreover, the political culture that empowered the army
rural poverty, ultranationalism, weak civilian control
would not automatically have disappeared simply because the navy held strategic primacy.
In short, a navy-centered Japan would most plausibly have been a wealthier, less overextended, more diplomatically integrated power,
aligned with the Anglo-American maritime order
and avoiding the catastrophic continental war that destroyed the empire in 1945
but it would still have been navigating the same harsh structural constraints
that made Japanese grand strategy so difficult in the first place.

items.question: What If Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829?
human_answers: The Know-Nothings don't exist yet in the 1820s. That said, there is something that might alienate him from the nascent Whigs - he's a Freemason, and a pretty involved one - he was Grand Master of the Grand Orient of France during Napoleon's entire reign as emperor, founded the National Lodge of Spain, and that aspect in particular helped hurt his legitimacy among the Spanish when he was made king there. Now, the period where Joseph would enter American politics in your scenario largely coincides with the spread of the Anti-Masonic movement in New York, and their members would largely go on to integrate the Whig party later down the line. In the other hand, as time passed, the Anti-Masonic aspect was diluted so much that they ended up running a Mason as their 1832 presidential candidate, who even defended the Order in a speech before the convention that nominated him, so he might go either way.

In 1908? Highly doubtful, given Bonaparte's Catholic faith. That wouldn't have played at all in much of the South (not that it would have mattered much in terms of getting votes for the GOP there), and might have been a hindrance elsewhere. If he had somehow gotten the nomination, his running mate would certainly have been a Protestant from (likely) the midwest (Albert Beveridge?); TR would have had to do some strenuous campaigning on his behalf especially if Bryan (often referred to as "the Protestant pope") had been his opponent. The result would have been close if Bonaparte had won, and he'd have had to go to great lengths to demonstrate his independence from the Vatican. Still, the idea is intriguing: imagine the polling place schizophrenia of the Irish community in Boston, for example, given how accustomed that segment was to voting a straight Democrat ticket at the time. Also fascinating: Bonaparte was a strong advocate for civil rights for African-Americans. Had he somehow been elected, perhaps the entire cause of civil rights might have been advanced five years or so.
items.original_question: What if Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829? Joseph Bonaparte in the early 1830s. ​ Yes, this is completely unrealistic, but it's not quite as outlandish as an actual ASB (hence why I'm posting it on here), as it was theoretically something that could have happened. Joseph Bonaparte had lived in the US since 1817, seemed to have been relatively well-liked during his time in America, and to be a senator you need to be a US citizen for at least nine years. Theoretically, had the former king of Naples and then Spain had desired it, he could have very well becoming a senator by the beginning of the Jacksonian period, when both of New Jersey's seats in the US senate were up for grabs in the 1828-29 senate elections. For this scenario, Joseph Bonaparte comes to decide he wants to integrate himself in the United States. After becoming a US citizen in 1819, Joseph manages to be elected to the US Senate representing New Jersey in the 1828-29. replacing Theodore Frelinghuysen from our own timeline. What exactly happens, domestically, and in terms of the US' relationships with foreign countries, and in any other conceivable aspect, in this timeline where a former monarch manages to become a US Senator at the beginning of the Jackson administration.

items.model_answer:
If Joseph Bonaparte had become a U.S. Senator in 1829, the event itself would have required a significant departure from both constitutional law and his own circumstances, and its consequences would have rippled through American politics, diplomacy, and the broader Atlantic world.

To begin with the legal hurdle: the U.S. Constitution requires senators to have been citizens for at least nine years and to be inhabitants of the state they represent. Joseph Bonaparte, the elder brother of Napoleon and former King of Naples and Spain, arrived in the United States in 1815 and lived primarily at his estate, Point Breeze, in Bordentown, New Jersey. For him to be seated as a senator in 1829, he would have had to have naturalized very shortly after his arrival (he never did, in reality) and to have been formally accepted as a New Jersey inhabitant. The New Jersey legislature, which still chose senators in that era, would have had to elect a former Bonapartist monarch—a politically charged act in itself.

Assuming all that, his presence in the Senate would have been a sensation. He would have entered just as Andrew Jackson was beginning his presidency, a moment of sharpening partisan divisions between Jacksonian Democrats and the emerging National Republicans (soon Whigs). Joseph was cultured, liberal-leaning by European standards, and friendly with figures like Nicholas Biddle, Henry Clay, and Daniel Webster. He likely would have aligned with the anti-Jackson coalition, especially during the Bank War, where his connections to Biddle and the Second Bank of the United States would have made him a natural defender of the Bank. His vote and prestige might have strengthened the pro-Bank forces, though probably not enough to overcome Jackson's veto.

Diplomatically, his seating would have caused real friction. The Bourbon Restoration governments of France and Spain regarded the Bonapartes as dangerous exiles; having one as a sitting U.S. legislator would have complicated relations with both Paris and Madrid at a delicate time, particularly as the United States was negotiating spoliation claims with France (resolved in 1831) and watching the July Revolution unfold in 1830. Joseph might have served as an informal back-channel to French liberals and even to his nephew Louis-Napoleon, future Napoleon III. Conversely, Latin American republics, some of which had once considered offering Joseph a throne, might have viewed his elevation as a symbolic alignment of the United States with anti-Bourbon, post-revolutionary legitimacy.

Domestically, his senatorship would have raised durable questions about the role of foreign-born aristocrats in American republican government, possibly accelerating nativist sentiment a decade before it crystallized in the 1840s. It might also have encouraged other European exiles—Polish, Italian, and German liberals who flocked to the U.S. in this era—to seek political office, subtly Europeanizing the political class.

On a personal level, the role would have anchored Joseph in America. In actual history, he returned to Europe in 1832 and died in Florence in 1844. A senatorial career might have kept him at Point Breeze, made him a lasting fixture of Philadelphia–New York high society, and perhaps drawn his nephew Louis-Napoleon (who briefly visited the U.S. in 1837) into a more American orbit, with incalculable consequences for the later Second French Empire.

In short, Joseph Bonaparte's hypothetical 1829 Senate seat would have been a constitutional curiosity, a boost to the anti-Jackson opposition, a diplomatic irritant with Europe's restored monarchies, and a striking symbol of how thoroughly the wreckage of the Napoleonic order had washed up on American shores.

edus.text: If Joseph Bonaparte had become a U.S. Senator in 1829,
the event itself would have required a significant departure from both constitutional law and his own circumstances,
and its consequences would have rippled through American politics, diplomacy, and the broader Atlantic world.
To begin with the legal hurdle:
the U.S. Constitution requires senators to have been citizens for at least nine years
and to be inhabitants of the state they represent.
Joseph Bonaparte, the elder brother of Napoleon and former King of Naples and Spain,
arrived in the United States in 1815
and lived primarily at his estate, Point Breeze, in Bordentown, New Jersey.
For him to be seated as a senator in 1829,
he would have had to have naturalized very shortly after his arrival
(he never did, in reality)
and to have been formally accepted as a New Jersey inhabitant.
The New Jersey legislature,
which still chose senators in that era,
would have had to elect a former Bonapartist monarch
—a politically charged act in itself.
Assuming all that,
his presence in the Senate would have been a sensation.
He would have entered just as Andrew Jackson was beginning his presidency,
a moment of sharpening partisan divisions between Jacksonian Democrats and the emerging National Republicans (soon Whigs).
Joseph was cultured, liberal-leaning by European standards,
and friendly with figures like Nicholas Biddle, Henry Clay, and Daniel Webster.
He likely would have aligned with the anti-Jackson coalition,
especially during the Bank War,
where his connections to Biddle and the Second Bank of the United States would have made him a natural defender of the Bank.
His vote and prestige might have strengthened the pro-Bank forces,
though probably not enough to overcome Jackson's veto.
Diplomatically, his seating would have caused real friction.
The Bourbon Restoration governments of France and Spain regarded the Bonapartes as dangerous exiles;
having one as a sitting U.S. legislator would have complicated relations with both Paris and Madrid at a delicate time,
particularly as the United States was negotiating spoliation claims with France
(resolved in 1831)
and watching the July Revolution unfold in 1830.
Joseph might have served as an informal back-channel to French liberals
and even to his nephew Louis-Napoleon, future Napoleon III.
Conversely, Latin American republics,
some of which had once considered offering Joseph a throne,
might have viewed his elevation as a symbolic alignment of the United States with anti-Bourbon, post-revolutionary legitimacy.
Domestically, his senatorship would have raised durable questions about the role of foreign-born aristocrats in American republican government,
possibly accelerating nativist sentiment a decade before it crystallized in the 1840s.
It might also have encouraged other European exiles
—Polish, Italian, and German liberals who flocked to the U.S. in this era—
to seek political office,
subtly Europeanizing the political class.
On a personal level, the role would have anchored Joseph in America.
In actual history, he returned to Europe in 1832
and died in Florence in 1844.
A senatorial career might have kept him at Point Breeze,
made him a lasting fixture of Philadelphia–New York high society,
and perhaps drawn his nephew Louis-Napoleon
(who briefly visited the U.S. in 1837)
into a more American orbit,
with incalculable consequences for the later Second French Empire.
In short,
Joseph Bonaparte's hypothetical 1829 Senate seat would have been a constitutional curiosity,
a boost to the anti-Jackson opposition,
a diplomatic irritant with Europe's restored monarchies,
and a striking symbol of how thoroughly the wreckage of the Napoleonic order had washed up on American shores.

items.question: What If Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg?
human_answers: I mean, that was more or less the agreement. The Prussians, or more likely Brandenburgers, most likely considered that they would not control Prussia, would be a power on the level of Saxony or Bavaria. Prussia would be divided between Austria (Silesia + border areas), Saxony (Magdeburg/Halberstadt), Sweden (Pomerania), Russia (East Prussia), and possibly others for the Rhineland territories. The kingdom would be drastically reduced, possibly returning to approximately the size of the central Electorate of Brandenburg, destroying its status as a great power. France would likely gain the Austrian Netherlands unless Austria withdrew from the deal. However, I'm not sure if they would do that. What, Germany? The kingdom that united the German kingdoms is no longer a great power. France, which became a republic in OTL, may very well not experience total collapse, instead becoming a constitutional monarchy. Eliminating the entire process of potentially creating Germany. Honestly, the idea of Germany may very well never leave the drawing board. Austria didn't really want to unify the German kingdoms; it was quite happy with the kingdoms being linked to it but not absorbed. Perhaps some form of federation of northern Germany will occur, but that's not a certainty.

I think it depends on the exact settlement. What are the full concessions Prussia is forced to make? Does Frederick II remain in power or does he abdicate or just maybe try in die on the battlefield if it seems like all is lost? Are events in the west impacted, the Franco-British peace settlement? And how is the domestic situation in Russia impacted with Elizbeth living longer? And do changes in Russia spill over into Poland ie with the election for the successor to Augustus III? Then I think you really have to run through the events of the 1770-80s to figure out what the international scene looks like by the 1790s which in tern dictates how much room to maneuver Austria has in Germany as the subject of Imperial reform becomes a pressing issue. If we go with a healthy butterfly net and assume the war mostly ends as IOTL but with Austria regaining Silesia then yes, Austria retains preeminence in Germany and Prussia is knocked down a peg to the level of the other Electors. That certainly changes Austria's strategic outlook. I think there would be less pressure to secure Bavaria on the death of Max III. Since the claims were mostly fabricated Joseph may just let it pass to Charles Theodore without incident. The Balkans are probably where you would first see the new strategic situation begin to change things. To some extent that depends on the fate of Russia. Again, assuming a butterfly net that still places Catherine on the throne with a similar eye cast towards the south and things get interesting. Without the threat of Prussia to the north Austria is better positioned to make gains in the Balkans. IOTL the Prussians were fairly obsessed with blocking any Austrian gains to the south which would strengthen Austria and upset the relative balance of power between the two. I still think the Greek Plan is a fantasy but its entirely possible that Austria recovers something along the lines of the Passarowitz borders, perhaps incrementally over the course or the rest of the century. IOTL Austria almost took Oltenia but instead opted for Bukovina when Prussia redirected everyone towards a partition of Poland. ITTL attention Austria will be focused squarely to the south and the Danube so gains in Serbia, Bosnia and Wallachia are likely but Moldavia less so. Poland meanwhile probably does not undergo partition and remains a Russian client state in the near term. Although its also possible in a different context post ATL Seven Years War that the Polish Royal election in 1764 leads to a falling out between Russia and Austria. Then the next big question is whether the French revolution still breaks out and still proceeds as IOTL and what kind of state Austria is in internally at the end of Joseph II's reign. Presumably even if the Josephine reforms spark a backlash Austria is much better positioned to ride them out with the southern border secure and gains already made from the Ottomans and with no Prussia threat in the north. So even if the Austrian Netherlands break out in rebellion Joseph or Leopold would be able to put down the revolt more easily without it posing any kind of existential threat.

Considering that theoretically the agreement signed between Russia, Austria and Saxony, envisaged a territorial exchange between Royal Prussia and Courland ( with the recognition that the Wettins would retain the throne of the PLC ) while the Habsburgs would recover Silesia or parts of it, that said, the internal balance of the HRE, would be brought back to the previous Leopoldine period, with Vienna as the undisputed leader, and therefore there would be more room for maneuver to try to pass a new package of imperial reforms, certainly France gaining control of the Austrian Netherlands, would not let the imperial princes of the Rhineland and the Hanoverians sleep peacefully, but unfortunately the latter pay the price of having sided with Prussia or of wanting to remain neutral, regarding the possible idea of German unification, it is difficult for the Habsburgs to show a real interest, when they would prefer to maintain the Status Quo or at most consolidate their position in Swabia / Bavaria ( I could see the Bavarian crisis being easily resolved through an agreement, with Charles Theodore inheriting a good part of the duchy, while Vienna annexes small border areas ) finally I am of the opinion that in this scenario, the role of leadership of the Protestant front ( in Otl led by Berlin ) will be taken by the Hanover, who paradoxically will have to review their political priorities ( especially from the London point of view ), because with their choices they will find themselves diplomatically isolated, therefore they will necessarily have to be more active on the continent

It was already happening: Elizabeth could not force Buturlin to get out of his bases and start acting against Prussia. The only meaningful operation was capture of Kolberg and even it was to provide a secure supply line because the Austrians were refusing to do so and getting supplies from the PLC was extremely problematic. Among the Russian military (except those safely away from the front) there was not too much of an appetite for the further fighting and definitely no serious anymosity toward Fritz. Rumyantsev in OTL was quite happy when PIII made peace and Russian #2 general was Fritz’s admirer. It would take very little time for Russia, no matter who was in charge, to figure out that Prussia is more convenient ally than the Hapsburgs. Even under Elizabeth, no matter what the politicians in St.Petersburg were deciding, relations between the Russian and Austrian commanders hd been steadily deteriorating since Kolberg. The Austrians could not reconquer Silesia on their own and the Russian commanders were not willing to keep doing the Austrian job, especially after Doun failed in obligations to provide them with the food and was very cautious in risking the Austrian troops. Anyway, even in OTL, Fritz was playing a second fiddle to CII until she managed to screw up her foreign policy to a degree which gave Fritz “an opening”.
items.original_question: What if Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg? She lives between a few months to a few years longer in this scenario. Peter III does not withdraw Russian troops from the Seven Years War, the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg does not materialize. Now, nobody was interested in total defeat of Prussia, it would remain a viable country but remains a second rate power in Europe, Silesia would go back to Austria, there would be possibly other territorial concessions as well. What happens to Germany long term in this timeline? Austria obviously becomes the natural candidate for unification of the country but the timeline will likely change.

items.model_answer:
If Empress Elizabeth of Russia had lived beyond January 1762, the so-called "Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg" would never have occurred, and the long-term trajectory of Germany would have been profoundly altered.

In the immediate term, Russia would have remained in the anti-Prussian coalition alongside Austria, France, Sweden, and Saxony. By late 1761, Frederick II of Prussia was in a desperate position: his army was exhausted, his treasury empty, Berlin had already been briefly occupied by Russian forces in 1760, and the fortress of Kolberg had fallen. Without Peter III's accession and his sudden withdrawal of Russia from the war (and return of conquered East Prussia), it is highly likely that Frederick would have been crushed within a year. Prussia would probably have been partitioned: Russia annexing East Prussia outright, Austria recovering Silesia and possibly Glatz, Saxony regaining its territorial integrity and perhaps gaining Magdeburg, and Sweden recovering parts of Pomerania. Prussia might have been reduced to the Brandenburg core, a second-rate north German state.

The long-term consequences for Germany would be enormous. The Habsburg monarchy under Maria Theresa and Joseph II would emerge as the unchallenged dominant German power, restoring Austrian primacy within the Holy Roman Empire and reversing the dualism that had defined German politics since 1740. Without a strong Prussia, the "kleindeutsch" (small-German) path to unification under Hohenzollern leadership becomes nearly impossible to imagine. Instead, any future German consolidation would likely follow a "großdeutsch" trajectory centered on Vienna, incorporating the Austrian lands and perhaps developing into a looser, Habsburg-led federation rather than a centralized nation-state.

The ripple effects would extend further. Russia's enlarged western frontier through East Prussia would reshape the Baltic balance and possibly alter the dynamics of the Polish partitions—indeed, Poland might not have been partitioned at all, or only between Russia and Austria, since a weakened Prussia would not have been able to demand its share in 1772. The French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars would unfold against a very different German backdrop, with no Prussian military tradition of Rossbach and Leuthen to draw upon, and no Prussian reform movement of Stein, Hardenberg, and Scharnhorst emerging in response to Jena. There would be no Bismarck, no 1871 Reich in its recognizable form, and consequently the entire militarist-authoritarian Prussian legacy that shaped 19th- and 20th-century German history would be absent.

In short, Elizabeth's longer life would likely have produced a Catholic, Habsburg-centered, more decentralized German world—closer in character to the old Holy Roman Empire than to the Prussian-led nation-state that actually emerged, with cascading consequences for European history that are difficult to overstate.

edus.text: If Empress Elizabeth of Russia had lived beyond January 1762,
the so-called "Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg" would never have occurred,
and the long-term trajectory of Germany would have been profoundly altered.
In the immediate term, Russia would have remained in the anti-Prussian coalition alongside Austria, France, Sweden, and Saxony.
By late 1761, Frederick II of Prussia was in a desperate position:
his army was exhausted,
his treasury empty,
Berlin had already been briefly occupied by Russian forces in 1760,
and the fortress of Kolberg had fallen.
Without Peter III's accession and his sudden withdrawal of Russia from the war
and return of conquered East Prussia,
it is highly likely that Frederick would have been crushed within a year.
Prussia would probably have been partitioned:
Russia annexing East Prussia outright,
Austria recovering Silesia and possibly Glatz,
Saxony regaining its territorial integrity and perhaps gaining Magdeburg,
and Sweden recovering parts of Pomerania.
Prussia might have been reduced to the Brandenburg core,
a second-rate north German state.
The long-term consequences for Germany would be enormous.
The Habsburg monarchy under Maria Theresa and Joseph II would emerge as the unchallenged dominant German power,
restoring Austrian primacy within the Holy Roman Empire
and reversing the dualism that had defined German politics since 1740.
Without a strong Prussia,
the "kleindeutsch" (small-German) path to unification under Hohenzollern leadership becomes nearly impossible to imagine.
Instead, any future German consolidation would likely follow a "großdeutsch" trajectory centered on Vienna,
incorporating the Austrian lands
and perhaps developing into a looser, Habsburg-led federation rather than a centralized nation-state.
The ripple effects would extend further.
Russia's enlarged western frontier through East Prussia would reshape the Baltic balance
and possibly alter the dynamics of the Polish partitions—
indeed, Poland might not have been partitioned at all,
or only between Russia and Austria,
since a weakened Prussia would not have been able to demand its share in 1772.
The French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars would unfold against a very different German backdrop,
with no Prussian military tradition of Rossbach and Leuthen to draw upon,
and no Prussian reform movement of Stein, Hardenberg, and Scharnhorst emerging in response to Jena.
There would be no Bismarck,
no 1871 Reich in its recognizable form,
and consequently the entire militarist-authoritarian Prussian legacy that shaped 19th- and 20th-century German history would be absent.
In short, Elizabeth's longer life would likely have produced a Catholic, Habsburg-centered, more decentralized German world—
closer in character to the old Holy Roman Empire than to the Prussian-led nation-state that actually emerged,
with cascading consequences for European history that are difficult to overstate.

items.question: What If New Spain kept appointing a tlatoani?
human_answers: Yes, really. The social organization was hierarchical and defined by race, as many are even today, with the whites at the top. Again nothing unheard of. It's also true that the Peninsulars were usually assigned the top positions in the Viceroyalties, but even there there were exceptions. Three criollos were viceroys in New Spain and two more in Peru. Apart of that, there was no legal impediment for marriages between whites, mestizos and indios, with the children of such unions considered belonging to the upper class. "Rigid caste systems" never allow marriages outside one's caste and even less allow upwards movement. In many cases, mestizos bribed their way into the white class. Ironically, there were also cases where mestizos bribed their way down to be considered indios, because that put them outside the control from the Inquisition. Black people got it worse, certainly, but even there the social system never reached the hysteric levels of the United States. Intermarriage was complex due to slavery, but still legal. The first registered marriage between a white man and a black woman happened in 1564 in Florida. Of course, the whitest the skin of the children were, the better future they had.

It wouldn't give any advantages to the Spanish, the entire coalition hated the Mexica, keeping him around is not helping them score any points with them. In OTL, the local nobility got incorporated into the Spanish aristocracy, through marriage or by appointment as cacique (lord) of a region. By the Independence War, the most ardent loyalists were the natives, which had the most to lose, together with the Spanish, from a change in government. The enconmienda phase (1500s) was brutal, but by the 1600s, things had settled, and life was back to normal, with a Spanish/Native aristocracy above mestizo and native peasants. The worst abuses to the natives were behind, and the native nobility thrived. Unless there is no total victory, and the Spanish make the the Mexica vassals instead, then they will be in a need for someone to stay in charge. After a few decades, that might even go away if there is a Spanish-Mexica match, the children will be considered Spanish in less than two generations. Unlike the Inca, which I think could survive as a figurehead in Cuzco, the Tlatoani's case is more complicated.
items.original_question: What if New Spain kept appointing a tlatoani? When we think of the Fall of the Aztec Empire, we think of the Spanish coming in and overthrowing the existing order and building New Spain upon the ashes of the Aztec Empire. Well, the answer is a lot more complicated than that thought. One aspect from the Aztec Empire Spain kept was the position of a Tlatoani. Initially, the last sovereign of the Aztec Empire, Cuauhtémoc, was kept alive until Hernan Cortes killed him while bringing along to Honduras. However, Hernan then appointed a person named Tlacotzin (A former advisor of Cuauhtémoc) as tlatoani, (Though he was titled Cuauhtlatoani) but he died the next year before he could return to Tenochtitlan. So, Cortes then appointed a commoner named Motelchiuhtzin net, then he died fighting the Chichimeca up north. Then a man named Xochiquentzin ruled until he died of natural causes. So after that stint, the Spanish appointed Tlatoanis from the previous Aztec dynasty, who were both Tlatoani and Governor of Tenochtitlan (By this point Mexico City) under the Spanish colonial government of New Spain. It started with Panitzin and ended with Cipac. The last one got into frequent disputes over legal issues and disagreements on taxes with the colonial authorities. Afterwards, in just 1565, the Spanish ceased appointing a member of the former dynasty of Tlatoani. But they did continue to appoint a native Judge-governor until Mexican independence in 1821, who were either indigenous or mixed descent and many were descendants of Aztec nobility, though not of the royal dynasty. What if the Spanish continued to appoint continued a blood member of the previous Aztec Empire as "Tlatoani," and continues this until Mexican independence? How would a direct descendent of the Aztec emperors affect the search for a Mexican monarch? Could we see a movement similar to the "Inca Plan" where the Mexicans elect a native Nahuatl as Emperor instead of a European Prince or later Iturbide?

items.model_answer:
If New Spain had continued appointing a tlatoani, the colonial system would have maintained a more visible continuity with Aztec political structures, though the position's actual power would have remained subordinate to Spanish authority.

In reality, the Spanish did initially preserve the office of tlatoani in Tenochtitlan (renamed Mexico City) after the conquest. The last widely recognized tlatoani appointed under Spanish oversight was Don Juan Velázquez Tlacotzin, who served briefly in the 1520s. The position gradually lost significance as the Spanish consolidated direct colonial administration through the viceroyalty system.

Had the practice continued systematically throughout the colonial period, several outcomes seem plausible:

**Symbolic legitimacy**: A perpetual tlatoani would have provided indigenous communities with a recognized figurehead, potentially easing some tensions by maintaining the appearance of indigenous political participation. This could have functioned similarly to how the Spanish used indigenous nobility (caciques) in local governance.

**Limited practical authority**: The tlatoani would likely have been restricted to ceremonial roles and local administrative functions, serving Spanish interests rather than exercising genuine sovereignty. The position would have been carefully controlled to prevent it from becoming a rallying point for resistance.

**Cultural preservation**: Maintaining the office might have helped preserve certain Nahua political traditions, language, and customs longer than they otherwise survived, though heavily modified by Spanish and Catholic influence.

**Potential complications**: A continuous line of tlatoque could have created succession disputes, competing claims to legitimacy, or provided a focal point for indigenous resistance movements—reasons why the Spanish ultimately allowed the institution to fade.

The counterfactual hinges on whether Spanish colonial interests would have been better served by this symbolic continuity or by the more direct control they actually implemented.

items.question: What If Almanzor had never risen to power in al-Andalus?
human_answers: I had to read about Ghalib because my knowledge of him is quite limited. Overall, he seems to be a competent Saqaliba (slave-soldier) leader and served three caliphs. I don't see why he would try to reshape the composition of the caliphate as Al-Mansur did when trying to use Berbers against the rest of Islamic Iberia. Ghālib's rise coincides with the retirement of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III from active military command following his defeat at the Battle of Simancas in 939. So he came to serve under the first caliph and had a life of distinguished service fighting against Vikings, Moroccans, Fatimids, and Christians from northern Iberia. Gaining his freedom and patronage from the Umayyad. Perhaps it will have a greater influence from the Saqaliba in general within the caliphate. But to be honest, overall, they were good slave soldiers, and in the OTL, when the caliphate began to collapse, they were the ones who desperately fought against the Berbers to try to keep the caliphate alive and prevent the sackings of the city of Córdoba. I think one factor that made them generally better managers than the Mamluks in Egypt was that the ṣaqāliba were much less institutionalized and more integrated into local society. This was largely because Andalusian power was always balanced by military pluralism. With Arabs, Berbers, local Andalusians (the Muwallads), Ṣaqāliba, and Christian mercenaries, this balance prevented a single military group from monopolizing the state, as the Mamluks had done. So a Mameluke is freed to never cease being a Mameluke, while a ṣaqāliba is freed to cease being a ṣaqāliba. I'd guess that overall, you have a continuation of the status quo of the period, with a normal caliph (not the puppets of the period). There will be ethnic tensions that rise and fall depending on the situation, disputes over spheres of influence, campaigns in North Africa against the Fatimids (and in the future the Berber caliphates if they rise to power), and campaigns against Christians in the north (Kingdom of Leon), which may or may not succeed depending on the general, as happened in the OTL. It's difficult to say whether this prevents the reconquest of Iberia, but it certainly prevents the implosion of the caliphate of OTL. I would say that what will have the greatest impact on the survival of the Caliphate is not the Christians in the north, but rather the possible rise of the Almoravids.

I think that after ibn Abi Amir is killed, Ghalib is hailed as a hero by the Arab ruling class. As hajib, the old general, committed to the survival of the Caliphate as an institution, would free Hisham II from his irrelevance and perhaps have advisors train the boy-Caliph for rule. Once he reaches the age of maturity, Hisham takes power, albeit he mostly delegates authority to capable bureaucrats. His rule might be an extension of his father’s, a time of peace and prosperity and a golden age of the arts and sciences. The Christians are still too disorganized and weak to push into al-Andalus. Sancho III of Navarre is likely never even born as a result of butterflies. So no Jimenez dynasty either. Christian Spain remains small and disunited while Cordoba remains quietly strong and prosperous. I agree, the real threat to Cordoba wouldn’t be from the north, but from the south. So Cordoba focuses on maintaining hegemonic control over Morocco for strategic purposes. And without the constant warfare against the Christians, I think this will create a favorable situation for the Umayyads in Morocco. So no Almoravids. Fanatical tribes from the desert are repelled by strong Umayyad clients. Once Hisham passes away, he likely leaves an heir. This heir would inherit a strong and stable state, one that is durable for the century to come…
items.original_question: What if No Almanzor Ibn Abi Amir ‘al-Mansur’, better known Latinized as Almanzor, was the Hajib (chamberlain) and de facto ruler of the Caliphate of Qurtubah (Córdoba) from 978 to 1002 AD. A highly ambitious man, ibn Abi Amir would rise through the collection of various powerful offices over the course of the 960s and 970s as an administrator. Through this and his alliance with Subh, mother of the Umayyad boy-caliph Hisham II, ibn Abi Amir would become the most powerful man in al-Andalus by 980. Except, he wasn’t alone. He shared this spotlight with Ghalib ibn Abd al-Rahman ‘al-Siqlabi’ (the Slav), a widely-respected octogenarian general who had served both of Hisham’s predecessors. The two men formed an alliance with one another following the death of Caliph al-Hakam II in 976, allowing for them to rise the ranks of the Caliphate. However by 980 the two men had fallen out, and were increasingly at odds. That year, while together on campaign against the Christians, Ghalib attempted to murder ibn Abi Amir during a feast. The injured ibn Abi Amir would escape with his life and then proceed to capture Ghalib’s fortress in Madinat Salim (Medinaceli). This would lead to a brief civil war between the two, culminating in 981 with the Battle of Torrevicente. There, Ghalib’s army of Andalusi soldiers and his Christian allies would initially rout the Berber troops of ibn Abi Amir. However, Ghalib would unexpectedly die of seemingly natural causes in the middle of the battle, allowing for ibn Abi Amir to claim victory and the mantle of ‘al-Mansur’. Al-Mansur would go on to rule al-Andalus with an iron fist for the next two decades, sidelining the Umayyads, Arab nobility, and Muwalladi (native Iberian Muslims) alike while utilizing increasing numbers of Berber troops to repeatedly devastate the Christian north. While al-Mansur would lead al-Andalus to its peak of dominance over the whole of Iberia, he would also destroy its literal and cultural wealth while gutting its institutions. Upon his death in 1002 the Caliphate was a house of cards waiting to collapse, which it did after Abd al-Rahman ‘Sanchol’, better known as Sanchuelo, attempted to directly usurp the Umayyads as Caliph himself in 1009. This led to the 22-year-long Fitna (unrest) of al-Andalus, ending with Córdoba in ruins and the Caliphate shattered into 30+ petty kingdoms known as Taifas . A situation that would enable the Reconquista to gain steam, culminating in the capture of Tulaytulah (Toledo) by the Christians in 1085. Had Ghalib succeeded in the attempt on his life, ibn Abi Amir would have never become al-Mansur. The Umayyads would have maintained control over their Caliphate. Al-Andalus wouldn’t come to be dominated by a single dictatorial ruler. And the seeds of the Fitna wouldn’t be planted. The Reconquista will unfold differently, or even not at all. What are your thoughts on this scenario? I’ve come to believe that it represents the best chance the Caliphate of Córdoba had at ensuring long-term survival. Averting Almanzor and his excesses would blunt the height of Andalusi authority, but paradoxically preserve the state itself. Of course, stability following his death wouldn’t be ensured, and Ghalib wouldn’t have much longer to live anyway. However, the two had taken care of most rivals, and Ghalib was in good standing with the old guard of al-Andalus. Caliph Hisham II can actually grow up and become a proper ruler, preserving the legitimacy of the Caliphate itself. And without Almanzor, you don’t see increasing numbers of Berber tribesmen relocated to Iberia, provoking ethnic strife.

criteria.3-4: Mentions the Christian north only generically, ignoring how Almanzor's campaigns, tribute, devastation, or lack thereof would change incentives.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that fewer Almanzorid raids could alter Christian consolidation, but gives limited detail on political fragmentation, tribute, or military balance.
criteria.7-8: Balances competing effects: less devastation of Christian polities versus a more stable Cordoban caliphate, with plausible implications for Leon, Castile, Navarre, and frontier warfare.
criteria.9-10: Develops a coherent long-term trajectory for northern Iberia, including dynastic butterflies, frontier institutions, Christian disunity or consolidation, and how Cordoba's stability affects Reconquista timing.

criteria.9-10: Integrates North Africa into the long-range chain, including plausible effects on Umayyad hegemony, later Almoravid emergence or containment, and the balance between southern threats and northern Christian pressure.

items.model_answer:
If Almanzor (al-Mansur ibn Abi Aamir) had never risen to power in al-Andalus, the trajectory of the Iberian Peninsula in the late 10th and early 11th centuries would likely have been dramatically different.

Without Almanzor's military campaigns (978-1002), the Christian kingdoms of the north—León, Castile, Navarre, and the Catalan counties—would probably have consolidated power earlier and more securely. Almanzor's devastating raids, which sacked Santiago de Compostela, Barcelona, and León among dozens of other targets, temporarily reversed Christian expansion and kept the northern kingdoms weak and divided. His absence would have allowed these polities to develop stronger institutions and potentially begin the Reconquista a generation or two earlier.

The Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba itself would likely have faced a different fate. Almanzor effectively usurped power from the legitimate caliph Hisham II, ruling as a military dictator while maintaining the fiction of caliphal authority. Without his iron grip, the caliphate might have experienced internal instability sooner, but it also might have avoided the catastrophic collapse that followed his son's failed attempt to claim the caliphate in 1009. The fitna (civil war) that shattered al-Andalus into the taifa kingdoms was directly precipitated by the power vacuum and resentments created by Almanzor's dictatorship.

Culturally and economically, al-Andalus might have flourished differently. Almanzor's military focus drained resources that could have supported the remarkable intellectual and artistic achievements Córdoba was known for. A more stable, less militarized caliphate might have extended the golden age of Andalusi culture.

In sum, without Almanzor, Christian Spain would likely have grown stronger sooner, and Muslim Spain might have fragmented differently—possibly avoiding the sudden collapse into taifas, but also losing the temporary military resurgence that made late 10th-century al-Andalus so formidable.

items.question: What If In 1972 have Nixon make America the definitive winners in Vietnam before his re-election
human_answers: No there was still a path to victory as late as Watergate. The ARVN with US air support and a shitload of supplies showed it didn't need US ground troops to win battles in 1972 and 1973, and sometimes won without US air support too, and still was winning battles into late 1974 before their supplies and manpower reserves gave out. The problem was Watergate meant Nixon did not have the political capital to prevent Congress from reducing supplies to the ARVN, and then Ford had the same problem, but also couldn't get airstrikes approved for Phouc Long (the lack of which explicitly accelerated the NVA's final offensive by a year). NVA planners actually considered 1976 to be their last shot at winning, as after that point the ARVN would have gotten over its teething troubles So extra US aid means the ARVN wins more of the smaller engagements and US air support smacks the first post cease fire NVA Corps level offensive. That buys another year without lots (possibly any) of American deaths and thus less resistance to having airpower smack the NVA again when they try their "do or die" offensive in late 1975-early 1976. If that gets fought off, that's probably the last chance as the Sino-Vietnamese border is heating up and the ARVN will have gotten over its teething troubles, while the Soviets had become increasingly unwilling to resupply the NVA after the ceasefire

Yes, if the US could have continued the war, then the war would have continued. That's axiomatic. But it couldn't, so it didn't. Remember your Clausewitz: if your armies in the field are still capable of fighting, but there is no political support for continuing the war, then the war is over. They couldn't muster the political capital because the US had already lost. South Vietnam hadn't been defeated yet, but the writing was on the wall in 1972. The major US operations of that year weren't about winning the war - they were about getting favourable conditions for US withdrawal. Arguably everything after Nixon took power was about getting favourable conditions for US withdrawal. You don't agree to withdraw your troops from a theatre of war while your opponent leaves 200,000 of theirs because you're winning. You don't sign a peace agreement that leaves your opponent in control of territory you were trying to defend because you're winning.

Without fundamental reforms, the South Vietnamese government could not achieve any tactical victories, let alone destroy most of the northern army. I believe OP refers to the US destroying most of the North Vietnamese army. However, I doubt the South Vietnamese government was so incompetent as to be destroyed by local warlords and rebellious peasants. And the more the Americans suppressed these local forces, the more they aligned themselves with the Northern government. Things there somehow like Afganistan. Either a fundamental reshaping of the South Vietnamese government is necessary (which I don't think could be achieved during Nixon's term) or complete military control. This would require a large number of troops stationed in every town to maintain order in place of the South Vietnamese government. Not American, so from some Asia ally, maybe South Korean? This could come at a significant political cost and carries the risk of war with China.

By 1972 there were only around 50,000 American soldiers in Vietnam, which means with a POD of January 1, 1972, any military victories would be by the South Vietnamese ground forces, supported by US air power. I feel that the incompetence of the South Vietnamese army is greatly overstated. They were reliant on American support, but with that support they were a fairly decent force. Edit: I mean to say that the ARVN could not achieve any tactical victories is ridiculous. Look at the actual 1972 offensive of OTL. What I’m saying is basically exactly what happened. South Vietnamese ground forces defeated a northern invasion with the help of American air power. The North Vietnamese suffered 100,000 casualties. If you scale up the size of the offensive ITTL and/or the scale of the defeat, it’s not hard to get to losses that become pretty disastrous for the north Vietnamese war fighting capabilities.

The problem is doing what it would take to win Vietnam starting after Nixon is in office and winning by Fall of 72 is NOT going to make Nixon popular. It is going to take a massive build up a huge expenditure of money an increased draft and a lot of dead young men. In effect to massively over simplify you would have to form a line across the country and start marching north while keep a secure boarder. The U.S. got fascinated by the helicopters ability to drop troops wherever. But lost track that holding a small area of land doesn’t do any good. Imagine fighting WW2 only with airborne troops. Sure they are useful to capture a key point but to trully accomplish anything you need to match on the ground to join up with them and secure an area. Doing this in the S.E.A. Jungle is going to be a mess. This mess was somewhat avoided in WW2 because when fighting in that kind of area vs Japan both sides were “foreigners” and we had more support from the locals. But yo take the local? You need to stand on and hold the land. ALL the land, if you hold any hive area but large parts are not occupied by your troops then the other guys just slip away to areas your troops aren’t at. I never understood why this wasn’t pretty obvious. I can only think it WAS obvious but being as the U.S. didn’t what to commit that kind of level of force it was ignored in favor of the new high tech way of fighting. Which in defense of it, it worked in a stand up fight against traditional armies but what cost the U.S. the war was not traditional armies. So to win Vietnam the cost is going to be very high and it won’t help Nixon at all

criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, distinguishes propaganda victory from durable strategic victory, and rigorously tests feasibility against military, domestic, and diplomatic limits.

items.model_answer:
If Nixon had achieved a definitive American victory in Vietnam before his 1972 re-election, the consequences would have been profound across multiple dimensions:

**Military and Strategic Implications:**
A decisive victory would have required either a massive escalation of force—potentially including invasion of North Vietnam, mining Haiphong harbor earlier and more aggressively, or even tactical nuclear weapons—or a sudden collapse of North Vietnamese resistance. The former would have risked direct confrontation with China and the Soviet Union, while the latter was highly unlikely given Hanoi's commitment. Assuming some combination of intensified bombing, ground operations into the North, and cutting the Ho Chi Minh Trail succeeded in forcing North Vietnam's surrender or complete withdrawal, South Vietnam would have been preserved as an independent, non-communist state.

**Domestic Political Impact:**
Nixon's landslide victory in 1972 would have been even more overwhelming. The antiwar movement would have been discredited or at least marginalized. The credibility gap and distrust of government that characterized the post-Vietnam era might have been significantly reduced. However, Watergate would likely still have occurred, though Nixon's position as a victorious wartime president might have given him more political capital to survive it.

**Cold War Dynamics:**
A clear American victory would have validated the domino theory and containment strategy, emboldening U.S. interventionism elsewhere. The Soviet Union and China would have faced a significant geopolitical setback. American credibility with allies would have been strengthened rather than damaged. The subsequent communist victories in Cambodia and Laos might have been prevented.

**Long-term Consequences:**
The "Vietnam Syndrome"—American reluctance to commit ground forces abroad—would not have developed, potentially leading to more interventions in the 1980s and beyond. The military reforms that emerged from Vietnam's lessons might have been delayed. Southeast Asia's development trajectory would have been dramatically different, with South Vietnam potentially following a path similar to South Korea or Taiwan rather than reunification under communist rule.

The human cost would have been substantial—likely hundreds of thousands more casualties on all sides to achieve such a victory.
