items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?

rubrics.question_focus: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling and technological feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer treats the premise carefully: fission is discovered early enough for a practical reactor around 1900, while still evaluating what supporting science, engineering, materials, and industrial capabilities would or would not plausibly exist.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or rejects the premise without analysis, or assumes modern nuclear technology simply appears in 1900.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges the premise but gives a shallow feasibility discussion with major anachronisms or missing constraints.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some key feasibility issues such as fuel, moderation, control, materials, or instrumentation, but unevenly.
criteria.7-8: Carefully distinguishes the fission discovery from the broader reactor-supporting technologies needed around 1900.
criteria.9-10: Rigorously explores what must change for a 1900 reactor to work, separating minimal plausible changes from implausible technological leaps.

criteria.name: Nuclear reactor mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explains the reactor-specific mechanisms relevant to a 1900-era practical reactor, including natural uranium, enrichment limits, moderators, neutron economy, control systems, heat removal, shielding, and reactor type.
criteria.1-2: Shows little understanding of how a reactor works or confuses fission with unrelated nuclear processes.
criteria.3-4: Mentions reactors generally but omits most key mechanisms or contains serious technical errors.
criteria.5-6: Covers several mechanisms, such as moderators or shielding, but misses important interactions or design constraints.
criteria.7-8: Explains most relevant mechanisms and connects them to 1900-era industrial capabilities.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent technical account of plausible reactor designs and bottlenecks, including tradeoffs among graphite, heavy water, natural uranium, control, cooling, and radiation safety.

criteria.name: Industrial and scientific context around 1900
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the answer situates the counterfactual in the actual capabilities of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, including chemistry, metallurgy, electrical instrumentation, steam engineering, mining, heavy water or graphite production, and radiation biology.
criteria.1-2: Uses a vague or fantasy-like 1900 setting with no attention to historical industrial limits.
criteria.3-4: Mentions the era but relies on broad claims without concrete scientific or industrial context.
criteria.5-6: Includes some period-appropriate constraints, such as weak electronics or immature radiation safety, but not systematically.
criteria.7-8: Grounds the scenario in credible 1900-era capacities and identifies where major bottlenecks would arise.
criteria.9-10: Integrates detailed period constraints across multiple sectors and shows how each would shape reactor deployment and consequences.

criteria.name: Long-range causal consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces plausible downstream effects of early nuclear reactors over decades, such as power generation, naval propulsion, weapons development, regulation, public health, environmental contamination, geopolitics, fossil fuel use, and scientific institutions.
criteria.1-2: Provides only immediate effects or unsupported claims about the future.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few downstream effects but lacks causal links or timeframe clarity.
criteria.5-6: Develops some medium- or long-term consequences, but misses major domains or treats them independently.
criteria.7-8: Builds a mostly coherent multi-decade chain from early reactors to industrial, military, medical, environmental, and political outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Presents a nuanced long-range trajectory with interacting feedback loops, path dependence, and plausible alternate historical branches.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly separates likely, possible, and speculative outcomes while avoiding internal contradictions, overconfidence, and conflicts with the stated counterfactual premise.
criteria.1-2: Is internally contradictory, overconfident, or incompatible with the premise.
criteria.3-4: Contains some hedging but also major unsupported certainties or inconsistent assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent, with moderate uncertainty awareness but some vague or conflicting claims.
criteria.7-8: Clearly signals uncertainty, explains assumptions, and maintains consistency across the scenario.
criteria.9-10: Precisely calibrates confidence, compares alternative pathways, and keeps all mechanisms and consequences logically consistent with the counterfactual.

items.model_answer:
If nuclear fission had been discovered and harnessed in a practical reactor around 1900, the trajectory of the twentieth century would have diverged dramatically across science, industry, geopolitics, and culture.

Scientifically, such a discovery would require a radically accelerated understanding of atomic structure. In our timeline, the electron was identified in 1897, the nucleus not until 1911, and fission itself only in 1938. For fission to be usable in 1900, physicists like Becquerel, the Curies, Rutherford, and Thomson would have had to leap past decades of incremental work, perhaps spurred by an unusually lucky experimental observation with uranium or thorium salts. This would have compressed the development of quantum mechanics and nuclear physics into the early Edwardian era, likely concentrating immense scientific prestige and funding in Europe — particularly France, Britain, and Germany — well before the rise of American dominance in physics.

Industrially, a working reactor in the 1900s would have arrived in a world still transitioning from coal and steam to electricity and oil. Cheap, dense thermal energy could have short-circuited the petroleum age. Electrification of cities, railways, and factories would have proceeded much faster, and the internal combustion engine — and with it the automobile and aviation industries — might have developed differently or more slowly, since the strategic urgency of oil would be reduced. Heavy industry, desalination, synthetic fertilizer production (the Haber-Bosch process arrived in 1909), and even early electric ships could have spread decades ahead of schedule. However, materials science of the era was inadequate for managing intense radiation, heat, and corrosion, so early reactors would likely have been crude, dangerous, and prone to catastrophic accidents that killed workers and contaminated regions — possibly creating a public backlash that shaped nuclear regulation far earlier.

Geopolitically, the consequences would be profound. If weaponization followed reactor technology — as it did historically — then a nuclear-armed great power could have emerged before World War I. The arms race between Britain, Germany, France, Russia, and Austria-Hungary in the 1900s and 1910s might have included fission devices, fundamentally altering or perhaps preventing the First World War as it actually unfolded. Colonial powers controlling uranium-bearing territories (the Belgian Congo, Czechoslovakia, the American West, Australia) would gain enormous leverage. Conversely, if early reactors remained purely civilian because the path to a bomb was not yet understood, an unprecedented era of cheap energy might have eased some of the resource competition that fueled imperial rivalry.

Culturally and socially, the early twentieth century's optimism about science — already strong — would have intensified into something close to techno-utopianism, with radium-and-atomic imagery saturating advertising, architecture, and politics even more than it briefly did in the 1900s–1930s. But the early, poorly understood health effects of radiation, layered onto an industrial workforce with no protections, would have produced enormous human costs, comparable to or worse than the radium-dial painters' tragedy on a mass scale. Public health, labor law, and environmental regulation might have evolved earlier in response.

In short, an 1900s nuclear reactor would have accelerated electrification and industrial capacity by roughly half a century, reshaped imperial geopolitics, possibly inserted nuclear weapons into the pre-WWI balance of power, and exacted a steep human and environmental price due to the era's primitive safety knowledge — making the twentieth century both more technologically advanced and, quite possibly, more dangerous than the one we actually experienced.

edus.text: If nuclear fission had been discovered and harnessed in a practical reactor around 1900,
the trajectory of the twentieth century would have diverged dramatically across science, industry, geopolitics, and culture.
Scientifically, such a discovery would require a radically accelerated understanding of atomic structure.
In our timeline, the electron was identified in 1897,
the nucleus not until 1911,
and fission itself only in 1938.
For fission to be usable in 1900, physicists like Becquerel, the Curies, Rutherford, and Thomson would have had to leap past decades of incremental work,
perhaps spurred by an unusually lucky experimental observation with uranium or thorium salts.
This would have compressed the development of quantum mechanics and nuclear physics into the early Edwardian era,
likely concentrating immense scientific prestige and funding in Europe — particularly France, Britain, and Germany —
well before the rise of American dominance in physics.
Industrially, a working reactor in the 1900s would have arrived in a world still transitioning from coal and steam to electricity and oil.
Cheap, dense thermal energy could have short-circuited the petroleum age.
Electrification of cities, railways, and factories would have proceeded much faster,
and the internal combustion engine — and with it the automobile and aviation industries — might have developed differently or more slowly,
since the strategic urgency of oil would be reduced.
Heavy industry, desalination, synthetic fertilizer production (the Haber-Bosch process arrived in 1909), and even early electric ships could have spread decades ahead of schedule.
However, materials science of the era was inadequate for managing intense radiation, heat, and corrosion,
so early reactors would likely have been crude, dangerous, and prone to catastrophic accidents
that killed workers and contaminated regions —
possibly creating a public backlash
that shaped nuclear regulation far earlier.
Geopolitically, the consequences would be profound.
If weaponization followed reactor technology — as it did historically —
then a nuclear-armed great power could have emerged before World War I.
The arms race between Britain, Germany, France, Russia, and Austria-Hungary in the 1900s and 1910s might have included fission devices,
fundamentally altering or perhaps preventing the First World War as it actually unfolded.
Colonial powers controlling uranium-bearing territories (the Belgian Congo, Czechoslovakia, the American West, Australia) would gain enormous leverage.
Conversely, if early reactors remained purely civilian because the path to a bomb was not yet understood,
an unprecedented era of cheap energy might have eased some of the resource competition
that fueled imperial rivalry.
Culturally and socially, the early twentieth century's optimism about science — already strong — would have intensified into something close to techno-utopianism,
with radium-and-atomic imagery saturating advertising, architecture, and politics even more than it briefly did in the 1900s–1930s.
But the early, poorly understood health effects of radiation, layered onto an industrial workforce with no protections, would have produced enormous human costs,
comparable to or worse than the radium-dial painters' tragedy on a mass scale.
Public health, labor law, and environmental regulation might have evolved earlier in response.
In short, an 1900s nuclear reactor would have accelerated electrification and industrial capacity by roughly half a century,
reshaped imperial geopolitics,
possibly inserted nuclear weapons into the pre-WWI balance of power,
and exacted a steep human and environmental price due to the era's primitive safety knowledge —
making the twentieth century both more technologically advanced and, quite possibly, more dangerous than the one we actually experienced.

items.question: What If Create an exotic party system
human_answers: Led to: Independent Growers Union Party: AKA the Green Farmers Party, Green and Grow Party ... ( In derogatory terms also referred to as the Goatwool Sock Party, the goats ) A split-off from the Farmers Union Party that contends that the latter has become too subservient to the big agricultural businesses, megafarms and meat-packing plants to the detriment of small family farms and independent growers. Quickly gained a following in rural New England, Colorado, New Mexico and parts of California. Also gained support from the microbrewery industry, whole food grocery chains and Willie Nelson... However while promoting small farms and orchards, they quickly adopted ideas of sustainable green farming which lead to talk radio now openly calling them 'that other green lefties'. The fact that they are also heavily promoting the legalization of marijuana does not help and lately their appeal with traditional small family farms - once their core constituents- has waned. Many of hem now lamenting that they "revolted against being pushed out by corporate megafarms, only to now be pushed out by hippie goat farmers". Still their upward trend has slowed but not stopped andbin the last elections they managed to get as many votes as the FUP. Platform : pro small farms, pro sustainable farming, pro farm subsides but vehement watchdog making sure said subsidies are not gobbled up by large agribusiness. Socially conservative to pro-busines, pro-family and pro states rights. However also pro marijuana and against fracking, pesticides and GMO seeds. Although not official, in analogy to the Democrat's mule and the Republican's elephants, political cartoonists have taken to depicting the IGUP as a small goat or a goat Inna farmers outfit. Apparently many IGUP members liked the idea and bumper stickers of goats driving tractors, goats headbutting mules and goats p.... against the leg of an elephant have become quite popular in rural parts of the states. Closely aligned with: Fraternal Order of Local and Small Businesses: Originally an action group turned political party, the FOLSBee is - as the name implies- pro-busines but against 'big business' and megacorporations running roughshod over small neighborhood mon-and-pop stores. Unsurprisingly they have a strong following on the local levels, in several smaller towns being the biggest party in city council. Their reach however declines with each superimposed layer of government and their overall impact in the state elections I negligible. Nationally, so far they have only yielded one senator and four congressmen in their 50 years of existence. The name invokes strong images of early 1900's idyllic New England town streets with lots of stores that are just known by the family name of their owner and it must be said that the FOLSBee is quite successful in playing on the nostalgic feel of that image. Their mythical hero is George Bailey, the community banker protagonist from Frank Capra's ' It's a Wonderful Life'. And like Bailey, their main tenet is that it is a local business' task to help it's community especially when this does not exclude getting ahead themselves as well. Therefore on a national level it should be the government's task to help small businesses helping the community. As a platform, they are rather conservative, pro gun rights, pro law and order and pro-busines. However they are quite effective as a watchdog making sure that every proposed business law is effectively helping ALL businesses an not just the ones big enough to afford their own lobbyists and their idea of 'a level playing field for all' also ties in with support for education and immigrants' rights. However like the IGUP, the FOLSBee also has taken on -critics say:'has been infiltrated by' - some rather leftist and environmentalist views. So they tend to promote public transportation over new highways (there are more clients at bus stops then at parking lots) green energy over fossil fuel (no startup will come to our city thinking 'Hey, let's build a car that runs on coal') public housing, a strong social welfare net and lately even state-run healthcare. So much like conservatives paint the IGUP as the party of goat wool sock wearing weed farmers, they taken to deride the FOLSBee as the party of hippie farmers market organic bath salt sellers. Like the IGUP, this has not really affected their base and although rather small nationally, by coordinating their programs with the IGUP 'goats' they are still on of the more influntial minor pressure parties. In political cartoons to the FOLSBee is usually represented as a Norman Rockwell-esque 1920's drug store owner. Typically he is standing behind a soda fountain doling out fatherly advice to a donkey or elephant sitting at the drug store counter.

Law and Order : Center-right to right-wing, MacArthurism, law and order, strong government, agrarianism (faction) Originally formed during the Dorr Rebellion, however, they soon grew to great lengths due to the Great Rebellion. As of now, they are the party in power and have a strong grasp over the country's House of Burgesses, most likely due to the recent riots in cities such as Cleaveland and St. Elmo. The party itself campaigns on the promises of strength, justice, and keeping the radicals in check. They are currently led by Premier Joe Pennacchio. Republican Moderate : Center to center-right, liberal-conservatism, economic conservatism, social liberalism, libertarianism (faction) Created in an attempt to oppose the religious fanatics of the state along with the dictatorial Alaskan Governor Ben Stevens. However, over time they became a national party and became a party full of moderates and centrists leaning towards the right. They are also the second biggest party in the House, they support religious freedom and economic conservatism. They are currently led by Deirdre Scozzfava. Nullifier : Center-right to center-right, nullification, economic liberalism, social conservatism, free-trade, states' rights (faction) The party of nullification and free trade, the Nullifiers were strong for a good many of years before the Republic of Dixie's secession, in which they were banned for treason, however, in the early '80s, they were unbanned and forced to start from the bottom up. However, they are doing well now, and are the third biggest party in the United States' House of Burgesses. They are currently led by Peter Lawler. Solidarity : Left-wing to center-left, populism, anti-authoritarianism, left-wing populism, workers' rights, social democracy (faction) The party originated from the Illinois Solidarity Party which had been formed to oppose local lunatic Hermyle LaRouche's antics, however, they eventually moved into the national arena. For a time, they were very strong, especially during the population's progressive sway during the 1990s, they have been slowly and surely losing seats each year, They are currently led by Adlai Stevenson IV. Southern : Center-left to far-right, southern interests, social conservatism, states' rights, southern secession (faction) The Southern Party was formed for southern interests, and their interests only. It was a miracle that they were unbanned in the early 2000s by Nullifier Premier James Q. Wilson. They are especially socially conservative, however, there are a few members who could be considered left-wing populists to some extent. They only contain seats that originate from the deep south. Currently led by Roy Moore. Peoples' Constitutional : Left-wing to left-wing, Chicano nationalism, Mexican-American interests, Christian socialism (faction) And last, but also least, the Peoples' Constitutional Party. Similar to the Southern Party, the PCs were formed to protect a specific group of peoples' interests. However, unlike the Southerners, the PCs fight for the rights of minorities, well, actually just those of Hispanic origin. There is also a strong Catholic Socialist faction in the party, most likely due to former leader Dolores Huerta. Currently led by Julian Castro.

- Puritan Party: Atl scenario where the Great Awakening leads to a political movement alongside the religious revival. - National Party: Atl scenario where the military plays a more important role in early US politics. The military takes control and declares that citizenship is only given to those who serve. The US becomes a one party state dominated by military leaders. - German American Party: German immigration to America occurs in even larger numbers than otl. German Americans demand German be declared a national "protected" language. They also fight against ethnic discrimination. - Monarchist Party:. The US tries out a Monarchy but it fails and Becomes a Republic. This party tries wishes to see the return of the Monarchy. - Colonization Party: A party of early abolitionists who focus there effort on the state and local level. Try to encourage slave states to allow slaves to earn their freedom under the condition that they be sent to Liberia after their enslavement ends.

I had a rather lengthy idea I've been toying around with for a party system for a work of fiction written in my Power Without Knowledge setting that I might write out today but on an unrelated note I've been mulling over the impact of a more successful Joseph Smith presidential run . I'm not suggesting that he win, or even that he not be assassinated, I'm just trying to puzzle out the consequences of his electoral platform surviving his death. Perhaps some sort of alliance with the Liberty Party ? Smith's platform included provisions shrinking the size of Congress and docking their pay, along with the elimination of courts martial and instituting the death penalty for public officials that didn't defend their constituents' constitutional rights, but what suggests at least some buy-in from the Liberty Party was a program of complete emancipation by 1850, with at least some degree of compensation financed by the sale of public land. Smith also argued for the annexation of Texas and Oregon. I understand it's a gamble of long odds (especially regarding constitutional changes and territorial expansion) but perhaps a pragmatic move to adopt compensation as a way to attract votes in slave states that would otherwise dig in their heels at any mention of abolition? It would also almost certainly require butterflying away the LDS move to Utah, leaving them a powerful swing constituency in Illinois. The idea of an openly abolitionist party arising in and surviving the 19th century and explicitly focused on the rights of minority religious and ethnic groups has a lot of promise. *EDIT- In keeping with my new Strange Bedfellows idea for an alternate American history in party systems here's my reinterpretation of the Second Party System: Federalist Party - The sole survivor of the First Party System and the Era of Good Feelings, the Federalist Party was able to claw its way back from the brink in the wake of the shattering of the National Republican Party following the much maligned 1824 election. Advocating a strong central government, Hamiltonian economics and infrastructure spending, the party was aided in its recovery by the influx of anti-Jacksonians leaving the disintegrating National Republicans. Nullifier Party - Intrinsically rooted in the fallout of the Era of Good Feelings, the Nullifier Party was shaped in it's early history by the rise of Andrew Jackson and the fallout of the Nullification Crisis of 1832. Considering himself cheated out of the presidency in 1824 Jackson had joined the Nullifiers out of a belief in populism and states' rights, though he would oppose the doctrine within the party known as "Hard Nullification" (the right of the states to cancel federal laws), instead advocating a policy of limiting government power at the federal level. While in office Jackson tended to side with Southern interests against abolitionism, opposed (but could not dismantle) the Bank of the United States and defied the Supreme Court in the lead up to the Trail of Tears. Liberty Party - As the 19th century went on, national expansion through the annexation of Texas and the Mexican-American War put the issue of slavery at the forefront of the nation's politics. The Federalists would side with northern industrial interests in opposition to the spread of the Peculiar Institution, while Nullifiers, viewing such attempts as federal overreach, became adamant defenders of it. Despite this focus on the issue it wouldn't be until the 1850's that the Liberty Party, the only explicitly abolitionist party in the Union, would gain traction beyond the local level. A party of minority rights and abolitionism, the Libertarians would lead a coalition of freedmen, Mormons and Owenite socialists of all stripes to political action, parlaying a pivotal influence in several midwestern states into a coalition with the Federalists in 1860.
items.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Divergence Logic
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer establishes a clear alternate-history or institutional premise that plausibly produces an exotic party system rather than merely listing random parties.
criteria.1-2: No clear divergence point or premise; parties appear arbitrary or unrelated to the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a premise, but the link to party formation is weak, vague, or mostly asserted.
criteria.5-6: Provides a recognizable divergence and explains some direct effects on party development.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible divergence with clear causal links to multiple party origins and alignments.
criteria.9-10: Develops a rich, internally grounded counterfactual premise whose institutional, social, and historical consequences strongly explain the whole party system.

criteria.name: Party System Breadth and Distinctiveness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer creates a varied, exotic, and politically meaningful set of parties with distinct identities, constituencies, ideologies, and roles.
criteria.1-2: Provides too few parties or parties are generic labels with little differentiation.
criteria.3-4: Includes several parties, but many overlap ideologically or lack clear bases of support.
criteria.5-6: Creates a functional multiparty system with some distinct platforms and voter blocs.
criteria.7-8: Offers a diverse party ecology with clear ideological niches, regional bases, factions, and political functions.
criteria.9-10: Presents a vivid, memorable, and exotic party system where each party has a distinctive history, constituency, symbolism, and strategic role.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanisms by which the new parties emerge, compete, evolve, and affect governance over time.
criteria.1-2: Little or no explanation of how parties form, gain support, or influence politics.
criteria.3-4: Gives limited mechanisms, mostly party platforms without electoral or social dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic formation causes, voter bases, and some electoral consequences.
criteria.7-8: Covers party origins, coalitions, regional strength, factional drift, electoral incentives, and policy effects.
criteria.9-10: Traces long-range dynamics across generations, including realignments, splinters, alliances, media framing, institutional pressures, and governing consequences.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence and Internal Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the created party system remains coherent across time, geography, ideology, and institutions without contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible timelines, or mutually incompatible party claims.
criteria.3-4: Has some coherent elements but frequent inconsistencies in ideology, chronology, or influence.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with minor unexplained jumps or tensions between party traits and outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains strong consistency across party histories, platforms, regions, and electoral status.
criteria.9-10: Shows excellent systemic coherence, with tensions explicitly explained as factions, compromises, historical legacies, or strategic adaptations.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Constraint Awareness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer balances imaginative exoticism with plausible political sociology and acknowledges uncertainty where appropriate.
criteria.1-2: Wildly implausible or deterministic; ignores political constraints and social realities.
criteria.3-4: Some plausible ideas, but relies heavily on unsupported leaps or overconfident claims.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible, though some assumptions or long-range outcomes are underjustified.
criteria.7-8: Balances creativity with realistic voter behavior, institutions, regional interests, and contingency.
criteria.9-10: Highly imaginative yet disciplined; clearly distinguishes likely outcomes from speculative ones and explains constraints, tradeoffs, and alternative possibilities.

items.model_answer:
An exotic party system would be a political party structure that deviates significantly from conventional models. Here are some creative possibilities:

**Rotating Ideology Parties**: Parties that systematically shift their platform every election cycle, forcing voters to engage with policies rather than tribal loyalty. A party might be conservative one term, progressive the next.

**Issue-Specific Parties**: Rather than broad coalitions, parties form around single issues and dissolve once that issue is resolved or becomes irrelevant. This creates fluid political landscapes where representatives must constantly build new coalitions.

**Sortition Parties**: Parties whose candidates and leadership are selected by lottery from qualified citizens rather than through internal elections, combining democratic representation with random selection to reduce careerism and elite capture.

**Algorithmic Parties**: Parties whose platforms are generated through direct digital democracy, where members vote on every policy position through secure apps, with AI aggregating preferences into coherent platforms while preventing manipulation.

**Expertise-Weighted Parties**: Systems where party members' votes on specific policies are weighted by demonstrated expertise in that domain, balancing populism with technocracy.

**Generational Parties**: Parties organized strictly by age cohorts, ensuring each generation has direct representation of its interests, with mandatory retirement as members age into the next bracket.

Each system would create different incentives, power dynamics, and representation patterns, fundamentally reshaping how political competition and governance function.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.

I actually like the idea of an improved dragon better than what we have with Starship (assuming it ever carries humans). As for using it for lunar missions. Do we need to recreate the Apollo Mission profile or can we build some sort of transfer craft a sort of tug or booster that can be docked with and used to get to and from the moon. We would need a way to refuel it in earth orbit but it may be one way to get Dragon to the moon. And long term it may be better. I have always thought that we needed some sort of “space craft” vs the way we do everything with the vehicle we use to get up and down from earth. That would I suppose be a big task to build and maintain and refuel this transfer vehicle. But it may allow a less powerful system to do the job. And once you have the hardware it is harder to cancel the thing. So we may actually get some long term use.

All true of course, also fully ignored in most cases and specifically in the articles/videos I cited above The "mantra" is simply that Dragon is cheaper and therefor better than Orion. Similar statements about Falcon versus SLS. One of the videos I didn't cite was in fact one that suggests Lunar HLS "Starship" will be used for ferrying the landing party from LEO to LLO where they would use Dragon to land on the Moon and then return to the HLS "Starship" to be ferried back to LEO where Dragon would be used to land on Earth. Ya, IIRC you lose the core stage. Ya it would be 'neat' but keep in mind the Super Draco's are not actually "throttleable" since they are supposed to be used as abort rockets and not landing rockets. items.original_question: What if Falcon/Dragon to the Moon? Kind of bouncing off this thread as I've run across some of the usual "hype" sources such as this and this , (nothing from SpaceX though which I think is telling) "bragging" about SpaceX's "great new plan" to send crew Dragon to the Moon "sooner than NASA or China" etc, et-al. (Of course they all simply ignore the issues with Dragon going beyond LEO and the fact Orion and SLS are designed to do exactly that but what would I expect ) So the question is essentially "What if SpaceX had continued to iterate and improve Dragon and Falcon Heavy for use in Lunar missions? Granting that as I pointed out here that there's likely no "place" for such a move since the SpaceX to Mars focus was pretty much baked in since the start and with such a short timeline getting a plausible POD is going to be problematic I do wonder if a bit more focus on "Dear Moon" along with Cargo/Crew Dragon couldn't set up a premise where the eventual "HLS" might end up more realistic? Anyway, open for thoughts and comments Randy

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the premise that SpaceX continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions, rather than shifting back to actual-history Starship-centered development or unrelated Apollo/SLS narratives.
criteria.1-2: Mostly ignores the premise or treats actual Starship development as unchanged and central.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar use but frequently reverts to actual-history assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains the premise in broad terms, with some unsupported or inconsistent deviations.
criteria.7-8: Consistently explores a Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar path while noting relevant actual-history constraints.
criteria.9-10: Fully anchors the scenario in sustained Falcon Heavy/Dragon investment and carefully distinguishes counterfactual changes from real events.

criteria.name: Technical mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer identifies the key engineering mechanisms needed for crewed lunar missions using Falcon Heavy and Dragon, such as translunar injection, docking, life support duration, radiation, lunar orbit operations, landing architecture, refueling, and return capability.
criteria.1-2: Provides vague claims with little or no technical mechanism discussion.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few hardware elements but misses major mission-critical requirements.
criteria.5-6: Covers several core mechanisms but leaves important gaps such as landing, refueling, or return strategy.
criteria.7-8: Explains most major mechanisms and tradeoffs in a plausible mission architecture.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly connects Falcon Heavy, Dragon modifications, transfer stages, docking/refueling, lunar landing, and Earth return into a technically coherent architecture.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the quality of the answer's extended reasoning from early SpaceX development choices through NASA procurement, mission cadence, economics, infrastructure, Starship opportunity costs, and possible lunar program outcomes.
criteria.1-2: Lists isolated effects with no causal chain or timeline.
criteria.3-4: Gives a shallow sequence of consequences with weak links between causes and effects.
criteria.5-6: Presents a recognizable medium-term chain but skips key transitions or feedback effects.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent long-range chain across technology, funding, operations, and institutional responses.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced multi-stage causal model showing how early Falcon Heavy/Dragon choices propagate into lunar architecture, market position, NASA strategy, and later SpaceX priorities.

criteria.name: Plausibility and uncertainty calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer avoids overclaiming and properly calibrates uncertain outcomes, especially around Falcon Heavy performance limits, Dragon upgrade feasibility, cost advantages, NASA willingness, and whether such a path would outperform or delay Starship.
criteria.1-2: Makes sweeping deterministic claims unsupported by constraints.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty superficially but still relies on strong unsupported conclusions.

items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Crew Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions, the trajectory of both the company and U.S. human spaceflight in the late 2010s and early 2020s would likely have looked quite different.

The original 2017 announcement of a Falcon Heavy–launched lunar tourism flight, using a modified Crew Dragon to send two private citizens on a free-return trajectory around the Moon, was quietly shelved in favor of focusing resources on Starship. Had SpaceX pursued that path instead, the most immediate technical work would have involved upgrading Crew Dragon for deep-space conditions: improved radiation shielding, a higher-velocity reentry heat shield capable of handling lunar return speeds (around 11 km/s rather than the 7.8 km/s of low Earth orbit return), enhanced life support for a roughly week-long mission, and better communications and navigation for cislunar space. Falcon Heavy itself would likely have needed human-rating certification, something it was never designed for, requiring additional structural margins, abort-mode analyses, and probably reinforcement of its triple-core configuration.

A plausible mission architecture would have been a single Falcon Heavy launching Crew Dragon directly onto a translunar trajectory for a circumlunar flyby, similar to Apollo 8 but without lunar orbit insertion, since Dragon's SuperDraco-based propulsion lacks the delta-v for orbital capture and return. A lunar landing would have required a separately launched lander and likely orbital rendezvous, an architecture SpaceX never seriously pursued with this hardware.

The broader consequences could have included an earlier private crewed lunar flyby, possibly by 2020 or 2021, beating NASA's Artemis program to cislunar space with humans. It would have given the United States a crewed lunar capability years before SLS/Orion flew Artemis I uncrewed in 2022. However, it would almost certainly have slowed Starship development by diverting engineering talent and capital, potentially delaying the fully reusable super-heavy-lift system that NASA ultimately selected for the Artemis III lunar landing. SpaceX likely also would not have won the HLS contract in 2021, since that award was explicitly tied to Starship.

Commercially, a successful circumlunar tourism flight could have opened a small but high-profile market for lunar tourism, though the per-seat costs would have remained extremely high compared to the long-term economics Starship promises. Strategically, Elon Musk's Mars-focused vision would have been compromised, since Falcon Heavy and Dragon are fundamentally dead-end architectures for interplanetary settlement. In essence, the counterfactual trades a near-term lunar achievement for a likely multi-year delay in the more transformative reusable-launch revolution.

items.question: What If the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto?
human_answers: The only time Aircraft Carriers carry out multi-day attacks on the same location is when they either are providing air cover to an invasion force or have total air superiority. If Pearl Harbour had been a single raid each day for two days the raid on the second day would have suffered serious losses and the patrol aircraft may have located the Carriers which then becomes a very big question of risking a Carrier. Aircraft Carriers are great at projecting power in that they represent overwhelming firepower from unexpected directions at any time. For example look at the exercises carried out between the cold war Royal Navy and the USA. I think it was HMS Ark Royal which involved HMS Ark Royal being the aggressor and striking US bases on the US Eastern Sea Board. up to a week of operations with strikes on a daily basis and undetected due to sneaky sneaky tactics. Aircraft Carriers are also hideously vulnerable to attrition and easily overwhelmed while in contact with shore based aircraft. Naval Aircraft are compromises due to structural needs and limitations caused by operational environment. The exact same engine in an airframe designed with the same technology will result in a land based aircraft of higher basic capability. The further technology has improved the smaller the difference in performance. During 1940's this difference was massive. Size constraints include wingspan, height and weight. Takeoff distance is also important. Range suffers because you need to hit takeoff speed much sooner. What all of this leads to is the fact the Royal Navy could not safely carry out more than a single night of attacks. The Raid was split into two waves due to time it took to launch the loaded aircraft then spot the next wave on the flight deck. Number of aircraft in an attack is also determined by speed at which aircraft could be launched. Even today the raid count is determined by rate of aircraft launch and form up time. j If the Royal Navy had 4 Fleet Carriers available the raid would still have been a single night. However the number of aircraft in each raid would have changed. With 4 carriers the raid would have likely been 80 Swordfish in two waves and it would also have been possible to attempt to wipe out the local airbases in order to do a daylight follow up. The Fighters from 4 Carriers would have been able to fend of larger opposition. If the aircraft compliment was the same as HMS Ilustrious then you could plan on 60 Fulmar's to be available. The likelihood is however that had 4 Carriers been available the air group would be Swordfish, Fulmar's and Sea Gladiators with 60 fighters in Fleet being impossible at this time of the war. 40 Swordfish with Torpedo's and 40 with bombs and flares equals Taranto being removed as a Naval Base for a full year with few Oil storage tanks remaining and the ships in the harbour being severely damaged and total constructive losses. Photos of Taranto pre war show the ships moored stern in at a the docks and essentially tied together. This being hit by 250 or 500lb bombs would decimate the Italian ships due to very week deck armour. 20 to 50 mm is very light and even a 250lb SAP bomb should go through. If 6 ships and tied together you create a 60m by 140m target square as a minimum with plenty of HE and fuel to burn in the ships. Swordfish Dive Bombing was fairly accurate. 40 Torpedo armed and 32 bombers with 8 Flare dropping aircraft equals insane damage levels.

The Brits achieved miracles with a bunch of obsolete biplanes ... The first wave, 12 aircraft, consisted of 6 Swordfish armed with torpedoes, 2 two with flares plus four 250 lb (110 kg) bombs, and 4 with six bombs. The second wave , 8 aircraft, 5 with torpedoes, 2 with flares pus four bombs. Total attack force, 20 aircraft, of which only 11 actually carried a torpedo ! (contrast Pearl Harbor, Japanese attack force= 353 aircraft) The Brits don't need more 'waves', they need more aircraft and more carriers... Which means a POD of 1 April 1918 (April Fools day === how appropriate ) and a replacement of the 'Bomber will always get through' nonsense with one of 'By 1940 our carrier fleet will sink your battleship fleet' (it's debatable when this would be accepted, HOWEVER :- By 1918, the RN had between 650 and 936 Short 184 torpedo bombers. In 1919, the RN had taken delivery of 90 Sopwith Cuckoo torpedo bombers (the had ordered 230 but then the war ended). So, even in 1918, some-one in the RN was having some 'modern' thoughts

items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a second attack at Taranto following their successful November 1940 raid, several significant outcomes could have emerged:

**Immediate tactical gains:** A follow-up strike could have finished off damaged Italian battleships still in harbor, particularly the Littorio and Caio Duilio, which were eventually repaired and returned to service. The Vittorio Veneto, which escaped damage in the first raid, would have been a prime target. Destroying these ships permanently would have given Britain overwhelming naval superiority in the Mediterranean for years.

**Strategic Mediterranean control:** With Italy's battle fleet effectively eliminated rather than merely crippled, British convoys to Malta and North Africa would have faced far less threat. This could have accelerated the North African campaign and reduced the siege pressures on Malta, potentially shortening the war in that theater by months.

**Operational challenges:** The Italians would have been on high alert after the first attack, with enhanced anti-aircraft defenses, more barrage balloons, additional smoke screens, and possibly relocated ships. The element of surprise—critical to the first raid's success—would be gone. British losses would likely have been significantly higher, potentially making the operation prohibitively costly.

**Broader implications:** A devastating second blow might have forced Italy to adopt an even more defensive naval posture, essentially conceding Mediterranean control. However, it could also have prompted Germany to divert more Luftwaffe resources to the Mediterranean earlier, changing the dynamics of the Battle of Britain's aftermath.

The British ultimately chose not to attempt a second raid, likely weighing the diminished surprise factor against the risks to their limited carrier aircraft resources.

items.question: What If Vichy France had sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944?
human_answers: When the Allies invaded NW Africa, the French colonies of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia Kesselrings command was approved to recruit patriotic French to resist the Allies. The proposed infantry division never materialized. Enough men were found for a weak battalion, but after the unhealthy and unreliable were rejected there were enough to form a single over strength company. Given the German shortage of up to date equipment, particularly artillery and motor transport. The extra 100,000 French would be armed with the usual mix of older & obsolescent weapons, often in inferior numbers, like most other ground combat formations in Rundsteadts OB West. Just maybe there would be a SS 'Frankreich' division with good equipment, but otherwise its going to be leftovers, horse drawn artillery, little or no medium and heavy artillery, no supporting armor other than a few obsolescent R35 or D2 tanks, pitiful air support, inferior AT guns, French made MG vs the MG 34 or MG42. Compounding all this is the chronic German shortages of artillery ammunition and fuel. If the 100,000 French soldiers are used to offset other soldiers who are then sent to other front the questions is who? The overaged German reservists of the Bodenstang formations? The Ossies from Poland, Urkraine, Beylo Russ, ect... ? The elite Panzer Truppen? If the French are just added on top of the others, with no transfers, then its just the same inadequate equipment spread across a increase of 5% or 10% of men. A second given is the relatively small number of French soldiers who volunteered for the crusade in the east. The members of the Charlemagne division totaled far less than 100,000 through the entire war. Probably less than 50,000 served in that formation. While volunteers could be found to fight in the east, there was no similar movement in the west. The Milcie managed to recruit young men who wanted to avoid labor service, but that relatively large body failed to volunteer or participate in the battle of France. Most deserted long before the Allied armies over ran the police districts the Milcie units were assigned to.
items.original_question: Impact of French soldiers in the Atlantic Wall? I just read that after the Dieppe Raid Pétain was so enthusiastic and convinced Germany would win that he actually offered French troops to the Reich, only to be turned down by a less than convinced Hitler. But what could have been the impact of let's say 100,000 French soldiers helping Germany on D-Day? I assume they would have to be conscripted from the industrial workforce in Germany? In that case, would that impact production? And what could be the performance of those soldiers fighting clearly for Germany as late as 1944?

items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had openly committed 100,000 French troops to defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, the consequences would have been significant on military, political, and social levels, though probably not decisive in altering the ultimate outcome of the war.

Militarily, the Atlantic Wall in mid-1944 was thinly manned in many sectors, particularly in Normandy, where second-rate static divisions composed of older Germans, Osttruppen (former Soviet POWs), and convalescents formed much of the garrison. An additional 100,000 reasonably trained French soldiers could have plugged gaps, freed German field divisions for the mobile reserve, or thickened beach defenses. However, their combat value would have been doubtful. Vichy's armed forces after November 1942, when the Germans dissolved the Armistice Army, were minimal, and any new force would have lacked modern equipment, armor, and air support. Morale and reliability would also have been low: French conscripts fighting alongside Germans against an Allied liberation force—including Free French units—would likely have suffered mass desertions and surrenders, much as the Osttruppen did on D-Day. The Allies' overwhelming naval gunfire, air superiority, and logistical might would still have prevailed, though casualties on Omaha or other beaches could have been higher, and the breakout from the bocage might have been delayed by days or weeks.

Politically, the impact would have been far more profound than the military one. Vichy's claim to be a legitimate, sovereign French government protecting French interests rested on the fiction of neutrality and reluctant collaboration. Openly fielding 100,000 troops in German uniform or under German command would have shattered that fiction completely, transforming Vichy into an unambiguous Axis co-belligerent. This would have devastated whatever residual support Pétain still commanded among conservative French citizens, the Catholic hierarchy, and the colonial administration. Recruitment on such a scale would also have required either mass conscription—impossible to enforce given the strength of the Resistance and the draft-dodging that already plagued the Service du Travail Obligatoire—or a dramatic expansion of fascist volunteer formations like the Milice and LVF, neither of which ever attracted more than a few thousand committed recruits.

For the French Resistance and the postwar settlement, the effects would have been severe. The Resistance would have gained enormous legitimacy and recruits, and Allied willingness to recognize de Gaulle's Provisional Government would have accelerated. The épuration after liberation would almost certainly have been bloodier and more extensive, with collaboration prosecuted on a scale resembling postwar Yugoslavia rather than the relatively contained French purges that actually occurred. Pétain, Laval, and the entire Vichy apparatus would have faced near-universal condemnation, and France's diplomatic position in 1945—already weakened—would have been further compromised, possibly costing it its occupation zone in Germany or its permanent seat on the UN Security Council, both of which Churchill and Roosevelt granted partly to bolster a friendly postwar France.

In short, the deployment would probably have stiffened German defenses marginally, accelerated Vichy's moral collapse dramatically, and produced a far harsher reckoning with collaborators after liberation, without changing the war's outcome.

items.original_question: What if World War I had occurred 9 years earlier? The First Moroccan Crisis occurred between 1905 and 1906 during the Russo-Japanese War. Although this event did not escalate into a full-scale military conflict, it was resolved through the Algeciras Conference. However, tensions between the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente grew stronger. Then, in 1911, the Second Moroccan Crisis took place. At this time, there were talks of a potential war, but ultimately it was resolved through international negotiations. Despite these series of events, in 1914, World War I broke out due to the assassination of the Austrian Archduke and the subsequent invasion of Serbia. This raises an interesting question. During the July Crisis in the OTL, there were numerous efforts to avoid war, but in the end, the arrogance of autocratic monarchs and the complex web of interests caused tensions to escalate and ultimately explode. What if such a chain reaction and explosion had occurred during the First Moroccan Crisis? What if the First Moroccan Crisis had escalated into a full-blown war, leading to World War I happening 9 years earlier than in the OTL? What could have been the consequences of such a scenario? Here are the questions in English: 1. In 1905, how does the military strength of countries such as the United Kingdom, France, the Russian Empire, the German Empire, Austria-Hungary, and the Kingdom of Italy compare to that of 1914 in OTL? Which country would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL when the war begins? 2. In 1905, the ruling party of the United States is the Republican Party, and the president is Theodore Roosevelt. If a world war were to occur during his presidency, what would America's stance be? Would Teddy Roosevelt maintain neutrality throughout, or would he eventually push for involvement? And how would Roosevelt's vision for the post-war world differ from Wilson's? 3. The Russian Empire, after the Russo-Japanese War in OTL, pursued reforms like constitutional monarchy changes and Stolypin’s agricultural reforms. However, in this TL, war breaks out before such reforms happen. What impact do you think this would have on Russia? I believe Russia would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL. However, there is also this possibility: "Unlike in OTL, there would be no Duma, and no legitimate or proper opposition parties. As a result, although there are many opposing forces, they would not form a cohesive alliance, and there would be no single negotiation channel." "This would make it harder for the anti-government factions to gain representation throughout Russia. Therefore, after the revolution, it would be more difficult to quickly take over the government and establish a revolutionary regime." 4. What do you think is the most likely outcome of the world war in this alternate timeline?

items.model_answer:
If World War I had broken out in 1905 instead of 1914, the conflict would have looked quite different in character, scale, and outcome, though many of the same underlying tensions would still have driven it.

In 1905, the alliance system was not yet fully formed. The Anglo-Russian Entente of 1907 had not been signed, and Britain's commitments to France through the Entente Cordiale (1904) were still fresh and untested. Britain might well have stayed neutral, especially since Anglo-German naval rivalry had not yet reached its fever pitch—the dreadnought race only began in 1906. Without Britain, Germany would have faced a less encircled strategic situation, and the Royal Navy's blockade, which proved decisive in starving Germany of resources, would not have existed.

Russia would have been an especially weak participant, having just lost the Russo-Japanese War and convulsed by the 1905 Revolution. A war in this moment might have collapsed the Tsarist regime even faster than 1917 did, possibly producing an earlier revolution—though without Lenin's wartime return via Germany, its character would be unpredictable.

Militarily, the war would have been less industrialized. Machine guns were less ubiquitous, barbed wire less standardized in military doctrine, and aircraft barely existed (the Wright brothers had flown only in 1903). Poison gas, tanks, and submarine warfare on a strategic scale would not yet have been developed. The result might have been a shorter, more mobile war resembling the Franco-Prussian War in style, with decisive battles rather than years of trench stalemate. The Schlieffen Plan existed in draft form but had not been refined; a German offensive through Belgium might have succeeded more easily against an unprepared France.

The likely outcome would have been a German victory on the continent within a year or two, producing a Mitteleuropa under Berlin's economic and political dominance. Without the catastrophic casualties of 1914–1918, without the Treaty of Versailles, and without the specific humiliations that fueled Nazism, the twentieth century would lack many of its defining traumas—but it would also lack the democratic openings, the collapse of empires (Habsburg, Ottoman, Romanov) might have been delayed, and colonial systems would have persisted longer. A triumphant Imperial Germany, however, would likely have generated its own backlash and a later, perhaps even larger, war of revenge from France and Russia.

edus.text: If World War I had broken out in 1905 instead of 1914,
the conflict would have looked quite different in character, scale, and outcome,
though many of the same underlying tensions would still have driven it.
In 1905, the alliance system was not yet fully formed.
The Anglo-Russian Entente of 1907 had not been signed,
and Britain's commitments to France through the Entente Cordiale (1904) were still fresh and untested.
Britain might well have stayed neutral,
especially since Anglo-German naval rivalry had not yet reached its fever pitch
the dreadnought race only began in 1906.
Without Britain, Germany would have faced a less encircled strategic situation,
and the Royal Navy's blockade, which proved decisive in starving Germany of resources, would not have existed.
Russia would have been an especially weak participant,
having just lost the Russo-Japanese War
and convulsed by the 1905 Revolution.
A war in this moment might have collapsed the Tsarist regime even faster than 1917 did,
possibly producing an earlier revolution
though without Lenin's wartime return via Germany,
its character would be unpredictable.
Militarily, the war would have been less industrialized.
Machine guns were less ubiquitous,
barbed wire less standardized in military doctrine,
and aircraft barely existed
the Wright brothers had flown only in 1903.
Poison gas, tanks, and submarine warfare on a strategic scale would not yet have been developed.
The result might have been a shorter, more mobile war resembling the Franco-Prussian War in style,
with decisive battles rather than years of trench stalemate.
The Schlieffen Plan existed in draft form
but had not been refined;
a German offensive through Belgium might have succeeded more easily against an unprepared France.
The likely outcome would have been a German victory on the continent within a year or two,
producing a Mitteleuropa under Berlin's economic and political dominance.
Without the catastrophic casualties of 1914–1918,
without the Treaty of Versailles,
and without the specific humiliations that fueled Nazism,
the twentieth century would lack many of its defining traumas
but it would also lack the democratic openings,
the collapse of empires (Habsburg, Ottoman, Romanov) might have been delayed,
and colonial systems would have persisted longer.
A triumphant Imperial Germany, however, would likely have generated its own backlash
and a later, perhaps even larger, war of revenge from France and Russia.

items.question: What If A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections
human_answers: Think about it--when Truman lost, it wasn't *just* because Democrats had been in power a long time. It was *also* because Harry Truman never saw a hornet's nest he didn't want to kick, a temperamental flaw that contributed to a sense of chaos in all walks of life. Combine that with the endemic corruption issues that come from twenty years in power, and you've got a recipe for a one term president. A distinct but similar dynamic appears with the coming of Nixon. Nobody believed LBJ about anything by 1968, and that rubbed off on Humphrey, who was (ironically) more upright but much weaker than Johnson, and the Hump never could shake the Credibility Gap issues he inherited. The loss of trust on all fronts created widespread anger and chaos followed in the wake of that anger. Add to that the endemic corruption issues that come from eight years of Kennedy and Johnson, and you've got a recipe for a Nixon win. No surprise, this is basically the exact same setup that takes down Nixon and Ford. What you might notice here is that the personality flaws of the individual in the White House combine with the problems of institutional corruption that arise after years in power to create a scandal unique to the time and place that ends up consuming everyone involved. I would imagine that a Bush I who gets a second term--by *some* miracle--is going to make some similar mistakes to the ones his son made. They had many of the same advisors, after all. Here, Bush I had none of Bush II's cocksure self assurance to distract from whatever Middle East quagmire he drags the US into, and I think he would crash and burn more quickly in terms of public approval. You might imagine a scenario where Clinton's scandals + much better Perot popular vote= an apparent Bush landslide, where Bush makes the error of mistaking his opponents' divisions for his own strength. I won't get into details because it's current politics, but if you want an example of just such an outcome, look at the results of the last UK general election. The bigger question to me is why America would turn to a plutocrat like Rockefeller after 16 years of "Greed is Good."

Okay, the idea is that this story is loosely based on some ideas from other users who wrote their stories*. The general idea is to create a story with some overall meaning using all of this. So, the story is about how, before the 1988 elections, a recession (like the one in the 90s) occurs. This causes Bush to win by a much smaller margin than OTL (301-236 EVs), resulting in the Democrats gaining more seats in the Senate and the House. This leads to Bush panicking, causing him to try to appease both Reaganite Republicans and more moderate Republicans, although I haven't decided what his cabinet would look like. Anyway, because of this, the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait is delayed until August 18, 1991. Furthermore, Iraq decides to invade the east coast of Saudi Arabia on December 26, 1991, that is, 130 days after the invasion of Kuwait. This leads to larger chain reactions overall, but they are not important at this moment. Two important points should also be added: 1. There were no Yugoslav Wars, therefore Bush was perhaps less concerned about the situation developing in the Balkans and set an earlier deadline (than OTL) for a ceasefire in Iraq, which ended on February 24, 1992. 2. The Iraqi Civil War did not end until 1993, so there was an incentive to be more attentive to the problems of other countries. This resulted in a much more effective Gulf War, and Saddam was overthrown a few days before the coalition reached Baghdad, but these are details. What you're probably wondering is... how did Bush win the 1992 election? Well, it was for several reasons. Like the Gulf War, the fact that the Soviet Union was doing stupid things, that the US was able to recover from the recession thanks to contracts with Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and most importantly, that each and every one of Bill Clinton's sex scandals was revealed. Ultimately, the election ended in a landslide victory for Bush (343-195 EVs). Bush's second term was relatively fruitful**. In foreign policy, he had some relative successes, such as Somalia, and some major successes, such as Rwanda. The economy was booming, and everything was going well. But people were starting to get tired of 16 years of Republican presidency and a Democratic option that wasn't showing it could win 4 elections in a row. Therefore, the Democratic primaries would be an opportunity to determine who could win the 1996 election once and for all. I have a vague idea of who the Democratic candidates might be in the primaries; they would be: ● Jay Rockefeller – He would be the one to win because of his establishment base and because he represents a remnant of the New Deal era, making him the best candidate. ● Henry Cisneros – The surprise candidate of the primaries, someone no one expected to win so many states, even though he's a senator who won the 1990 midterm Senate elections. I think he would come in second or third. ● Jesse Jackson – I'm sure he would see this as the perfect opportunity to run in the 1996 elections. He would run with the rainbow coalition and say that the reason they didn't win the last election was because Bill Clinton was a moderate white Southerner and, above all, a womanizer. Therefore, I see him coming in second or third, but I highly doubt the establishment would want him as their candidate. ● Bill Bradley – He would be the progressive candidate the establishment would prefer over Jackson, but I doubt he would win many states, to be honest. ● Joe Biden - Same as Bradley, but being liberal, not progressive. ● Kent Conrad - Okay, I'd have to justify myself here.
