items.question: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?
human_answers: Define failed - do you just mean the fighter planes are sitting armed in their revetments, the AA guns (both fleet and land based) are manned, the ships are at condition ZED, the radar stations are manned, and the Air Information Center has been set up (probably not fully manned but at least some minimal level of staffing). This gets you raid warning, fighters get into the air in time to meet the raid, and the ships in port and ready to take the punch. That is not done due any specific intelligence about an attack it is simply done as a response to the war warnings of late November. Between fighter defenses and AA fire and planes not making it back to the carriers the Japanese lose somewhere between 1/3 and 1/2 of their attacking aircraft. Damage to the Pacific Fleet is a lot less because the ships are buttoned up and a lot less planes are destroyed on the ground because they are either in the air or in protected revetments or at least dispersed. Losses to fighter pilots are higher because of more guys getting shot down but they also take their measure of the Japanese. That constitutes failure for the Japanese, particularly given the losses in trained air crews. What it means going forward I'm not sure but it sure is an ugly start. Or, do you mean by failure the US does all of the above but also has knowledge a Japanese carrier task force is going to attack Oahu during the morning of 7 December from a position between 200-250 miles north of Oahu. This means every available attack aircraft on Oahu is bombed up and ready to go (6 B-17s, 21 B-18s, 5 A-20s, 23 SBDs, 8 SB2Us) and Kimmel is able to position Enterprise and Lexington 150 miles to the southwest of where the KB is expected to be operating as well as sending the small number of submarines he has in port to the north as well. By the way, Kimmel also has a moment of profound insight and realizes the safest place for his fat slow battleships is sitting in port at Condition ZED. That scenario has the US forces on island ready to take the punch and the US has about 180 attack aircraft of various types ready to throw at the KB to include roughly the equivalent of seven squadrons of US Navy and US Marine Corps dive bombers the most effective weapon in the US arsenal. Scenario One is quite realistic and only needs some fairly minor PODs to make it work. Scenario Two is a lot less realistic but if you squint hard enough you can probably come up with some PODs that still make it work. Scenario One the attacking aircraft get butchered but the KB likely gets away clean. Scenario Two the attacking aircraft get butchered and Nagumo loses at least two carrier maybe as many as four depending on the breaks.

I do not disagree with the analysis above, but I would take a different path in logical application from the same starting point. Define failure. What if the Japanese failed to attack Pearl Harbor at all. What if on the morning of 7 December the seas were unexpectedly, and unseasonably rough enough to preclude any launch of aircraft. The invasion of Malaya started four hour earlier, and it is too late to cancel attacks on US possession in the western Pacific. Conditions are not much better on the eighth. Kido Butai trundles back home to Japan, undetected by US aircraft.. This may seem like a "what if Japan declared war, and did not attack Pearl Harbor" scenario but it is not. The key difference is, what if Japan launched surprise attacks all over Asia without declaring war, and its most powerful naval assets were non-combat effective for the first 25 days of the war? Comments?

I'm not too familiar either with how much intelligence the US had on Japan pre-Pearl Harbor, but I do know that a Japanese submarine was sunk by the US just hours before Pearl Harbor, and the message either was ignored or received too late to mobilize the dock. I could totally see an early warning, through this incident, cause Pearl Harbor to mobilize and allow for Japanese pilots to lose the element of surprise. Assuming the Japanese ships aren't found and only the planes are destroyed, this would make Japan more cautious against the US, since the Pacific Fleet wouldn't be as weak as it was after Pearl Harbor in our timeline. Additionally, because of the warning, there might be less civilian causalities and so, in the United States, there is anger at being attacked, there wouldn't be the rallying cry of "OMG THEY MURDERED A BUNCH ON INNOCENT AMERICANS!" But, overall, Pearl Harbor not being totally destroyed is definitely an interesting and plausible scenario that would have an impact on WWII.
items.original_question: What if the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed? This was something that popped into my head. What if the USA has gained early warning of Pearl Harbor and had managed to defeat the attack? I am not too familiar with the intelligence background of it but I do believe I heard that there were some potential early signs before the attack that were ignored. If say the USA had received information a few days in advance and was able to crush the japanise attack and keep many of their best ships in a strong position in Hawaii now much would it change the pacific campaign? Would America be able to defeat Japan early maybe before the Nazis even fall?

rubrics.question_focus: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise definition and plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what 'the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed' means and grounds that point of divergence in plausible December 1941 conditions.
criteria.1-2: Leaves 'failed' undefined or assumes an incoherent premise, such as Japan never being at war while still discussing Pearl Harbor effects.
criteria.3-4: Gives a vague failure premise, e.g. 'the U.S. was ready,' with little explanation of warning, weather, intelligence, or defensive readiness.
criteria.5-6: Defines a recognizable failure scenario, such as effective U.S. warning or poor Japanese launch conditions, but with limited support for plausibility.
criteria.7-8: Specifies a plausible point of divergence, such as radar response, submarine warning, war-warning readiness, or bad seas, and explains why it could occur.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes multiple plausible meanings of failure, such as failed surprise versus carrier losses versus aborted strike, and evaluates their different implications.

criteria.name: Military-mechanism fidelity in the immediate battle
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately reasons through the operational consequences at Oahu and for Kido Butai, including aircraft, ships, radar, AA readiness, and carrier vulnerability.
criteria.1-2: Makes major military errors, such as treating battleships as able to chase Japanese carriers immediately or ignoring carrier aviation entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions reduced damage or more Japanese losses but gives little operational mechanism for how this happens.
criteria.5-6: Covers some key mechanisms, such as U.S. fighters getting airborne, AA guns manned, ships buttoned up, or aircraft dispersed.
criteria.7-8: Explains several interacting mechanisms, including warning time, U.S. air response, Japanese aircrew losses, harbor damage reduction, and likely Japanese withdrawal.
criteria.9-10: Provides a detailed and balanced operational analysis, including distinctions between losing attacking aircraft and losing Japanese carriers, realistic U.S. strike capacity, and uncertainty in outcomes.

criteria.name: Pacific War downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer coherently traces how a failed Pearl Harbor attack affects Japan's early-war operations, U.S. naval power, and the broader Pacific campaign.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to sweeping conclusions, such as instant Japanese defeat or no U.S. entry, without causal support.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one downstream effect, such as a stronger U.S. Pacific Fleet, but does not connect it to later campaigns.
criteria.5-6: Discusses plausible medium-term effects, such as less battleship damage, preserved aircraft, Japanese caution, or altered timing in the Pacific.
criteria.7-8: Connects immediate survival of U.S. assets and Japanese aircrew losses to early-war operations in the Philippines, Dutch East Indies, Coral Sea, Midway, or carrier strategy.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain across 1941-1943, accounting for Japan's simultaneous offensives, logistics, carrier attrition, U.S. mobilization, and possible changes to major battles.

criteria.name: Political and strategic effects on U.S., Japan, and Allies
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the diplomatic, public-opinion, alliance, and grand-strategic consequences of a failed or blunted Pearl Harbor attack.
criteria.1-2: Ignores political effects or claims the U.S. would not enter the war despite Japanese attacks on U.S. or Allied possessions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions U.S. anger or morale but treats public reaction as the only strategic consequence.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that the U.S. likely still enters the war if Japan attacks U.S./Allied territories, though public shock and propaganda may differ.
criteria.7-8: Explains how a failed Pearl Harbor affects U.S. mobilization, Roosevelt's political position, Japanese strategic confidence, and Allied coordination.
criteria.9-10: Nuances political consequences by separating scenarios: aborted attack, failed surprise, heavy Japanese losses, or carrier defeat, and explains how each changes U.S. resolve and Japanese decision-making.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains internal consistency, avoids overclaiming, and signals uncertainty where the counterfactual branches depend on contested assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contains contradictions, impossible sequences, or deterministic claims unsupported by the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but mixes incompatible scenarios or overstates outcomes without caveats.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent and acknowledges at least one uncertainty, but leaves some causal leaps or scenario ambiguity unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Separates assumptions clearly, uses conditional language, and avoids conflating a failed air raid with destruction of the Japanese carrier force.
criteria.9-10: Consistently tracks branches, probabilities, and dependencies, explicitly noting where outcomes hinge on warning time, U.S. strike effectiveness, Japanese carrier losses, or wider Japanese operations.

items.model_answer:
If the attack on Pearl Harbor had completely failed, the trajectory of World War II and the postwar world would likely have looked quite different, though the broad outcome—Allied victory—would probably have remained the same.

A "complete failure" could mean several things: Japanese carriers detected and intercepted before launching, the strike force losing most of its aircraft, or inflicting negligible damage on the U.S. Pacific Fleet. In any of these scenarios, Japan would have suffered a devastating early loss of its naval aviation, which was the cutting edge of its military power. The Imperial Japanese Navy had concentrated six fleet carriers and its best pilots in the Kido Butai; losing them at the outset would have crippled Japan's ability to conduct offensive operations across the Pacific. Campaigns against the Philippines, Malaya, the Dutch East Indies, and Wake Island might have stalled or unfolded much more slowly, since Japanese expansion relied heavily on carrier-based air cover.

The political consequences in the United States would also have been significant. Pearl Harbor's shock galvanized American public opinion, transforming a divided, isolationist-leaning country into one unified for total war. A failed attack—especially one repulsed before serious damage—might still have brought the U.S. into the war, since Japan had declared its intentions, but the emotional intensity and the "Remember Pearl Harbor" rallying cry would have been muted. Roosevelt would still have asked for a declaration of war, but mobilization and public commitment might have been somewhat less fevered.

Strategically, the U.S. Pacific Fleet's battleships would have remained intact. Ironically, this might not have been as advantageous as it sounds, because the war proved that aircraft carriers, not battleships, were decisive. Still, with the fleet operational, the U.S. could have pursued a more aggressive early strategy, possibly relieving the Philippines or contesting Japanese advances sooner. The disastrous early months of 1942 might have been avoided.

For Japan, a failed Pearl Harbor would likely have accelerated defeat. Without crippling the U.S. fleet, Japan could not have established its defensive perimeter, and the industrial mismatch between the two powers would have told even more quickly. The war in the Pacific might have ended a year or more earlier, potentially before the atomic bombs were ready, which raises the intriguing possibility that nuclear weapons would not have been used against Japan—and perhaps would have made their combat debut elsewhere, or not at all in that war.

In Europe, Hitler's decision to declare war on the United States four days after Pearl Harbor was tied to Japan's apparent success. A humiliating Japanese failure might have made him hesitate, potentially delaying U.S. entry into the European theater and complicating the Atlantic strategy, though American involvement there was probably inevitable.

In short, a failed Pearl Harbor attack would likely have shortened the Pacific War, preserved more lives in 1942, possibly prevented the atomic bombings, and altered the political mythology that shaped American identity for decades afterward.

human_answers: The one thing that keeps coming to me is Nixon would have the greatest meltdown in political history, screaming bloody murder then the Eastern Establishment has screw him for a third and final time. Even in OTL 68 a lot of the GOP had in fact become very weary over backing Nixon over his defeats in 1960, and 1962 in California. Now this last minute scandal, Nixon messing with the peace talks, cost him and the Republicans the election for a third time. At the very best, Tricky Dick might become a Secretary of State under a future Republican president and a Statesman, but the White House is forever gone. GOP swings back to the Rockefeller Republicans like George Romney and Nelson Rockefeller himself, but could also swing to Reagan. McGovern quickly makes a peace deal for Vietnam and pulls out. The South eventually falls. But we wash our hands of that conflict. McGovern would see to a second wind of the Great Society and likely see to a very liberal and Leftist Supreme Court along with many other Judges and at least some mild liberal reforms passed in Congress.

items.original_question: The Highest Patriotism: What if George McGovern became President in 1968 ​ The initial frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 1968 was President Johnson of course, but an insurgent primary challenge from one Senator Eugene McCarthy set off a spark that would blow open a wide power vacuum in the Democratic party following Johnson's withdrawal from consideration. Johnson had endorsed Hubert Humphrey, his ambitious VP, but he chose not to run in the primaries, instead gaining support through backroom deals with delegates to win at the convention. This led to a bitter primary fight between McCarthy and Robert F. Kennedy, who had jumped into the race shortly before Johnson's withdrawal. As the primaries carried on, this fight would all come to a head with the hotly-contested California primary. Both campaigns put valiant efforts and loads of funding into this contest, but in the end, McCarthy would narrowly prevail, winning 45% to Kennedy's 42% and taking all of California's delegates. Kennedy would immediately announce his withdrawal from the nomination after the loss, but refused to make an endorsement. When it came to the convention, however, most of Kennedy's delegates coalesced around McCarthy, leading to a deadlocked convention between him and Humphrey. Kennedy had only privately backed McCarthy, even though he hated the man. With the convention at an impasse, Kennedy looked for an alternate who could emerge as a compromise candidate, despite his own ego making him hurt that no matter what, it wasn't going to be him. That man was none other than Senator from South Dakota George Stanley McGovern. McGovern was a Kennedy ally who had served as his brother's director for Food for Peace and an ambassador to the Peace Corps his brother founded. However, he was also firmly of the anti-war wing of the party and was more amenable to McCarthy and his delegates than Kennedy, whom McCarthy deeply despised. McCarthy vowed to stay in, but as more and more Kennedy-turned-McCarthy delegates flipped to McGovern, he saw the writing on the wall. After six more ballots, McCarthy would release his delegates, with all but a few holdouts voting for McGovern on the next ballot. However, the race was not over yet. There still was not an agreed upon consensus, and it would take more backroom dealing to put McGovern over the hump. To that, Kennedy looked to the Texas delegation, which was backing Humphrey, led by the old friend of his brother's, Governor John Connally. Kennedy aimed to make a deal with Connally to give his delegates over to McGovern in exchange for major concessions. Initially resistant, and more and more concessions being offered, Connally would finally accept the offer on one singular condition; he would be made VP. With the two coming to an agreement, Texas would announce the switch of its delegates to McGovern, putting him over the line to win the nomination after 10 ballots, and Connally was selected as McGovern's running mate. Republican nominee Richard Nixon had a strong lead in early polls, and it looked as if the McGovern/Connally ticket was heading for a demolishment. Some polls even had McGovern losing Texas despite Connally's presence on the ticket. But slowly McGovern chipped at Nixon. Nixon was seen as a crooked insider and someone who would do anything to win, while McGovern appeared to be more honest in his approach. However, the race still remained in Nixon's favor weeks before the election, despite McGovern's best efforts. Then, a bombshell emerged. Johnson, who had only tacitly supported McGovern, if only for his buddy Connally becoming VP if they won, had leaked to the press that Nixon attempted to sabotage the peace talks occurring in Vietnam. McGovern didn't wish to make the campaign dirty, but he still called the reports "troubling" and placed serious question into his opponent's integrity while not outright placing guilt, which helped his honest image even further, and painted an even greater contrast between the two men . In the end, it was close, but... McGovern/Connally (Democratic) - 279 electoral votes, 42.62% Nixon/Agnew (Republican) - 182 electoral votes, 41.04% Wallace/LeMay (American Independent) - 77 electoral votes, 16.01% ​ ...the last second scandal proved to be just enough for McGovern to win this election by the slimmest of margins. If he had lost any of the states of California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas, or Wisconsin, with Texas being decided by just 1.04% for him and only winning 39.74% of the vote there, this election would have been thrown to the House of Representatives, and all of them, decided by only a few points each, had flipped, than Nixon would have won an outright majority himself. George McGovern was never meant to win this election, but through a deadlocked convention, backroom deals, and scandals, it was the honest prairie man that triumphed over them all.

# The Highest Patriotism: What If George McGovern Became President in 1968?

This is a fascinating counterfactual, though it requires us to first acknowledge an important historical fact: George McGovern did not actually run as the Democratic nominee in 1968. That year, Hubert Humphrey won the Democratic nomination after Robert Kennedy's assassination, and Richard Nixon won the general election. McGovern entered the 1968 race late, primarily as a placeholder for Kennedy delegates after RFK's death, and did not seriously contend for the nomination. He became the Democratic nominee in 1972, when he lost in a landslide to Nixon.

That said, let us imagine the counterfactual: McGovern somehow secures the 1968 nomination and defeats Nixon. The likely consequences would have been profound.

**Vietnam War**: McGovern was the most consistent and forceful antiwar voice in the Senate. His famous 1970 "Chamber of Horrors" speech ("This chamber reeks of blood") signaled he would have moved rapidly toward withdrawal. A McGovern presidency would likely have ended American involvement in Vietnam by 1969 or 1970, sparing tens of thousands of American lives and hundreds of thousands of Southeast Asian lives. However, the fall of Saigon would likely have come sooner, and McGovern would have faced fierce political backlash from conservatives and the military establishment over "losing" Vietnam.

**Domestic Policy**: McGovern championed a guaranteed minimum income, expanded welfare, tax reform targeting the wealthy, and significant defense cuts. With Democratic majorities in Congress, some version of these proposals might have advanced, fundamentally reshaping the American social safety net in ways more akin to Western European social democracies.

**The Cold War and China**: This is where things get complicated. Nixon's opening to China in 1972 was politically possible precisely because of his anti-communist credentials. McGovern might have favored such an opening ideologically but faced enormous domestic resistance. Détente with the Soviet Union might have proceeded differently—perhaps more idealistically but less strategically.

**Watergate and Political Realignment**: There would have been no Watergate scandal, fundamentally altering the trajectory of American distrust in government. However, McGovern's defense cuts and Vietnam withdrawal would likely have provoked a powerful conservative backlash, possibly accelerating the rise of Reaganite conservatism in 1972 or 1976.

**Civil Rights and Culture**: McGovern's presidency would have aligned the federal government more firmly with the cultural left during a period of intense social upheaval, potentially deepening the cultural polarization that defined subsequent decades.

The title "highest patriotism" comes from McGovern's own framing—that dissent against an unjust war was the highest form of love for country. A McGovern presidency would have tested whether American voters embraced that vision, and the ensuing political realignment would likely have looked very different from the one we actually got.

edus.text: This is a fascinating counterfactual,
though it requires us to first acknowledge an important historical fact:
George McGovern did not actually run as the Democratic nominee in 1968.
That year, Hubert Humphrey won the Democratic nomination after Robert Kennedy's assassination,
and Richard Nixon won the general election.
McGovern entered the 1968 race late,
primarily as a placeholder for Kennedy delegates after RFK's death,
and did not seriously contend for the nomination.
He became the Democratic nominee in 1972,
when he lost in a landslide to Nixon.
That said, let us imagine the counterfactual:
McGovern somehow secures the 1968 nomination and defeats Nixon.
The likely consequences would have been profound.
McGovern was the most consistent and forceful antiwar voice in the Senate.
His famous 1970 "Chamber of Horrors" speech ("This chamber reeks of blood") signaled he would have moved rapidly toward withdrawal.
A McGovern presidency would likely have ended American involvement in Vietnam by 1969 or 1970,
sparing tens of thousands of American lives and hundreds of thousands of Southeast Asian lives.
However, the fall of Saigon would likely have come sooner,
and McGovern would have faced fierce political backlash from conservatives and the military establishment over "losing" Vietnam.
McGovern championed a guaranteed minimum income, expanded welfare, tax reform targeting the wealthy, and significant defense cuts.
With Democratic majorities in Congress,
some version of these proposals might have advanced,
fundamentally reshaping the American social safety net in ways more akin to Western European social democracies.
This is where things get complicated.
Nixon's opening to China in 1972 was politically possible precisely because of his anti-communist credentials.
McGovern might have favored such an opening ideologically
but faced enormous domestic resistance.
Détente with the Soviet Union might have proceeded differently—
perhaps more idealistically but less strategically.
There would have been no Watergate scandal,
fundamentally altering the trajectory of American distrust in government.
However, McGovern's defense cuts and Vietnam withdrawal would likely have provoked a powerful conservative backlash,
possibly accelerating the rise of Reaganite conservatism in 1972 or 1976.
McGovern's presidency would have aligned the federal government more firmly with the cultural left during a period of intense social upheaval,
potentially deepening the cultural polarization that defined subsequent decades.
The title "highest patriotism" comes from McGovern's own framing—
that dissent against an unjust war was the highest form of love for country.
A McGovern presidency would have tested whether American voters embraced that vision,
and the ensuing political realignment would likely have looked very different from the one we actually got.

items.question: What If A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)
human_answers: The problem is that everything becomes possible with enough wankium, hence the implied 'it would be best achieved by starting very early on, as per the other thread'; otherwise it's not a Challenge, an exploration of history and factors, rather an exercise in taking OTL and changing it all to successful/lucky/positive events while applying a large butterfly net. No assassination of AII; so he gets scared and Stolypin's reforms are implemented earlier and more decisively; but then, Japan still lucks out in War and so people are angry; WWI however you like, except with less Russian losses; Revolution happens later so Russia wins or at least doesn't lose as much, so the Mensheviks come into power and start building a social democracy in Russia; a couple decades of luck preventing any bad luck until the Nazis go West, while Russia prepares herself for being attacked; so when they come they are pushed back faster and with less losses, leading to a well-integrated post-WWII Russia that can enjoy a few decades of growth, has larger borders, and as a result reaches 300M by 2000 as you asked. But somehow, I don't think that's really what you are after, are you?

I do think early PoDs (which naturally make our world unrecognisable and certainly butterfly the birth of Lenin) are more plausible if you want Russia thoroughly similar to Scandinavia. But the 20th century is a good time for catching up, for radical jumps, for deep transformations, as OTL has also shown, only not in the way the OP desires. Steering a course between Bolshevik tyranny of OTL and its most likely counterpart, continuation of a relatively autocratic tsardom, is not impossible. Neither are the population numbers. A solid multi-party democracy, well, if it works in India, why not in Russia. But you could call what is required for it a good run of sixes, or a healthy dose of wankium. I've dabbled in that in Feeble Constitution , so I'll not dwell on the path of February 1917 consolidating with different policies after the April Days. Instead, I can see both earlier and later PoDs. For a good planning thread on a later PoD (basically SR victory in the Civil War), you could have a look at @galileo-034 's Century of the Common Man . Though this may not entirely fulfill your OP challenge - Lenin would not be an obscure footnote here, and instead die in 1918. So maybe let's go with the one big earlier opportunity - a successful revolution of 1905. @Powdermonkey started a TL on this last year. I'd be thrilled to see where this could go. One could argue that the path towards what the OP describes is still stony and uphill. How one would tackle the Great War problem is still up in the air, among other things. But still probably one path worth exploring more here since it hasn't been done often, I think.
items.original_question:
AHC: A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)

The goal is simple - we want to have a 20th century in which Russia avoids the interlocked chain of events leading to a century of trumas as IOTL. In this world, Russia becomes a vibrant multi party democracy, heavily integrated with the rest of Europe and with its intellectual and cultural elites intact. It follows an economic model analogous to the Social Market Economy of post ww2 Germany or even the Nordic Model if things go very positively. Its population is over 300 mln people by 1991 (the year the USSR collapsed IOTL). In this world, Vladimir Lenin is still born (despite the butterfly effect) and still becomes a revolutionary but he dies as an obscure, disillusioned theoretician. His last work, Delusions of the Proletariat , is a scathing critique of the supposed naivety of the working class, lured into capitalism through voting rights and social safety nets. It sells less than 500 copies. When the internet era arrives (either sooner or later than IOTL), Lenin is included in various "10 Failed Radicals You Have Never Heard of" type of articles on various history-related websited but is otherwise a forgotten figure.

# A Drastically Better Russian 20th Century: A Counterfactual History

If Russia's 20th century had gone drastically better, the most plausible turning point lies in the years between 1905 and 1917, where small changes could have cascaded into a fundamentally different trajectory for Russia and the wider world.

## The Point of Divergence

The most realistic divergence begins with the 1905 Revolution producing a genuine constitutional monarchy rather than Nicholas II's reluctant October Manifesto followed by reactionary backsliding. Imagine Nicholas II either dying earlier (perhaps from his hemophiliac son's condition never arising, removing Rasputin's influence) or genuinely committing to Pyotr Stolypin's reforms. Stolypin's agrarian reforms, which were beginning to create a class of prosperous independent peasants (the *kulaks* in a non-pejorative sense), would have continued past his 1911 assassination. Russia's pre-war industrial growth—already running at roughly 8% annually—would have compounded into the 1920s.

## Avoiding the Great War, or Surviving It

In the strongest counterfactual, Russia avoids entry into World War I, perhaps by Sergei Sazonov or a more cautious foreign minister recognizing that Serbia is not worth a general European war. Without Russian mobilization, the July Crisis might have remained localized. Alternatively, Russia enters the war but a more competent General Staff and a constitutional government weather the strain. Either way, no February Revolution, no Bolshevik seizure of power in October, no civil war that killed perhaps 10 million people.

## The Cascading Consequences

Without the Bolshevik Revolution, the 20th century looks radically different. There is no Soviet Union, no Comintern radicalizing European politics, and crucially, no existential anti-communist panic in Germany that helped propel Hitler to power. The Nazi movement, deprived of its central "Judeo-Bolshevik" enemy and the chaos of a Versailles-era Europe terrified of revolution, likely remains a fringe phenomenon. The Holocaust as we know it does not occur. World War II in Europe is either averted or fought on dramatically different terms.

Domestically, Russia by the 1930s would likely be a flawed but functioning constitutional state—probably still authoritarian-leaning, with persistent inequality and nationalities problems, but with a literate population, a growing middle class, and a market economy integrated with Europe. No Holodomor kills millions of Ukrainians. No Great Terror executes nearly a million people. No Gulag system processes 18 million prisoners. The collectivization famines, the deportations of entire nationalities under Stalin, the suppression of religion and culture—none of this happens.

## The Longer Shadow

By 2000, Russia would probably have a population significantly larger than its actual ~145 million—demographers estimate Soviet-era excess mortality and lost births at 50-60 million people. Russian science, which produced extraordinary work even under Soviet constraints, would likely have flourished without the persecution of geneticists under Lysenko, the philosophers expelled in 1922, and the countless scientists who died in the camps. The Cold War as a 45-year global confrontation does not occur, meaning no proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Angola, or Afghanistan in the forms we knew them, and no nuclear arms race accumulating 70,000 warheads at peak.

## Caveats

A "drastically better" Russia is not utopian. Russian nationalism, antisemitism (the pogroms predated the Bolsheviks), imperial pretensions over the borderlands, and the tension between Westernizers and Slavophiles would all persist. A constitutional Russia might still have fought wars, oppressed minorities, and experienced authoritarian relapses. But the sheer scale of human catastrophe associated with the actual Russian 20th century—arguably the single most violent national experience of the modern era outside of China's mid-century—would have been avoided, and with it many of the worst features of global history from 1917 onward.

items.question: What If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up?
human_answers: I agree with most of what you said but that’s not quite what happened to Hua - he was backed by Ye Jianying, an ‘elder’, and implemented reforms while publicly proclaiming his support of Mao Zedong Thought. It was Hua who saw the reintroduction of "material incentives". However Hua relied on collective leadership and as Ye's health decline Hua was outflanked by Deng, who took a much harsher stance of de-Maoification despite being economically similar to Hua. I’m going to go on a bit of a tangent to explain why I agree with the rest of what you said and think some equivalent to reform and opening was the most likely outcome - Deng spent the 80s balancing the other “elders” and younger officials. As @Georg von Frundsberg said, other elders were more 'conservative' but generally embraced reform - while younger officials like Hu and Zhao were aggressively reformist. Deng himself was a lot closer to the centre than is remembered - on agriculture for example Zhao Shukai had a good article about how Deng was slow to embrace reform and one of his signature reforms, "household production" (allowing households to dictate production instead of communes) was only adopted by central diktat in 1982 after years of discussion. However throughout the tumultuous 80s political instability remained, culminating in 1989, the removal of Zhao Ziyang and the introduction of martial. Deng was ont he defence for three years until 1992, at which point he returned to power by coordinating “reformist” officials through the southern tour. Deng enjoyed is last five years at his relative peak of influence and admiration since he had outlived everyone else. I mention this to show though that Reform and Opening up was somewhat inevitable. There was a large chunk of the elders that were open to reform and an even larger pool of younger officials. Someone sometime was going to remove the Gang of Four and the only real question left was how much reform and when. To return to OP’s question, the only real alternative to reform and opening up was a coup. People were tired of the stagnant economy and the damage done by the cultural revolution was significant - in certain periods it was closer to a civil war, as PLA and militia fought in the streets. If the government tried to stick with central planning it would be removed by the majority of officials, and if not by them then a popular uprising.

Without reform and opening up in 1978 I think the only alternative would be to chug along with five year plans and central planning. This was attempted immediately after Mao's death, but it failed because everyone believed that continuing that way was a dead end, so it's plausible but unlikely that the Communist Party goes down that path. There's reason to believe that the Cultural Revolution was launched in part as a reaction to the bureaucracy and corruption of the Stalinist party-state, as a way to try and find an alternative to it, which was eventually put to bed in 1968 when Mao sent in the PLA. Broadly, you can characterise the initial years of the Cultural Revolution as the 'left-wing' attempt to find an alternative to the Soviet model, and Reform and Opening up as the 'right-wing' attempt to find an alternative in the wake of the GPCR's failure. Maybe they could've made it work, compared to the post-war Soviet communist party, the Chinese communist party was far more afraid of stagnancy and was far more willing to put themselves behind ambitious economic programmes (this is probably the main the reason they carried out Reform and Opening up and the USSR didn't), and maybe that allows them to pull through and create a creating a working planned economy that marches proudly into the 21st century, avoiding concessions to market economics. Most people will probably dismiss this possibility. It is perhaps more likely that the whole thing ossifies and stagnates at some point, prompting the party to do something like reform and opening up at a later date. If the party has reached Soviet levels of complacency and don't do anything, the system will begin to rot, the black market will explode and you'll get something like North Korea. I don't think Chinese citizens would be as poor as North Koreans are though, considering the collapse of North Korea's living standards was largely caused by the disappearance of Soviet economic aid, something China stopped receiving long before then, but I'm not wholly sure on that one. EDIT: I can't believe I forgot to mention this, but people associated with China's New Left movement often look favourably upon Belarus' Market Socialism as an alternative to what happened in China, with all the social chaos it caused. I am not entirely familiar with how Market Socialism works in Belarus, but in a journal article by Chinese economists praising the Belarusian model they take a liking to the dominance of state-owned companies, central planning, strong leadership and stronger social security and welfare than what exists in China and the rest of the ex-USSR. I don't really know much about how things actually work in practice in Belarus and if it's at all feasible China could copy this economic model, but it gives some pointers.

He was weak. At the time, the Chinese Communist Party was filled with veteran figures who had followed Mao since its early days. In such a situation, Hua Guofeng was merely a novice. As the elders pushed for reform, the young Hua Guofeng could not hold his ground. The Gang of Four, who had driven the Cultural Revolution, were not elders either; they relied on Mao’s personal trust. Hua Guofeng found himself caught between the Gang of Four and the veteran elders. While suppressing the Gang of Four, he also had to confront the elders who were advocating reform. Faced with such an overwhelming burden, Hua Guofeng was simply too young and lacked the political influence to manage it. Unlike the Soviet Communist Party, the Chinese Communist Party had a much stronger tendency to pursue “a today different from yesterday” rather than “a today the same as yesterday.” Even if the result turned out to be disastrous, they were still more inclined to act proactively and at least try to do something. Is this what you mean? If that is true, then it seems that for the PRC, it was ultimately a matter of timing—it would have carried out reform and opening up sooner or later. Then, in your view, is a scenario in which the PRC becomes like North Korea impossible? I mean a situation in which a particular vested elite seizes control of the bureaucracy and the military, crushes all resistance, and pushes for isolation in order to preserve its own power even at the cost of weakening the state’s capabilities. Certainly, the politics of the PRC and North Korea were different. In the PRC, even after Mao had secured absolute power, figures like Deng Xiaoping at least managed to survive by keeping a low profile. As a result, change became possible after Mao’s death. By contrast, in North Korea, Kim Il Sung had already eliminated all alternative forces by the 1960s, and from the 1970s onward he was able to prepare to pass power on to his son.
items.original_question: What if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Unlike in OTL, assume that a POD occurred in the succession struggle after Mao Zedong’s death. Or, if you prefer, assume that the Cultural Revolution itself unfolded differently. In any case, because of this change, Deng Xiaoping either never came to power or was removed partway through. Reform and Opening Up did not take place in the 1980s. Post in thread 'What if succession had occurred in China after Mao's death?' Feb 5, 2025 And I could see Lin being not really into the idea of Mao Anying succeeding Mao lead to a more serious involvement by Lin Biao in Project 571 or an equivalent plot, as opposed to IOTL where his son was the main driving force behind it. Whiteshore (For example, something like this.) What do you think would have happened if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Would the PRC have eventually collapsed under economic crisis, or would it have endured like North Korea? Would the CCP have fallen because its claim to rule lost credibility? criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the premise that the PRC never undertakes Reform and Opening Up, while accurately grounding the divergence in late-1970s CCP politics after Mao, including Hua Guofeng, Deng Xiaoping, party elders, the Gang of Four, and the legacy of the Cultural Revolution.

criteria.3-4: Acknowledges the premise but relies on vague or inaccurate history; key actors such as Hua, Deng, elders, or the Gang of Four are missing or misrepresented.
criteria.5-6: Provides a basically accurate post-Mao setup and identifies a plausible point of divergence, but with limited detail or some inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Accurately situates the counterfactual in CCP succession politics and explains why avoiding reform would require specific political changes or blockages.
criteria.9-10: Maintains strict premise discipline and uses precise historical anchoring to show what institutional, factional, and ideological conditions would have had to differ for reform never to occur.

criteria.name: Causal mechanism coverage inside the CCP
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the political mechanisms that could prevent, delay, or replace reform, including elite bargaining, elder authority, bureaucratic incentives, military support, ideological legitimacy, and possible coups or purges.
criteria.1-2: Offers only broad claims such as 'China would be poor' without explaining how the CCP avoids reform.
criteria.3-4: Mentions leadership conflict or ideology but gives little causal detail about how anti-reform forces prevail or why reformist forces fail.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some relevant mechanisms, such as conservative dominance, Hua retaining power, Deng losing influence, or stronger Maoist control, but underdevelops their interaction.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple interacting mechanisms, including elite coalitions, PLA or elder support, bureaucratic resistance, and legitimacy pressures.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust causal account of how a non-reform path is sustained over decades despite strong pro-reform pressures within the CCP and society.

criteria.name: Economic and social trajectory plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer develops plausible long-run economic and social outcomes for a China without Reform and Opening Up, including central planning, agricultural organization, industrial productivity, living standards, black markets, urban-rural dynamics, and comparisons to the USSR, North Korea, Belarus, or other socialist models where appropriate.
criteria.1-2: Makes implausible or unsupported economic claims, such as instant superpower status or total collapse without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Gives a simplistic outcome, such as 'China becomes North Korea' or 'China stays poor,' with little attention to scale, resources, or institutional differences.
criteria.5-6: Discusses stagnation, planning, poverty, or black markets in a plausible way but omits important sectors such as agriculture, industry, or trade.
criteria.7-8: Traces credible economic and social effects across sectors and decades, distinguishing China from Soviet, North Korean, or Belarusian analogues.
criteria.9-10: Presents a nuanced economic-social trajectory with clear mechanisms linking non-reform policies to productivity, state capacity, welfare, inequality, unrest, and informal markets over the long run.

criteria.name: Long-range geopolitical and institutional consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer coherently follows downstream effects beyond the 1980s, including China's global trade position, relations with the US and USSR/Russia, East Asian production networks, Hong Kong/Taiwan dynamics, military modernization, state capacity, and the survival or transformation of CCP rule.
criteria.1-2: Ignores long-term consequences or jumps directly to a final outcome without intervening reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few downstream effects but treats them as disconnected or inevitable.
criteria.5-6: Covers some long-range consequences, such as slower growth, weaker global influence, or possible instability, but with limited causal linkage.
criteria.7-8: Connects domestic non-reform choices to international trade, diplomacy, military capacity, and regime durability across several decades.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent multi-decade chain showing how no Reform and Opening Up reshapes China's domestic institutions, global economic integration, regional politics, and CCP survival prospects.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, plausible, and unlikely scenarios; avoids overconfident determinism; handles alternative paths such as delayed reform, neo-Maoist isolation, Soviet-style stagnation, market socialism, coup, or popular upheaval; and avoids internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Presents a single dogmatic outcome with major contradictions or no acknowledgement of uncertainty.
criteria.3-4: Allows for uncertainty only superficially and contains tension between claims, such as saying reform was impossible while also assuming reform-like outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes more than one possible path but does not clearly rank probabilities or resolve tensions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely from less likely scenarios and explains why some alternatives, such as North Korea-style isolation or delayed reform, are more or less plausible.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, compares competing scenarios, states assumptions, and preserves logical consistency throughout the counterfactual chain.

items.model_answer:
If the People's Republic of China had never undertaken Reform and Opening Up beginning in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, the trajectory of China and the world over the past four decades would look profoundly different.

Domestically, China would likely have remained a centrally planned command economy along the lines it inherited from the Mao era. Without the dismantling of the people's communes, the introduction of the household responsibility system, and the creation of Special Economic Zones in places like Shenzhen and Zhuhai, agricultural productivity would have stagnated, and the explosive growth of light industry, manufacturing, and private enterprise would not have occurred. The lifting of roughly 800 million people out of poverty—arguably the largest reduction of poverty in human history—would not have happened, or would have proceeded far more slowly. Urbanization would have been suppressed, since the strict hukou system and state allocation of labor would have remained largely intact. China's GDP, which grew from around $150 billion in 1978 to over $17 trillion today, would almost certainly be a small fraction of its current size, and per capita income would resemble that of countries like North Korea, Cuba, or perhaps a somewhat more developed version of late-Soviet economies.

Politically, the legitimacy of the Chinese Communist Party has rested heavily since 1989 on a tacit bargain: the Party delivers rising living standards in exchange for political acquiescence. Without reform, that bargain would not exist, and the regime would have had to rely entirely on ideological mobilization and coercion, as in the Mao years. It is plausible the PRC would have experienced more frequent instability, factional purges, or even regime collapse along the lines of the Soviet Union and Eastern Bloc states in 1989–1991. Alternatively, it might have evolved into a more isolated, hereditary, dynastic system resembling North Korea, though its sheer size makes that comparison imperfect.

Internationally, the consequences would be enormous. China would not have become "the world's factory," meaning the global supply chains that lowered consumer prices in the West from the 1990s onward would never have materialized in the same form. Other economies—possibly Mexico, Southeast Asia, or India—might have absorbed more of that manufacturing role. Foreign direct investment patterns, the WTO (which China joined in 2001), and the entire architecture of globalization would look quite different. The United States would not have a peer competitor of China's current scale; the post-Cold War "unipolar moment" might have extended much longer. Taiwan, Hong Kong, and the broader East Asian security order would also be reshaped: Hong Kong's 1997 handover would have occurred under far more fraught conditions, and Taiwan would face a much weaker, poorer, and less militarily capable mainland.

Culturally and technologically, China would not have produced companies like Huawei, Alibaba, Tencent, or BYD, nor would it host the world's largest internet population. Chinese students and scholars would not have flowed in large numbers to Western universities, and the cultural exchange of the past forty years—both ways—would be drastically diminished.

In short, without Reform and Opening Up, China would likely be a much poorer, more isolated, and politically more brittle state, while the global economy of the 21st century would be smaller, less integrated, and structured around a different set of industrial powers.

edus.text: If the People's Republic of China had never undertaken Reform and Opening Up beginning in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping,
the trajectory of China and the world over the past four decades would look profoundly different.
Domestically, China would likely have remained a centrally planned command economy along the lines it inherited from the Mao era.
Without the dismantling of the people's communes, the introduction of the household responsibility system, and the creation of Special Economic Zones in places like Shenzhen and Zhuhai,
agricultural productivity would have stagnated,
and the explosive growth of light industry, manufacturing, and private enterprise would not have occurred.
The lifting of roughly 800 million people out of poverty—arguably the largest reduction of poverty in human history—
would not have happened, or would have proceeded far more slowly.
Urbanization would have been suppressed,
since the strict hukou system and state allocation of labor would have remained largely intact.
China's GDP, which grew from around $150 billion in 1978 to over $17 trillion today,
would almost certainly be a small fraction of its current size,
and per capita income would resemble that of countries like North Korea, Cuba, or perhaps a somewhat more developed version of late-Soviet economies.
Politically, the legitimacy of the Chinese Communist Party has rested heavily since 1989 on a tacit bargain:
the Party delivers rising living standards in exchange for political acquiescence.
Without reform,
that bargain would not exist,
and the regime would have had to rely entirely on ideological mobilization and coercion, as in the Mao years.
It is plausible the PRC would have experienced more frequent instability, factional purges, or even regime collapse along the lines of the Soviet Union and Eastern Bloc states in 1989–1991.
Alternatively, it might have evolved into a more isolated, hereditary, dynastic system resembling North Korea,
though its sheer size makes that comparison imperfect.
Internationally, the consequences would be enormous.
China would not have become "the world's factory,"
meaning the global supply chains that lowered consumer prices in the West from the 1990s onward would never have materialized in the same form.
Other economies—possibly Mexico, Southeast Asia, or India—
might have absorbed more of that manufacturing role.
Foreign direct investment patterns, the WTO (which China joined in 2001), and the entire architecture of globalization would look quite different.
The United States would not have a peer competitor of China's current scale;
the post-Cold War "unipolar moment" might have extended much longer.
Taiwan, Hong Kong, and the broader East Asian security order would also be reshaped:
Hong Kong's 1997 handover would have occurred under far more fraught conditions,
and Taiwan would face a much weaker, poorer, and less militarily capable mainland.
Culturally and technologically, China would not have produced companies like Huawei, Alibaba, Tencent, or BYD,
nor would it host the world's largest internet population.
Chinese students and scholars would not have flowed in large numbers to Western universities,
and the cultural exchange of the past forty years—both ways—would be drastically diminished.
In short,
without Reform and Opening Up,
China would likely be a much poorer, more isolated, and politically more brittle state,
while the global economy of the 21st century would be smaller, less integrated, and structured around a different set of industrial powers.

items.question: What If the Vickers Wellington had been produced with a stressed-skin airframe instead of its geodetic fabric-covered structure?
human_answers: Picked this up from John Dell, whose site is quite often mentioned here, a long time ago. Geodetic structures only show advantages for big aircraft - e.g. a small geodetic fighter would be a non-starter. The advantages of Geodetic aircraft are better the bigger the aircraft - From this point of view it is a shame the Warwick + Windsor were so late. The main Geodetic structures (fuselage + wings) are built as whole units - So it is harder to break up the structure into subassemblies for distributed manufacture. Advantages of Geodetic over steel-tube, wooden formers and fabric covering are... Much greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage, and more g force. No internal bracing - so unobstructed space within for passengers, fuel tanks + other equipment. The potential for cheaper construction if planned + implemented properly and a very large production run with no changes in the primary structure - It may take more people to construct a geodetic aircraft but many more of them will be low-skilled, lower-waged workers. Drag difference between the two types is probably not much. Advantages of Steel tube, wooden formers and fabric covering over Geodetic are... Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Much more cost-effective for short production runs. Advantages of Geodetic over all wood stressed structures (i.e. Mosquito) Potentially greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage. Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production (Wood-workers are some of the most skilled factory workers around and therefore have higher wages and take longer to train) - In actual fact during WWII this was not such a great problem, because so many wood-working companies (i.e. furniture makers) were closed there was a relative glut of wood workers available. Not susceptible to woodworm or termites - a real danger in tropical climates. Advantages of Wooden stressed structures over Geodetic The wooden aircraft should have a lower drag, because of its smooth finish. Wood was more readily available, whereas aviation alloys were in short supply. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make a profit out of a short production run. Advantages of Geodetic over Fully-stressed skin metal aircraft Ability to absorb more battle damage + keep flying (but not necessarily protect the crew) Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production - not actually realised by Vickers. Uses less metal, a particular advantage if aviation alloys are scarce. Advantages of fully stressed metal skin over geodetic Lower drag (smoother skin). More suitable for cabin pressurisation. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make profit out of smaller production run (but still nowhere near that possible with wooden + steel tube structures). Maybe more crew protection. Possibilities for weight saving by integrating structures (eg a fuel tank or firewall could be an integral part of the main structure rather than being something added after the main structure is built - this becomes increasingly important).

Specification B.1/35 was effectively a replacement for the Hampden and Wellington which were designed to meet Specification B.9/32. What became the Halifax began as the HP.55 with 2 Hercules class engines to Spec B.1/35, then the HP.56 with 2 Vultures to Spec. P.13/36, then the HP.57, 59 & 63 with 4 Merlins and the HP.61 with 4 Hercules engines. Handley Page delivered its 500th and last Hampden in July 1940 and its first production Halifax in August 1940. English Electric built 770 Hampdens which were delivered from March 1940 to March 1942. English Electric's Hampden production overlapped with its Halifax production because the first one was delivered in October 1941. The Halifax was also built by Fairey, the London Aircraft Production Group and Rootes. The Warwick was designed to meet Spec. B.1/35 with 2 Hercules class engines too, which was changed to 2 Vulture class engines, but still to B.1/35 rather than the later B.12/36 or P.13/36. If its development had proceeded as smoothly as the Halifax it's likely that this would have happened. Weybridge would have switched from the Wellington to the Warwick in the summer of 1940. Chester may have swiched in August 1940 too, after delivering the 200 Wellingtons ordered 1937-38. The next batch of Wellingtons ordered IOTL (550 in May 1939) would have been the first batch of Warwicks. Blackpool didn't get its first Wellington contract until December 1939 and commenced deliveries in August 1940. Based on the above a contract for 500 Warwicks would have been let instead. 750 Wellingtons were ordered from the Castle Bromwich factory in December 1939 IOTL. It was cancelled before any were built, I don't know when and why, but it was probably so it could concentrate on building Spitfires. The factory also received orders for 650 Lancasters and Lincolns from September 1941 to June 1944 of which 300 were delivered from December 1943 to August 1945. Although the Warwick was only built at Weybridge (first delivery June 1942) it was also ordered from the Blackpool and Chester factories. So contradicting what I wrote in Message 8, if the stressed-skin Warwick is allowed to evolve in the same way that the Halifax did, we may see it built by the thousand at the Vickers factories at Blackpool, Chester and Weybridge instead of most of the OTL Wellingtons and all the OTL Warwicks. Depending upon how the TTL version compares to the Lancaster it might be built at Castle Bromwich too instead of the Lancasters it built IOTL.

items.model_answer:
The Vickers Wellington's geodetic structure was one of the most distinctive design features of any WWII bomber, so replacing it with a conventional stressed-skin airframe would have produced significant trade-offs.

**Advantages of a stressed-skin alternative:**

A stressed-skin Wellington would likely have been faster and more aerodynamically efficient. The geodetic framework covered in fabric created considerable drag compared to smooth metal skin. You'd probably gain 15-25 mph in top speed, improving both operational effectiveness and survivability. Manufacturing would have been more straightforward using conventional techniques already widespread in the industry, potentially allowing faster production ramp-up and easier subcontracting to firms unfamiliar with Barnes Wallis's complex geodetic construction.

**What would be lost:**

The geodetic structure's remarkable damage tolerance was its greatest asset. The basketweave framework could absorb tremendous battle damage—Wellingtons routinely returned with large sections of fabric torn away and structural members severed, yet remained flyable because loads redistributed through the lattice. A stressed-skin design would be far more vulnerable to catastrophic failure from battle damage or flak, as skin ruptures and frame damage would compromise structural integrity much more severely.

Weight savings would also disappear. The geodetic structure was exceptionally light for its strength, and a conventional airframe achieving equivalent strength would likely be heavier, reducing payload or range.

**The broader impact:**

A stressed-skin Wellington would have been a more conventional but less remarkable aircraft—faster and easier to build, but more fragile and less forgiving in combat. Given that Wellingtons served extensively in the early war years when losses were high and fighter opposition fierce, the survivability advantage of the geodetic structure was probably more valuable than the speed penalty it imposed. The design's ability to bring crews home despite severe damage saved lives and maintained operational strength during critical periods.

In essence, you'd trade the Wellington's extraordinary toughness for conventional performance gains—a questionable exchange for a night bomber operating in hostile airspace.

items.question: What If Napoleon Bonaparte had never risen to power? How would the French Revolution and the wars against the coalitions have unfolded?
human_answers: Alternate-history counterfactuals hinge on small changes producing large downstream effects. Removing Napoleon Bonaparte from the post‑Revolutionary scene doesn’t collapse the French Revolution into a single predictable path; it produces several plausible trajectories shaped by institutional weaknesses, military fortunes, political culture, and international reaction. Below are the most likely variants, their mechanics, and consequences for the war with the Coalition. Summary framing The Revolution’s radical phase (1789–1794) already created durable structural changes: the abolition of feudal privileges, administrative centralization, secular legal reform impulse, and mass mobilization through levée en masse. Those foundations would continue to shape France even without Napoleon. The crucial variables that Napoleon exploited were France’s exhausted but vast manpower, a cohort of competent generals, political instability in Paris, and the European monarchies’ inability to coordinate consistently. Removing Napoleon changes leadership quality and political stability more than the Revolution’s underlying transformations. The outcome of the wars and the Revolution’s political evolution become probabilistic. Two broad families of outcomes dominate: (A) a prolonged Revolutionary/Republican instability with periodic military rule; or (B) an eventual conservative reaction producing a restored monarchy or authoritarian regime under different leaders. Which emerges depends on battlefield results, coalition cohesion, and French political resilience. Probable short‑ to medium‑term scenarios (1797–1815) 1) Revolutionary Directory survives longer but weakens (most likely) With no singular strategic and political talent to convert victories into regime consolidation, the Directory (or a Directory‑like government) would probably limp on. It was already corrupt, factionalized, and unpopular. Military successes would be more uneven. Generals like Moreau, Masséna, Hoche, and Augereau were capable but less politically adroit than Napoleon; they could win theaters but lacked Napoleon’s combination of operational audacity and political ambition. France would likely fight the Coalition to a military stalemate in some theaters, win in others. The levée en masse still supplies manpower: the Republic probably avoids complete defeat but also fails to secure sweeping victories that produce durable peace treaties like those Napoleon negotiated (Amiens/Pressburg/Tilsit analogues would be much harder). Domestic politics: repeated coup attempts, revolts, and coups from both Jacobin and Thermidorian factions. A series of short‑lived regimes and military interventions remain likely until a stronger political solution emerges. 2) A different military strongman rises (plausible) Absent Napoleon, another general could emulate his path. Generals such as Moreau, Masséna, or even Murat might build regional power bases and attempt coups. Any successful military politician would face harder constraints: fewer early spectacular victories (no Italian campaign miracle) and less charisma to exploit domestic exhaustion. But given the Directory’s fragility, a coup‑by‑general remains a strong possibility, producing an authoritarian government similar in form but different in policy from Napoleonic France. If such a figure consolidated power, reforms (legal codification, administrative centralization, meritocratic promotion) could still appear, albeit more modest or delayed. 3) Restoration or conservative stabilization (possible) If the Coalition’s coordination improves and France suffers significant strategic defeats (for instance, if Britain finances continental armies more effectively and Austria/Russia coordinate), royalist and moderate elements could reassert themselves. A negotiated restoration of the Bourbon monarchy or a constitutional monarchy under a conservative regime could occur by the early 1800s. That outcome would reverse some revolutionary gains (partial restoration of elite influence, rollback of some laws) but would struggle to erase deep administrative and social changes already entrenched. Popular resistance would be uneven; rural conservatism in some regions might favor restoration while urban and veteran constituencies resist. Would France win the war against the Coalition? Definitive “win” like the Napoleonic domination of Europe is unlikely without Napoleon’s genius for campaign strategy and diplomacy. France would probably avoid outright conquest by the Coalition but also unlikely to subdue Europe. Most likely military outcome: protracted war with shifting front lines, localized French successes, and negotiated settlements that leave France enlarged territorially in some terms (the Republic might keep some Belgian/Northern Italian gains) but not hegemonic across Europe. If the Coalition obtained decisive coordination and a string of victories (e.g., crushing France in the field and occupying Paris), they could force a restoration. Conversely, if French generals achieve enough operational successes, a compromise peace establishing France as a major but not dominant continental power would follow. Long‑term institutional and global consequences Legal and administrative legacies: the drive for rationalized administration, standardized law, and secular meritocracy likely persists. Even a restored monarchy would inherit the Napoleonic (or proto‑Napoleonic) bureaucracy and many reformist laws because they were efficient and staffed by a new elite. Nationalism and conscription: mass armies and national mobilization create durable national identities and military-industrial practices across Europe. Revolutions and reforms elsewhere accelerate without Napoleon, but not necessarily with the same geopolitical footprint. Colonial and global effects: without the Napoleonic reshuffle (e.g., the sale of Louisiana to the U.S.), colonial transfers follow different paths. Britain remains dominant at sea; colonial contests continue but with alternate timings. Legal codification (Civil Code) may emerge differently or later. The idea of a rational civil code was already present among reformers; in one variant it is completed by another jurist or regime, preserving many modern legal foundations of continental law. Concrete examples and plausible anecdotes Example: A Moreau‑led stabilization. Moreau secures victory over Austrian forces in Germany, returns to Paris, negotiates a constitutional settlement limiting radicalism, and avoids imperial pretensions. France keeps the Rhineland and revenues sufficient to sustain influence but not empire. Example: Coalition success and Bourbon restoration. Improved Anglo‑Austrian‑Russian coordination defeats French armies, occupies Paris, restores the Bourbons with constitutional limits. Local reforms (metric system, secular administration) remain because they are functional; émigrés regain some property through compensation rather than wholesale reversal. Net assessment Napoleon’s absence reduces the likelihood of France conquering Europe and exporting Napoleonic institutions by force. It increases the probability of prolonged internal instability, fragmented military outcomes, and either a delayed authoritarian consolidation under another general or a conservative settlement restoring monarchy with revolutionary reforms partially retained. The Revolution’s social, administrative, and legal transformations mostly survive in adapted form; its geopolitical expansion and specific legacy (Napoleonic Code, Europe‑wide redrawing) are weaker or redistributed differently. Time note: analysis reflects scholarship and primary evidence available through May 2024.

criteria.9-10: Builds a sustained long-range chain showing which revolutionary/Napoleonic legacies likely persist, weaken, arrive later, or take different institutional and global forms.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control

criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty and offers more than one scenario, though likelihoods or dependencies are underdeveloped.

items.model_answer:
If Napoleon Bonaparte had never risen to power, the trajectory of the French Revolution and the wars against the European coalitions would likely have unfolded in a far messier and more uncertain fashion, though the broad currents of change in Europe would not have disappeared.

By 1799, when Napoleon staged the Coup of 18 Brumaire, the Directory was already politically bankrupt, financially exhausted, and militarily strained. Without Napoleon, some other figure—possibly General Jean Victor Moreau, Lazare Hoche (had he not died in 1797), or a politician like the Abbé Sieyès working with a more pliable general—would probably have attempted a similar consolidation of power. France in 1799 was almost destined for some kind of authoritarian correction, because the Directory could neither suppress royalist insurrection nor neo-Jacobin revival without leaning on the army. The result, however, might have been a weaker, more collegial military regime, perhaps a true oligarchic republic rather than a personal dictatorship evolving into empire.

The wars of the coalitions would likely have ended sooner and less decisively. France's revolutionary armies had already shown, before Napoleon, that they could defend the natural frontiers (Rhine, Alps, Pyrenees). Generals like Moreau, Jourdan, and Masséna were highly capable. But none possessed Napoleon's combination of strategic boldness, political ambition, and propaganda instinct. The Second Coalition (1798–1802) might still have been defeated or negotiated into a stalemate, leaving France in possession of Belgium, the Rhineland, and dominant influence in northern Italy and the Netherlands, but without the dramatic expansion that followed Austerlitz, Jena, and Wagram. A general European peace, similar to Amiens but more durable, becomes plausible by around 1801–1803, since neither Britain nor Austria would have had the same existential reason to keep fighting an expansionist emperor.

Domestically, the consolidating reforms Napoleon imposed—the Civil Code, the Concordat with the Papacy, the Bank of France, the prefectoral system, the lycées—would have come more slowly, piecemeal, and with continuing political instability. France might have oscillated between conservative republican governments and renewed Jacobin or royalist threats, perhaps experiencing a Bourbon restoration earlier, possibly through negotiation rather than foreign invasion. Alternatively, a moderate constitutional monarchy under the Orléans branch—an outcome that eventually arrived in 1830—could have emerged decades sooner.

For the rest of Europe, the absence of Napoleonic conquest would have profound consequences. The Holy Roman Empire might have survived longer, since it was Napoleon who dissolved it in 1806. The German states would not have been consolidated through the Confederation of the Rhine, slowing but not preventing eventual German nationalism. Spain would not have suffered the Peninsular War, meaning the Spanish American independence movements—triggered largely by the collapse of royal authority after 1808—would have been delayed or taken very different forms. Russia would not have been invaded in 1812, preserving the prestige of the ancien régime there and perhaps slowing reformist currents. Prussia would not have undergone its humiliation at Jena and the subsequent Stein-Hardenberg reforms that modernized its state and military.

Ideologically, however, the revolutionary genie was already out of the bottle. The ideas of popular sovereignty, legal equality, secular government, and nationalism would still have spread, but more through example and gradual diffusion than through the bayonets of the Grande Armée. The 19th-century European order would likely have lacked both the dramatic codification of revolutionary principles that Napoleon exported and the powerful conservative backlash embodied by the Congress of Vienna. The result might have been a slower, more uneven, but perhaps less violent transition toward the liberal and national movements that defined the century.

In short, without Napoleon, the Revolution would not have been "ended" by a single charismatic figure who simultaneously preserved and betrayed it. Europe would have avoided fifteen years of continent-wide warfare, but it would also have lost the brutal accelerant that spread revolutionary institutions far beyond France's borders.
