criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Case Distinctions
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly interprets “emptied by half” as a physical counterfactual involving vacuum and distinguishes the crucial geometries: top half empty versus bottom half empty, rather than treating it as ordinary air above water.
criteria.1-2: Treats the scenario as a normal half-full glass or simple evaporation/spilling, with little recognition of vacuum or geometry.
criteria.3-4: Mentions vacuum or missing air but gives a single undifferentiated outcome and misses why which half is empty matters.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that a vacuum half is unstable and notes at least one relevant geometry, but only partially contrasts top-empty and bottom-empty cases.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes top vacuum from bottom vacuum and explains that the outcomes differ because air can enter one but not the other.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, including ordinary air/water baseline, top-half vacuum collapse, and bottom-half vacuum suction/water-hammer case as separate physical evolutions.

criteria.name: Early-Time Fluid and Gas Dynamics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates causal fidelity for the first microseconds to milliseconds: air molecule motion into an exposed vacuum, limited liquid expansion, surface boiling into vacuum, and formation of pressure waves.
criteria.1-2: Gives physically implausible early behavior, such as water instantly filling all space or the vacuum persisting unchanged without explanation.
criteria.3-4: States that air rushes in or water boils but with vague, incorrect, or badly timed mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Covers some correct early mechanisms, such as air entering the top vacuum and water vapor forming, but omits timing or pressure-wave consequences.
criteria.7-8: Accurately explains rapid air inflow, weak water vapor formation, vacuum collapse, and the resulting pressure disturbance over microsecond-to-millisecond scales.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent early-time sequence with appropriate relative timescales, molecular speeds, air filling the exposed vacuum, boiling being cut short there, and shock/pressure waves propagating through air, water, and glass.

criteria.name: Bottom-Vacuum Long-Range Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer follows the distinctive downstream chain when the empty half is below the water: atmospheric pressure pushes glass and water together, the assembly accelerates, water impacts the bottom, and the glass breaks via water hammer.
criteria.1-2: Misses the bottom-vacuum case entirely or predicts a gentle settling with no major forces.
criteria.3-4: Mentions suction or collapse but does not connect it to acceleration, impact, or breakage.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that atmospheric pressure drives motion and may break the glass, but the causal chain is incomplete or weakly explained.
criteria.7-8: Explains that trapped vacuum prevents air cushioning, causing glass and water to accelerate together and collide sharply, likely breaking the glass.
criteria.9-10: Fully traces the bottom-vacuum sequence: suction from external air pressure, minimal vapor cushioning, rapid closure in milliseconds, incompressible-water impact, water-hammer shock, bottom failure, splashing, shards, and possible upward motion of remaining glass.

criteria.name: Physical Plausibility, Scale, and Quantitative Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response uses reasonable magnitudes and avoids exaggerated or understated physics for forces, speeds, timescales, sounds, and structural damage.
criteria.1-2: Uses wildly implausible scales, such as nuclear explosions, instant freezing, or no noticeable effect despite vacuum collapse.
criteria.3-4: Gets the qualitative direction partly right but gives misleading magnitudes or unsupported dramatic claims.
criteria.5-6: Provides broadly plausible effects but with limited scale calibration or some questionable estimates.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable qualitative or approximate scales: microseconds for air motion, milliseconds for shocks/collapse, loud bang, strong but localized breakage.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates the scenario very well, distinguishing rapid but non-explosive top-vacuum collapse from the more destructive bottom-vacuum water-hammer event, with plausible timing, speeds, pressures, and damage.

criteria.name: Chain Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a consistent causal timeline, handles dependencies and assumptions explicitly, and avoids contradictions such as simultaneous persistent vacuum and full air equalization.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or disconnected claims that cannot all be true under the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has a rough story but includes causal gaps, reversed ordering, or unacknowledged assumptions that undermine the scenario.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent but leaves some dependencies unclear, such as whether air has access to the vacuum or whether the glass can withstand the shock.
criteria.7-8: Presents a consistent timeline with clear assumptions, plausible contingencies, and few internal tensions.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a tightly ordered long-range causal chain, explicitly conditions outcomes on geometry and glass strength, calibrates uncertainty without evasion, and avoids all significant physical contradictions.

items.model_answer:
If a glass of water suddenly emptied by half, several physical phenomena would occur depending on the mechanism:

**If the water simply vanished (hypothetical scenario):**
The remaining water would experience a sudden drop in hydrostatic pressure at its surface. The water level would instantly be lower, and the glass would become lighter by the mass of the disappeared water (roughly 100-125 grams for a typical glass). The center of mass of the glass-water system would shift upward relative to the base.

**If the water rapidly drained out:**
- The water would flow out following gravity and fluid dynamics principles
- Air would rush in to replace the volume previously occupied by water, potentially creating gurgling sounds
- The outflow rate would depend on the opening size and would follow Torricelli's law (similar to √(2gh), where h is the height of water above the opening)
- Surface tension effects might cause the remaining water to oscillate briefly before settling

**Physical consequences:**
- The hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of the glass would drop by approximately half (pressure = ρgh, where h is halved)
- The weight pressing down on the table would decrease by about 100-125 grams
- If you were holding the glass, you'd feel it suddenly become lighter
- Temperature would remain essentially unchanged (assuming no evaporation)

**If this happened via instantaneous evaporation:**
- It would require enormous energy input (~250 kJ for 125g of water)
- The surrounding air would cool dramatically as it supplied this latent heat
- Water vapor would rapidly expand into the space and surrounding area

The most realistic scenario would be rapid drainage, which follows well-understood fluid mechanics principles.

items.question: What If Humanity Tried to Evacuate the Entire Earth?
human_answers: There are a bunch of science fiction movies where, because of pollution, overpopulation, or nuclear war, humanity abandons Earth. But lifting people into space is hard. Barring a massive reduction in the population, is launching the whole human race into space physically possible? Let’s not even worry about where we’re headed—we’ll assume we don’t have to find a new home, but we can’t stay here. [Image: image] To figure out if this is plausible, we can start with an absolute baseline energy requirement: four gigajoules per person. No matter how we do it, whether we use rockets or a cannon or a space elevator, moving a 65-kilogram person—or 65 kilograms of anything—out of the Earth’s gravity well requires at least this much energy. \[\text{Gravitational potential energy} = \frac{1}{2} \times 65\mathrm{kg} \times \text{(Earth escape velocity)}^{2}\] The energy required to lift something away from the Earth is equal to its kinetic energy if it were moving at Earth’s escape velocity. How much is four gigajoules? It’s about a megawatt-hour, which is what a typical US household consumes in electricity in a month or two. It’s the amount of stored energy in a cargo van full of AA batteries or 90 kg of gasoline. [Image: image] Four gigajoules times seven billion people gives us \(2.8 \times 10^{18}\) joules, or 8 petawatt-hours. This is about five percent of the world’s annual energy consumption. A lot, but not impossible. But this is just a minimum. In practice, everything depends on our means of transportation. If we’re using rockets, it’s going to take a lot more. This is because of a fundamental problem with rockets: they have to lift their own fuel. Let’s return for a moment to those 90 kilograms of gasoline (about 30 gallons), because they help illustrate a central problem in space travel. If we want to launch a 65-kilogram spaceship, we need to burn around 90 kilograms of fuel. (Gasoline has an energy per pound comparable to that of rocket fuel, so we’ll stick with that example). We load that fuel on board—and now our spaceship weighs 155 kilograms. A 155-kilogram spaceship requires 215 kilograms of fuel, so we load another 125 kilograms on board ... Fortunately, we’re saved from an infinite loop—where we add 1.3 kilograms for every 1 kilogram we add—by the fact that we don’t have to carry that fuel all the way up. We burn it as we go, so we get lighter and lighter, which means we need less and less fuel. But we do have to lift the fuel partway. The formula for how much propellant we need to burn to get moving at a given speed is given by the Tsiolkovsky Rocket equation: \[\Delta v = v_\text{exhaust} \ln \frac {m_\text{start}} {m_\text{end}}\] \(m_\text{start}\) and \(m_\text{end}\) are the total mass of the ship+fuel before and after the burn, and \(v_\text{exhaust}\) is the “exhaust velocity” of the fuel, a number that’s between 2.5-4.5 km/s for rocket fuels. What’s important is the ratio between \(\Delta v\) and \(v_\text{exhaust}\) — the speed we want to be going compared to the speed that the propellant exits our rocket. The kilograms of fuel needed per kilogram of ship is e to the power of this number, which gets big very fast. For leaving Earth, we need a \(\Delta v\) of upwards of 13 km/s, and \(v_\text{exhaust}\) isn’t much higher than 4.5 km/s, which gives a fuel-to-ship ratio of at least \(\text{e}^{\frac{13}{4.5}} \approx 20\). The upshot is that to overcome Earth’s gravity using traditional rocket fuels, a one-ton craft needs 20 to 50 tons of fuel. Launching all of humanity (total weight: around 400 million tons) would therefore take tens of trillions of tons of fuel. That’s a lot; if we were using hydrocarbon-based fuels, it would represent a decent chunk of the world’s remaining oil reserves. And that’s not even worrying about the weight of the ship itself, food, water, or our pets (there are probably around a million tons of pet dog in the US alone). We’d also need fuel to produce all these ships, to transport people to the launch sites, and so forth. It’s not necessarily completely impossible, but it’s certainly outside the realm of plausibility. But rockets aren’t our only option. As crazy as it sounds, we might be better off trying to (1) literally climb into space on a rope, or (2) blow ourselves off the planet with nuclear weapons. These are actually serious—if audacious—ideas for launch systems, both of which have been bouncing around since the start of the Space Age. [Image: image] The first approach is the “space elevator” concept, a favorite of science fiction authors. The idea is that we connect a tether to a satellite orbiting far enough out that the tether is held taut by centrifugal force. Then we can send climbers up the rope using ordinary electricity and motors, powered by solar power, nuclear generators, or whatever works best. The biggest engineering hurdle is that the tether would have to be several times stronger than anything we can currently build. There are hopes that carbon nanotube-based materials could provide the required strength—adding this to the long list of engineering problems which can be waved away by tacking on the prefix “nano-”. The second approach is nuclear pulse propulsion, a surprisingly plausible method for getting huge amounts of material moving really fast. The basic idea is that you toss a nuclear bomb behind you and ride the shockwave. You’d think the spacecraft would be vaporized, but it turns out that if it has a well-designed shield, the blast flings away before it has a chance to disintegrate. If it could be made reliable enough, this system would in theory be capable of lifting entire city blocks into orbit, and could—potentially—accomplish our goal. The engineering principles behind this were solid enough that in the 1960s, under the guidance of Freeman Dyson, the US government actually tried to build one of these spaceships. The story of that effort, dubbed Project Orion, is detailed in the excellent book (http://www.amazon.com/Project-Orion-Story-Atomic-Spaceship/dp/0805059857) of the same name by Freeman’s son George Dyson. Advocates for nuclear pulse propulsion are still disappointed that the project was cancelled before any prototypes were built. Others argue that when you think about what they were trying to do—put our entire nuclear arsenal in a box, hurl it high into the atmosphere, and nuke it repeatedly—it’s terrifying that it got as far as it did. So the answer is that while sending one person into space is easy, getting all of us there would tax our resources to the limit and possibly destroy the planet. It’s a small step for a man, but a giant leap for mankind.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Humanity Tried to Evacuate the Entire Earth?

criteria.name: Physical Baseline and Scale of the Evacuation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer grounds the counterfactual in the basic physics and scale of lifting all humans out of Earth's gravity well.
criteria.1-2: Ignores gravity, escape energy, population scale, or treats evacuation as trivially easy.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that space launch is hard but gives little or no quantitative sense of energy or mass.
criteria.5-6: Identifies escape velocity or energy-per-person scale and recognizes billions of people make the task enormous.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable estimates for human mass, escape energy, and total energy demand, with mostly correct order-of-magnitude reasoning.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes the theoretical minimum energy from practical requirements and accurately scales from one person to all humanity.

criteria.name: Launch Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the causal constraints of plausible evacuation methods, especially rockets, space elevators, and nuclear pulse propulsion.
criteria.1-2: Relies on magical or unsupported transport methods without addressing physical mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions rockets or future technology but misses the main limiting mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Explains that rockets require large fuel mass and that alternative launch systems might reduce but not eliminate the problem.
criteria.7-8: Correctly discusses rocket mass ratio, fuel burden, and at least one serious alternative such as space elevators or nuclear pulse propulsion.
criteria.9-10: Accurately compares multiple mechanisms, including why rockets scale poorly and why alternatives face extreme engineering, safety, or materials constraints.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the downstream consequences of evacuating Earth beyond the initial launch problem.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'people leave Earth' with no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences but without causal connection or prioritization.
criteria.5-6: Covers major follow-on needs such as ships, supplies, launch sites, energy production, and coordination.
criteria.7-8: Connects launch requirements to industrial mobilization, resource extraction, ecological damage, social disruption, and survival logistics.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain from physical launch constraints through global infrastructure, biosphere loss, orbital staging, governance, and post-Earth survival limits.

criteria.name: Plausibility and Uncertainty Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer makes appropriately qualified claims about what is physically possible, technologically feasible, and socially plausible.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims that are physically wrong or unsupported, such as declaring evacuation easy with current technology.
criteria.3-4: Uses vague feasibility claims without separating physics, engineering, economics, and politics.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that evacuation is not strictly forbidden by physics but is far beyond current practical capability.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty across scenarios, noting assumptions about population, payload mass, destination, time horizon, and technology level.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes theoretical minima from real-world execution, identifies dominant uncertainties, and avoids overconfident predictions.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Counterfactual Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer remains internally consistent with the premise that humanity must leave Earth and cannot solve the problem by simply staying.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or contains major internal inconsistencies about energy, mass, or destination.
criteria.3-4: Partly follows the premise but repeatedly shifts to unrelated solutions such as fixing Earth without answering evacuation feasibility.
criteria.5-6: Mostly stays on the evacuation scenario, with minor inconsistencies or unsupported jumps.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent counterfactual frame and avoids double-counting, impossible shortcuts, or contradictory assumptions.
criteria.9-10: Uses the premise rigorously, keeps assumptions explicit, and ensures all causal claims about launch, resources, and survival are mutually compatible.

items.model_answer:
Evacuating the entire human population of Earth—roughly 8 billion people—is so far beyond current or near-future capability that it's essentially a thought experiment in scale rather than engineering. Still, walking through the numbers is illuminating.

The fundamental bottleneck is launch capacity. SpaceX's Starship, when fully operational, is designed to carry around 100 people to orbit per flight (and far fewer on long-duration interplanetary trips). Even optimistically assuming 100 passengers per launch, evacuating 8 billion people would require 80 million launches. If we somehow built and launched one Starship every single hour without pause, it would take more than 9,000 years. To finish in a single human lifetime (say 80 years), we'd need to launch roughly 2,700 rockets every day—about 110 per hour, worldwide. For comparison, humanity currently launches around 200 rockets per *year* globally.

The fuel demand alone is staggering. Starship uses about 4,600 tonnes of methane and liquid oxygen per launch. Eighty million launches would consume on the order of 370 billion tonnes of propellant—comparable to a significant fraction of Earth's accessible natural gas reserves, plus the enormous industrial infrastructure to liquefy oxygen at that rate. Producing that much methane and oxygen would itself require energy on the scale of decades of current global electricity production.

Then there's the destination problem. Low Earth orbit can't hold 8 billion people for long; they need somewhere to go. The Moon and Mars combined have essentially zero existing habitats. Building life support, food production, radiation shielding, and pressurized living space for billions on another world is a construction project orders of magnitude larger than all human construction ever performed, and it must happen *before* the evacuees arrive. Mars receives a launch window only every 26 months, and a one-way trip takes 6–9 months, so the throughput limits are even harsher than the launch numbers suggest.

Logistics on the ground would also collapse the plan. Choosing who flies first, maintaining food, water, power, and civil order during a multi-century evacuation, and keeping industrial supply chains running while simultaneously dismantling them is a contradiction that no government structure has ever managed.

The realistic conclusion is that mass evacuation isn't a survival strategy for humanity. If Earth becomes uninhabitable on a short timescale, the most that could plausibly escape is a tiny seed population—perhaps thousands to millions over many decades—not the species as a whole. For any threat short of total planetary destruction, fixing Earth is vastly cheaper and faster than leaving it. That's why serious "planetary defense" and climate efforts focus on keeping Earth livable rather than packing our bags.

SpaceX's Starship, when fully operational, is designed to carry around 100 people to orbit per flight
and far fewer on long-duration interplanetary trips.
Even optimistically assuming 100 passengers per launch, evacuating 8 billion people would require 80 million launches.
If we somehow built and launched one Starship every single hour without pause,
it would take more than 9,000 years.
To finish in a single human lifetime (say 80 years),
we'd need to launch roughly 2,700 rockets every day—about 110 per hour, worldwide.
For comparison, humanity currently launches around 200 rockets per year globally.
The fuel demand alone is staggering.
Starship uses about 4,600 tonnes of methane and liquid oxygen per launch.
Eighty million launches would consume on the order of 370 billion tonnes of propellant
comparable to a significant fraction of Earth's accessible natural gas reserves,
plus the enormous industrial infrastructure to liquefy oxygen at that rate.
Producing that much methane and oxygen would itself require energy on the scale of decades of current global electricity production.
Then there's the destination problem.
Low Earth orbit can't hold 8 billion people for long;
they need somewhere to go.
The Moon and Mars combined have essentially zero existing habitats.

Building life support, food production, radiation shielding, and pressurized living space for billions on another world is a construction project orders of magnitude larger than all human construction ever performed,
and it must happen before the evacuees arrive.
Mars receives a launch window only every 26 months,
and a one-way trip takes 6–9 months,
so the throughput limits are even harsher than the launch numbers suggest.
Logistics on the ground would also collapse the plan.

Choosing who flies first, maintaining food, water, power, and civil order during a multi-century evacuation, and keeping industrial supply chains running while simultaneously dismantling them is a contradiction
that no government structure has ever managed.
The realistic conclusion is that mass evacuation isn't a survival strategy for humanity.
If Earth becomes uninhabitable on a short timescale,
the most that could plausibly escape is a tiny seed population—perhaps thousands to millions over many decades—
not the species as a whole.
For any threat short of total planetary destruction, fixing Earth is vastly cheaper and faster than leaving it.
That's why serious "planetary defense" and climate efforts focus on keeping Earth livable rather than packing our bags.

items.question: What If Everyone Had Exactly One Soulmate?
human_answers: What a nightmare that would be. There are a lot of problems with the concept of a single random soul mate. As Tim Minchin put it in his song If I Didn’t Have You: (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gaid72fqzNE) Your love is one in a million You couldn’t buy it at any price. But of the 9.999 hundred thousand other loves, Statistically, some of them would be equally nice. But what if we did have one randomly-assigned perfect soul mate, and we couldn’t be happy with anyone else? Would we find each other? We’ll assume your soul mate is set at birth. You know nothing about who or where they are, but—as in the romantic cliché—you’ll recognize each other the moment your eyes meet. Right away, this raises a few questions. For starters, is your soul mate even still alive? A hundred billion or so humans have ever lived, but only seven billion are alive now (which gives the human condition a 93% mortality rate). If we’re all paired up at random, 90% of our soul mates are long dead. [Image: image] That sounds horrible. But wait, it gets worse: A simple argument shows we can’t just limit ourselves to past humans; we have to include an unknown number of future humans as well. See, if it’s possible for your soul mate to be in the distant past, then it also has to be possible for soul mates to be in the distant future. After all, your soul mate’s soul mate is. So let’s assume your soul mate lives at the same time as you. Furthermore, to keep things from getting creepy, we’ll assume they’re within a few years of your age. (This is stricter than the standard age gap creepiness formula (http://xkcd.com/314/), but if we assume a 30-year-old and a 40-year-old can be soul mates, then the creepiness rule is violated if they accidentally meet 15 years earlier.) With the same-age restriction, most of us have a pool of around half a billion potential matches. But what about gender and sexual orientation? And culture? And language? We could keep using demographics to try to break things down further, but we’d be drifting away from the idea of a random soul mate. In our scenario, you don’t know anything about who your soul mate will be until you look into their eyes. Everybody has only one orientation—toward their soul mate. The odds of running into your soul mate are incredibly small. The number of strangers we make eye contact with each day is hard to estimate. It can vary from almost none (shut-ins or people in small towns) to many thousands (a police officer in Times Square). Let’s suppose you lock eyes with an average of a few dozen new strangers each day. (I’m pretty introverted, so for me that’s definitely a generous estimate.) If 10% of them are close to your age, that’s around 50,000 people in a lifetime. Given that you have 500,000,000 potential soul mates, it means you’ll only find true love in one lifetime out of ten thousand. [Image: image] But with the threat of dying alone looming so imminently, society could restructure to try to enable as much eye contact as possible. We could put together massive conveyer belts to move lines of people past each other … [Image: image] ... but if the eye contact effect works over webcams, we could just use a modified version of ChatRoulette. [Image: image] If everyone used the system for eight hours a day, seven days a week, and if it takes you a couple seconds to decide if someone’s your soul mate, this system could—in theory—match everyone up with their soul mates in a few decades. (I modeled a few simple systems to estimate how quickly people would pair off and drop out of the singles pool. If you want to try to work through the math for a particular setup, you might start by looking at derangement problems (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derangement).) In the real world, many people have trouble finding any time at all for romance—few could devote two decades to it. So maybe only rich kids would be able to afford to sit around on SoulMateRoulette. Unfortunately for the proverbial 1%, most of their soul mates are to be found in the other 99%. If only 1% of people use the service, then 1% of that 1% would find their match through this system—one in ten thousand. The other 99% of the 1% (“We are the zero point nine nine percent!”) would have an incentive to get more people into the system. They might sponsor projects akin to One Laptop Per Child (but with a sleazier vibe). Careers like “cashier” and “police officer in Times Square” would become high-status prizes because of the eye contact potential. People would flock to cities and public gathering places to find love—just as they do now. But even if a bunch of us spent years on SoulMateRoulette, another bunch of us managed to hold jobs that offered constant eye contact with strangers, and the rest of us just hoped for luck, only a small minority of us would ever find true love. The rest of us would be out of luck. Given all the stress and pressure, some people would fake it. They’d want to join the club, so they’d get together with another lonely person and stage a fake soul mate encounter. They’d marry, hide their relationship problems, and struggle to present a happy face to their friends and family. (Of course, this never happens in our world.) All in all, the world of random soul mates is an even lonelier one than ours. I prefer Tim Minchin’s take on things: With all my heart and all my mind I know one thing is true: I have just one life and just one love and, my love, that love is you. And if it wasn't for you, baby, I really think that I would have somebody else.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Everyone Had Exactly One Soulmate?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the specific premise that every person has exactly one soulmate and that this constraint meaningfully changes human mating, search, and social systems.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or rejects the premise; treats soulmates as ordinary dating preferences or gives a generic romance answer.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one soulmate but applies the idea inconsistently or relies mostly on vague emotional claims.
criteria.5-6: Maintains the one-soulmate premise in most reasoning, with some attention to exclusivity and rarity.
criteria.7-8: Consistently explores how exclusivity, recognition, and random pairing would affect individuals and society.
criteria.9-10: Fully commits to the premise and derives nuanced consequences from exact one-to-one soulmate assignment across populations and time.

criteria.name: Search Probability and Demographic Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly analyzes the odds of finding one's soulmate using population size, age cohorts, geography, mortality, future generations, and encounter rates.
criteria.1-2: Provides no quantitative or demographic reasoning; assumes everyone easily finds their soulmate.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes finding a soulmate is hard but gives little support or implausible numbers.
criteria.5-6: Uses basic population or probability reasoning, though with gaps or oversimplified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains why random assignment makes discovery unlikely, considering age, location, and encounter frequency.
criteria.9-10: Offers strong probabilistic reasoning, including issues like past/future humans, same-age restrictions, lifetime encounters, and the scale mismatch between candidates and meetings.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Social and Technological Adaptation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream systems society might build or reshape to locate soulmates, such as mass screening, online matching, urbanization, labor incentives, surveillance, or institutional matchmaking.
criteria.1-2: Does not discuss societal or technological adaptation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions dating apps or matchmaking superficially without causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several adaptations but does not explain their feasibility, limits, or incentives.
criteria.7-8: Explains plausible systems for increasing encounters and how they would alter behavior, work, status, and infrastructure.
criteria.9-10: Develops a rich, mechanism-level account of large-scale soulmate search systems, including participation constraints, unequal access, dropout effects, and unintended consequences.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer builds coherent causal chains from the soulmate premise to long-term effects on family formation, inequality, mental health, culture, economics, and institutions.
criteria.1-2: Lists disconnected effects or makes abrupt unsupported claims.
criteria.3-4: Includes some consequences but weakly links them to the premise.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly coherent chain from soulmate scarcity to personal or social outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Connects multiple domains through credible causal pathways over time.
criteria.9-10: Shows sophisticated long-range reasoning, tracing feedback loops among search pressure, loneliness, marriage norms, labor markets, inequality, deception, and cultural values.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer states assumptions, acknowledges uncertainty, avoids internal contradictions, and distinguishes necessary consequences from speculative ones.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or changes the rules of the scenario without notice.
criteria.3-4: Contains noticeable unsupported certainty or inconsistent assumptions about how soulmates work.
criteria.5-6: States some assumptions and avoids major contradictions, but uncertainty handling is limited.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates assumptions from conclusions and qualifies uncertain social or numerical predictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, keeps all assumptions consistent, and flags alternative outcomes under different soulmate-recognition or assignment rules.

items.model_answer:
If every person on Earth had exactly one soulmate—a single, uniquely compatible partner predetermined by some cosmic mechanism—the consequences would be strange, often tragic, and would reshape society in profound ways.

The first problem is mathematical. With roughly 8 billion people alive and tens of billions more who have ever lived, the odds of crossing paths with your one soulmate are vanishingly small. Even assuming your soulmate is alive at the same time, lives on the same continent, and speaks a language you could learn, the probability of meeting them in a lifetime is on the order of one in millions. Most people would die without ever encountering their match. The romantic ideal would, in practice, become a guarantee of romantic loneliness for the overwhelming majority.

This depends on whether soulmates must be contemporaries. If they can be separated by centuries, the situation becomes worse: your soulmate might have lived in 14th-century Mongolia or won't be born for another 300 years. If they must be contemporaries, the system implies a tightly orchestrated demographic balance—equal numbers of compatible people born within overlapping lifespans—which raises questions about how the universe enforces this pairing.

Society would likely respond by industrializing the search. Governments or private companies would build massive databases—DNA, biometrics, behavioral profiles—trying to algorithmically identify pairings. Travel and migration patterns would change as people roam the world looking for their match. A new global ethics would emerge around questions like: Are you obligated to wait? Is marrying a non-soulmate a moral failure or a pragmatic choice? What happens when one soulmate dies young, leaving the other alone forever?

The institution of marriage would split. A small number of "verified" soulmate couples would be celebrated almost religiously, while the rest of society would form ordinary, chosen relationships now culturally regarded as second-best. This could either devalue ordinary love or, in a healthier reaction, push society to reject the soulmate framework entirely as cruel cosmic luck.

There are also biological complications. If soulmate compatibility is genetic, populations might converge or diverge in ways that disrupt the gene pool. If it's psychological, childhood environment becomes fate. If it's mystical, then free will in love essentially disappears—your most important relationship is dictated rather than built.

The deepest implication is philosophical. Human relationships derive much of their meaning from being chosen and cultivated, from the work of compatibility rather than its discovery. A soulmate system would replace love-as-craft with love-as-lottery. For the lucky few who find their match it would feel transcendent; for everyone else, it would turn ordinary, hard-won love into a consolation prize. Most likely, humanity would be worse off—not because soulmates are a bad idea, but because guaranteeing exactly one would make love rarer, more fragile, and more dependent on chance than it already is.

edus.text: If every person on Earth had exactly one soulmate—a single, uniquely compatible partner predetermined by some cosmic mechanism—
the consequences would be strange, often tragic, and would reshape society in profound ways.
The first problem is mathematical.
With roughly 8 billion people alive and tens of billions more who have ever lived, the odds of crossing paths with your one soulmate are vanishingly small.
Even assuming your soulmate is alive at the same time, lives on the same continent, and speaks a language you could learn,
the probability of meeting them in a lifetime is on the order of one in millions.
Most people would die without ever encountering their match.
The romantic ideal would, in practice, become a guarantee of romantic loneliness for the overwhelming majority.
This depends on whether soulmates must be contemporaries.
If they can be separated by centuries, the situation becomes worse:
your soulmate might have lived in 14th-century Mongolia
or won't be born for another 300 years.
If they must be contemporaries,
the system implies a tightly orchestrated demographic balance—equal numbers of compatible people born within overlapping lifespans—
which raises questions about how the universe enforces this pairing.
Society would likely respond by industrializing the search.
Governments or private companies would build massive databases—DNA, biometrics, behavioral profiles—trying to algorithmically identify pairings.
Travel and migration patterns would change as people roam the world looking for their match.
A new global ethics would emerge around questions like:
Are you obligated to wait?
Is marrying a non-soulmate a moral failure or a pragmatic choice?
What happens when one soulmate dies young, leaving the other alone forever?
The institution of marriage would split.
A small number of "verified" soulmate couples would be celebrated almost religiously,
while the rest of society would form ordinary, chosen relationships now culturally regarded as second-best.
This could either devalue ordinary love
or, in a healthier reaction, push society to reject the soulmate framework entirely as cruel cosmic luck.
There are also biological complications.
If soulmate compatibility is genetic,
populations might converge or diverge in ways that disrupt the gene pool.
If it's psychological,
childhood environment becomes fate.
If it's mystical,
then free will in love essentially disappears—your most important relationship is dictated rather than built.
The deepest implication is philosophical.
Human relationships derive much of their meaning from being chosen and cultivated, from the work of compatibility rather than its discovery.
A soulmate system would replace love-as-craft with love-as-lottery.
For the lucky few who find their match it would feel transcendent;
for everyone else, it would turn ordinary, hard-won love into a consolation prize.
Most likely, humanity would be worse off—
not because soulmates are a bad idea,
but because guaranteeing exactly one would make love rarer, more fragile, and more dependent on chance than it already is.

items.question: What If Earth's Landmasses Were Rotated by 90 Degrees?
human_answers: It would profoundly alter our biosphere in general and public radio in particular. Socke asks what would happen if the Earth’s surface were slid around by 90 degrees, putting our current North and South Poles on the equator. We’re not changing the tilt of the Earth’s axis; we’re just imagining that the surface were arranged differently. [Image: image] We’ll pick the Greenwich meridian for our new equator, putting the new North and South poles in the Indian ocean (0N, 90E) and off the coast of Ecuador (0N, 90W). India, Indonesia, and Ecuador would become polar, while Europe, Antarctica, and Alaska would become tropical. Where would the deserts and forests be? What areas would get better or worse? This stuff is complicated. In a moment, we'll start using wild speculation to reshape the face of the planet. But first, a brief story to illustrate just how mind-bogglingly complicated this stuff is: In Chad, on the southern outskirts of the Sahara, there’s valley called the Bodélé Depression. It was once a lakebed, and the dry dust in the valley floor is full of nutrient-rich matter from the microorganisms that lived there. From October to March, winds coming in from the east are pinched between two mountain ranges. When the surface winds climb over 20 mph, they start picking up dust from the valley. This dust is blown westward, all the way across Africa, and out over the Atlantic. That dirt—from one small valley in Chad—supplies over 50% of the nutrient-rich dust that helps fertilize the Amazon rainforest (http://iopscience.iop.org/1748-9326/1/1/014005). At least, according to that one study. But if it's right, it wouldn’t be a crazy anomaly. This kind of complexity is found everywhere. The basic building blocks of our world are crazy. This is why we can be so certain about large-scale patterns like global warming, where we understand the overall physics pretty well—energy comes in, less energy goes out, so the average temperature rises—but have a harder time predicting how it will affect any particular place or specific species. So even if I were a climate expert—which I’m definitely not—there’d be no way to answer this question with certainty. There are just too many variables. Instead, think of what follows as a rough sketch of some of the things this alternate Earth could contain. To start, here’s a map of our reshuffled world: [Image: image] (An equirectangular projection, by the way. This type of equirectangular projection, centered on a north-south meridian instead of the equator, is specifically called a Cassini projection, so a good name for our alternate Earth might be "Cassini".) Let’s imagine that this alternate Earth develops over millions of years, with ecosystems and climate zones settling out. Then one day we wake up to find our current civilization has been magically transported there—cities and all. What would they find? The climate on the rotated Earth would depend heavily on the details of ocean and atmospheric heat circulation (http://eesc.columbia.edu/courses/ees/climate/lectures/gen_circ/index.html). We'll guess at some of that, but for now, let's assume this world has extremes which are similar to ours. So let's add some ice and permafrost near the poles and in mountainous areas: [Image: image] Next, we should fill in some green areas and deserts. The locations of these depend heavily on rainfall, so we’ll need to sketch out some winds. The main driver of our weather is the sun, which heats air near the equator more than at the poles. Hot air rises at the equator and then flows poleward, and cooler air moves in across the surface toward the equator. This circulation is called a Hadley cell (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadley_cell). [Image: image] Hadley cells shift north and south of the Equator with the seasons. At this time of year on our Earth, the sun is directly overhead at about 10°N, which is why hurricanes are forming near that latitude right now. Because of the Coriolis effect, the surface winds in a Hadley cell flow from east to west. Further north, for most of the temperate zones, the prevailing surface winds are west to east. (At times, there are also east-to-west winds circulating around the poles.) So let’s fill in some wind patterns—keeping in mind that in reality things would be further complicated by land interactions and the location of persistent high and low pressure systems. [Image: image] Sinking air is cool and dry, so land under the outer edges of the Hadley cells tends to be arid. These regions, lying a bit poleward of 30 degrees, are known as the horse latitudes (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_latitudes). [Image: image] The rising air at the equator carries moisture from the ocean, which then condenses into rain, so tropical areas are usually wet and thick with growth. Areas near the equator are sometimes dominated by a seasonal monsoon cycle (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon). In temperate zones, things are more variable. Weather there is dominated by the movement of jet streams and fronts, and depends heavily on geography. Most of the United States is in this type of region. With all that in mind, let’s fill in some arid and lush areas: [Image: image] (Climates can be hard to predict—for example, in our world, Somalia and French Guiana both sit on the equator, at the eastern coast of a continent, and seem like they should both receive a tropical sea breeze. But coastal French Guiana is dense rain forest while coastal Somalia is an arid desert. The explanation involves the monsoon cycle.) And just for fun, here’s a wild guess as to where the hurricane basins would be: [Image: image] Let’s take a closer look at each continent. North America has a range of climates similar to what it had before, but flipped north-south. The Arctic Canadian provinces are now tropical, while Central America is icy and polar. Hurricanes threaten Greenland, Baffin Island, and the Maritimes. Tropical moisture from Baffin Bay and the northwest (formerly north) Atlantic mixes with cool air flowing down through the US from the Rockies, creating a new Tornado Alley in the prairies inland from Hudson Bay. South America looks sort of like the old Europe. It's cool and temperate along the Brazilian coast, with boreal forests and grasslands across much of its width. In the south, the boreal vegetation gives way to polar tundra, and eventually to the massive icebound Andes, which cut the continent off from the frozen polar waters. The Amazon, which in our world carries more water than the next seven largest rivers put together, is reduced to something akin to the Mississippi. Asia is flipped in the same way North America was, with the Siberian coast facing an enclosed tropical sea. The Indian subcontinent and north (formerly southeast) Asia form the new Siberia. The Gobi Desert is no longer in the rain shadow of the Himalayas, but doesn't exactly become tropical. Europe resembles the old southeast Asia. Great Britain and Ireland look like the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo. Iceland resembles our Philippines. Central Europe is the new New Guinea, with the Alps the only place on the Equator with permanent glaciers. Africa is rotated 90 degrees, with south (formerly west) Africa becoming tropical rainforest and north (formerly east) Africa an arid desert. On our Earth, North America is the only continent where tornadoes are common, but in this world, they're frequent in East Africa as well. Australia is cooler and wetter, with forests across the northern (formerly western) regions. Antarctica is a clear winner. Without its ice cap, it’s a bit smaller than we remember, but most of it is blanketed with highland rainforest. There are alpine zones around the mountains to the south and west. The researchers at McMurdo and Scott Base on Ross Island wake up to a tropical paradise. If any of them find they miss the frozen wastelands, they can always put in for a transfer to Costa Rica. Now, let’s see how the world’s largest cities fare: [Image: image] Some cities get colder. Mexico City, high in the polar mountains, is buried beneath an ice sheet. Jakarta is the new Svalbard—a desolate coastal rock too far north even for most Norwegians. Kolkata and Delhi are icebound, sealed off from the warmer world by the Himalayas. Hong Kong, Manila, Karachi, and Mumbai are similar to our world’s Anchorage or Reykjavik—the ocean isn’t frozen, but it sure is cold. A few cities remain perfectly habitable, albeit with some changes: Seoul, Osaka, Tokyo, Shanghai, and New York City are among the least-affected cities, with climates roughly similar to their previous ones. Shanghai does get colder, but seasonal extremes in all five cities get milder—particularly in Seoul—and substantially wetter. Cairo is moved slightly south. It’s now surrounded by coastal savannah, with spots of rain forest found around the mouth of the Nile. Though it moves closer to the equator, it doesn’t actually get hotter. São Paulo and Buenos Aires cool down a bit. They’re now on the northern coast of a South America, which occupies a Canadalike range of latitudes. Their climate is somewhere between that of our New England and that of our Regular England. Los Angeles is cool and mild. The steady sea breeze carrying moisture up into the San Gabriel mountains makes LA one of the rainiest places in the new US. It closely resembles a wetter version of our Seattle. And a few cities get much hotter. Moscow is extremely hot and very dry, with a climate somewhere between our Phoenix and our Baghdad. Russians, who have been surviving in Russia for centuries, shrug with resignation. London sits in a steamy jungle straddling the equator, with a climate generally resembling Manila's. The food is still bland, the Thames is full of piranha, and it's the only place on Earth where tigers apologize as they attack you. At the beginning, I mentioned the impact on public radio. To explain, let’s consider one more scenario. Namely, what if this change were made on our Earth, over a fairly short time? We’re assuming that all the material is magically shifted around, so there are no massive tsunamis or earthquakes. Even so, it would definitely still be a catastrophe. For starters, the ice caps would melt long before new ones could develop, pushing the ocean up by a few hundred feet. The reshuffling of climate zones would come as a huge shock to the biosphere, leading to collapse of the food chain and eventually to mass extinctions at every level. But if the shift happened just right—and Michael Bay were telling the story—then as the waters of the Gulf of Mexico began to cool and the Mississippi slowed and became an estuary, the region’s wildlife would spread inland. And one morning, Minnesotans would wake up to the sight of floating rafts of fire ants (http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2011/04/pictures/110425-fire-ants-life-rafts-swarms-science-proceedings/), followed by five million lost, hungry alligators … [Image: image] … leading a harrowing, surprisingly bloody “News from Lake Wobegon” segment on what would become the final, fatal broadcast of A Prairie Home Companion.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Earth's Landmasses Were Rotated by 90 Degrees?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly applies the specific premise: Earth's landmasses/surface features are rotated 90 degrees relative to the spin axis while axial tilt, solar forcing, rotation, and basic planetary physics remain unchanged.
criteria.1-2: Misunderstands the premise, changes Earth's tilt/orbit/rotation, or treats the scenario as physical tectonic rotation with irrelevant catastrophes only.
criteria.3-4: Partly recognizes land relocation but confuses poles/equator, latitude changes, or rotates only selected continents inconsistently.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the 90-degree landmass relocation and notes latitude shifts, but leaves important geographic implications vague or uneven.
criteria.7-8: Accurately tracks the new polar/equatorial placement of major regions and preserves unchanged planetary drivers with only minor slips.
criteria.9-10: Precisely and consistently applies the rotated-surface premise across continents, oceans, cities, climates, and biosphere without introducing premise-breaking assumptions.

criteria.name: Climate and Geophysical Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the main physical mechanisms determining the rotated Earth's outcomes, including latitude, insolation, atmospheric circulation, ocean currents, mountains, rain shadows, ice, deserts, monsoons, and storms.
criteria.1-2: Gives unsupported guesses about hot/cold regions with little or no climate mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions latitude or temperature but omits most circulation, ocean, precipitation, and topographic effects.
criteria.5-6: Explains several key mechanisms such as equatorial heating, polar ice, and rainfall, but treatment is shallow or misses major interactions.
criteria.7-8: Covers Hadley cells, prevailing winds, ocean moderation, mountains, deserts, forests, ice, and storm zones with generally sound causal links.
criteria.9-10: Integrates atmospheric and ocean circulation, seasonal shifts, topography, hydrology, cryosphere, and ecological feedbacks into a nuanced, question-specific climate sketch.

criteria.name: Regional and Downstream Consequence Specificity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives concrete, plausible consequences for major regions and human/ecological systems affected by the 90-degree rotation.
criteria.1-2: Offers only broad statements such as 'everything changes' without region-specific consequences.
criteria.3-4: Names a few places but gives sparse, generic, or implausible outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several continents or cities and some ecological/human impacts, though coverage is incomplete or uneven.
criteria.7-8: Provides plausible outcomes for most major continents, selected cities, ecosystems, agriculture, sea ice, deserts, forests, and hazards.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a rich global assessment including continents, oceans, cities, biomes, agriculture, hydrology, disease/habitat shifts, extreme weather, and civilization-level disruptions.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer links immediate geographic relocation to medium- and long-term climate, ecological, sea-level, and societal consequences in a coherent sequence.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or jumps directly to outcomes without causal sequencing.
criteria.3-4: Has simple cause-effect links but chains are short, incomplete, or frequently illogical.
criteria.5-6: Builds some coherent chains from latitude to climate to ecosystems or society, but misses timescales or feedbacks.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes immediate shock from long-term equilibration and traces multi-step effects through climate, biosphere, and human systems.
criteria.9-10: Maintains robust long-range reasoning across timescales, including transient catastrophe, ice-cap adjustment, sea-level change, ecosystem succession, extinctions, migration, and infrastructure stress.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately acknowledges uncertainty while avoiding internal contradictions and overconfident false precision in this complex climate counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Makes definitive but unsupported predictions, contradicts itself, or ignores uncertainty entirely.
criteria.3-4: Includes token caveats but still gives conflicting or overprecise regional claims.
criteria.5-6: Shows moderate uncertainty awareness and few major contradictions, though some claims exceed the available reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates confidence well, flags dependencies such as ocean circulation and monsoons, and keeps regional claims mostly consistent.
criteria.9-10: Expertly balances speculation and mechanism, states assumptions, marks uncertain cases, avoids false precision, and maintains consistency across all described effects.

items.model_answer:
If Earth's landmasses were rotated 90 degrees, the consequences would be profound and multifaceted, affecting climate, ocean currents, biodiversity, and human civilization.

**Climate and Temperature Distribution**

The most dramatic changes would occur in global climate patterns. Currently, most landmasses are concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere, with Antarctica isolated at the South Pole. A 90-degree rotation would redistribute land across different latitudinal zones, fundamentally altering heat absorption and reflection. Land heats and cools more rapidly than ocean, so regions that were previously oceanic would experience more moderate temperatures, while newly positioned landmasses would face more extreme seasonal variations.

If major continents shifted toward equatorial regions, they would absorb more solar radiation, potentially increasing global temperatures. Conversely, if large landmasses moved toward polar regions, increased ice sheet formation could raise Earth's albedo (reflectivity), potentially triggering cooling or even glaciation cycles.

**Ocean Circulation and Currents**

Ocean currents depend heavily on continental configurations. The current system—including the Gulf Stream, Antarctic Circumpolar Current, and thermohaline circulation—exists because of how landmasses channel and deflect water flow. Rotating continents would completely reorganize these patterns. The thermohaline circulation, which drives global heat distribution and nutrient cycling, could be disrupted or reconfigured entirely, leading to regional climate extremes and altered marine productivity.

**Atmospheric Circulation**

Mountain ranges and large landmasses influence atmospheric circulation by creating barriers to wind flow and generating monsoon systems. A 90-degree rotation would relocate mountain chains like the Himalayas, Andes, and Rockies, fundamentally changing precipitation patterns. Regions currently receiving monsoon rains might become arid, while deserts could transform into fertile zones.

**Biodiversity and Ecosystems**

Ecosystems are finely tuned to their current climatic conditions. A sudden rotation would place tropical species in temperate or polar climates and vice versa, causing mass extinctions. Marine ecosystems would face similar disruption as ocean temperatures, currents, and nutrient availability shifted. Evolutionary adaptation would take millions of years, and many species would not survive the transition.

**Human Civilization**

Human societies are built around current geographic realities—coastlines, river systems, agricultural zones, and climate patterns. A 90-degree rotation would render most infrastructure obsolete. Coastal cities might find themselves inland or underwater depending on new sea levels and continental positions. Agricultural breadbaskets could become uninhabitable, triggering food crises. The geopolitical map would be redrawn entirely.

**Conclusion**

A 90-degree rotation of Earth's landmasses would trigger cascading changes across every Earth system, from atmospheric and oceanic circulation to the survival of species and human societies. The planet would eventually reach a new equilibrium, but the transition would be catastrophic for existing life.

items.question: What If All the Raindrops in a Storm Merged into One Giant Drop?
human_answers: It’s midsummer. The air is hot and heavy. Two old-timers sit on the porch in rocking chairs. [Image: image] On the horizon to the southwest, ominous-looking clouds begin to appear. The towers build as they draw closer, the tops spreading out into an anvil shape. [Image: image] They hear the tinkling of wind chimes as gentle breeze picks up. The sky begins to darken. Air holds water. If you walled off a column of air, from the ground up to the top of the atmosphere, and then cooled the column of air down, the moisture it contained would condense out as rain. If you collected the rain in the bottom of the column, it would fill it to a depth of anywhere between zero and a few dozen centimeters. That depth is what we call the air’s total precipitable water. [Image: image] Normally, the TPW is one or two centimeters. Satellites measure this water vapor content for every point on the globe, producing some truly beautiful maps (http://tropic.ssec.wisc.edu/real-time/mimic-tpw/natl/main.html). We’ll imagine our storm measures 100 kilometers on each side and has a high TPW content of 6 centimeters. This means the water in our rainstorm would have a volume of: \[100\textrm{km}\times100\textrm{km}\times6\textrm{cm}=0.6\textrm{km}^3\] That water would weigh 600 million tons (which happens to be about the current weight of our species). Normally, a portion of this water would fall, scattered, as rain—at most, 6 centimeters of it. In this storm, all that water instead condenses into one giant drop, a sphere of water over a kilometer in diameter. We’ll assume it forms a couple kilometers above the surface, since that’s where most rain condenses (http://rsd.gsfc.nasa.gov/912/edop/misc/1736.pdf). [Image: image] The drop begins to fall. For five or six seconds, nothing is visible. Then, the base of the cloud begins to bulge downward. For a moment, it looks a little like a funnel cloud is forming. Then the bulge widens, and at the ten-second mark, the bottom of the drop emerges from the cloud. [Image: image] The drop is now falling at 90 meters per second (200 mph). The roaring wind whips up the surface of the water into spray. The leading edge of the droplet turns to foam as air is forced into the liquid. If it kept falling for long enough, these forces would gradually disperse the entire droplet into rain. Before that can happen, about 20 seconds after formation, the edge of the droplet hits the ground. The water is now moving at over 200 m/s (450 mph). Right under the point of impact, the air is unable to rush out of the way fast enough, and the compression heats it so quickly that the grass would catch fire if it had time. Fortunately for the grass, this heat lasts only a few milliseconds because it’s doused by the arrival of a lot of cold water. Unfortunately for the grass, the cold water is moving at over half the speed of sound. [Image: image] If you were floating in the center of this sphere during this episode, you wouldn’t have felt anything unusual up until now. It’d be pretty dark in the middle, but if you had enough time (and lung capacity) to swim a few hundred meters out toward the edge, you’d be able to make out the dim glow of daylight. [Image: image] As the raindrop approached the ground, the buildup of air resistance would lead to an increase in pressure that would make your ears pop. But seconds later, when the water contacted the surface, you’d be crushed to death—the shock would briefly create pressures exceeding those at the bottom of the Marianas Trench. The water plows into the ground, but the bedrock is unyielding. The pressure forces the water sideways, creating a supersonic omnidirectional jet that destroys everything in its path. [Image: image] The wall of water expands outward kilometer by kilometer, ripping up trees, houses, and topsoil as it goes. The house, porch, and old-timers are obliterated in an instant. Everything within a few kilometers is completely destroyed, leaving a pool of mud down to bedrock. The splash continues outward, demolishing all structures out to distances of 20 or 30 kilometers. At this distance, areas shielded by mountains or ridges are protected, and the flood begins to flow along natural valleys and waterways. The broader region is largely protected from the effects of the storm, though areas hundreds of kilometers downstream experience flash flooding in the hours after the impact. News trickles out into the world about the inexplicable disaster. There is widespread shock and puzzlement, and for a while, every new cloud in the sky causes mass panic. Fear reigns supreme as the world fears rain supreme, but years pass without any signs of the disaster repeating. Atmospheric scientists try for years to piece together what happened, but no explanation is forthcoming. Eventually, they give up, and the unexplained meteorological phenomenon is simply dubbed a “Skrillex Storm”—because, in the words of one researcher, “It had one hell of a drop.”

items.model_answer:
If every raindrop in a typical thunderstorm merged into a single giant drop before hitting the ground, the result would be catastrophic — far more like an asteroid impact than a rainstorm.

A moderate thunderstorm might drop on the order of 10 million to a billion liters of water across its footprint. Compressed into one sphere, even 10 million liters would form a drop about 27 meters across; a billion liters would make one roughly 125 meters in diameter, weighing a million tons. At the upper end of severe storms (which can dump trillions of liters), you'd get a sphere a kilometer or more wide.

Surface tension cannot hold a drop that large together — water's cohesion only stabilizes droplets up to about 5–6 millimeters before they break apart from air resistance. So in reality the "giant drop" would shatter immediately. But if we imagine it magically holding together until impact, here's what would happen:

Falling from cloud base (roughly 1–2 km up), the drop would accelerate under gravity. Air resistance scales with cross-section, but the mass scales with volume, so terminal velocity rises dramatically with size. A 100-meter water sphere would reach speeds of several hundred meters per second — comparable to a small meteor. The kinetic energy of a million-ton mass moving at, say, 200 m/s is around 20 trillion joules, equivalent to roughly 5 kilotons of TNT, similar to a small nuclear weapon.

Impact effects would include a crater tens of meters deep, a violent shockwave flattening trees and buildings for kilometers, and a massive splash sending a tsunami of water and debris outward. The air displaced by the falling sphere would itself produce a hurricane-force downburst preceding the impact. Anything directly beneath would be obliterated not by drowning but by hydraulic pressure — water at those speeds behaves like concrete.

Meanwhile, the rest of the storm's region would receive essentially no rain at all, since all the moisture is concentrated in one place. So you'd trade a beneficial soaking of a wide area for a localized natural disaster — a strong argument for why evolution and physics favor rain arriving as billions of tiny, gentle drops.

edus.text: If every raindrop in a typical thunderstorm merged into a single giant drop before hitting the ground,
the result would be catastrophic —
far more like an asteroid impact than a rainstorm.
A moderate thunderstorm might drop on the order of 10 million to a billion liters of water across its footprint.
Compressed into one sphere, even 10 million liters would form a drop about 27 meters across;
a billion liters would make one roughly 125 meters in diameter, weighing a million tons.
At the upper end of severe storms (which can dump trillions of liters), you'd get a sphere a kilometer or more wide.
Surface tension cannot hold a drop that large together —
water's cohesion only stabilizes droplets up to about 5–6 millimeters before they break apart from air resistance.
So in reality the "giant drop" would shatter immediately.
But if we imagine it magically holding together until impact,
here's what would happen:
Falling from cloud base (roughly 1–2 km up), the drop would accelerate under gravity.
Air resistance scales with cross-section,
but the mass scales with volume,
so terminal velocity rises dramatically with size.
A 100-meter water sphere would reach speeds of several hundred meters per second —
comparable to a small meteor.
The kinetic energy of a million-ton mass moving at, say, 200 m/s is around 20 trillion joules,
equivalent to roughly 5 kilotons of TNT,
similar to a small nuclear weapon.
Impact effects would include a crater tens of meters deep,
a violent shockwave flattening trees and buildings for kilometers,
and a massive splash sending a tsunami of water and debris outward.
The air displaced by the falling sphere would itself produce a hurricane-force downburst preceding the impact.
Anything directly beneath would be obliterated
not by drowning but by hydraulic pressure —
water at those speeds behaves like concrete.
Meanwhile, the rest of the storm's region would receive essentially no rain at all,
since all the moisture is concentrated in one place.
So you'd trade a beneficial soaking of a wide area for a localized natural disaster —
a strong argument for why evolution and physics favor rain arriving as billions of tiny, gentle drops.

items.question: What If Everyone on Earth Pointed a Laser Pointer at the Moon?
human_answers: Not if we use regular laser pointers. The first thing to consider is that not everyone can see the Moon at once. We could gather everyone in one spot, but we learned our lesson about that (http://what-if.xkcd.com/8/) a few weeks ago. Instead, let’s just pick a time when the Moon is visible to as many people as possible. Since about 75% of the world’s population lives between 0°E and 120°E (http://www.good.is/posts/mapping-the-world-s-population-by-latitude-longitude/), we should try this while the Moon is somewhere over the Arabian Sea. We can try to illuminate either a new moon or a full moon. The new moon is darker, making it easier to see our lasers. But the new moon is a trickier target, because it’s mostly visible during the day—washing out the effect. Brightness aside, an ideal time would probably be 2:00 PM EST on December 27th, 2012, when a full moon will be high in the sky above Mumbai and Islamabad. At that point, the Moon will be visible to approximately five billion people—most of Asia, Europe, and Africa—about as many as can ever see it at one time. But let’s pick a quarter moon instead, so we can see the effect on the dark side. We’ll avoid the December 21st quarter moon to avoid encouraging any Mayan nonsense, and pick the one on January 4th, 2013, half an hour after midnight (GMT). It’ll be day in East Asia but night in Africa and Europe. Here’s our target: [Image: image] The typical red laser pointer is about 5 milliwatts, and a good one has a tight enough beam to actually hit the Moon—though it’d be spread out over a large fraction of the surface when it got there. The atmosphere would distort the beam a bit, and absorb some of it, but most of the light would make it. [Image: image] Let’s assume everyone has steady enough aim to hit the Moon, but no more than that, and the light is spread evenly across the surface. At half an hour after midnight (GMT), everyone aims and presses the button. This is what happens: [Image: image] Well, that’s disappointing. It makes sense, though. Sunlight bathes the Moon in a bit over a kilowatt of energy per square meter. Since the Moon’s cross-sectional area is around 10^13 square meters, it’s bathed in about 10^16 watts of sunlight—ten petawatts, or two megawatts per person—far outshining their five milliwatt laser pointer. There are varying efficiencies in each part of this system, but none of it changes that basic equation. [Image: image] 5 milliwatts is wimpy. We can do better. A 1-watt laser is an extremely dangerous thing. It’s not just powerful enough to blind you—it’s capable of burning skin and setting things on fire. Obviously, they’re not legal for consumer purchase in the US. Just kidding! You can pick one up for $300 (http://www.wickedlasers.com/arctic). So suppose we spend the $2 trillion to buy one-watt green lasers for everyone. (Memo to presidential candidates: this policy would win my vote.) In addition to being more powerful, green laser light is nearer to the middle of the visible spectrum, so the eye is more sensitive to it and it seems brighter. Here’s the effect: [Image: image] Dang. The laser pointers we’re using put out about 150 lumens of light (more than most flashlights) in a beam 5 arc-minutes wide. This lights up the surface of the Moon with about half a lux (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lux) of illumination—compared to about 130,000 lux from the sun. (Even if we aimed them all perfectly, it would only manage half a dozen lux over about 10% of the Moon’s face.) By comparison, the full moon lights up the Earth’s surface with about one lux of illumination—which means that not only would our lasers be too weak to see from Earth, but if you were standing on the Moon, the laser light on the landscape would be fainter than Moonlight is to us on Earth. [Image: image] With advances in lithium batteries and LED technology over the last ten years, the high-performance flashlight market has exploded. But it’s clear that flashlights aren’t gonna cut it. So let’s skip past all of that and give everyone a Nightsun. You may not recognize the name, but chances are you’ve seen one in operation: It’s the searchlight mounted on police and Coast Guard helicopters. With an output on the order of 50,000 lumens, it’s capable of turning a patch ground from night to day. The beam is several degrees wide, we’ll want some focusing lenses to get it down to the half-degree needed to hit the Moon. Here’s the effect: [Image: image] It’s hard to see, but we’re making progress! The beam is providing 20 lux of illumination, outshining the ambient light on the night half by a factor of two! However, it’s quite hard to see, and it certainly hasn’t affected the light half. [Image: image] Let’s swap out each Nightsun for an IMAX projector array—a 30,000-watt pair of water-cooled lamps with a combined output of over over a million lumens. [Image: image] Still barely visible. [Image: image] At the top of the Luxor Hotel in Las Vegas is the most powerful spotlight on Earth. Let’s give one of them to everyone. [Image: image] Oh, and let’s add a lens array to each so the entire beam is focused on the Moon: [Image: image] Our light is definitely visible, so we’ve accomplished our goal! Good job, team. [Image: image] … Well. The Department of Defense has developed megawatt lasers, designed for destroying incoming missiles in mid-flight. The Boeing YAL-1 was a megawatt-class chemical oxygen iodine laser mounted in a 747. It was an infrared laser, so it wasn’t directly visible, but we can imagine building a visible-light laser with similar power. Let’s give one to everyone. [Image: image] Finally, we’ve managed to match the brightness of sunlight! We’re also drawing five petawatts of power, which is double the world’s average electricity consumption. [Image: image] Ok, let’s mount a megawatt laser on every square meter of the surface of Asia. Powering this array of 50 trillion lasers would use up Earth’s oil reserves in approximately two minutes, but for those two minutes, the Moon would look like this: [Image: image] The Moon shines as brightly as the midmorning sun, and by the end of the two minutes, the lunar regolith is heated to a glow. [Image: image] Ok, let’s step even more firmly outside the realm of plausibility. The most powerful laser on Earth is the confinement beam at the National Ignition Facility (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Ignition_Facility), a fusion research laboratory. It’s an ultraviolet laser with an output of 500 terawatts. However, it only fires in single pulses lasting a few nanoseconds, so the total energy delivered is about equivalent to a quarter-cup of gasoline. Let’s imagine we somehow found a way to power and fire it continuously, gave one to everyone, and pointed them all at the Moon. Unfortunately, the laser energy flow would turn the atmosphere to plasma, instantly igniting the Earth’s surface and killing us all. But let’s assume that the lasers somehow pass through the atmosphere without interacting. Under those circumstances, it turns out Earth still catches fire. The reflected light from the Moon would be four thousand times brighter than the noonday sun. Moonlight would become bright enough to boil away Earth’s oceans in less than a year. But forget the Earth—what would happen to the Moon? The laser itself would exert enough radiation pressure to accelerate the Moon at about one ten millionth of a gee. This acceleration wouldn’t be noticeable in the short term, but over the years, it adds up to enough to push it free from Earth orbit. … If radiation pressure were the only force involved. 40 megajoules of energy is enough (http://www.psfc.mit.edu/library1/catalog/reports/2000/09rr/09rr011/09rr011_full.pdf) to vaporize a kilogram of rock. Assuming Moon rocks have an average density of about 3 kg/liter, the lasers would pump out enough energy to vaporize four meters of lunar bedrock per second: \[\frac{5\text{ billion people}\times 500\frac{\mathrm{terawatts}}{\text{person}}}{\pi\times\text{Moon radius}^2}\times20\frac{\mathrm{megajoules}}{\mathrm{kilogram}}\times 3\frac{\mathrm{kilograms}}{\mathrm{liter}}\approx4 \frac{\mathrm{meters}}{\text{second}}\] However, the actual lunar rock won’t evaporate that fast—for a reason that turns out to be very important. When a chunk of rock is vaporized, it doesn’t just disappear. The surface layer of the Moon becomes a plasma, but that plasma is still blocking the path of the beam. Our laser keeps pouring more and more energy into the plasma, and the plasma keeps getting hotter and hotter. The particles bounce off each other, slam into the surface of the Moon, and eventually blast away into space at a terrific speed. This flow of material effectively turns the entire surface of the Moon into a rocket engine—and a surprisingly efficient one, too. Using lasers to blast off surface material like this is called laser ablation, and it turns out to be a promising method for spacecraft propulsion (http://materials.web.psi.ch/Publications/Publ_MatDev_files/2010/Claude_JPP_2010.pdf). The Moon is massive, but slowly and surely the rock plasma jet begins to push it away from the Earth. (The jet would also scour clean the face of the Earth and destroy the lasers, but we’re pretending for the moment that they’re invulnerable.) The plasma also physically tears away the lunar surface, a complicated interaction that’s tricky to model. But if we make the wild guess that the particles in the plasma exit at an average speed of 500 kilometers per second, then it will take a few months for the Moon to be pushed out of range of our laser. It will keep most of its mass, but escape Earth’s gravity and enter a lopsided orbit around the sun. Technically, the Moon won’t become a new planet, under the IAU definition of a planet. Since its new orbit crosses Earth’s, it will be considered a dwarf planet like Pluto. This Earth-crossing orbit will lead to periodic unpredictable orbital perturbation. Eventually it will either be slingshotted into the Sun, ejected toward the outer Solar System, or slammed into one of the planets—quite possibly ours. I think we can all agree that in this case, we’d deserve it. Scorecard: [Image: image] And that, at last, is enough power.
