items.question: What If a 100-Foot Diamond Meteor Hit Earth at Light Speed?
human_answers: Nothing made of matter can go at the speed of light. But that’s ok—we can get close enough! No matter how fast you push something, it will never quite get up to light speed. This seems like it can’t be right, but it is. Our universe has some weird rules. But the closer something gets to the speed of light, the more energy and momentum it has—and this energy and momentum go up without limit. We’ll start slow and work our way up. 1 kilometer per second: If we drop the meteor from the edge of space, 100 kilometers up, it’ll punch through the atmosphere without slowing down too much and hit the ground moving about Mach 3—over a kilometer a second. As it falls, it compresses the air in front of it. When the air is compressed, it heats it up. (This is the same thing that heats up spacecraft and meteors—actual air friction has little to do with that.) By the time it reaches the ground, the lower surface will have heated to over 500℃, which is enough to glow visibly. When it hits the ground, two minutes after it was released, it makes a crater 300 meters across—the size of a school, shattering into fragments in the process. [Image: image] 11 kilometers per second: If we set the diamond in space a little ways away from the Earth, and let it fall toward us, it will hit at about 11 kilometers per second. This is Earth’s escape velocity, and anything that hits the Earth from space will—thanks to gravity—be going at least that fast. At 11 kilometers per second, the brief descent would be visible as a fireball. The energy of the impact would be comparable to a small atomic bomb, and the crater it would create would be a kilometer across—a little smaller than Meteor Crater in Arizona. [Image: image] 72 kilometers per second: This is just about the fastest that anything can hit the Earth if it’s orbiting the Sun. The Leonid meteor shower hits at this speed. Oddly, the speed that something is going doesn’t really affect how deeply it digs into the ground. Isaac Newton came up with a very clever idea (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_depth) for estimating how deeply projectiles will go in their targets before stopping. It turns out that no matter how fast a projectile is going, if it hits something that’s about the same density, it will only go about one body-length in. [Image: image] However, it will make quite a splash. The 72-kilometer-per-second diamond sphere blasts out a crater over two kilometers across, with an energy release comparable to that of the biggest fusion bombs. Here’s where things get weird. 3,000 kilometers per second = 0.01c: This would be pretty bad. The thing that makes this a little unpredictable is the fact that at speeds in the range of hundreds of kilometers per second, the air begins to undergo nuclear fusion (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0032063389900305) (Google that paper title to find the full text). This, combined with plain old plasma heating, may manage to eat apart the diamond sphere completely before it reaches the ground. But it doesn’t do the ground much good. The sphere doesn’t spread out enough to make a difference, and it still hits the ground in roughly one spot. The blast releases a thousand times more energy than the largest nuclear weapon, devastating whatever region it came down over. It gouges out a massive crater—though not the biggest one Earth has ever seen. [Image: image] 0.99c: This is where relativity kicks in. At these speeds, the bonds holding the sphere together are completely irrelevant. It’s just a collection of carbon atoms moving so fast that Lorentz contraction flattens the whole thing into a pancake (although we wouldn’t be able to see that visually (http://www.math.ubc.ca/~cass/courses/m309-01a/cook/terrell1.html)). The SRIM (http://www.srim.org/) particle physics simulation tool can help answer some questions about what happens when it hits. The carbon atoms in the ball carry about 70 GeV of energy each. They’re actually moving too fast to fuse directly with the air—they just pass through it completely. The air molecules punch three meters into the face of the ball before coming to a rest inside it, and it arrives at the ground with a bunch more matter in it than it started with. It’s also expanding rapidly. When it hits the surface, it disintegrates completely, digging downward and outward, carving a cone-shaped path down through the bedrock. The impact depth equation no longer applies, since the atoms are literally passing through each other. The energy cracks a hole in the crust and blows open a crater so big you can see the molten mantle. This delivers the energy of 50 dinosaur-killing Chicxulub impacts—enough to cause a mass extinction, if not end life completely. [Image: image] I’ve always thought that one of the the great things about physics is that you can add more digits to any number and see what happens and nobody can stop you. 0.9999999c: At this speed, every carbon molecule carries 25 TeV of energy, comparable to particles in the beam of the Large Hadron Collider. A little faster, and we might spot Higgs bosons in the impact debris. As it stands, the whole thing hits the planet with about the kinetic energy of the orbiting Moon. It’s enough to punch a gaping hole in the mantle and shake up the surface across the whole planet, turning it molten. This probably ends all life on and around Earth. Oops, cat stepped on my keyboard again and I added a bunch more 9s. 0.9999999999999999999999951c The fastest object (with mass) in recorded history might be the Oh-My-God particle (no relation to the God particle), a proton from space that plowed into the atmosphere over Utah in 1991. It was moving at 99.99999999999999999999951% of the speed of light, which meant it packed the kinetic energy of a baseball—in a single proton. The cascade of particles it blasted apart dwarfed anything the LHC could produce. Nobody knows how it got to be moving so fast. Particles moving that fast hit the Earth a handful of times a year. They seem to come from the general direction of exploding galaxies, but what happened to to make them leave in such a hurry—and why they haven’t slowed down more before they got here—is something of a mystery. Let’s give Aidan’s diamond meteor the speed of the Oh My God particle. These speeds are so high that my copy of SRIM flatly refuses to simulate them. However, we can get some idea from looking at how cosmic rays cascade through rock. The diamond sweeps out a column of atmosphere without seeming to notice and disappears into the crust. A cloud of expanding plasma and radiation grows around the entry point as the energy ripples outward through the body of the planet. Forty milliseconds later the entire far side expands outward in an incandescent cloud. The diamond meteor, and the cascade of particles it created as it collided with the crust, is spread out throughout the body of our planet. The superheated planet glows brighter than the sun. The momentum would be enough to knock the Earth into a different orbit—but the Earth is no more. The energy deposited is ten thousand times greater than the planet’s gravitational binding energy, and the planet is blown into an expanding cloud of plasma, with a particularly energetic streamer extending away from the far side of the impact site, out into space. The Sun hiccups and flares as it absorbs waves of dust. The surfaces of Mars and Venus are scoured clean by the waves of incredibly high-energy plasma. [Image: image] And in the distant future, an alien astronomer on a world hundreds of light-years from Earth frowns at a beeping detector, and wonders what violent event would make a particle move so fast.

items.model_answer:
A 100-foot diamond meteor traveling at the speed of light is, of course, physically impossible — any object with mass requires infinite energy to reach c — but if we set aside relativity's prohibition and just compute the kinetic energy as though such an impact could occur, the result would be one of the most catastrophic events imaginable.

First, the mass. A 100-foot diameter sphere has a volume of roughly 14,800 cubic feet, or about 420 cubic meters. Diamond has a density of around 3,500 kg/m³, giving the meteor a mass of roughly 1.47 million kilograms (1.47 × 10⁶ kg).

If we naively use the classical kinetic energy formula KE = ½mv² with v = c (3 × 10⁸ m/s), we get about 6.6 × 10²² joules. That's already roughly 100 times the energy of the dinosaur-killing Chicxulub impact, enough to extinguish nearly all complex life on Earth.

But at light speed we should use the relativistic energy expression, and here the math breaks down — the Lorentz factor γ goes to infinity, so the total energy diverges to infinity. Even at 99.9999% of light speed, the kinetic energy of that diamond would be on the order of 10²⁶ joules or more, comparable to the gravitational binding energy of the Earth itself (around 2.5 × 10³² J only at extreme γ factors).

Practically, the consequences would be:

The meteor would not "hit" the planet in any normal sense. Atmospheric atoms in its path would interact with such violence that each collision would behave like a particle-accelerator event, producing showers of exotic particles and gamma radiation. The atmosphere wouldn't slow it meaningfully — it would punch through in microseconds while triggering a cascade of relativistic debris.

On contact with the ground, the energy deposition would vaporize not just the impact site but a huge volume of crust, mantle, and possibly punch clean through the planet. The Earth could be shattered, partially ejected into space, or — if the energy is high enough — fully unbound, with its fragments dispersed into a debris cloud orbiting the Sun.

A blast of gamma rays and relativistic ejecta would sterilize nearby planets, and the explosion would be visible across the solar system, briefly outshining the Sun.

In short: at any meaningful fraction of light speed, the diamond's composition becomes irrelevant. It is no longer a meteor — it is a cosmic-scale energy weapon, and Earth simply ceases to exist as a coherent world.

items.model_answer:
If modern China had fully replaced Chinese characters (hanzi) with a phonetic script—most plausibly Hanyu Pinyin, which was developed in the 1950s precisely with this possibility in mind—the consequences would have rippled across literacy, culture, politics, and China's global position in complex ways.

The most immediate effect would have been on literacy. Mao Zedong himself reportedly favored eventual romanization, and reformers argued that characters were too difficult for mass education. A phonetic script would have dramatically shortened the time needed to achieve basic literacy, possibly accelerating rural education in the 1950s–70s and boosting economic development somewhat earlier. Printing, typewriting, and early computing would also have been far simpler, sparing China decades of input-method engineering (though ironically, by the 1990s Chinese character input became efficient enough that this advantage shrank).

The cultural costs would have been severe. Classical Chinese literature, philosophy, poetry, and historical records rely heavily on characters for meaning, because Mandarin has extensive homophony—dozens of distinct morphemes share the same syllable like "shi" or "yi." A pinyin-only text of classical poetry or even a newspaper would be ambiguous in ways characters effortlessly resolve. Either Chinese would have had to undergo significant lexical reform (replacing monosyllabic literary words with disyllabic spoken equivalents, as Vietnamese did when it abandoned chữ Nôm for the Latin alphabet), or readers would lose direct access to most pre-modern texts. Within a generation or two, classical literature would become the domain of specialists, much as it did in Vietnam and Korea after their own script reforms.

Politically, the script unifies a country whose "dialects"—Cantonese, Hokkien, Shanghainese, Hakka—are mutually unintelligible spoken languages. Characters allow a Cantonese speaker and a Mandarin speaker to read the same newspaper. A pinyin script based on Mandarin pronunciation would have privileged Mandarin even more starkly, likely accelerating the decline of regional languages and possibly fueling resentment in places like Guangdong, Fujian, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. Taiwan and overseas Chinese communities would almost certainly have refused to follow, deepening a cultural rift.

Internationally, China's soft power would look different. Japan and Korea, which historically borrowed characters, would have lost a visible cultural anchor to China; the East Asian "Sinographic sphere" would have fragmented further. On the other hand, foreigners would find written Chinese vastly easier to learn, possibly increasing global engagement with Chinese-language media.

Finally, there is the question of identity. Characters are not merely a writing system in China but a civilizational symbol stretching back over three thousand years, tied to calligraphy, seals, couplets, and national self-image. Abandoning them would have been experienced by many as a rupture comparable to Atatürk's Turkish script reform—modernizing and clarifying, but also severing a population from its own past. It is largely for this reason that the reform was quietly shelved after the 1950s in favor of simplified characters, a compromise that preserved continuity while easing learning. In the counterfactual, China would be more literate sooner, more linguistically homogenized, more globally accessible in print—but culturally thinner and historically more distant from itself.

edus.text: If modern China had fully replaced Chinese characters (hanzi) with a phonetic script
most plausibly Hanyu Pinyin
which was developed in the 1950s precisely with this possibility in mind
the consequences would have rippled across literacy, culture, politics, and China's global position in complex ways.
The most immediate effect would have been on literacy.
Mao Zedong himself reportedly favored eventual romanization
and reformers argued that characters were too difficult for mass education.
A phonetic script would have dramatically shortened the time needed to achieve basic literacy
possibly accelerating rural education in the 1950s–70s
and boosting economic development somewhat earlier.
Printing, typewriting, and early computing would also have been far simpler
sparing China decades of input-method engineering
though ironically, by the 1990s Chinese character input became efficient enough
that this advantage shrank.
The cultural costs would have been severe.
Classical Chinese literature, philosophy, poetry, and historical records rely heavily on characters for meaning
because Mandarin has extensive homophony
dozens of distinct morphemes share the same syllable like "shi" or "yi."
A pinyin-only text of classical poetry or even a newspaper would be ambiguous
in ways characters effortlessly resolve.
Either Chinese would have had to undergo significant lexical reform
replacing monosyllabic literary words with disyllabic spoken equivalents
as Vietnamese did when it abandoned chữ Nôm for the Latin alphabet
or readers would lose direct access to most pre-modern texts.
Within a generation or two, classical literature would become the domain of specialists
much as it did in Vietnam and Korea after their own script reforms.
Politically, the script unifies a country whose "dialects"—Cantonese, Hokkien, Shanghainese, Hakka—are mutually unintelligible spoken languages.
Characters allow a Cantonese speaker and a Mandarin speaker to read the same newspaper.
A pinyin script based on Mandarin pronunciation would have privileged Mandarin even more starkly
likely accelerating the decline of regional languages
and possibly fueling resentment in places like Guangdong, Fujian, Hong Kong, and Taiwan.
Taiwan and overseas Chinese communities would almost certainly have refused to follow
deepening a cultural rift.
Internationally, China's soft power would look different.
Japan and Korea, which historically borrowed characters, would have lost a visible cultural anchor to China
the East Asian "Sinographic sphere" would have fragmented further.
On the other hand, foreigners would find written Chinese vastly easier to learn
possibly increasing global engagement with Chinese-language media.
Finally, there is the question of identity.
Characters are not merely a writing system in China
but a civilizational symbol stretching back over three thousand years
tied to calligraphy, seals, couplets, and national self-image.
Abandoning them would have been experienced by many as a rupture comparable to Atatürk's Turkish script reform
modernizing and clarifying
but also severing a population from its own past.
It is largely for this reason that the reform was quietly shelved after the 1950s in favor of simplified characters
a compromise that preserved continuity while easing learning.
In the counterfactual, China would be more literate sooner, more linguistically homogenized, more globally accessible in print
but culturally thinner and historically more distant from itself.

items.question: What If Japan Had Attacked the Panama Canal Instead of Pearl Harbor?
human_answers: > So I want to know, did the Japanese Navy have the ability to destroy it in a surprise attack, let's say on 1941 Dec 7? I'm asking if the Japanese Navy had the ability.

The Canal is 8400 miles from Tokyo, compared to 4000 miles for Pearl Harbour. The Japanese carriers are stated of having a range of 10,000 miles at a cruising speed of about 16 knots, but remember that drag varies as the square of speed.

Destroying those locks is going to be harder than you think. They are very large, at 110 feet x 1,050 feet, and the lock gates have to have been built to stand up to accidental collisions with large ships (at low speed, admittedly).
items.original_question: 1941 年 12 月 7 日，日本是否可以在突然袭击中瞄准巴拿马运河而不是珍珠港？这个问题来自一个稍微相关的问题。第二次世界大战时，美国大部分工业都位于东海岸，包括所有航母和战列舰的造船业。如果巴拿马运河沉没，将大大减少美国海军在太平洋的后勤保障。所以我想知道，日本海军是否有能力在突然袭击中摧毁它，比如1941年12月7日？到目前为止我所知道的： - 巴拿马运河每条航道有 6 个水闸。这些锁有混凝土墙，但有空心钢门，根据这部纪录片：https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d-CaBIKTl4M，在 1:11:00 你可以看到它们是一个空心框架。一枚炸弹或鱼雷可能会在上面炸出一个洞，但可能不足以立即耗尽船闸的水。 - 日本俯冲轰炸机接受过训练，他们在二战早期（珊瑚海、中途岛）遭受的许多航母打击就证明了这一点。注意，我说的是打击，不一定是杀戮。我回顾了这两场战斗，很多次，美国航母都被击中了，但都幸存了（当时美国航母似乎比日本航母坚强得多）。 我只是想指出日本俯冲轰炸机似乎训练有素且准确性良好。 - 编辑：潘

items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the outcome of World War II would likely have been dramatically different, though not necessarily in Japan's favor.

**Strategic Impact:**

Destroying or severely damaging the Panama Canal would have been a more devastating blow to American logistics than Pearl Harbor. The Canal was critical for moving the U.S. Pacific Fleet between oceans—without it, ships would need to travel around South America, adding weeks to deployment times. This would have significantly hampered America's ability to fight a two-ocean war against both Japan and Germany.

**The Critical Difference:**

However, Pearl Harbor's actual value to Japan wasn't just the damage inflicted—it was that it failed to provoke immediate American capitulation while simultaneously enraging the American public. An attack on the Panama Canal, being on the mainland and affecting a vital economic artery, might have produced even greater American fury and resolve.

**Tactical Challenges:**

Attacking the Canal would have been extraordinarily difficult. It was much farther from Japanese bases than Hawaii, requiring a longer, more vulnerable approach. The lock system, while vulnerable, would have required precision bombing or sabotage rather than the naval aviation strike that worked at Pearl Harbor. Japan would have needed to commit substantial resources with uncertain results.

**The Bigger Picture:**

Most importantly, attacking the Canal instead of Pearl Harbor would have left the U.S. Pacific Fleet intact and operational. Those carriers, battleships, and supporting vessels that were damaged or destroyed at Pearl Harbor would have remained a potent threat. Japan's entire strategy depended on crippling American naval power in the Pacific to buy time for consolidating their territorial gains. Without neutralizing the fleet, Japan would have faced immediate, overwhelming naval opposition.

**Likely Outcome:**

Japan probably still loses the war, possibly faster. The industrial and demographic advantages of the United States were simply too great. An intact Pacific Fleet could have contested Japanese expansion from day one, while American resolve to rebuild Canal infrastructure would have been absolute. Japan's best-case scenario—forcing a negotiated peace—would have been even less achievable without first removing American naval power from the Pacific theater.

nodes.text: If Japan had attacked the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor in December 1941,
the outcome of World War II would likely have been dramatically different,
though not necessarily in Japan's favor.
Destroying or severely damaging the Panama Canal would have been a more devastating blow to American logistics than Pearl Harbor.
The Canal was critical for moving the U.S. Pacific Fleet between oceans—
without it, ships would need to travel around South America,
adding weeks to deployment times.
This would have significantly hampered America's ability to fight a two-ocean war against both Japan and Germany.
However, Pearl Harbor's actual value to Japan wasn't just the damage inflicted—
it was that it failed to provoke immediate American capitulation
while simultaneously enraging the American public.
An attack on the Panama Canal, being on the mainland and affecting a vital economic artery, might have produced even greater American fury and resolve.
Attacking the Canal would have been extraordinarily difficult.
It was much farther from Japanese bases than Hawaii,
requiring a longer, more vulnerable approach.
The lock system, while vulnerable, would have required precision bombing or sabotage rather than the naval aviation strike that worked at Pearl Harbor.
Japan would have needed to commit substantial resources with uncertain results.
Most importantly, attacking the Canal instead of Pearl Harbor would have left the U.S. Pacific Fleet intact and operational.
Those carriers, battleships, and supporting vessels that were damaged or destroyed at Pearl Harbor would have remained a potent threat.
Japan's entire strategy depended on crippling American naval power in the Pacific
to buy time for consolidating their territorial gains.
Without neutralizing the fleet, Japan would have faced immediate, overwhelming naval opposition.
Japan probably still loses the war, possibly faster.
The industrial and demographic advantages of the United States were simply too great.
An intact Pacific Fleet could have contested Japanese expansion from day one,
while American resolve to rebuild Canal infrastructure would have been absolute.
Japan's best-case scenario—forcing a negotiated peace—
would have been even less achievable
without first removing American naval power from the Pacific theater.

items.question: What If Eighteenth-Century European Armies Had Returned to the Crossbow?
human_answers: Yes, a trained archer can probably put more effective shots on an unarmored target than a trained musketman of the 18th century. The problem is that word trained.

One often missed factor is that arrows are delicate and require skilled fletchers to make them. The English invasion of France under Edward IV in 1475 required two years lead time producing enough arrows to supply his troops on campaign.

There have already been some good explanations, regarding relative ease of use for muskets, as well as less training required to use, but I have not seen two constants of campaigning considered: Rain and Disease. Gunpowder and bowstrings both need to be kep...

There's a lot of very good answers already; but I'd like to add on to what @Schwern has said from a Japanese perspective. When the musket was introduced in Japan in the 16th century, it quickly overtook archery in terms of importance.
Schwern had a lot of very good points, but there are other factors as well. - siege warfare.
items.original_question: 18世纪盔甲逐渐被淘汰，为什么射箭没有卷土重来？即使我们考虑到训练一个人使用弓比训练火枪要繁琐得多，为什么强弩没有卷土重来呢？据报道，其有效射程为 300m，仍然比 18 世纪的滑膛步枪好得多，而且可能也更准确。一支由14世纪强弩手组成的军队似乎比一支燧发枪手组成的军队有更多的战术选择，那么为什么十字弓没有卷土重来呢？

items.model_answer:
If eighteenth-century European armies had returned to the crossbow as a primary infantry weapon, the consequences would have rippled through tactics, logistics, industry, and ultimately the geopolitical balance of the period.

The first thing to recognize is why armies had abandoned the crossbow in the first place. By 1700, the smoothbore flintlock musket with a socket bayonet had become the standard infantry weapon not because it was more accurate or faster-firing than a crossbow (in raw mechanical terms, a trained crossbowman could match or exceed a musketeer's three rounds per minute, and was far more accurate at moderate range), but because muskets were vastly easier to mass-produce to a uniform standard, required less individual skill, carried a bayonet for shock action, produced terrifying noise and smoke that affected morale and cavalry horses, and could penetrate the heavier armor that crossbows had struggled against in the sixteenth century. A return to crossbows would mean abandoning these advantages.

Tactically, the linear formations that defined the age—long thin lines delivering volley fire—were built around the musket's characteristics: short effective range (around 80–100 meters), inaccuracy compensated by mass, and the bayonet for close combat. Crossbows would have encouraged either a return to deeper formations with pavise-bearers or large skirmishing screens making use of the weapon's better accuracy and its silent, smokeless discharge. Battlefields would have been quieter and visually clearer, since gunpowder smoke would no longer blanket engagements after the first few volleys. Officers could actually see what was happening, command-and-control would improve, and aimed fire would matter more than volume.

However, the crossbow's killing power against eighteenth-century targets would have been a serious problem. A heavy military crossbow could pierce mail and even some plate at close range, but soldiers of this period wore no armor at all. Against unarmored men a musket ball delivered far more shocking, often unsurvivable trauma than a bolt, and crossbows would have produced fewer immediate casualties per hit. Combined with their lack of a practical bayonet equivalent, crossbow-armed infantry would have been at the mercy of cavalry, which dominated open ground when not deterred by massed musketry and bayonet hedges. Pike support might have had to be reintroduced, undoing a century of tactical simplification.

Logistically, a crossbow army would have escaped dependence on saltpeter, sulfur, and the elaborate powder-mill infrastructure that constrained eighteenth-century campaigns. Wet weather, which routinely crippled flintlock armies, would matter much less. Powder magazines—major strategic targets and accident risks—would shrink. On the other hand, bolts are heavier and bulkier per shot than musket cartridges, steel prods require skilled craftsmen, and the spanning mechanisms (cranequins or windlasses for heavy bows, goat's-foot levers for lighter ones) demanded maintenance by armorers rather than the simple repair flintlocks needed in the field.

The strategic implications follow from these trade-offs. A power that retained muskets while its rivals reverted to crossbows would enjoy a decisive battlefield advantage, particularly in the open-field set-piece engagements that decided wars like the War of the Austrian Succession and the Seven Years' War. Frederick the Great's Prussia, whose entire military system rested on rapid platoon-volley musketry, would have rolled over crossbow-armed opponents. Conversely, in colonial and irregular warfare—forest fighting in North America, mountain campaigns, sieges, naval boarding actions where sparks were dangerous—the crossbow's silence, accuracy, and independence from powder might have given it genuine niche utility, much as it retained some use among hunters and partisans into the nineteenth century.

In the longer view, a wholesale return to crossbows would have stalled the technological trajectory that led from flintlock to rifled musket to breech-loader. The enormous state investment in firearms manufacture drove standardization, interchangeable parts, and eventually industrial mass production; routing that investment into bowyery instead would have slowed the military-industrial integration of European states. By the Napoleonic era, any crossbow-armed army facing French columns supported by massed artillery and skirmishing voltigeurs would have been annihilated, because the crossbow has no answer to cannon, and shock action by determined infantry would overrun bowmen unable to fix bayonets.

In short, the return would have been a romantic blunder. The crossbow had real virtues the musket lacked—accuracy, silence, weather resistance, no logistical tail of powder—but it could not deliver the casualty-producing shock, the moral effect, the cavalry-deterring bayonet, or the industrial scalability on which eighteenth-century warfare depended. Any state that tried it would have been defeated by neighbors who did not, and the experiment would have ended within a single major war.

edus.text: If eighteenth-century European armies had returned to the crossbow as a primary infantry weapon,
the consequences would have rippled through tactics, logistics, industry, and ultimately the geopolitical balance of the period.
The first thing to recognize is why armies had abandoned the crossbow in the first place.
By 1700, the smoothbore flintlock musket with a socket bayonet had become the standard infantry weapon
not because it was more accurate or faster-firing than a crossbow
in raw mechanical terms, a trained crossbowman could match or exceed a musketeer's three rounds per minute, and was far more accurate at moderate range
but because muskets were vastly easier to mass-produce to a uniform standard,
required less individual skill,
carried a bayonet for shock action,
produced terrifying noise and smoke that affected morale and cavalry horses,
and could penetrate the heavier armor that crossbows had struggled against in the sixteenth century.
A return to crossbows would mean abandoning these advantages.
Tactically, the linear formations that defined the age were built around the musket's characteristics:
short effective range,
inaccuracy compensated by mass,
and the bayonet for close combat.
Crossbows would have encouraged either a return to deeper formations with pavise-bearers
or large skirmishing screens making use of the weapon's better accuracy and its silent, smokeless discharge.
Battlefields would have been quieter and visually clearer,
since gunpowder smoke would no longer blanket engagements after the first few volleys.
Officers could actually see what was happening,
command-and-control would improve,
and aimed fire would matter more than volume.
However, the crossbow's killing power against eighteenth-century targets would have been a serious problem.
A heavy military crossbow could pierce mail and even some plate at close range,
but soldiers of this period wore no armor at all.
Against unarmored men a musket ball delivered far more shocking, often unsurvivable trauma than a bolt,
and crossbows would have produced fewer immediate casualties per hit.
Combined with their lack of a practical bayonet equivalent,
crossbow-armed infantry would have been at the mercy of cavalry,
which dominated open ground when not deterred by massed musketry and bayonet hedges.
Pike support might have had to be reintroduced,
undoing a century of tactical simplification.
Logistically, a crossbow army would have escaped dependence on saltpeter, sulfur, and the elaborate powder-mill infrastructure
that constrained eighteenth-century campaigns.
Wet weather, which routinely crippled flintlock armies, would matter much less.
Powder magazines would shrink.
On the other hand, bolts are heavier and bulkier per shot than musket cartridges,
steel prods require skilled craftsmen,
and the spanning mechanisms demanded maintenance by armorers rather than the simple repair flintlocks needed in the field.
The strategic implications follow from these trade-offs.
A power that retained muskets while its rivals reverted to crossbows would enjoy a decisive battlefield advantage,
particularly in the open-field set-piece engagements that decided wars like the War of the Austrian Succession and the Seven Years' War.
Frederick the Great's Prussia, whose entire military system rested on rapid platoon-volley musketry, would have rolled over crossbow-armed opponents.
Conversely, in colonial and irregular warfare
the crossbow's silence, accuracy, and independence from powder might have given it genuine niche utility,
much as it retained some use among hunters and partisans into the nineteenth century.
In the longer view, a wholesale return to crossbows would have stalled the technological trajectory that led from flintlock to rifled musket to breech-loader.
The enormous state investment in firearms manufacture drove standardization, interchangeable parts, and eventually industrial mass production;
routing that investment into bowyery instead would have slowed the military-industrial integration of European states.
By the Napoleonic era, any crossbow-armed army facing French columns supported by massed artillery and skirmishing voltigeurs would have been annihilated,
because the crossbow has no answer to cannon,
and shock action by determined infantry would overrun bowmen unable to fix bayonets.
In short, the return would have been a romantic blunder.
The crossbow had real virtues the musket lacked—accuracy, silence, weather resistance, no logistical tail of powder—
but it could not deliver the casualty-producing shock, the moral effect, the cavalry-deterring bayonet, or the industrial scalability
on which eighteenth-century warfare depended.
Any state that tried it would have been defeated by neighbors who did not,
and the experiment would have ended within a single major war.

items.question: What If the Black Death Had Devastated Poland?
human_answers: Poland wasn't actually "spared", it was merely less affected than the rest of Europe. That graphic is incorrect (or rather, incomplete), since a substantial number of both Poland and Milan's population did in fact die of the plague.
There are three types of plague, Pneumonic, Bubonic, and Septicemic all of which are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. People infected by fleas get the bubonic form of the plague.

ANOTHER EXPLANATION REGARDING POLAND IS THAT IT HAD A LOT OF JEWS, PARTICULARLY IN URBAN SETTINGS; NOW, WHY WERE Jews Less Affected? > And even if Jews died at a lesser rate, it can be attributed to the sanitary practices Jewish law.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Historical Baseline Accuracy
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the counterfactual against the real historical baseline: Poland was not fully spared by the Black Death, but was generally less affected than many parts of Europe, with regional variation and uncertain evidence.
criteria.1-2: Treats Poland as completely untouched or invents a premise with little relation to the Black Death or medieval Poland.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes the Black Death context but gives a crude or inaccurate baseline, such as assuming total immunity or total devastation without nuance.
criteria.5-6: States that Poland was less affected than much of Europe and explores devastation, but with limited attention to uncertainty or regional variation.
criteria.7-8: Accurately distinguishes myth from evidence, notes that Poland still suffered plague impacts, and defines a plausible higher-mortality counterfactual.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual using cautious baseline claims, avoids overreliance on misleading plague maps, and specifies severity, geography, and timing of Poland’s hypothetical devastation.

criteria.name: Plague Mechanism and Demographic Causality
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of how a severe outbreak would affect population, labor, settlement, agriculture, urban life, and minority communities through plausible plague transmission and mortality mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Provides no causal mechanism for devastation or relies on magical, racial, or biologically false explanations.
criteria.3-4: Mentions deaths generally but does not explain transmission, demographic collapse, labor effects, or differential vulnerability.
criteria.5-6: Connects higher mortality to labor shortages, abandoned land, and urban disruption, but mechanisms remain broad or incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Explains plausible bubonic/pneumonic/septicemic plague dynamics, population loss, labor scarcity, migration, and effects on towns, farms, Jews, and elites.
criteria.9-10: Integrates disease biology, trade routes, settlement patterns, sanitation claims with caveats, and differentiated mortality into a coherent demographic mechanism.

criteria.name: Political and Institutional Long-Range Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly traces how a devastated Poland could alter state capacity, monarchy, nobility, military power, relations with Lithuania, the Teutonic Order, Bohemia, Hungary, and later regional balance.
criteria.1-2: Ignores politics entirely or makes implausible claims unrelated to medieval Central Europe.
criteria.3-4: Mentions political weakness or collapse vaguely without explaining institutional or geopolitical pathways.
criteria.5-6: Links depopulation to weaker taxation, military recruitment, or noble bargaining power, but downstream effects are thin.
criteria.7-8: Plausibly traces effects on the Piast/Jagiellonian trajectory, Polish-Lithuanian relations, Teutonic conflict, and regional power balances.
criteria.9-10: Builds a nuanced multi-generation chain from mortality to fiscal capacity, elite politics, military outcomes, dynastic unions, and altered Eastern/Central European development.

criteria.name: Economic, Social, and Cultural Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of major long-term societal effects, including serfdom, wages, land use, urbanization, Jewish communities, migration, religious interpretations, and social conflict.
criteria.1-2: Offers only generic catastrophe language with no Poland-specific social or economic consequences.
criteria.3-4: Mentions economic decline or social unrest but lacks specific mechanisms or medieval Polish context.
criteria.5-6: Discusses labor scarcity, wages, land abandonment, or peasant status, but misses important urban, religious, or minority dimensions.
criteria.7-8: Covers several major effects, including agriculture, towns, labor relations, migration, Jewish communities, and possible scapegoating or legal changes.
criteria.9-10: Explores interacting long-range effects on manorialism, serfdom, urban networks, ethnic/religious minorities, cultural memory, and Poland’s role in European migration and trade.

criteria.name: Coherence, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a logically consistent counterfactual chain, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, and avoids internal contradictions or unsupported deterministic claims.
criteria.1-2: Is incoherent, self-contradictory, or presents impossible outcomes as certain.
criteria.3-4: Contains some plausible points but jumps across centuries without causal links or contradicts its own premise.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly coherent scenario but overstates certainty or leaves major causal gaps.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal chain, flags uncertainty, offers alternatives, and avoids strong contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a tightly reasoned long-range scenario with explicit assumptions, probabilistic language, competing pathways, and careful separation of evidence, inference, and speculation.

items.model_answer:
If the Black Death had devastated Poland as severely as it did Western Europe, the consequences would have been profound and far-reaching:

**Demographic and Economic Impact**

Poland would have lost 30-60% of its population, similar to Western European losses. This would have crippled agricultural production, caused labor shortages, and disrupted trade routes. The relatively prosperous Polish economy of the 14th century would have contracted sharply, delaying the kingdom's expansion and development.

**Political Consequences**

King Casimir III the Great's ambitious state-building projects would likely have stalled. Without sufficient population and tax revenue, his administrative reforms, castle construction, and territorial consolidation would have been severely hampered. Poland's ability to resist external pressures from the Teutonic Knights, Bohemia, and the Golden Horde would have weakened considerably.

**The Union with Lithuania**

The 1385 Union of Krewo, which joined Poland and Lithuania, might never have occurred or would have created a much weaker entity. A devastated Poland would have been a less attractive partner for Lithuania, potentially altering the entire geopolitical structure of Eastern Europe. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which became one of Europe's largest states, might not have emerged as a major power.

**Jewish Communities**

Poland became a refuge for Jewish populations fleeing persecution during the Black Death era. If Poland had been equally devastated, these communities would have had nowhere to go, fundamentally altering Jewish demographic patterns in Europe and eliminating what became one of the world's largest Jewish populations.

**Long-term Regional Balance**

A weakened Poland would have shifted the balance of power eastward. The Teutonic Order might have conquered more territory, Russia could have expanded westward earlier, and the Ottoman advance into Europe might have proceeded differently without a strong Polish-Lithuanian buffer state.

items.model_answer:
If Europe had unified early like China, the trajectory of world history would have been dramatically different across political, economic, cultural, and technological dimensions.

**Political and Military Consequences**

A unified Europe would have created the world's most powerful state for much of history. With a population and resource base comparable to or exceeding China's, unified Europe could have projected overwhelming military force. The internal wars that devastated Europe—the Thirty Years' War, Napoleonic Wars, World Wars I and II—would never have occurred, saving tens of millions of lives. However, this unity might have enabled more effective colonial expansion, potentially intensifying rather than limiting European imperialism. The competitive state system that drove European military innovation might have been replaced by a more conservative imperial structure, though the sheer scale of a unified Europe could have compensated through centralized research programs.

**Economic Development**

The economic implications are complex. Europe's fragmentation created competitive pressures that arguably accelerated the Industrial Revolution—rival states raced to adopt new technologies and economic systems. A unified Europe might have developed more slowly, resembling China's periods of technological stagnation despite early advantages. Alternatively, unified administration could have created the world's largest integrated market centuries earlier, with standardized laws, currencies, and infrastructure enabling unprecedented economic efficiency. The absence of internal tariffs and trade barriers would have facilitated commerce on a continental scale.

**Cultural and Intellectual Impact**

European cultural diversity would have been significantly diminished. The rich tapestry of distinct national literatures, artistic traditions, and philosophical schools emerged partly from political fragmentation. A unified Europe might have developed a dominant imperial culture, suppressing regional identities much as China's imperial system promoted cultural homogenization. However, the Enlightenment and Scientific Revolution might have unfolded differently—either stifled by centralized orthodoxy or amplified by coordinated intellectual institutions spanning the continent.

**Global Power Dynamics**

A unified Europe would have fundamentally altered the global balance of power. The Ottoman Empire would have faced an overwhelmingly superior adversary, likely preventing its expansion into Europe entirely. The Americas might have been colonized by a single European empire rather than competing powers, creating a very different New World political landscape. The rise of the United States might have been prevented or delayed if faced with a unified European colonial administration. China and a unified Europe would have been the world's two superpowers, potentially leading to earlier and more intensive contact between these civilizations.

**The Unification Challenge**

The critical question is whether early European unification was even feasible. Europe's geography—with numerous peninsulas, mountain ranges, and islands—created natural divisions that China's river valleys did not. Europe's linguistic diversity far exceeded China's, and the absence of a unifying script like Chinese characters made cultural integration harder. The Roman Empire came closest to unifying Europe but collapsed under administrative strain and external pressure. Any early unified Europe would have required either a more successful Roman Empire, a different outcome to the barbarian migrations, or perhaps Islamic conquest succeeding where it historically failed.

In summary, early European unification would have created a superpower that dominated global affairs but might have sacrificed the competitive dynamism that made Europe so transformative in the early modern period. The world would likely be more politically stable but potentially less innovative, with profound implications for democracy, industrialization, and cultural diversity.

edus.text: If Europe had unified early like China,
the trajectory of world history would have been dramatically different across political, economic, cultural, and technological dimensions.
A unified Europe would have created the world's most powerful state for much of history.
With a population and resource base comparable to or exceeding China's,
unified Europe could have projected overwhelming military force.
The internal wars that devastated Europe—the Thirty Years' War, Napoleonic Wars, World Wars I and II—would never have occurred,
saving tens of millions of lives.
However, this unity might have enabled more effective colonial expansion,
potentially intensifying rather than limiting European imperialism.
The competitive state system that drove European military innovation might have been replaced by a more conservative imperial structure,
though the sheer scale of a unified Europe could have compensated through centralized research programs.
The economic implications are complex.
Europe's fragmentation created competitive pressures that arguably accelerated the Industrial Revolution—
rival states raced to adopt new technologies and economic systems.
A unified Europe might have developed more slowly,
resembling China's periods of technological stagnation despite early advantages.
Alternatively, unified administration could have created the world's largest integrated market centuries earlier,
with standardized laws, currencies, and infrastructure enabling unprecedented economic efficiency.
The absence of internal tariffs and trade barriers would have facilitated commerce on a continental scale.
European cultural diversity would have been significantly diminished.
The rich tapestry of distinct national literatures, artistic traditions, and philosophical schools emerged partly from political fragmentation.
A unified Europe might have developed a dominant imperial culture,
suppressing regional identities much as China's imperial system promoted cultural homogenization.
However, the Enlightenment and Scientific Revolution might have unfolded differently—
either stifled by centralized orthodoxy
or amplified by coordinated intellectual institutions spanning the continent.
A unified Europe would have fundamentally altered the global balance of power.
The Ottoman Empire would have faced an overwhelmingly superior adversary,
likely preventing its expansion into Europe entirely.
The Americas might have been colonized by a single European empire rather than competing powers,
creating a very different New World political landscape.
The rise of the United States might have been prevented or delayed
if faced with a unified European colonial administration.
China and a unified Europe would have been the world's two superpowers,
potentially leading to earlier and more intensive contact between these civilizations.
The critical question is whether early European unification was even feasible.
Europe's geography—with numerous peninsulas, mountain ranges, and islands—created natural divisions
that China's river valleys did not.
Europe's linguistic diversity far exceeded China's,
and the absence of a unifying script like Chinese characters made cultural integration harder.
The Roman Empire came closest to unifying Europe
but collapsed under administrative strain and external pressure.
Any early unified Europe would have required either a more successful Roman Empire,
a different outcome to the barbarian migrations,
or perhaps Islamic conquest succeeding where it historically failed.
In summary, early European unification would have created a superpower that dominated global affairs
but might have sacrificed the competitive dynamism that made Europe so transformative in the early modern period.
The world would likely be more politically stable but potentially less innovative,
with profound implications for democracy, industrialization, and cultural diversity.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Japan Had Attacked the Soviet Far East in World War II?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Discipline and Historical Baseline
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately establishes the real historical baseline—Khalkhin Gol/Nomonhan, Japan's north-vs-south strategic debate, the 1941 Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact, Soviet force posture in Siberia, and Japan's resource constraints—before reasoning from the altered premise of a Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East.
criteria.1-2: Misstates core facts or ignores the actual strategic context; treats the scenario as generic Japan-vs-USSR war.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few relevant facts but with major omissions or inaccuracies about timing, motives, or military conditions.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly correct baseline, including Japan's strategic choices and Soviet-Japanese tensions, but lacks detail or nuance.
criteria.7-8: Accurately grounds the counterfactual in the north-south debate, Khalkhin Gol lessons, neutrality pact, and Japanese resource problems.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the divergence point and explains why the real-world decision favored attacking southward rather than Siberia, using the baseline to constrain all later reasoning.

criteria.name: Military Feasibility and Operational Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the plausibility of the military analysis: Japanese Kwantung Army capabilities, Soviet Far Eastern defenses, terrain, logistics, armor/artillery/airpower balance, naval irrelevance or limits, and the likely operational tempo of a campaign in Siberia and Manchuria.
criteria.1-2: Offers implausible military claims, such as easy Japanese conquest of Siberia or Soviet collapse without logistical analysis.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes that fighting would be difficult but gives vague or one-sided operational reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Discusses major military factors such as logistics, terrain, and Soviet strength, though some mechanisms remain underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Gives a coherent operational picture showing why Japan would struggle to achieve decisive gains against Soviet Far Eastern forces.
criteria.9-10: Integrates force quality, geography, supply lines, seasonal effects, Soviet reserves, and Japanese strategic limitations into a highly plausible campaign assessment.

criteria.name: Interaction with the German-Soviet War
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer reasons through effects on Operation Barbarossa, Stalin's transfer or retention of Siberian divisions, the defense of Moscow, Soviet war production, German strategy, and whether a two-front Soviet war meaningfully changes the Eastern Front.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the German-Soviet war or makes unsupported claims that Germany automatically wins or nothing changes.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Moscow or Siberian divisions but treats them simplistically without causal linkage.
criteria.5-6: Explains that a Japanese attack could limit Soviet redeployments and pressure Moscow, but leaves key timing and scale issues vague.
criteria.7-8: Carefully connects Japanese action to Soviet force allocation, Moscow's defense, German opportunities, and limits on Axis coordination.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced, timing-sensitive analysis of whether and how a Far Eastern front could alter Barbarossa, while avoiding deterministic claims.

criteria.name: Pacific, Resource, and Allied Downstream Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of long-range consequences beyond the immediate Soviet front: Japan's oil problem, whether it still attacks Southeast Asia or Pearl Harbor, US embargo and entry into the war, Allied aid to the USSR, Chinese theater effects, and global Axis coordination.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on Siberia and ignores Japan's resource crisis, the United States, China, and the Pacific War.
criteria.3-4: Mentions oil or Pearl Harbor but gives disconnected or contradictory downstream effects.
criteria.5-6: Addresses several major consequences, such as delayed or altered Pacific War and resource shortages, but lacks a full chain.
criteria.7-8: Explains how attacking north would affect Japan's oil strategy, US relations, Southeast Asia, China, and Allied support to the USSR.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent global cascade linking Japan's northern war to Pacific timing, US entry, resource exhaustion, Soviet aid routes, and Axis strategic coordination.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration, Causal Coherence, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer presents a logically consistent long-range counterfactual with explicit uncertainty, avoids overclaiming, distinguishes likely from possible outcomes, and maintains internal consistency about timing, alliances, and strategic choices.
criteria.1-2: Is deterministic, internally contradictory, or relies on unsupported speculation and hindsight.
criteria.3-4: Shows some causal reasoning but contains major leaps, inconsistent assumptions, or exaggerated certainty.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a plausible main line with moderate uncertainty, though some causal links are thin or underqualified.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes while keeping the chain of events consistent across theaters.
criteria.9-10: Offers a disciplined counterfactual with explicit contingencies, alternative branches, calibrated probabilities, and no significant contradictions.

items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East during World War II instead of pursuing its southern expansion, the war's trajectory would have changed dramatically across multiple theaters.

**Strategic Context**

Japan faced a critical choice in 1941. Historically, it chose the "southern strategy" (attacking Southeast Asia and the Pacific) over the "northern strategy" (attacking the Soviet Union). This decision came after the Nomonhan Incident in 1939, where Soviet forces decisively defeated Japanese troops, and was reinforced by the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact of April 1941.

**Immediate Military Consequences**

An attack on the Soviet Far East would have forced Stalin to fight a true two-front war. During the critical months of late 1941, when German forces approached Moscow, the Soviets transferred approximately 15-20 divisions from Siberia westward—troops that proved decisive in the winter counteroffensive. Without these reinforcements, Moscow might have fallen, potentially collapsing Soviet resistance entirely.

However, Japan would have faced enormous logistical challenges. The Soviet Far East offered limited strategic objectives, poor infrastructure, and harsh terrain. Unlike resource-rich Southeast Asia, Siberia provided little oil, rubber, or other materials Japan desperately needed. The Trans-Siberian Railway would have been vulnerable but difficult to permanently sever.

**Impact on the Pacific War**

Without Japanese aggression in Southeast Asia and Pearl Harbor, the United States might have remained neutral longer or entered the war differently. Britain would have retained Malaya, Singapore, and Burma, but also would have received no American Pacific support. The resource crisis that drove Japanese expansion would have remained unresolved, potentially crippling Japan's war effort within months.

**Long-term Outcomes**

The most likely scenario is a grinding stalemate in Siberia while Japan's economy collapsed from resource starvation. Germany might have achieved greater success against the USSR initially, but Japan would have been a weaker, resource-starved ally. The absence of Pearl Harbor would have fundamentally altered American involvement, possibly delaying or preventing the Pacific War as we know it.

Ultimately, Japan's southern strategy, while ending in defeat, was more rational given its resource needs. A northern attack would have traded uncertain gains in Siberia for the certain loss of access to Southeast Asian resources, likely leading to an even swifter Japanese collapse.

items.question: What If Gunpowder-Era Fortresses Were Built as Circles or Squares Instead of Stars?
human_answers: Star forts or bastion forts are designed to enable enfilade (or flanking) fire: shooting on the line of attackers from the side, significantly increasing firing efficiency of the defender. Flanking fire allows guns placed in the side wall of the bastion (pr...

Imagine that you are defending a fort with old-fashioned round bastions in the Middle Ages. Your walls are high, but once the enemy comes close and starts scaling the walls, very few of your defenders can engage them.

These outcroppings are called Bastions and they became common when muskets and cannons became common in European warfare. The problem with a square or circle forts is that when the enemy has reached the wall, they are in your dead zone.

items.model_answer:
Star forts emerged in the 15th and 16th centuries as a direct response to the failure of older medieval designs against gunpowder artillery. To understand what would have happened if engineers had stuck with circles or squares, you have to look at the specific geometric problems that the star shape solved.

The fundamental issue with round and square fortresses in the gunpowder era was twofold: vulnerability to cannon fire and the creation of "dead ground" that defenders could not cover.

Round towers and circular curtain walls, which had been the gold standard in the high medieval period, performed poorly against cannons because their curved surfaces, while good at deflecting arrows and trebuchet stones, presented a continuously perpendicular face to a besieger who positioned his guns correctly. More importantly, cannons firing back from a round wall had limited traverse, and any attacker who reached the base of the wall entered a blind spot that defenders on top could not shoot into without exposing themselves dangerously over the parapet.

Square fortresses had the opposite but equally fatal problem. Their corners created sharp angles where attackers could shelter, and defenders firing along the curtain walls could not cover the ground directly in front of the corner towers without crossfire from another tower. The corners themselves were also structurally weak points that concentrated stress and could be brought down by concentrated battery.

If gunpowder-era powers had been forced or had chosen to stick with these shapes, sieges would have become dramatically shorter and more decisive in favor of attackers. The roughly two-to-three-month siege that became typical of well-designed star forts in the 17th and 18th centuries might have collapsed to a matter of weeks. This in turn would have transformed warfare itself: campaigns of maneuver would have dominated over the siege-heavy warfare that characterized conflicts like the Eighty Years' War or the wars of Louis XIV. Defensive strategy as a whole would have been less viable, pushing states toward larger field armies and more decisive battle-seeking doctrines.

Architecturally, engineers would likely have compensated in other ways. You would probably see much thicker walls, possibly buried earthen ramparts replacing masonry entirely much earlier than they did historically, and elaborate outer works—ravelins, hornworks, and detached bastions—proliferating around the simple geometric core to provide the flanking fire that the main shape could not. In effect, the star fort might have re-emerged in piecemeal form as a halo of auxiliary structures rather than an integrated design.

Economically, fortification would have been cheaper per installation but required in greater numbers and with more frequent reconstruction after sieges. Cities like Vauban's frontier strongholds in France or the Dutch water-line fortresses, which historically held off armies for months and shaped the entire grand strategy of their nations, would have been far less effective at buying time. The strategic depth that fortifications provided to smaller powers like the Dutch Republic against larger neighbors would have largely disappeared, possibly leading to earlier consolidation of Europe under the largest military powers.

Finally, the cultural legacy would look quite different. The distinctive star-shaped footprints visible today in cities like Palmanova, Naarden, or Neuf-Brisach would not exist; instead, we might see rings of crumbling outer earthworks around simpler geometric cores, and the entire aesthetic vocabulary of early modern military engineering—so influential on urban planning—would be much less geometrically striking.

items.question: What If Germany Had Blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar in World War II?
human_answers: > ...but if the Strait is guarded such that they can't get them without braving an enfilading strafe of torpedoes, then it wouldn't do much good even if they knew where they are. From this comment by the OP, and others like it, it seems they don't appreciat...

Gibraltar during the war had a quite formidable British naval presence (Force H), an airfield, and significant coastal gun emplacements easily capable of covering the entire strait. > The primary batteries were a set of twin 9.2" naval guns guns at the sout...
While you are at it why not blockade the port of London? Isn't that a better target?

I'm not a historian nor a scholar of sorts, but I was lucky to be at the right place at the right time and found out from one of the most capable people who could answer this question. I lived in Madrid, Spain in the late 60s, early 70s.

Blockade requires local superiority To enforce a blockade at a chokepoint, you need to arrive there and stay there, winning any engagements. To win local engagements, you need to be stronger than an expected blockade-breaking force.

items.model_answer:
If Germany had successfully blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar in World War II, it would have fundamentally altered the Mediterranean theater and potentially the war's outcome.

**Strategic Consequences:**

A German blockade would have severed Britain's vital Mediterranean lifeline to Egypt, India, and the Far East. British forces would have been forced to route all supplies around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa, adding thousands of miles and weeks to supply times. This would have severely strained Britain's already overstretched merchant marine and made reinforcing North Africa, Malta, and the Middle East extremely difficult.

**How It Might Have Been Achieved:**

Germany would have needed to capture Gibraltar itself or secure Spanish cooperation to close the strait. Hitler attempted the latter through Operation Felix, planning to seize Gibraltar with Spanish assistance, but Franco refused to enter the war despite German pressure. Alternatively, Germany could have deployed U-boats, aircraft, and surface raiders to the western Mediterranean approaches, though maintaining such a blockade would have required bases in Spain or Spanish Morocco.

**Operational Impact:**

Malta would likely have fallen without resupply, eliminating the key base that disrupted Axis supply lines to North Africa. Rommel's Afrika Korps would have received more consistent supplies while British forces in Egypt faced critical shortages. This could have enabled an Axis conquest of Egypt, the Suez Canal, and potentially the Middle Eastern oil fields.

**Broader Implications:**

Control of the Middle East might have provided Germany with crucial oil resources and threatened British India. However, Germany still faced the fundamental problem of fighting a two-front war after invading the Soviet Union in 1941. Even with Mediterranean dominance, German resources were ultimately insufficient to defeat both the USSR and the Western Allies, especially after American entry into the war.

The blockade's success would have depended on timing, Spanish cooperation, and whether Germany could sustain it while fighting elsewhere.

edus.text: If Germany had successfully blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar in World War II,
it would have fundamentally altered the Mediterranean theater and potentially the war's outcome.
A German blockade would have severed Britain's vital Mediterranean lifeline to Egypt, India, and the Far East.
British forces would have been forced to route all supplies around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa,
adding thousands of miles and weeks to supply times.
This would have severely strained Britain's already overstretched merchant marine
and made reinforcing North Africa, Malta, and the Middle East extremely difficult.
Germany would have needed to capture Gibraltar itself
or secure Spanish cooperation to close the strait.
Hitler attempted the latter through Operation Felix,
planning to seize Gibraltar with Spanish assistance,
but Franco refused to enter the war despite German pressure.
Alternatively, Germany could have deployed U-boats, aircraft, and surface raiders to the western Mediterranean approaches,
though maintaining such a blockade would have required bases in Spain or Spanish Morocco.
Malta would likely have fallen without resupply,
eliminating the key base that disrupted Axis supply lines to North Africa.
Rommel's Afrika Korps would have received more consistent supplies
while British forces in Egypt faced critical shortages.
This could have enabled an Axis conquest of Egypt, the Suez Canal, and potentially the Middle Eastern oil fields.
Control of the Middle East might have provided Germany with crucial oil resources
and threatened British India.
However, Germany still faced the fundamental problem of fighting a two-front war after invading the Soviet Union in 1941.
Even with Mediterranean dominance, German resources were ultimately insufficient to defeat both the USSR and the Western Allies,
especially after American entry into the war.
The blockade's success would have depended on timing, Spanish cooperation, and whether Germany could sustain it while fighting elsewhere.

items.question: What If You Opened a 10-Meter Drain to Space at the Bottom of Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
# Opening a 10-Meter Drain to Space at Challenger Deep

Challenger Deep sits about 10,935 meters below sea level, where pressure reaches roughly 1,086 bar (about 1,071 atmospheres, or ~110 MPa). If you suddenly opened a 10-meter-diameter portal there that led directly to the vacuum of space, here's what would unfold.

**The Initial Flow**

Water would accelerate downward (well, "outward" through the drain) under that enormous pressure differential. Using Bernoulli's equation, the exit velocity would be roughly v = √(2P/ρ), giving about 465 m/s — faster than the speed of sound in air, though still well below water's sound speed (~1,500 m/s), so the flow wouldn't be choked the way a gas would be. Through a 10-meter (78.5 m²) opening, that's an initial volumetric flow of about **36,500 cubic meters per second**, or roughly 36 million liters per second. For comparison, that's about 1.5 times the Amazon River's average discharge, all pouring out of a single hole.

**What Happens to the Water in Space**

The moment water exits into vacuum, several things happen at once. The pressure drops from 1,086 bar to essentially zero, so the water flashes — some of it boils explosively into vapor, while the rest, losing the heat of vaporization, rapidly freezes into ice crystals. You'd get a fan-shaped plume of mixed vapor and ice grains shooting away from Earth. The bulk of the mass, however, is moving at only ~465 m/s, far less than Earth's escape velocity (11.2 km/s) or even low-orbit velocity (~7.8 km/s). So almost all of this water would arc back down and fall onto the planet as ice or rain elsewhere — it isn't actually leaving Earth.

**The Cavitation and Shock Effects Around the Drain**

Above the drain, the water column would drop pressure faster than the surrounding ocean could fill in. This creates massive cavitation — a roaring vortex of vaporized seawater. A bowl-shaped depression would form on the surface 11 km above, eventually developing into a swirling vortex (thanks to the Coriolis effect at ~11°N latitude) something like a giant bathtub drain. The surface dimple would be modest in depth (the flow is limited by what can be drawn from the surroundings), but the inflow currents would be ferocious near the opening, easily capable of pulling submarines, sediment, and anything else into the maw.

**The Long-Term Picture**

The ocean holds about 1.35 × 10¹⁸ m³ of water. At 36,500 m³/s, *if the rate stayed constant*, you'd need roughly **1.2 million years** to drain it all. But the rate wouldn't stay constant — as sea level dropped, pressure at the drain would decrease, and flow would slow proportionally to √(depth). Practically, the ocean would never fully empty this way; you'd asymptotically approach a state where sea level sits roughly at the depth of the drain. Long before that, of course, the climate, ecosystems, and continental shelves would be utterly transformed.

**The Hidden Catch**

Most of the "drained" water doesn't actually escape Earth's gravity. It's launched ballistically, reaches some apex above the atmosphere, and falls back — likely as catastrophic ice and steam precipitation distributed around the globe. So in truth, this isn't a drain at all. It's the world's most violent fountain, redistributing the Pacific Ocean across the rest of the planet, one Amazon-per-second at a time.
