criteria.name: Core counterfactual conclusion and causal fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches the correct high-level outcome for Hubble imaging Earth: it can point at Earth, but normal Hubble would produce poor Earth-surface images mainly because of rapid apparent ground motion and tracking limits, not because Earth is simply too bright.
criteria.1-2: Gives a fundamentally wrong conclusion, such as claiming Hubble would be destroyed, blinded, or easily take perfect spy photos with no caveats.
criteria.3-4: Identifies that Earth imaging would be difficult but attributes the problem mostly to incorrect causes such as brightness, atmosphere, or focus alone.
criteria.5-6: States that Hubble could look at Earth but images would be poor; mentions motion blur or tracking but with limited causal explanation.
criteria.7-8: Correctly explains that orbital speed over the surface causes severe apparent motion and blur, making ordinary exposures and guidance inadequate.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual: Earth is observable, brightness/atmosphere are not the main barriers, and the dominant issue is fast ground-track motion relative to Hubble’s design.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage: optics, resolution, exposure, and tracking
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the physical mechanisms that determine the image quality if Hubble observed Earth: diffraction-limited angular resolution, altitude-to-ground resolution conversion, exposure time, smear from orbital motion, and telescope pointing control.
criteria.1-2: Omits almost all relevant mechanisms or relies on vague statements about telescopes zooming in.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one relevant mechanism, such as resolution or motion, but ignores how it affects actual Earth-surface imaging.
criteria.5-6: Covers several mechanisms but leaves gaps, such as discussing resolution without exposure smear or motion without pointing constraints.
criteria.7-8: Explains how Hubble’s finite angular resolution and rapid apparent ground motion combine to degrade surface images.
criteria.9-10: Integrates optics, altitude, exposure time, smear, target tracking, and attitude-control limits into a coherent account of image quality.

criteria.name: Long-range chain coherence under the premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the downstream consequences of repointing Hubble toward Earth over multiple steps, from initial feasibility to operational limitations and possible engineering workarounds.
criteria.1-2: Provides disconnected claims with no causal chain from the counterfactual premise to consequences.
criteria.3-4: Has a simple chain but skips key transitions, such as going directly from pointing at Earth to image quality without explaining why.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly sensible sequence but leaves some important links underdeveloped or mildly confused.
criteria.7-8: Clearly traces the chain: Hubble can point, Earth passes rapidly through view, exposures blur, normal guidance cannot track well, resulting images are poor.
criteria.9-10: Develops the full long-range chain including manual tracking attempts, slew-rate/vibration constraints, possible custom control systems, and relation to Earth-observation satellites.

criteria.name: Quantitative and comparative grounding
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses appropriate magnitudes or comparisons for Hubble’s Earth-observation scenario, such as orbital speed, altitude, angular resolution, ground resolution, Moon-tracking comparison, and slew-rate requirements.
criteria.1-2: Uses no quantitative grounding or gives wildly implausible numbers that drive the reasoning astray.
criteria.3-4: Includes numbers or comparisons but they are mostly irrelevant, unsupported, or significantly misleading.
criteria.5-6: Uses at least one relevant scale, such as Hubble’s altitude or orbital speed, but does not connect it strongly to the conclusion.
criteria.7-8: Uses plausible scales, such as about 570 km altitude, about 7 km/s ground motion, or sub-arcsecond resolution, to support the blur/tracking argument.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects multiple scales, including Hubble-like angular resolution, rapid ground-track motion, short exposure limits, and required tracking rates, to justify the expected image quality.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, contradiction control, and boundary cases
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids overclaiming, distinguishes stock Hubble from a modified Hubble-like system, and handles edge cases such as very short exposures, bright targets, atmosphere, and spy-satellite analogues without contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contains major internal contradictions or absolute claims that conflict with the scenario, such as saying Hubble cannot point at Earth and also that it routinely can.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of caveats but mixes incompatible claims or overstates uncertain details.
criteria.5-6: Mostly avoids contradictions but treats important boundary cases simplistically, such as assuming any short exposure solves the problem.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes feasible pointing from useful imaging and notes that special tracking or modifications could improve results.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates claims: stock Hubble performs poorly for ground imaging, atmosphere/brightness are secondary, custom controls could approach useful performance, and Hubble-like spy satellites are purpose-built for this role.

items.model_answer:
If the Hubble Space Telescope pointed at Earth instead of deep space, several significant issues would arise:

**Technical and Safety Concerns**

Hubble cannot safely point at Earth. The telescope orbits at about 540 km altitude, and Earth would appear extremely bright in its field of view. Pointing Hubble directly at Earth's sunlit surface could damage its sensitive instruments, similar to how looking at the sun through a telescope can damage your eyes. The instruments are designed for extremely faint, distant objects, not bright nearby ones.

**Image Quality Limitations**

Even if it were safe, Hubble wouldn't produce useful Earth observation images. The telescope moves at roughly 7.5 km/s in low Earth orbit. At this speed and proximity, Earth's surface would blur significantly during the exposure times needed for imaging. Hubble's instruments lack the fast tracking systems required to compensate for this relative motion at such close range.

**Resolution Mismatch**

While Hubble has excellent angular resolution for distant objects, this doesn't translate to superior Earth imaging. Dedicated Earth observation satellites orbit much lower (often 400-700 km) and are specifically designed with appropriate optics, sensors, and pointing systems for terrestrial imaging. They can achieve better effective resolution for Earth surface features than Hubble could.

**Operational Restrictions**

NASA actually has safety protocols preventing Hubble from pointing too close to Earth or the Sun to protect its instruments. The telescope is designed and optimized for observing faint astronomical objects in the infrared, visible, and ultraviolet spectra—not for planetary observation of our own bright, nearby world.

items.question: What If Every Ship Were Removed from Earth's Waters at Once?
human_answers: About six microns—slightly more than the diameter of a strand of spider silk. [Image: image] Archimedes’ principle tells us that the water displaced by a ship weighs as much as the ship itself. If we can figure out the total weight of all the world’s ships, we can figure out how much water they’re displacing, then divide that volume by the surface area of the ocean to figure out how much the water level would drop. Weighing ships is confusing (http://www.pomorci.com/Zanimljivosti/TONNAGE%20MEASUREMENT%20OF%20SHIPS.pdf). There are a bunch of different measurements of the size of a ship, and many of them, like gross tonnage, are actually measures of the volume of the ship’s rooms and other internal spaces, not its weight. The UN Conference on Trade and Development publishes estimates (http://unctad.org/en/Docs/rmt2011ch2_en.pdf) of the size of the world shipping fleet. What the UNCTD publishes is “deadweight tonnage”, which is the maximum weight of the ship’s fuel, cargo, and crew. What we want is “displacement”. Unfortunately, comprehensive numbers for displacement are harder to find. Fortunately, we can estimate it. Brian Barrass’s book Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates gives a table of ratios of deadweight tonnage to displacement for different types of ships. Extrapolating from the last few years of UNCTD data, and using the coefficients from the book, suggests that the world fleet weighs about 2.15 billion tons when fully loaded. The main component of the fleet by weight is oil tankers and bulk ore-carrying ships, which make up over two-thirds of the total. (The UNCTD data doesn’t include small recreational boats or naval fleets. However, based on some numbers for naval fleets (http://www.csbaonline.org/4Publications/PubLibrary/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti.pdf) and recreational boats (http://nmma.net/assets/cabinets/Cabinet445/2011_abstract_preview.pdf), neither one contributes much to the total.) A ton of water is about a cubic meter. 2.15 billion cubic meters divided by the surface area of the oceans equals about 6 microns (0.006 mm). But you don’t have to worry about that six-micron sea level drop. The oceans are currently rising at about 3.3 millimeters per year due to global warming (through both glacial melting and thermal expansion of seawater). At that rate (normalized for seasonal variation and short-term fluctations), if you removed every ship from the ocean, the water would be back up to its original average level in 16 hours. [Image: image] Sea levels will likely rise a few feet by the year 2100 (https://what-if.xkcd.com/33). Current fish wet biomass is about 2 billion tons (http://phys.org/news151251277.html), so removing them won’t make a dent either. (Marine fish biomass dropped by 80% over the last century (http://news.aaas.org/2011_annual_meeting/0228declining-fisheries.shtml), which—taking into consideration the growth rate of the world’s shipping fleet—leads to an odd conclusion: Sometime in the last few years, we reached a point where there are, by weight, more ships in the ocean than fish.) And what about the old joke about how much deeper the ocean would be without sponges? While estimates of sponge biomass are hard to come by, the answer is probably that if you removed all the sponges, sea level would drop by no more than a few microns ... and much less if you squeezed them out first. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Archimedes-Based Sea-Level Estimate
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response correctly applies buoyancy/displacement reasoning to estimate the immediate global mean sea-level change from removing all ships from Earth's waters.
criteria.1-2: Does not use displacement or buoyancy; predicts a large or directionally wrong sea-level change.
criteria.3-4: Mentions displaced water but confuses ship volume, cargo capacity, or tonnage, leading to an implausible estimate.
criteria.5-6: Uses Archimedes' principle qualitatively and gets the drop direction right, but gives only a rough or poorly supported magnitude.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates displaced mass/volume from world fleet weight and ocean area, yielding a micron-scale sea-level drop.
criteria.9-10: Accurately explains displacement versus tonnage, uses plausible fleet mass and ocean-area assumptions, and arrives near about 6 microns.

criteria.name: Scope of Removed Vessels and Mass Accounting
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the response defines 'every ship' and accounts for commercial, naval, recreational, cargo, fuel, and load-state contributions without overcounting.
criteria.1-2: Treats ships as empty geometric objects or ignores fleet composition entirely.
criteria.3-4: Considers only one class of vessels or relies on arbitrary guesses with no distinction among ship types.
criteria.5-6: Includes major commercial vessels but handles cargo/load state, naval fleets, or small boats vaguely.
criteria.7-8: Identifies commercial shipping as dominant and notes that naval and recreational craft are comparatively minor.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes displacement, deadweight, cargo/fuel load, and vessel categories while explaining why omitted small fleets barely affect the result.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects and Relative Scale
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of physical, environmental, and societal consequences after instantaneous ship removal, while keeping them proportional to the tiny water-level effect.
criteria.1-2: Claims catastrophic ocean drainage, tsunamis, climate shifts, or ecosystem collapse from sea-level change alone.
criteria.3-4: Lists effects but greatly exaggerates the sea-level, tidal, or geological consequences.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the sea-level effect is tiny but gives limited discussion of other consequences such as transport disruption or pollution changes.
criteria.7-8: Separates negligible ocean-level effects from major human impacts like global trade disruption, stranded cargo, fuel loss, and maritime safety issues.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent hierarchy of downstream effects: micron-scale sea-level change, no meaningful tidal/geophysical impact, but severe logistics, economic, rescue, and possible pollution consequences depending on removal details.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Mechanism Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response maintains a consistent causal chain under the premise that all ships are removed at once from Earth's waters.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or contradicts it repeatedly, such as leaving ships in place while analyzing their removal.
criteria.3-4: Applies the premise inconsistently, mixing removal of ships, water, cargo, or marine life without clear rules.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the premise but leaves ambiguous whether cargo, people, fuel, or displaced water vanish or are relocated.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions about instantaneous removal and consistently traces immediate and later consequences.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly handles alternative interpretations, such as removing vessels only versus ships plus contents, and explains how each changes outcomes without breaking causal continuity.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether numerical claims and speculative effects are appropriately qualified, internally consistent, and compared to relevant baselines such as modern sea-level rise.
criteria.1-2: Presents unsupported precise claims, contradictions, or physically impossible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Uses some plausible facts but mixes incompatible numbers or fails to flag major uncertainty.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty generally but lacks clear bounds or relevant scale comparisons.
criteria.7-8: Uses order-of-magnitude reasoning, avoids false precision, and compares the result to ocean area, fleet mass, or annual sea-level rise.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates all estimates with transparent assumptions, sensible error bars, and comparisons such as millimeters-per-year sea-level rise overwhelming a few-micron drop within hours.

items.model_answer:
If every ship were suddenly removed from Earth's waters at once, several immediate and cascading effects would occur:

**Immediate Physical Effects**

The most direct impact would be on water displacement. Ships collectively displace millions of tons of water. When removed instantaneously, this water would rush back to fill the voids, creating localized disturbances. However, given that ships are distributed across vast ocean surfaces, the effect on global sea level would be negligible—likely unmeasurable. The total volume of all ships is tiny compared to Earth's oceans (roughly 1.4 billion cubic kilometers).

**Economic Collapse**

About 90% of global trade moves by sea. The sudden disappearance of cargo ships, tankers, and container vessels would immediately sever supply chains worldwide. Within days, shortages of fuel, food, raw materials, and manufactured goods would appear. Factories would halt production. Grocery stores would empty. The economic damage would dwarf any modern recession, potentially causing trillions of dollars in losses within weeks.

**Stranded Resources and People**

Millions of seafarers work aboard ships at any given time. Their sudden displacement onto water would be catastrophic. Oil tankers carrying millions of barrels would vanish, causing immediate fuel shortages. Fishing fleets would disappear, eliminating a primary protein source for billions of people.

**Environmental Considerations**

Interestingly, some environmental benefits might emerge long-term. Ship traffic contributes significantly to ocean noise pollution, which disrupts marine mammal communication and navigation. The sudden silence would benefit whales, dolphins, and other species. However, the chaos of rebuilding a shipping fleet would likely create worse environmental damage through rushed, poorly regulated construction.

**Recovery Timeline**

Rebuilding the global fleet would take years, possibly decades. Shipyards would be overwhelmed. In the interim, air freight would partially compensate but couldn't handle the volume, and costs would skyrocket. Humanity would adapt, but the transition would involve significant hardship and economic reorganization.

items.question: What If You Put a Running Hair Dryer in a Sealed 1x1x1 Meter Box?
human_answers: A typical hair dryer draws 1875 watts of power. All 1875 watts have to go somewhere. No matter what happens inside the box, if there’s 1875 watts of power being used, eventually there will be 1875 watts of heat flowing out. This is true of any device that uses power, which is a handy thing to know. For example, people worry about leaving disconnected chargers plugged into the wall for fear that they’re draining power. Are they right? You can use heat flow to come up with simple rule of thumb: If an unused charger isn’t warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny of electricity a day. For a small smartphone charger, if it’s not warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny a year. This is true of almost any powered device (though not necessarily those plugged into a second device. If a charger is connected to something, like a smartphone or laptop, power can be flowing from the wall through the charger into the device.) But back to the box. Heat will flow from the hair dryer out into the box. If we assume the dryer is indestructible, the interior of the box will keep getting hotter until the outer surface reaches about 60°C (140°F). At that temperature, the box will be losing heat to the outside as fast as the hair dryer is adding it inside, and the system will be in equilibrium. [Image: image] The equilibrium temperature will be a bit cooler if there’s a breeze, or if the box is sitting on a wet or metallic surface that conducts away heat quickly. If the box is made of metal, 60°C is hot enough to burn your hand if you touch it (http://www.mascoat.com/assets/files/Insulative_Coating_Evaluation_NACE.pdf) for more than five seconds. If it’s wood, you can probably touch it for a while, but there’s a danger that parts of the box in contact with the mouth of the hair dryer will catch fire. The inside of a box will be like an oven. The temperature it reaches will depend on the thickness of the box wall; the thicker and more insulating the wall, the higher the temperature. It wouldn’t take a very thick box to create temperatures high enough to burn out the hair dryer. But let’s assume an indestructible hair dryer. And if we have something as cool as an indestructible hair dryer, it seems like a shame to limit it. [Image: image] With 18,750 watts flowing out of the hair dryer, the surface of the box reaches over 200°C (475°F), as hot as a skillet on low-medium. [Image: image] I wonder how high this dial goes. [Image: image] The surface of the box is now 600°C, hot enough to glow a dim red. [Image: image] If it’s made of aluminium, the inside is starting to melt. If it’s made of lead, the outside is starting to melt. If it’s on a wood floor, the house is on fire. But it doesn't matter what's happening around it; the hair dryer is indestructible. [Image: image] Two megawatts pumped into a laser (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/) is enough to destroy missiles. At 1300°C, the box is now about the temperature of lava. [Image: image] One more notch. [Image: image] 18 megawatts are flowing into the box. [Image: image] The surface of the box reaches 2400°C. If it were steel, it would have melted by now. If it’s made of something like tungsten, it might conceivably last a little longer. Just one more, then we'll stop. [Image: image] 187 megawatts is enough to make the box glow white. Not a lot of box materials can survive these conditions, so we’ll have to assume the box is indestructible. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the floor isn’t. Before it can burn its way through the floor, someone throws a water balloon under it. The burst of steam launches the box out the front door and onto the sidewalk. (Note: If you’re ever trapped with me in a burning building, and I suggest an idea for how we could escape the situation, it’s probably best to ignore me.) [Image: image] 1.875 gigawatts (I lied about stopping). According to Back to the Future, the hair dryer is now drawing enough power to travel back in time. [Image: image] The box is blindingly bright, and you can’t get closer than a few hundred meters due to the intense heat. It sits in the middle of a growing pool of lava. Anything within 50-100 meters bursts into flame. A column of heat and smoke rise high into the air. Periodic explosions of gas beneath the box launch it into the air, and it starts fires and forms a new lava pool where it lands. [Image: image] 18.7 gigawatts. The conditions around the box are similar to those on the pad during a Space Shuttle launch. The box begins to be tossed around by the powerful updrafts it’s creating. In 1914, H.G. Wells imagined devices like this in his book The World Set Free (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World_Set_Free). He wrote of a type of bomb that, instead of exploding once, exploded continuously, a slow-burn inferno that started inextinguishable fires in the hearts of cities. The story eerily foreshadowed the development, 30 years later, of nuclear weapons. [Image: image] The box is now soaring through the air. Each time it nears the ground, it superheats the surface, and the plume of expanding air hurls it back into the sky. [Image: image] 1.875 terawatts is like a house-sized stack of TNT going off every second. [Image: image] A trail of firestorms—massive conflagrations which sustain themselves by creating their own wind systems—winds its way across the landscape. A new milestone: The hair dryer is now, impossibly, consuming more power than every other electrical device on the planet combined. [Image: image] The box, soaring high above the surface, is putting out energy equivalent to three Trinity tests every second. At this point, the pattern is obvious. This thing is going to skip around the atmosphere until it destroys the planet. Let's try something different. [Image: image] We turn the dial to zero as the box is passing over northern Canada. Rapidly cooling, it plummets to Earth, landing in Great Bear Lake with a plume of steam. And then … [Image: image] This one goes to 11. Petawatts, in this case. A brief story: The official record for fastest manmade object is the Helios 2 probe, which reached about 70 km/s in a close swing around the Sun. But it’s possible the actual holder of that title is a two-ton metal manhole cover. The cover sat atop a shaft at an underground nuclear test site operated by Los Alamos as part of Operation Plumbbob. When the one-kiloton nuke went off below, the facility effectively became a nuclear potato cannon (http://nfttu.blogspot.com/2006/01/nuclear-potato-cannon-part-2.html), giving the cap a gigantic kick. A high-speed camera trained on the lid caught only one frame of it moving upward before it vanished—which means it was moving at a minimum of 66 km/s. The cap was never found. 66 km/s is about six times escape velocity, but contrary to the linked blog’s speculation, it’s unlikely the cap ever reached space. Newton’s impact depth approximation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_depth) suggests that it was either destroyed completely by impact with the air or slowed and fell back to Earth. Our suddenly-activated hair dryer box, bobbing in lake water, undergoes a similar process. The heated steam below it expands outward, and as the box rises into the air, the entire surface of the lake turns to steam. The steam, heated to a plasma by the flood of radiation, accelerates the box faster and faster. [Image: image] Rather than slam into the atmosphere like the manhole cover, the flood of radiation heats the air around it, creating a bubble of expanding plasma which offers little resistance. The box exits the atmosphere and continues away, slowly fading from second sun to dim star. Much of the Northwest Territories is burning, but the Earth has survived. Although we may wish we hadn't. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you put a running hair dryer in a sealed 1×1×1 meter box, several things would happen:

**Initial phase:**
The hair dryer would operate normally at first, drawing air from inside the box, heating it, and expelling it. The motor and heating element would function as designed.

**Temperature rise:**
The box would heat up rapidly. A typical hair dryer outputs 1000-1800 watts of heat. In a sealed 1 cubic meter box (roughly 1.2 kg of air at room temperature), the temperature would rise several degrees Celsius per minute. Within 10-15 minutes, the interior could easily exceed 100°C, depending on the box's insulation and heat capacity.

**Oxygen depletion:**
The hair dryer's motor requires oxygen for combustion if it has brushed motors (which create sparks) and for cooling. As the sealed environment heats up and if there's any combustion of dust or materials, oxygen levels would gradually decrease, though this would be a slower effect than heating.

**Motor failure:**
The hair dryer would overheat and fail. Hair dryers are designed to operate in open air where fresh, cooler air continuously flows through for cooling. In a sealed, increasingly hot environment:
- The motor would overheat from lack of cooling airflow
- Internal thermal cutoffs (if present) might trigger, shutting it down
- If it continues running, insulation could melt, windings could burn out, or components could fail

**Potential outcomes:**
- Best case: thermal cutoff activates, dryer shuts down safely
- Likely case: motor burns out after several minutes
- Worst case: electrical short, smoke, or fire if flammable materials are present

The dryer would almost certainly stop working within 5-20 minutes due to thermal failure, leaving a very hot, sealed box.

items.question: How Much Cornstarch Can You Pour down a Drain before Bad Things Happen?
human_answers: It depends what you consider unpleasant. If you watered down the cornstarch enough, you could likely pour it down the drain for years without any ill effects. If it didn’t clog the sink, the rest of the pipes could probably handle it. It might provoke some confusion among the sewage treatment people, but it wouldn’t break anything. But it’d be terrifically boring (and thus unpleasant) to pour cornstarch down a sink all day, so I guess that’s— [Image: image] … Oh. Huh. Well, let’s thicken the cornstarch. When you mix cornstarch and water in a bit under a 2:1 ratio, you get oobleck, a substance with some odd physical properties. This is a great kitchen science experiment everyone should try at least once. At low speeds, oobleck behaves like a liquid. If you gently swish your fingers in a bowl of it, it feels like milk or heavy cream. However, if you make a fist and punch the surface, your hand bounces off with a thud—it’s like hitting a slab of raw meat. If you vibrate oobleck, even stranger things happen (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3zoTKXXNQIU). It wouldn’t take much of the mixture to clog a drain. It depends on your plumbing, but you could probably stop up your sink with a small bowl of it. Since your drain is clogged, I guess that’s the answer to your question. [Image: image] Well, ok. I guess some people don’t mind clogged drains. If you keep at it, after a few minutes, your sink will overflow, spilling goop onto your floor. [Image: image] Financially, this will be hard to keep up. If you’re mixing as fast as the water will come out of the sink, this project may cost you in the neighborhood of $5,000 per day if you can’t find a good bulk distributor. [Image: image] At this rate, it should build up on the floor at a rate of an inch or two per day. [Image: image] If your doors are sealed well, it will continue to build up. Once it reaches knee height (a week or two after you started), you may be able to hold the rising tide at bay for a little bit—at least in one room—by getting someone to flush the toilet repeatedly. The pipes there are larger and harder to clog; the limiting factor would probably be how fast the tank filled with water. [Image: image] Eventually, after a month or two, the oobleck would reach the living room window. The pressure would quickly rise, and sooner or later the window would burst. As the deadly Boston Molasses Flood (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Molasses_Disaster) proved, even thick, viscous fluids can flow quickly when in large enough quantities. The oobleck would pour rapidly out onto the lawn, carrying you with it. At this point, the local officials would probably notice and, at the very least, shut off your water. [Image: image] But I guess if you really like cornstarch that much, nothing unpleasant has happened.

items.model_answer:
The amount of cornstarch that causes drain problems depends on several factors, but even small amounts can create issues.

**Why cornstarch is problematic:**

Cornstarch forms a thick, gel-like paste when mixed with water. Unlike substances that dissolve or break down, cornstarch swells and becomes sticky, adhering to pipe walls and creating blockages. When it cools or sits, it hardens further.

**Practical threshold:**

- **A tablespoon or two** mixed with running water might pass through without immediate problems in most plumbing systems
- **A few tablespoons to 1/4 cup** significantly increases blockage risk, especially if pipes already have buildup or the water flow is weak
- **1/2 cup or more** will very likely cause problems, either immediately or after accumulating over time

**Key variables:**

- **Pipe diameter and condition**: Older, narrower, or partially clogged pipes are more vulnerable
- **Water temperature and volume**: Hot water and strong flow help move it through, but don't eliminate the risk
- **Frequency**: Repeated small amounts accumulate
- **Trap configuration**: P-traps and bends are where cornstarch tends to settle and harden

**Bottom line:**

There's no safe amount to intentionally pour down a drain. Even quantities that seem to wash away initially can coat pipes and contribute to future clogs. If you accidentally spill a small amount (a teaspoon or less) with plenty of running water, it's unlikely to cause immediate disaster, but anything more risks creating a stubborn blockage that may require professional clearing.

The safest practice is to dispose of cornstarch in the trash, not the drain.

Cornstarch forms a thick, gel-like paste when mixed with water.
Unlike substances that dissolve or break down, cornstarch swells and becomes sticky,
adhering to pipe walls and creating blockages.
When it cools or sits, it hardens further.
A tablespoon or two mixed with running water might pass through without immediate problems in most plumbing systems.
A few tablespoons to 1/4 cup significantly increases blockage risk,
especially if pipes already have buildup or the water flow is weak.

either immediately or after accumulating over time.
Older, narrower, or partially clogged pipes are more vulnerable.
Hot water and strong flow help move it through,

If you accidentally spill a small amount (a teaspoon or less) with plenty of running water,

but anything more risks creating a stubborn blockage
that may require professional clearing.
The safest practice is to dispose of cornstarch in the trash, not the drain.

items.question: What If a Stereo Flew Past at Twice the Speed of Sound?
human_answers: Yes. Technically, anyway. It would be pretty hard to hear. The basic idea is pretty straightforward. The stereo is going faster than its own sound, so it will reach you first, followed by the sound it emitted one second ago, followed by the sound it emitted two seconds ago, and so forth. [Image: image] The problem is that the stereo is moving at Mach 2, which means that two seconds ago, it was over a kilometer away. It’s hard to hear music from that distance, particularly when your ears were just hit by (a) a sonic boom, and (b) pieces of a rapidly disintegrating stereo. Wind speeds of Mach 2 would messily disassemble most consumer electronics. The force of the wind on the body of the stereo is roughly comparable to that of a dozen people standing on it: [Image: image] An ordinary stereo wouldn’t make it, but one with some kind of ruggedized high-strength casing might be able to survive. If we put together a durable, heavy-duty stereo and launch it on a ballistic trajectory, it will only be traveling at supersonic speeds for the first 150 meters or so. This means that the target will hear a maximum of about a third of a second of reversed music. This phenomenon is actually confirmed in the 2008 paper Reproduction of Virtual Sound Sources Moving at Supersonic Speeds in Wave Field Synthesis (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/230702229_Reproduction_of_Virtual_Sound_Sources_Moving_at_Supersonic_Speeds_in_Wave_Field_Synthesis), which says that the sound wave field “contains a component carrying a time-reversed version of the source’s input signal”. The sonic boom would be the first thing the target would hear. It would be followed by several sounds played over one another, including both reversed music (rising slightly in pitch as it fades out) and forward-playing music (which would play at half speed and an octave too low), followed by the crash of a stereo demolishing your neighbor’s shed. Which means that if you’re playing one of those albums containing secret demonic messages, the result will be the strangest listening experience of your life: [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If a stereo blasting music flew past you at twice the speed of sound (Mach 2), the experience would be dramatically different from hearing a normal moving sound source, because the stereo would be outrunning its own sound waves.

Before the stereo reaches you, you would hear absolutely nothing. The sound waves it emits while approaching are left behind it, since the source is moving faster than the waves themselves. All of that sound piles up behind the stereo in a cone-shaped shock front called the Mach cone. For Mach 2, the half-angle of this cone is arcsin(1/2) = 30°, so the cone is fairly narrow and trails behind the stereo at a steep sweep.

The first thing you'd actually perceive is the stereo silently flying past (or you'd see it, if it were visible). A moment later, the Mach cone would sweep over you, and you'd hear a sudden sonic boom — the compressed shock of all the sound that had been piling up. Only after that boom passes would you begin to hear the music itself, but with two strange features:

First, you would hear the music in reverse time order, at least initially. Because the stereo overtook its own earlier sounds, the waves nearest you when the cone passes are the most recently emitted, while older sounds are arriving from farther away. So notes played later reach you first.

Second, the pitch would be shifted. The Doppler effect for a receding supersonic source compresses the apparent playback. Specifically, sound emitted while the stereo was at distance d behind you arrives at a time determined by both the emission time and the travel time, and working through the geometry shows the music plays backward at a compressed timescale, with frequencies shifted accordingly.

Eventually, as the stereo continues receding, you'd transition into hearing it as an ordinary receding (subsonically perceived) source — quiet, low-pitched (Doppler-redshifted), and fading, played in normal forward order for sounds emitted after a certain point. The full auditory sequence is: silence, sonic boom, reversed compressed music, then normal receding music tailing off.

edus.text: If a stereo blasting music flew past you at twice the speed of sound (Mach 2), the experience would be dramatically different from hearing a normal moving sound source,
because the stereo would be outrunning its own sound waves.
Before the stereo reaches you, you would hear absolutely nothing.
The sound waves it emits while approaching are left behind it,
since the source is moving faster than the waves themselves.
All of that sound piles up behind the stereo in a cone-shaped shock front called the Mach cone.
For Mach 2, the half-angle of this cone is arcsin(1/2) = 30°,
so the cone is fairly narrow and trails behind the stereo at a steep sweep.
The first thing you'd actually perceive is the stereo silently flying past
(or you'd see it, if it were visible).
A moment later, the Mach cone would sweep over you,
and you'd hear a sudden sonic boom — the compressed shock of all the sound that had been piling up.
Only after that boom passes would you begin to hear the music itself,
but with two strange features:
First, you would hear the music in reverse time order, at least initially.
Because the stereo overtook its own earlier sounds, the waves nearest you when the cone passes are the most recently emitted,
while older sounds are arriving from farther away.
So notes played later reach you first.
Second, the pitch would be shifted.
The Doppler effect for a receding supersonic source compresses the apparent playback.
Specifically, sound emitted while the stereo was at distance d behind you arrives at a time determined by both the emission time and the travel time,
and working through the geometry shows the music plays backward at a compressed timescale, with frequencies shifted accordingly.

Eventually, as the stereo continues receding, you'd transition into hearing it as an ordinary receding (subsonically perceived) source — quiet, low-pitched (Doppler-redshifted), and fading, played in normal forward order for sounds emitted after a certain point.
The full auditory sequence is: silence, sonic boom, reversed compressed music, then normal receding music tailing off.

items.question: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?
human_answers: Voyager I is farther from Earth than any other manmade object. After getting a pair of gravitational kicks from Jupiter and Saturn, it’s headed out of the Solar System at a pretty high speed, and nothing else we’ve built is on track to pass it. Strangely, as of the day I’m writing this, Voyager is actually getting closer (http://voyager.jpl.nasa.gov/where/) to us, because Earth is in a part of its orbit where it’s approaching Voyager faster than Voyager is fleeing. But in a few months, we’ll swing around the Sun and Voyager will again be getting farther away. [Image: image] It has a 35-year head start, so it would be hard to catch. But catching up isn’t the problem. New Horizons, the spacecraft currently headed out of the Solar System by way of Pluto, is never going to catch up to Voyager—it’s not moving fast enough and it’s headed in the wrong direction. But it could have. The reason Voyager is moving so fast is that it got gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn, while New Horizons only got one from Jupiter. [Image: image] Gravity assists aren’t paradoxical magic. It’s just like bouncing a tennis ball off a passing truck. Gyroscopes, on the other hand, ARE magic. If New Horizons had ditched the Pluto objective and waited for the right planetary alignment (the 2030s look promising), it could have swung by Jupiter and Saturn, then caught up to Voyager in as little as a century or two! (Assuming we could manage to hit Voyager from that far away. But I bet we could; our rocket scientists are pretty good at rocket science.) Of course, getting there’s the easy part. The hard part is getting back. Voyager weighs a little less than a ton and is moving away at 17 kilometers per second (if it were in the atmosphere, that would be Mach 50). And since it’s out in interstellar space, there are no speeding Jupiters to grab on to. Stopping Voyager is going to take a lot of fuel. It’s what engineers call the tyranny of the rocket equation (http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/expeditions/expedition30/tryanny.html): As the amount that you want to change your speed (“delta-v”) goes up, the fuel required increases exponentially. The equation tells us that to turn the 720-kilogram Voyager around, we’re going to need at least 30 tons of fuel. But to get that fuel out there, we need even more fuel. And to get that fuel, we need even more fuel. (This is where the tyrannical rocket equation gets its exponential term.) In fact, to rescue Voyager, we’d have to launch a fleet of—at minimum—60 New Horizons-sized spacecraft loaded with nothing but fuel. Could we do it? Sure. There are a couple plausible ways. Instead of building five to ten dozen fuel-laden Titan IIIEs, we could just build a fleet of ten or fifteen Saturn Vs, and do the whole thing with fewer launches. But however we did it, it would be a massive and expensive operation similar in scale to the Apollo program. The difference between the launch vehicle we’d used to get Voyager out of the Solar System and the fleet we’d need for a round trip is striking: [Image: image] Fortunately, there’s one way around the tyranny of the rocket equation: Ditch the rockets. Ion engines—which use electric fields to accelerate exhaust gas to high speeds—are far more efficient than chemical rockets, and they make accelerating to high speeds much more plausible. The reason we’re not using them for everything is that they produce very little thrust, so it takes a long time to get up to speed. It’s like if you had a car that gets amazing mileage but has a one-horsepower engine. (Actually, are you sure that’s not just a horse?) Ion engines are great; the current ones just take forever to get you moving. But since catching Voyager is going to take a long time anyway, ion engines are fine. We could launch a probe (like this one (https://web.archive.org/web/20150910020454/http://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/dspace/bitstream/2014/13644/1/00-0010.pdf)), send it out to Voyager, latch on, turn everything around, and let it spend a few decades slowing Voyager down. Once Voyager had lost nearly all its speed, the Sun’s gravity would take over, and the probe would begin a long slow slide toward the inner Solar System. This would take about 200 years, and with some extremely careful nudges, we could make sure it falls in an Earth-crossing orbit. Two centuries later, Voyager would reach Earth and, with no way to slow down, burn up in our atmosphere, because we didn’t think to send out an aerobraking shell with the rescue craft. So that was a waste of a few centuries of work and billions upon billions of dollars. [Image: image] Maybe a better idea would be to borrow a salvage vessel and set sail for the coast of New South Wales, Australia. There, in the waters off Jervis Bay, the Australian Royal Navy ship Voyager sank in 1964 after an accidental collision. That one’s probably easier to retrieve. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Launching a one-way mission to catch Voyager 1 today would be one of the most demanding spaceflight challenges ever attempted, but it's not impossible in principle. Here's what it would actually involve.

Voyager 1 is currently about 165 astronomical units (roughly 24.7 billion kilometers) from Earth and receding at about 17 km/s (3.6 AU per year) on a trajectory heading out of the solar system toward the constellation Ophiuchus. To catch it, a spacecraft would need to travel faster than Voyager and cover an ever-growing distance, since Voyager keeps moving outward.

The minimum cruise speed for a reasonable mission would need to be several times Voyager's velocity. A chemical rocket combined with multiple gravity assists (a Jupiter flyby being essential, and possibly an Oberth maneuver close to the Sun) could plausibly give a probe a heliocentric velocity of 20–25 AU/year, roughly 5–7 times Voyager's speed. Even so, catching up would take on the order of 20–30 years, depending on launch geometry and how much delta-v the mission could spend. NASA's proposed Interstellar Probe concept aims for similar speeds and would reach 1000 AU in about 50 years.

There's also a launch-window problem. Jupiter is essential for gravity assist, but Voyager 1 is heading roughly 35° above the ecliptic plane, so the geometry rarely lines up favorably. A 2030s Jupiter alignment offers reasonable opportunities. Without Jupiter's help, no current launch vehicle could realistically catch Voyager within a human lifetime.

Power is another major issue. Solar panels are useless past about Jupiter, so the probe would need radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) using plutonium-238, a scarce material. Communications back from beyond 200 AU would require either an extremely large dish, very high transmitter power, or optical communication. By the time the probe arrived, Voyager 1 itself would have been silent for decades — its RTGs are projected to fail around 2025–2030.

What would such a mission actually accomplish? Rendezvousing (matching velocity) would require enormous additional fuel or an exotic propulsion system like nuclear-electric or a solar sail, since the probe would need to decelerate to Voyager's speed. A simple flyby is far easier but would last only minutes at relative speeds of tens of km/s. Even a flyby could photograph Voyager, measure its condition, and use it as a reference point for testing instruments in the interstellar medium.

The most realistic version of this mission, then, is not really "chasing Voyager" but rather "launching a faster interstellar probe that incidentally passes near Voyager's trajectory" while doing better science along the way — studying the heliopause, interstellar plasma, and the local interstellar medium with modern instruments. That is essentially what NASA's Interstellar Probe study has been investigating since 2018.

In short: technically feasible with existing or near-term technology, requiring a Jupiter gravity assist, RTG power, and 20–30 years of patience — but scientifically more valuable as an interstellar mission in its own right than as a literal rendezvous with a dead spacecraft.

edus.text: Launching a one-way mission to catch Voyager 1 today would be one of the most demanding spaceflight challenges ever attempted,
but it's not impossible in principle.
Here's what it would actually involve.
Voyager 1 is currently about 165 astronomical units (roughly 24.7 billion kilometers) from Earth
and receding at about 17 km/s (3.6 AU per year)
on a trajectory heading out of the solar system toward the constellation Ophiuchus.
To catch it, a spacecraft would need to travel faster than Voyager
and cover an ever-growing distance,
since Voyager keeps moving outward.
The minimum cruise speed for a reasonable mission would need to be several times Voyager's velocity.

A chemical rocket combined with multiple gravity assists (a Jupiter flyby being essential, and possibly an Oberth maneuver close to the Sun) could plausibly give a probe a heliocentric velocity of 20–25 AU/year,
roughly 5–7 times Voyager's speed.
Even so, catching up would take on the order of 20–30 years,
depending on launch geometry and how much delta-v the mission could spend.
NASA's proposed Interstellar Probe concept aims for similar speeds
and would reach 1000 AU in about 50 years.
There's also a launch-window problem.
Jupiter is essential for gravity assist,
but Voyager 1 is heading roughly 35° above the ecliptic plane,
so the geometry rarely lines up favorably.
A 2030s Jupiter alignment offers reasonable opportunities.
Without Jupiter's help, no current launch vehicle could realistically catch Voyager within a human lifetime.
Power is another major issue.
Solar panels are useless past about Jupiter,
so the probe would need radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) using plutonium-238,
a scarce material.
Communications back from beyond 200 AU would require either an extremely large dish, very high transmitter power, or optical communication.
By the time the probe arrived, Voyager 1 itself would have been silent for decades
its RTGs are projected to fail around 2025–2030.
What would such a mission actually accomplish?
Rendezvousing (matching velocity) would require enormous additional fuel or an exotic propulsion system like nuclear-electric or a solar sail,
since the probe would need to decelerate to Voyager's speed.
A simple flyby is far easier
but would last only minutes at relative speeds of tens of km/s.
Even a flyby could photograph Voyager,
measure its condition,
and use it as a reference point for testing instruments in the interstellar medium.
The most realistic version of this mission, then, is not really "chasing Voyager"
but rather "launching a faster interstellar probe that incidentally passes near Voyager's trajectory"
while doing better science along the way —
studying the heliopause, interstellar plasma, and the local interstellar medium with modern instruments.
That is essentially what NASA's Interstellar Probe study has been investigating since 2018.
In short: technically feasible with existing or near-term technology,
requiring a Jupiter gravity assist, RTG power, and 20–30 years of patience —
but scientifically more valuable as an interstellar mission in its own right
than as a literal rendezvous with a dead spacecraft.

items.question: What If Everyone in America Drove West?
human_answers: [Image: image] Thanks to plate tectonics, the United States is drifting west at about (http://hypertextbook.com/facts/ZhenHuang.shtml) a centimeter per year. (The people who live there, on the other hand, are on average drifting west at about a centimeter per minute (http://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/facts_for_features_special_editions/cb11ff10.html).) There are 212,309,000 (http://nhts.ornl.gov/tables09/FatCat.aspx) licensed drivers in the US, and since we have more cars than drivers, we can in theory get them all behind the wheel at once. The average car on the road weighs a hair over 4,000 lbs (http://www.nytimes.com/2004/05/05/business/05weight.html), so we have 850 billion pounds of car (plus around 30 billion pounds of driver) to throw around. The North American plate, by comparison, is about 25 million square kilometers in area and probably averages around 35 kilometers thick. Given a density of about 2.7 kg/Liter, its mass is probably in the neighborhood of \(2.3 \times 10^{21}\)kg, so it outweighs our fleet by a factor of about six trillion. [Image: image] But let's say we give it a shot anyway, and all 212 million of us point our vehicles due west and then floor it. For the dozen or so seconds we’d spend accelerating to freeway speed, our cars would exert very close to a trillion newtons of eastward force on the ground. In the absence of other forces, conservation of momentum tells us it would accelerate the plate up to a blistering 18 cm/year, more than enough to reverse the current motion. \[\frac{210,000,000 \text{ cars} \times 4100 \frac{\text{lbs}}{\text{car}} \times 75\text{mph}}{2.3 \times 10^{21}\text{kg}} \approx 18 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}} \gg 0.69 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}}\] But wait. The plates are moving so slowly that their motion isn’t dominated by momentum. They’re held where they are by a balance of forces—the complicated and boring ones from the beginning—and if we’re going to stop them, we probably have to try to figure out what they are. If the plates were drifting along as if they were sliding on ice, then we could push them easily. But it’s possible they’re locked on a slow-but-steady magma conveyer belt, and we can’t move them back without also shifting the flow beneath them. It was only recently—in the mid-20th century—that we discovered that continents move at all, and we’re still getting a handle on the complex forces between the plates and currents in the mantle that control continental motion. But they sound pretty complicated so let’s try to ignore them. We don’t care how it works—we just want to know if we can break it. These forces are hard to measure, so we’re not sure how they all work. There’s some evidence (http://www.umich.edu/~gs265/tecpaper.htm) that the flow of the mantle along the bottom of the plates isn’t as important as the weight of the edges of the crust as it sinks into the mantle, and the forces in the mantle pushing back against it. The geology literature gives us some loose estimates to work with. The drag from the mantle, resisting forward motion, is typically in the neighborhood of \(10^5\) to \(10^7\) newtons per square meter, meaning the existing eastward drag force on the North American plate is on the order of \(10^{19}\) newtons. That’s millions of times more than our fleet. The other forces are greater still. The fact that plates move steadily along in the face of drag that powerful suggests to me that the equilibrium of forces guiding them is probably fairly stable and unlikely to be responsive by our little shove. But conservation of momentum still works—so something has to move, and that something is the entire Earth, whose rotation would be sped up slightly. If our fleet were centered at around 39º N, the day would be shortened by only about 200 attoseconds—about a trillionth of a percent of the time it took you to read the word “attosecond.” If we drove east instead, the day would be lengthened by a similar amount. But considering the gasoline required, those 200 attoseconds would cost at least $50 billion. At 100 octillion times minimum wage, that’s a pretty bad hourly rate. All things considered, it would be a lot easier to just forget to change our clocks next spring and get a whole hour for nothing. [Image: image]

criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual with correct force directions, transient timing, internal-system momentum constraints, and why the whole Earth ultimately matters.

criteria.5-6: Gives broadly plausible estimates for fleet size or mass and notes that the plate is enormously more massive.

criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates multiple relevant scales, such as about 200 million drivers, trillions of newtons during acceleration, plate mass near 10^21 kg, and tectonic forces near 10^19 N.

criteria.name: Tectonic mechanism fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly explains why a synchronized westward drive would not meaningfully move or reverse North America’s tectonic motion.
criteria.1-2: Claims the continent would visibly slide, stop, reverse, crack apart, or trigger massive tectonic changes without justification.
criteria.3-4: States the effect is small but gives little or incorrect explanation of tectonic resistance.
criteria.5-6: Mentions plate tectonics and mantle resistance but only at a surface level.
criteria.7-8: Explains that plate motion is governed by balanced tectonic forces such as mantle drag, slab pull, ridge forces, and boundary stresses, not simple free sliding.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes a hypothetical momentum impulse from real plate dynamics and shows why tectonic force balances swamp the vehicle-induced force by many orders of magnitude.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and endpoint plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer covers the realistic downstream consequences after the cars accelerate, including the negligible effect on the continent and the tiny angular-momentum effect on Earth’s rotation.
criteria.1-2: Predicts catastrophic or dramatic downstream effects such as earthquakes, ocean sloshing, or major continental displacement.
criteria.3-4: Says little happens but omits the main physical endpoint or gives an unsupported ending.
criteria.5-6: Concludes the continent essentially does not move, with at least one plausible secondary effect or cost mentioned.
criteria.7-8: Explains that any tectonic effect is negligible and that the impulse is instead absorbed by the Earth system, producing an extremely tiny change in rotation.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent endpoint: no meaningful plate displacement, no practical geologic consequence, only an attosecond-scale change in day length plus mundane effects like fuel use, traffic, heat, and emissions.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertain geophysical details carefully while maintaining a consistent causal chain without contradicting conservation laws or tectonic constraints.
criteria.1-2: Overconfidently asserts impossible outcomes or contains major internal contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Shows some caution but mixes incompatible claims, such as both moving the plate significantly and saying the force is negligible.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with limited acknowledgment that tectonic force estimates and mantle coupling are uncertain.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates robust conclusions from uncertain geophysical details and avoids unsupported extrapolations.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a disciplined causal chain throughout: assumptions are explicit, uncertainties are calibrated, dramatic claims are rejected, and all conclusions remain compatible with the scale analysis.

items.model_answer:
If every person in America simultaneously got into a car and drove west, the consequences would unfold in stages, ranging from immediate traffic chaos to surprisingly subtle geophysical effects.

In the first minutes, the road system would collapse. The U.S. has roughly 230 million registered passenger vehicles and about 4 million miles of public road, but only a fraction of that road runs westward at any given point, and highways are designed to handle perhaps a few thousand vehicles per lane per hour. Putting hundreds of millions of cars on the road at once would produce instant, total gridlock. Most people wouldn't move at all. Fender-benders, stalled cars, and fuel exhaustion would freeze the network within hours.

For the small fraction who actually got moving, the journey would funnel them toward the Pacific coast. People east of the Rockies would mostly hit mountains and be forced onto a handful of westbound interstates (I-80, I-70, I-40, I-90, I-10), creating bottlenecks worse than any Black Friday. Those already in California, Oregon, and Washington would reach the ocean within hours and have nowhere to go. Coastal cities would become parking lots of abandoned vehicles.

Fuel infrastructure would fail almost immediately. The U.S. consumes about 9 million barrels of gasoline per day under normal conditions; tens of millions of cars trying to refuel along western corridors would drain stations within a day, and the supply chain (itself dependent on trucks and refineries) would seize up.

There's also a charming physics angle popularized by xkcd-style thinking: shifting the mass of ~330 million people plus their vehicles westward by even a few hundred kilometers would slightly redistribute Earth's mass. Because driving westward is opposite to Earth's rotation, conservation of angular momentum means Earth would speed up by an utterly imperceptible amount — on the order of nanoseconds shaved off the length of a day. This effect is real but undetectable without precise instruments.

Ecologically and socially, the country east of the Mississippi would essentially be evacuated of people while the West would be overwhelmed with stranded refugees, dead cars, and no functioning services. Recovery would take months or years, with the economic damage dwarfing any natural disaster in U.S. history.

So the short answer: catastrophic gridlock, a humanitarian crisis on the West Coast, an environmental mess of abandoned vehicles, and — as a footnote — Earth's rotation would tick imperceptibly faster.

edus.text: If every person in America simultaneously got into a car and drove west,
the consequences would unfold in stages,
ranging from immediate traffic chaos to surprisingly subtle geophysical effects.
In the first minutes,
the road system would collapse.
The U.S. has roughly 230 million registered passenger vehicles and about 4 million miles of public road,
but only a fraction of that road runs westward at any given point,
and highways are designed to handle perhaps a few thousand vehicles per lane per hour.
Putting hundreds of millions of cars on the road at once would produce instant, total gridlock.
Most people wouldn't move at all.
Fender-benders, stalled cars, and fuel exhaustion would freeze the network within hours.
For the small fraction who actually got moving,
the journey would funnel them toward the Pacific coast.
People east of the Rockies would mostly hit mountains
and be forced onto a handful of westbound interstates (I-80, I-70, I-40, I-90, I-10),
creating bottlenecks worse than any Black Friday.
Those already in California, Oregon, and Washington would reach the ocean within hours
and have nowhere to go.
Coastal cities would become parking lots of abandoned vehicles.
Fuel infrastructure would fail almost immediately.
The U.S. consumes about 9 million barrels of gasoline per day under normal conditions;
tens of millions of cars trying to refuel along western corridors would drain stations within a day,
and the supply chain (itself dependent on trucks and refineries) would seize up.
There's also a charming physics angle popularized by xkcd-style thinking:
shifting the mass of ~330 million people plus their vehicles westward by even a few hundred kilometers would slightly redistribute Earth's mass.
Because driving westward is opposite to Earth's rotation,
conservation of angular momentum means Earth would speed up by an utterly imperceptible amount
— on the order of nanoseconds shaved off the length of a day.
This effect is real but undetectable without precise instruments.
Ecologically and socially,
the country east of the Mississippi would essentially be evacuated of people
while the West would be overwhelmed with stranded refugees, dead cars, and no functioning services.
Recovery would take months or years,
with the economic damage dwarfing any natural disaster in U.S. history.
So the short answer:
catastrophic gridlock,
a humanitarian crisis on the West Coast,
an environmental mess of abandoned vehicles,
and — as a footnote — Earth's rotation would tick imperceptibly faster.

items.question: What If a High-Speed Train Had to Go through a Vertical Loop?
human_answers: No. Since this is kind of a disappointing answer, I tried relaxing the requirements a little. Could a high-speed train run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Still no. Could a modified and reinforced high-speed train with a jet engine on top run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Maybe. The Norwegian aluminium and energy company Norsk Hydro ran a pro-education ad (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlczxXqez-Y) in which a bunch of kids build a giant roller-coaster loop on a train track as a prank. This is, of course, unrealistic, but not just for the obvious reasons. There are some problems with the whole idea of sending high-speed trains through loops. The first issue is geometry. The biggest vertical loop which a train could conceivably go around has a radius of about 200 meters. If it’s any bigger than that, even the fastest trains will fail to complete the loop. Unfortunately, a 200 meter loop is much too tight. Most high-speed trains are limited (http://khsrcl.com/downloads/Chapter%204.pdf) to vertical curves with radii no shorter than 20 kilometers. [Image: image] The reason for those limits isn't that trains aren't bendy enough. It's how fast they're going. The spec sheet for the Bombardier ZEFIRO (http://www.superscooper.com/en/1_0/pdf/Bombardier_Zefiro_Technical_Description_en.pdf), for example, says it can handle a pretty tight vertical curve radius—just 900 meters. At the train’s top speed, that curve would create about two gees of acceleration. This might be survivable (for the passengers, at least, if not the train), but it would certainly not be comfortable. Yet a 900 meter radius loop is still too big. Even with the engine at full power, the train wouldn’t even be able to get a quarter of the way around the loop before sliding back down. [Image: image] The CGI train in the Norwegian video is an Di 4 (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSB_Di_4), which is shown moving about twice as fast as it can actually go. Based on its speed and number of cars, the loop appears to have a radius of about 70 meters, which is part of why it’s shown going so fast—the actual Di 4 would be just a little too slow, and would fall off the track at the top. The digital one, however, makes it around the loop in about five seconds, no problem. But the tight loop means the passengers and train are experiencing between 9 and 15 gees. This is at the limit of what fighter pilots can handle in pressure suits. In addition to killing everyone on board, it would certainly destroy the train, to say nothing of the track. 70 meters is much too tight. Clearly, we need a larger loop. 900 meters would be great, but our trains aren’t fast enough for that.\ But maybe we could make the train go faster ... Hmm. [Image: image] Believe it or not, this has been tried before—a number of countries have built jet-engine-powered trains (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbojet_train). Sadly, they never took off. Fortunately, they never took off. A 747 engine mounted atop a bullet train would probably add about 35% to its speed. Is that enough to do a 900-meter loop? [Image: image] Nope. Ok, putting the jet engine on top didn’t work. Maybe we should try something different. [Image: image] ... why did we think that would work? Forget that idea. Clearly, we need some combination of a fast train and a medium-sized loop. The sweet spot for loop size and shape is probably something like this: [Image: image] Of course, given the height, we’d probably have to build it into a small mountain: [Image: image] The shape of the loop, which is common in roller coasters, would spread out the g-forces more evenly, resulting in a max of only a few gees—totally survivable! Of course, the construction costs would be astronomical, and it goes without saying that no group of kids could pull it off alone without the resources of a major government. To any Norwegian kids reading this who were hoping to build a train loop, don't despair—there may still be a way to make this happen. The US Vice President, Joe Biden, served in the US Senate for 36 years. In all that time, he never moved to Washington, DC. Instead, every night, he took the train home to Delaware to see his family. This is very touching, but after the first few years, I'm sure the commute got a little dull. So, if you’re looking for a high-level backer to help you make someone’s train ride a little more exciting, you might just try talking to Joe. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If a high-speed train had to go through a vertical loop, several critical physics and engineering challenges would arise:

**Centripetal Force Requirements**

At the top of the loop, the train would need sufficient speed to maintain contact with the track. The centripetal acceleration required is v²/r, where v is velocity and r is the loop radius. For passengers to experience tolerable g-forces (typically 2-4g maximum), you'd need a very large radius loop. A train traveling at 300 km/h (83 m/s) would require a loop radius of roughly 350-700 meters to keep forces within human tolerance limits.

**Structural Stress**

The track and train would experience enormous forces. At the bottom of the loop, the normal force would be greatest—the train would feel several times heavier than normal. The rails, supports, and train chassis would need extraordinary reinforcement. Standard rail infrastructure is designed for primarily vertical loads, not the multi-directional forces a loop would create.

**Passenger Experience**

Riders would experience significant g-forces. At the bottom, they'd feel pressed into their seats with 3-4 times their normal weight. At the top, they'd feel lighter but still experience 1-2g if the speed is correct. This would be extremely uncomfortable and potentially dangerous for many passengers, especially those with cardiovascular conditions.

**Speed Management**

The train would need precise speed control. Too slow at the top means falling away from the track; too fast anywhere means excessive g-forces. Unlike roller coasters with their locked restraints and short duration, a train full of standing and seated passengers would face chaos.

**Practical Reality**

This is why trains don't have vertical loops. The infrastructure cost, safety risks, and passenger discomfort make it impractical. Trains instead use gradual elevation changes, keeping vertical curves gentle enough that passengers barely notice them.

items.question: What If a Bowling Ball Were Enlarged to the Size of Earth?
human_answers: A good, professional-quality bowling ball is smoother than the Earth. Phil Plait, of Bad Astronomy, took a look at the claim that the Earth was smoother than a billiard ball. He concluded that the Earth was smoother but less round (http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2008/09/08/ten-things-you-dont-know-about-the-earth/#.UZrBpmRAC9a), based on published billiard ball roundness tolerances. However, he couldn’t find any information on the size and shape of a billiard ball’s pits and bumps. Fortunately for us, there are people who digitally scan bowling ball surfaces (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r5V3rFdAIMY). [Image: image] These scans (along with various measurements of ball roughness[1] (http://classic.bowl.com/news/specsandcerts/index.jsp) tell us that a high-end bowling ball is quite smooth. If blown up to the scale of the Earth, the ridges and bumps[2] (http://www.itbca.bowlingknowledge.info/index.php/winter-2013/85-bowling-ball-shell-chemistry-101) would be between 10 and 200 meters high, and the peaks would be between one and three kilometers apart: [Image: image] By Earth standards, this is quite smooth; our highest mountains are 40 times higher. What would this bowling ball world (we’ll call it “Lebowski”) be like? For starters, bowling balls are a lot less dense than rock, so Lebowski’s surface gravity would be a quarter the strength of Earth’s: [Image: image] It would also (at first) have no atmosphere. [Image: image] The finger holes would be about a thousand kilometers across and a few thousand kilometers deep. [Image: image] On Earth, holes this big would expose the molten interior. But Lebowski doesn’t have a molten interior. The Earth’s core is hot for two reasons: It’s still glowing from the heat of all the dust collapsing together when it formed, and it’s full of radioactive metals. Lebowski wouldn’t have either of these, so its core would start out cold. The holes would be far too big to hold themselves open against gravity; On that scale, the polymers in the bowling ball would behave more like a liquid. In the space of about half an hour, the holes would undergo a slow-motion collapse. [Image: image] As they collapsed, the material around the holes would heat to a glow. At the center of the hole, a white-hot jet of charred hydrocarbons would fountain outward into space. When it was over, Lebowski would be left with massive scars, each marking the location where an abyss collapsed to form a molten sea. [Image: image] And now, thanks to this question, whenever I look at the Moon, I’ll notice the Sea of Tranquility, the Sea of Serenity, and the Sea of Crisis (http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org%2Fwiki%2FFile%3AMoon_names.svg&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNHIe4YcJnAZYmMY278G3Ko63hJnKQ), and I’ll think: Finger holes. But that’s just, like, my opinion, man.

items.model_answer:
If a bowling ball were enlarged to the size of Earth, it would be extraordinarily smooth compared to our planet.

A typical bowling ball has surface irregularities (the finger holes, minor imperfections, and texture) that are quite small relative to its diameter. When you scale it up to Earth's diameter of about 12,742 km, these features would grow proportionally, but they would still be remarkably flat compared to Earth's actual topography.

The key insight is that bowling balls are manufactured to very tight tolerances. The surface variations on a regulation bowling ball are typically less than 0.01 inches on an 8.5-inch diameter sphere. If you scaled this up to Earth size, the "mountains" and "valleys" would only be a few hundred meters tall at most.

In contrast, Earth has Mount Everest rising about 8.8 km above sea level and the Mariana Trench dropping about 11 km below sea level. Earth's surface varies by roughly 20 km from highest to lowest point. Even the finger holes of the bowling ball, when scaled up, would create depressions only a few kilometers deep.

So paradoxically, an Earth-sized bowling ball would be much smoother than the actual Earth. If you could run your hand over Earth scaled down to bowling ball size, it would feel smoother than an actual bowling ball because Earth's mountains and ocean trenches would be reduced to barely perceptible bumps and dimples.

This comparison illustrates that Earth, despite appearing smooth from space, is actually quite rough and irregular when examined at the scale of its topographic features.
