edus.text: If you tried to hold an airplane to the ground with a rope,
the outcome would depend entirely on the strength of the rope compared to the thrust force generated by the aircraft's engines.
When an airplane's engines run at full throttle,
they produce enormous thrust forces.
For a commercial airliner like a Boeing 737, this is roughly 20,000-27,000 pounds of thrust per engine
so 40,000-54,000 pounds total.
A fighter jet can produce even more relative to its weight.
The rope would need to withstand this entire thrust force.
If the rope's tensile strength is less than the thrust,
it will snap.
Most common ropes would fail immediately—
even heavy-duty climbing ropes typically break around 5,000-10,000 pounds of force.
Weak rope:
It would snap almost instantly once the engines spool up to significant power,
and the plane would accelerate forward normally.
Very strong rope/cable:
If you used something like a steel cable with sufficient tensile strength
the rope could theoretically hold—
but now you've created a different problem.
The attachment points become critical.
The anchor point in the ground would fail.
The attachment point on the aircraft would fail.
The engines would continue running against the resistance, potentially overheating or suffering damage.
Perfect scenario:
With an indestructible rope and perfect anchoring,
the airplane would simply sit there with engines screaming, unable to move forward.
The brakes would be irrelevant at this point.
Eventually you'd need to reduce throttle
to prevent engine damage from prolonged operation at high power without airflow.
This scenario is somewhat similar to engine run-up tests,
where aircraft are chocked and braked while engines are tested at high power—
but these are done carefully at partial throttle,
not full takeoff power for extended periods.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in. [Image: image] The impact could trigger an earthquake. Denali (also known as Mount McKinley) is a mountain in Alaska that sits just to the south of a major fault line.[1]Roger A. Hansen, Earthquake and Seismic Monitoring in Denali National Park (http://www.nps.gov/akso/nature/science/ak_park_science/PDF/2006Vol5-1/Earthquake-Monitoring.pdf), National Park Service This fault is active,[2]Alaska Earthquake Information Center, M 7.9 Denali Fault earthquake of November 3, 2002 (http://www.aeic.alaska.edu/Denali_Fault_2002/) and we know that drilling can trigger earthquakes.[3]Van der elst NJ, Savage HM, Keranen KM, Abers GA. Enhanced remote earthquake triggering at fluid-injection sites in the midwestern United States (http://www.sciencemag.org/content/341/6142/164.abstract). Science. 2013;341(6142):164-7. Earthquakes can happen at any time, so there's always a chance that dropping a mountain any distance could trigger one. So could kicking a tree. The only way to find out for sure would be to try it.[4]This article has an awful lot of citations. Assuming it didn't trigger an earthquake, the impact wouldn't be all that dramatic. If you were standing on the mountain when it happened, you'd definitely feel a jolt, but it probably wouldn't even be enough to knock you down. [Image: image] When the mountain hit the ground, the rock under it would be damaged, but only a little. The granite base is strong enough to hold up under the tremendous resting weight of a mountain;[5]Citation: The rock was holding up a mountain when you got there. the shockwave from dropping it an inch doesn't add too much pressure on top of that, and the rock would survive with a little minor cracking. People nearby would definitely feel the impact, and probably hear it; the sound would likely resemble the crack of a lightning strike (if you were standing near the mountain) fading into a long, deep rumble.[6]Citation: A dream I had once. The vibration would be equivalent to that of a 3.5-magnitude earthquake[7]For more on the specific seismic details, see Stein, Seth, and Michael Wysession. "Earthquakes." An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and Earth Structure. Malden, MA: Blackwell Pub., 2003. 241 (http://books.google.com/books?id=-z80yrwFsqoC&lpg=PA241&ots=nrVTZ77_mJ&pg=PA241#v=onepage&q&f=false). Print.; at worst, it would knock a few pictures off the wall if you happened to be living next to the mountain. Frankly, I'd be more worried about debris flying out of the gap.[8]If your magical mountain-cutter put air in the space where the rock used to be, you should avoid standing near the crack when it falls. The air will come jetting out from the closing crack, spraying rocks and dust at speeds approaching, or even—thanks to some fun heat-related effects—exceeding, Mach 1. [Image: image] Oh. You again. Ok. Dropping from a height of one foot wouldn't be all that different. [Image: image] The mountain would hit the ground at 2.5 m/s, or roughly walking speed. The shockwave from that impact would be in the range of 50 megapascals of pressure,[9]You can calculate the peak pressure of the compressive strain wave in the rock using the Joukowsky equation, which says that the peak pressure of the compressive wave in a material is (material's density)x(speed at impact)x(the speed of sound in the material). This equation is is normally used in fluid mechanics, but it works fine here, too! (http://www.win.tue.nl/analysis/reports/rana06-08.pdf) which granite can handle without too much trouble.[10]Bhat HS, Sammis CG, Rosakis AJ. The Micromechanics of Westerley Granite at Large Compressive Loads (http://www.rosakis.caltech.edu/downloads/pubs/2011/181%20The%20Micromechanics%20of%20Westerley.pdf). Pure Appl. Geophys. 2011;168(12):2181-2198. [11]"... for a plane shock wave ... granite will stand a compressive stress of 3000-4000 MPa elastically before failing." Persson, Per-Anders, Roger Holmberg, and Jaimin Lee. Rock Blasting and Explosives Engineering (http://books.google.com/books?id=sdLO5HESJwgC&lpg=PA5&ots=-SJy8Yx-ea&pg=PA5#v=onepage&q&f=false). Boca Raton, FL: CRC, 1994. 5-6. Print. [Image: image] Ok. Let's jump straight to the end of John-Clark's question: [Image: image] After falling from summit height to base height—about 5 kilometers—the mountain would be moving at roughly the speed of sound. The last two impacts were pretty minor. This one wouldn't be. The jolt to the ground would be as violent as in a magnitude 7 earthquake.[12]In addition, there's a good chance that a shock this large will release some existing seismic energy; see: U.S. Congress, Office of Technology Assessment, Seismic Verification of Nuclear Testing Treaties (http://www.princeton.edu/~ota/disk2/1988/8838/883809.PDF), P. 715, OTA-ISC-361 (Washington, DC: U.S. Government Printing Office, May 1988). There wouldn't exactly be a crater, but the mountain would definitely not be shaped like it used to be. The pressure from the impact would be high enough to produce some unusual geologic strutures. If you put a lump of coal under the meteor, the impact would be enough to convert it to diamond (and, unfortunately, smash it to bits).[13]French B. M. (1998) Traces of Catastrophe: A Handbook of Shock-Metamorphic Effects in Terrestrial Meteorite Impact Structures., Chapter 4 (http://www.lpi.usra.edu/publications/books/CB-954/chapter4.pdf), LPI Contribution No. 954,Lunar and Planetary Institute, Houston. 120 pp The good news is that, the last time a magnitude 7+ earthquake hit Denali, no one was killed.[2]Alaska Earthquake Information Center, M 7.9 Denali Fault earthquake of November 3, 2002 (http://www.aeic.alaska.edu/Denali_Fault_2002/) Let's just hope nobody is on the mountain itself when we do this. [Image: image] Ok. Last one. We'd need to lift the mountain out of the atmosphere, out past the orbit of the GPS satellites, to the very outer limits of the Earth's gravity well. Then we let go. [Image: image] It would hit Alaska at 10 kilometers per second. The Last Frontier would not fare well. A 50-mile-wide crater would have obliterated Denali National Park. Anchorage would be buried under three meters of gravel.[14]Purdue University ImpactEarth asteroid impact simulator (http://www.purdue.edu/impactearth/) The shaking, combined with the debris falling into the ocean, would cause tsunamis across the Pacific. Across North America, the ground would tremble. A wind would sweep in from the northwest. The sky would darken. In 1815, Mount Tambora erupted in the largest volcanic event in recorded history. The resulting global veil of aerosols made 1816 the "year without a summer". Snow fell in Massachusetts in June, ice formed on rivers in Pennsylvania in August, and frost killed most of the spring crops. The cooling effects lingered for several years. The Alaska impact would be far worse. Over the next few months, the skies around the globe fill with dust. Summer is canceled and winter arrives. Global temperatures would drop by 5 to 20 degrees Celsius and stay that way for a year or more.[15]Covey, C, S Thompson, P Weissman, and M Maccracken. "Global Climatic Effects Of Atmospheric Dust From An Asteroid Or Comet Impact On Earth." Global and Planetary Change 9, no. 3-4 (1994): 263-273. On the plus side, we would not be engulfed in a global firestorm. When the Chicxulub comet hit the Yucatan peninsula 65 million years ago, it blasted molten debris into space. This debris fell back to Earth around the world, heating the atmosphere and igniting global firestorms. These may have played a role in the mass extinctions.[16]I don't have a citation for this. But, c'mon, it's a 'global firestorm'. Can you really imagine that every species made it through unscathed? However, our mountain would carry only about 10% of the energy of the Chicxulub impactor, which means that it wouldn't be capable of igniting global firestorms.[17]Osinski, G. R., and E. Pierazzo. "Environmental Effects of Impact Events." In Impact Cratering Processes and Products. (http://books.google.com/books?id=3Vzky11ZR3UC&lpg=PA149&ots=8kqLGZFB1g&pg=PA151#v=onepage&q&f=false). Chicester: Wiley, 2012. 151. The firestorms would, in fact, only cover some of North America. So that's a relief. The northern hemisphere would be covered in ice, but our species would probably manage to limp through. Civilization, on the other hand, might well collapse. A total collapse of modern civilization would be a serious blow to the already sluggish economy, and the economic damage could amount to $80 trillion per year (the total value of all human goods and services). All in all, it would have serious implications for the upcoming elections. And that's that. We've dropped the mountain from as high as it can be dropped, and I hope John-Clark is proud of the resulting devastation. Thanks for reading, and— [Image: image] No, that doesn't actually make sense. The Earth's gravitational pull doesn't— [Image: image] Dropping it from higher up won't do anything; there won't be enough force pulling it toward the— [Image: image] Ok. Fine. You win. We'll try it. [Image: image] Oops.

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Immediate Kinematics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise as a massive mountain suddenly losing its bottom inch, leaving a one-inch unsupported gap that closes under gravity, and computes or qualitatively estimates the short fall accurately.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise or treats the mountain as disappearing, exploding, floating, or collapsing from summit height without justification.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes a small vertical drop but gives highly implausible timing, speed, or motion, or ignores gravity-driven closure.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that the mountain drops only about one inch and the motion is brief, but with little quantitative grounding.
criteria.7-8: Gives plausible estimates for closure time and impact speed, e.g. tens of milliseconds and under 1 m/s, with mostly sound reasoning.
criteria.9-10: Accurately derives or explains the one-inch free fall, about 70 ms closure time, and modest impact speed while avoiding overstatement.

criteria.name: Impact, Stress, and Seismic Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly analyzes the mechanical impact of the mountain landing after a one-inch fall, including stress waves, rock strength, seismic shaking, and earthquake-triggering uncertainty.
criteria.1-2: Claims inevitable continent-scale destruction, no effect at all, or other outcomes incompatible with the small drop and huge mass.

items.model_answer:
If the bottom inch of a massive mountain suddenly vanished, the mountain would experience catastrophic structural failure and collapse.

Here's what would happen:

**Immediate structural failure**: Mountains are held up by the compressive strength of rock at their base. An entire mountain weighing billions of tons rests on its foundation. If even one inch of that foundation disappeared, the overlying rock would have nothing supporting it. The mountain would instantly begin to fall under its own weight.

**Collapse dynamics**: The mountain wouldn't fall as a single rigid block. Instead, it would undergo rapid, chaotic disintegration. The immense weight would cause the rock layers to shear, fracture, and pulverize as they dropped. The collapse would propagate upward through the mountain structure at roughly the speed of sound in rock (several kilometers per second).

**Energy release**: The gravitational potential energy released would be enormous. For a mountain like Everest (roughly 8.8 km tall with a mass on the order of 10^15 kg), dropping even one inch (2.54 cm) would release energy equivalent to a significant earthquake—potentially magnitude 7 or higher. The actual collapse would release far more energy as the entire structure came down.

**Ground effects**: The impact would generate powerful seismic waves, causing earthquake-like shaking for hundreds of kilometers. A massive debris avalanche would spread outward from the base, potentially traveling many kilometers and burying surrounding valleys.

**Atmospheric effects**: The collapse would generate enormous dust clouds, blast waves, and potentially pyroclastic-density-current-like flows of pulverized rock and air.

In essence, removing that bottom inch would trigger one of the most violent geological catastrophes imaginable—the instantaneous destruction of the entire mountain.

items.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up. It's hard to get to orbit because you have to go so fast. Space isn't like this: [Image: image] Space is like this: [Image: image] Space is about 100 kilometers away. That's far away—I wouldn't want to climb a ladder to get there—but it isn't that far away. If you're in Sacramento, Seattle, Canberra, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Phnom Penh, Cairo, Beijing, central Japan, central Sri Lanka, or Portland, space is closer than the sea. Getting to space[1]Specifically, low Earth orbit, which is where the International Space Station is and where the shuttles could go. is easy. It's not, like, something you could do in your car, but it's not a huge challenge. You could get a person to space with a small sounding rocket the size of a telephone pole. The X-15 aircraft reached space[2]The X-15 reached 100 km on two occasions, both when flown by Joe Walker. just by going fast and then steering up.[3]Make sure to remember to steer up and not down, or you will have a bad time. [Image: image] But getting to space is easy. The problem is staying there. Gravity in low Earth orbit is almost as strong as gravity on the surface. The Space Station hasn't escaped Earth's gravity at all; it's experiencing about 90% the pull that we feel on the surface. To avoid falling back into the atmosphere, you have to go sideways really, really fast. The speed you need to stay in orbit is about 8 kilometers per second.[4]It's a little less if you're in the higher region of low Earth orbit. Only a fraction of a rocket's energy is used to lift up out of the atmosphere; the vast majority of it is used to gain orbital (sideways) speed. This leads us to the central problem of getting into orbit: Reaching orbital speed takes much more fuel than reaching orbital height. Getting a ship up to 8 km/s takes a lot of booster rockets. Reaching orbital speed is hard enough; reaching to orbital speed while carrying enough fuel to slow back down would be completely impractical.[5]This exponential increase is the central problem of rocketry: The fuel required to increase your speed by one km/s multiplies your weight by about 1.4. To get into orbit, you need to increase your speed to 8 km/s, which means you'll need a lot of fuel: $ 1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\approx 15$ times the original weight of your ship. Using a rocket to slow down carries the same problem: Every 1 km/s decrease in speed multiplies your starting mass by that same factor of 1.4. If you want to slow all the way down to zero—and drop gently into the atmosphere—the fuel requirements multiply your weight by 15 again. These outrageous fuel requirements are why every spacecraft entering an atmosphere has braked using a heat shield instead of rockets—slamming into the air is the most practical way to slow down. (And to answer Brian's question, the Curiosity rover was no exception to this; although it used small rockets to hover when it was near the surface, it first used air-braking to shed the majority of its speed.) How fast is 8 km/s, anyway? I think the reason for a lot of confusion about these issues is that when astronauts are in orbit, it doesn't seem like they're moving that fast; they look like they're drifting slowly over a blue marble. But 8 km/s is blisteringly fast. When you look at the sky near sunset, you can sometimes see the ISS go past ... and then, 90 minutes later, see it go past again.[6]There are some good apps and online tools to help you spot the station, along with other neat satellites. My favorite is ISS Detector (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.runar.issdetector), but if you Google you can find lots of others. In those 90 minutes, it's circled the entire world. The ISS moves so quickly that if you fired a rifle bullet from one end of a football field,[7]Either kind. the International Space Station could cross the length of the field before the bullet traveled 10 yards.[8]This type of play is legal in Australian rules football. Let's imagine what it would look like if you were speed-walking across the Earth's surface at 8 km/s. To get a better sense of the pace at which you're traveling, let's use the beat of a song to mark the passage of time.[9]Using song beats to help measure the passage of time is a technique also used in CPR training, where the song "Stayin' Alive" is used to . suppose you started playing the 1988 song by The Proclaimers, I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles). That song is about 131.9 beats per minute, so imagine that with every beat of the song, you move forward more than two miles. In the time it took to sing the first line of the chorus, you could walk from the Statue of Liberty all the way to the Bronx: [Image: image] It would take you about two lines of the chorus (16 beats of the song) to cross the English Channel between London and France. The song's length leads to an odd coincidence. The interval between the start and the end of I'm Gonna Be is 3 minutes and 30 seconds,[10]Based on timing from the official Youtube video (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbNlMtqrYS0) and the ISS is moving at 7.66 km/s. This means that if an astronaut on the ISS listens to I'm Gonna Be, in the time between the first beat of the song and the final lines ... [Image: image] ... they will have traveled just about exactly 1,000 miles.

criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that staying in orbit requires large sideways velocity and that rocket-braking to a few mph means removing most of it.
criteria.9-10: Uses the orbital-speed insight as the central causal premise, explicitly correcting the intuition that space is hard mainly because it is high up.

criteria.name: Rocket-equation and fuel-mass consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures why carrying enough propellant to slow from orbital speed to a few mph is impractical, including compounding mass penalties.
criteria.1-2: Claims rockets could simply slow the craft without addressing fuel mass, or gives physically impossible fuel assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Says it would need 'a lot of fuel' but gives no mechanism for why this becomes prohibitive.
criteria.5-6: Explains that propellant requirements are very large and reduce payload, but lacks rocket-equation-style compounding.
criteria.7-8: Accurately describes exponential or multiplicative mass growth from needing propellant to brake, plus propellant to carry that propellant.
criteria.9-10: Connects the full mission penalty: reaching orbit while carrying deorbit/braking fuel is vastly harder, making near-zero-speed reentry impractical compared with aerobraking.

criteria.name: Atmospheric entry, heat shield, and aerobraking mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains how normal reentry uses the atmosphere to dissipate kinetic energy and how rocket braking would change heating, trajectory, and landing dynamics.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the atmosphere or incorrectly says heat shields are unnecessary simply because rockets exist.

criteria.7-8: Explains that slowing before dense atmosphere would greatly reduce heating but requires enormous propellant; also notes remaining descent/terminal landing issues.

items.model_answer:
Using rockets to slow a spacecraft from orbital velocity to just a few miles per hour during reentry is theoretically possible but practically extraordinarily difficult, primarily because of the enormous amount of propellant required.

A spacecraft in low Earth orbit travels at roughly 17,500 mph (about 7.8 km/s). To shed all that velocity with rockets instead of using atmospheric drag, you would need to perform a propulsive deceleration burn nearly equal in magnitude to the burn that originally got the craft into orbit. The rocket equation makes this brutal: every kilogram of payload you want to land softly requires several kilograms of propellant, and that propellant itself must be carried up to orbit in the first place. For typical chemical rockets with specific impulses around 300–450 seconds, fully canceling orbital velocity propulsively requires a propellant mass fraction comparable to launch—roughly 80–90% of the vehicle's mass at the start of the burn must be fuel. Reaching the surface at only a few miles per hour would also require a final hover/landing burn similar to what lunar landers perform, adding still more propellant.

The advantages of this approach would be significant. The spacecraft would not encounter the searing 1,650 °C (3,000 °F) plasma of hypersonic reentry, so it would need no ablative heat shield, no thermal tiles, and no blunt-body shape designed to manage shock heating. The communications blackout caused by ionized plasma surrounding the vehicle would disappear. Astronauts would experience gentle, sustained deceleration rather than several g's of reentry loading, and the vehicle could land precisely at any chosen location rather than being constrained to a narrow reentry corridor. Reusability would be far simpler because the structure would not be repeatedly thermally shocked.

The disadvantages are why no one does it. The mass penalty is so severe that the rocket needed to launch such a "propulsive reentry" spacecraft would be vastly larger than current vehicles—you essentially have to launch the equivalent of two rockets' worth of fuel for one mission. The atmosphere provides "free" deceleration via drag, and trading that for propellant is uneconomical with current propulsion technology. There are also new risks: an engine failure during the deceleration burn would be unrecoverable, whereas a passive heat shield works without active systems.

SpaceX's Starship uses a hybrid approach that hints at the tradeoffs. It still relies on aerodynamic braking and heat tiles for the bulk of deceleration but uses a propulsive landing burn at the end. A purely propulsive reentry remains in the realm of thought experiment, more plausible for low-gravity, airless bodies like the Moon than for Earth, where the atmosphere is simply too useful a brake to ignore.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ... and how much they'd cost. Printing Wikipedia People have considered printing out Wikipedia before. A few years ago, student Rob Matthews printed every Wikipedia featured article (http://www.brandnew.uk.com/wikipedia-as-a-printed-book/), creating a book several feet thick. Of course, that's just a small slice of the best of Wikipedia; the entire encyclopedia would be a lot bigger. Wikipedia user Tompw (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User:Tompw) has set up a page (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_in_volumes) for calculating the size of the whole English Wikipedia in printed volumes. It would currently fill a lot of bookshelves. Keeping up with the edits would be harder. Keeping up The English Wikipedia currently receives about 125,000 to 150,000 edits each day, or 90-100 per minute.[1]ToolServer: Edit rate (http://toolserver.org/~emijrp/wmcharts/wmchart0001.php) We could try to define a way to measure the "word count" of the average edit, but that's hard bordering on impossible. Fortunately, we don't need to—we can just estimate that each change is going to require us to reprint a page somewhere. Many edits will actually change multiple pages—but many other edits are reverts, which would let us put back pages we've already printed.[2]The filing system for this would be staggering (http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_card_storage.NARA.jpg). One page per edit seems like a reasonable middle ground. For a mix of photos, tables, and text typical of Wikipedia, a good inkjet printer might put out 15 pages per minute. That means you'd only need about six printers running at any given time to keep pace with the edits. The paper would stack up quickly. Using Rob Matthews' book as a starting point, I did my own back-of-the-envelope estimate for the size of the current English Wikipedia. Based on the average length of featured articles vs. all articles, I came up with an estimate of 300 cubic meters for a printout of the whole thing.[3]That's a little larger than Tompw's estimate, but I'm assuming they're printed straight from the browser, which is less compact and includes images. By comparison, if you were trying to keep up with the edits, you'd print out 300 cubic meters every month. $500,000 per month Six printers isn't that many, but they'd be running all the time. And that gets expensive. The electricity to run them would be cheap—a few dollars a day. The paper would be about one cent per sheet, which means you'll be spending about a thousand dollars a day. You'd want to hire people to manage the printers 24/7, but that would actually cost less than the paper. Even the printers themselves wouldn't be too expensive, despite the terrifying replacement cycle. But the ink cartridges would be a nightmare. Ink A study by QualityLogic[4]QualityLogic: Cost of Ink Per Page Analysis (http://www.qualitylogic.com/tuneup/uploads/docfiles/QualityLogic-Cost-of-Ink-Per-Page-Analysis_US_1-Jun-2012.pdf), June 2012 found that for a typical inkjet printer, the real-life cost of ink ran from 5 cents per page for black-and-white to around 30 cents per page for photos. That means you'd be spending four to five figures per day on ink cartridges. You definitely want to invest in a laser printer. Otherwise, in just a month or two, this project could end up costing you half a million dollars: [Image: image] But that's not even the worst part. If, someday, Wikipedia decides to go dark (http://sys01-public.msnbc.msn.com/technology/wikipedia-goes-dark-piracy-bill-protest-day-117714) again, and you want to join the protest ... [Image: image] You'll have to get a crate of markers and color every page solid black yourself. I would definitely stick to digital.

items.model_answer:
Printing the entire English Wikipedia in real time is a fun thought experiment because Wikipedia is not a static target—it's constantly being edited, so "real time" means your printer has to keep up with the live edit stream while also catching up on the existing corpus.

As of now, the English Wikipedia contains roughly 6.8 million articles. If you exported them as plain prose (ignoring images, tables, and references) the text comes to something like 50–60 GB uncompressed, which works out to roughly 3 billion words. Printed as standard book pages (about 500 words per page), that's around 6 million pages, or roughly 3,000 typical 2,000-page volumes—a bookshelf about a third of a kilometer long.

Now add the "real time" constraint. English Wikipedia receives on the order of 1.5–2 edits per second on average, with bursts much higher during major events. Each edit can range from a typo fix (a few bytes) to a full article rewrite (tens of kilobytes). Even a modest average of 1 KB of new or changed text per second means about 86 MB of churn per day, or roughly 30 GB per year of pure delta text. To "print in real time" you'd need to reprint affected pages as edits arrive—meaning a continuous trickle of replacement pages plus a once-and-done bulk print of the existing 6 million pages.

A fast office laser printer handles maybe 50 pages per minute, or 72,000 pages per day. At that rate, printing the existing corpus alone would take about 83 days running 24/7, by which point Wikipedia would have grown by several hundred thousand new edits, and you'd never catch up with a single printer. To truly stay in real time you'd need to print roughly 6 million pages within a window short enough that the ongoing edit rate doesn't outpace you. Practically, this means parallelizing: about 100 industrial printers running continuously could finish the initial dump in under a day, after which a handful of printers could keep up with live edits (since 2 edits/second translates to only a few thousand reprinted pages per day, well within one fast printer's capacity).

The physical resources are substantial but not absurd. Six million pages is about 30 tonnes of paper, roughly 360 trees' worth of pulp. Toner would run into the hundreds of kilograms. Storage of the output would require something like 600 cubic meters of shelving—a small warehouse. Cost-wise, at maybe 5 cents per page for paper and toner, you're looking at $300,000 just for the initial print, plus ongoing costs for the edit stream.

The deeper problem, though, is conceptual: a printed snapshot is obsolete the instant it leaves the printer. To maintain a true real-time printed mirror, you'd need a system that not only prints new versions but somehow retracts or marks superseded pages—otherwise you accumulate a growing archive of stale versions rather than a current encyclopedia. In that sense, "printing Wikipedia in real time" reveals why the encyclopedia exists digitally in the first place: the medium of paper is fundamentally mismatched to a continuously edited collaborative document. You can capture Wikipedia, or you can keep it current, but on paper you cannot really do both at once.

edus.text: Printing the entire English Wikipedia in real time is a fun thought experiment
because Wikipedia is not a static target
it's constantly being edited
so "real time" means your printer has to keep up with the live edit stream
while also catching up on the existing corpus.
As of now, the English Wikipedia contains roughly 6.8 million articles.
If you exported them as plain prose
ignoring images, tables, and references
the text comes to something like 50–60 GB uncompressed
which works out to roughly 3 billion words.
Printed as standard book pages (about 500 words per page)
that's around 6 million pages
or roughly 3,000 typical 2,000-page volumes
a bookshelf about a third of a kilometer long.
Now add the "real time" constraint.
English Wikipedia receives on the order of 1.5–2 edits per second on average
with bursts much higher during major events.
Each edit can range from a typo fix (a few bytes) to a full article rewrite (tens of kilobytes).
Even a modest average of 1 KB of new or changed text per second means about 86 MB of churn per day
or roughly 30 GB per year of pure delta text.
To "print in real time" you'd need to reprint affected pages as edits arrive
meaning a continuous trickle of replacement pages
plus a once-and-done bulk print of the existing 6 million pages.
A fast office laser printer handles maybe 50 pages per minute
or 72,000 pages per day.
At that rate, printing the existing corpus alone would take about 83 days running 24/7
by which point Wikipedia would have grown by several hundred thousand new edits
and you'd never catch up with a single printer.
To truly stay in real time you'd need to print roughly 6 million pages within a window short enough that the ongoing edit rate doesn't outpace you.
Practically, this means parallelizing
about 100 industrial printers running continuously could finish the initial dump in under a day
after which a handful of printers could keep up with live edits
since 2 edits/second translates to only a few thousand reprinted pages per day
well within one fast printer's capacity.
The physical resources are substantial but not absurd.
Six million pages is about 30 tonnes of paper
roughly 360 trees' worth of pulp.
Toner would run into the hundreds of kilograms.
Storage of the output would require something like 600 cubic meters of shelving
a small warehouse.
Cost-wise, at maybe 5 cents per page for paper and toner, you're looking at $300,000 just for the initial print
plus ongoing costs for the edit stream.
The deeper problem, though, is conceptual
a printed snapshot is obsolete the instant it leaves the printer.
To maintain a true real-time printed mirror, you'd need a system
that not only prints new versions
but somehow retracts or marks superseded pages
otherwise you accumulate a growing archive of stale versions
rather than a current encyclopedia.
In that sense, "printing Wikipedia in real time" reveals why the encyclopedia exists digitally in the first place
the medium of paper is fundamentally mismatched to a continuously edited collaborative document.
You can capture Wikipedia, or you can keep it current
but on paper you cannot really do both at once.

items.question: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?
human_answers: As ridiculous as it sounds, this is—sort of—possible. Falling from great heights is dangerous.[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Republic_Presidential_Unit_Citation)] A balloon could actually help save you, although a regular helium one from a party obviously won't do the trick. [Image: image] If the balloon is large enough, you don't even need the helium. A balloon will act as a parachute, slowing your fall to non-fatal speeds. Avoiding a high-speed landing is, unsurprisingly, the key to survival. As one medical paper[1]De Haven H. Mechanical analysis of survival in falls from heights of fifty to one hundred and fifty feet (http://injuryprevention.bmj.com/content/6/1/62.3.long). Injury Prevention. 6(1):62-b-68. put it, It is, of course, obvious that speed, or height of fall, is not in itself injurious ... but a high rate of change of velocity, such as occurs after a 10 story fall onto concrete, is another matter. ... which is just a wordy version of the old saying, "It's not the fall that kills you, it's the sudden stop at the end." To act as a parachute, a balloon filled with air, rather than helium, would have to be 10 to 20 meters across—far too big to be inflated with portable tanks. A powerful fan could be used to fill it with ambient air, but at that point, you may as well just use a parachute. Helium The helium makes things easier. It doesn't take too many helium balloons to lift a person. In 1982, Larry Walters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Walters) flew across Los Angeles in a lawn chair lifted by weather balloons, eventually reaching several miles in altitude. After passing through LAX airspace, he descended by shooting some of the balloons with a pellet gun. On landing, Walters was arrested, although the authorities had some trouble figuring out what to charge him with. At the time, an FAA safety inspector told the New York Times, "We know he broke some part of the Federal Aviation Act, and as soon as we decide which part it is, some type of charge will be filed."[2]ARMCHAIR AIRMAN SAYS FLIGHT FULFILLED HIS LIFELONG DREAM (http://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/04/us/armchair-airman-says-flight-fulfilled-his-lifelong-dream.html?pagewanted=all), New York Times, July 4, 1982 A relatively small helium balloon—certainly smaller than a parachute—will suffice slow your fall, but it still has to be huge by party balloon standards. The biggest consumer rental helium tanks are about 250 cubic feet, and you'd need to empty at least 10 of them to put enough air in the balloon to support your weight. You'd have to do it quickly. The compressed helium cylinders are smooth and often quite heavy, which means they have a high terminal velocity. You'll only have a few minutes to use up all the cylinders. (As soon as you emptied one, you could drop it.) You can't get around this problem by moving your starting point higher. Since the upper atmosphere is pretty thin, anything dropped from the stratosphere up will accelerate to very high speeds until it hits the lower atmosphere, then fall slowly the rest of the way. This is true of everything from small meteors[3]By the time meteors hit the Earth, they have slowed down (http://www.geology.wisc.edu/~museum/meteorite.html) to a few hundred miles per hour. to Felix Baumgartner.[4]Jason Martinez, Falling Faster than the Speed of Sound (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/), Wolfram Blog, October 24, 2012 [Image: image] But if you inflated the balloons quickly, possibly by connecting many canisters to it at once, you'd be able to slow your fall. Just don't use too much helium, or you'll end up floating at 16,000 feet like Larry Walters.http://xkcd.com/1110 [Image: image] While researching this article,[5]Additionally, while researching impact speeds for this article, I came across a discussion (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=361878) on the Straight Dope Message Boards about survivable fall heights. One poster compared a fall from height to being hit by a bus. Another user, a medical examiner, replied (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showpost.php?p=7180162&postcount=40) that this was a bad comparison: "When hit by a car, the vast majority of people are not run over; they are run under. The lower legs break, sending them into the air. They usually strike the hood of the car, often with the back of the head impacting the windshield, "starring" the windshield, possibly leaving a few hairs in the glass. They then go over the top of the car. They are still alive, although with broken legs, and maybe with head pain from the nonfatal windshield impact. They die when they hit the ground. They die from head injury." The lesson: Don't mess with medical examiners. They're apparently pretty hardcore. I managed to lock up my copy of Mathematica several times on balloon-related differential equations, and subsequently got my IP address banned from Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=how+many+days+have+i+been+alive) for making too many requests. The ban-appeal form asked me to explain what task I was performing that necessitated so many queries, so this is what I put: [Image: image] I hope they understand.

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?

criteria.name: Physical feasibility and outcome plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a physically plausible conclusion about jumping from a plane with helium tanks and a giant balloon, including whether survival is possible only under extreme, carefully constrained conditions.
criteria.1-2: Claims the plan simply works or fails for obviously false reasons, with little relation to buoyancy, drag, or impact speed.
criteria.3-4: Gives a partly plausible outcome but misses key constraints such as balloon size, inflation time, or terminal velocity.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that a large balloon could slow descent, but treats survival, helium needs, or deployment as oversimplified.
criteria.7-8: Explains that survival is possible in principle if the balloon is large enough and deployed quickly, while noting major practical dangers.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes theoretical possibility from practical near-impossibility, tying survival to reduced landing speed, adequate balloon volume, deployment timing, and manageable descent.

criteria.name: Buoyancy, drag, and balloon-size reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly explains the relevant mechanisms: helium lift, air-filled balloon drag, parachute-like behavior, and the very large volume needed to affect a human fall.
criteria.1-2: Misstates basic physics, such as implying a small party balloon or single tank can meaningfully lift or stop a person.
criteria.3-4: Mentions helium or drag but confuses lift with parachute effects or gives highly unrealistic scale estimates.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the balloon must be very large and can act like a parachute, but gives limited or vague mechanism detail.
criteria.7-8: Accurately explains both buoyant lift and aerodynamic drag, including why party-scale balloons are inadequate.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent quantitative or semi-quantitative account of needed balloon volume, helium lift, drag area, and why an air-filled balloon could slow descent even without helium.

criteria.name: Deployment sequence and long-range causal chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the answer's treatment of the full chain of events after the jump: initial acceleration, tank handling, inflation, descent stabilization, possible overshoot into floating, and landing.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the sequence of events and treats the setup as if the balloon is instantly and safely usable.
criteria.3-4: Mentions falling or inflation but omits major timing or sequencing problems during free fall.
criteria.5-6: Covers several stages, such as falling, inflating, and landing, but leaves gaps in how one stage affects the next.
criteria.7-8: Builds a mostly coherent causal chain from exit to landing, including rapid inflation, tank disposal, slowing descent, and landing risks.
criteria.9-10: Tracks the full long-range scenario with strong causal continuity, including acceleration before deployment, limited time to empty tanks, changing descent rate, possible excessive lift, and final impact dynamics.

criteria.name: Treatment of altitude, atmosphere, and terminal velocity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly handles how starting altitude and atmospheric density affect falling speed, balloon behavior, and the usefulness of going higher.
criteria.1-2: Makes incorrect claims such as higher altitude always giving more time and therefore making the plan easy.
criteria.3-4: Mentions altitude but misses how thin air, acceleration, or terminal velocity change during descent.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that altitude affects fall speed and available time, but gives incomplete treatment of atmospheric density.
criteria.7-8: Explains that very high starts can cause high speeds in thin air before slowing in denser air, limiting the benefit of extra altitude.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects altitude, air density, terminal velocity, balloon expansion/drag, and descent timing, avoiding simplistic 'start higher' reasoning.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain details, avoids internal contradictions, and keeps speculative extensions consistent with the physics of the scenario.
criteria.1-2: Presents confident but inconsistent claims, such as saying the balloon both cannot help and can safely land the person without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but also contains contradictions or unjustified certainty about survival, tank counts, or balloon dimensions.
criteria.5-6: Generally avoids contradictions and acknowledges some uncertainty, though estimates or assumptions may be underexplained.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable caveats about equipment, human control, inflation rate, and landing conditions while maintaining a consistent conclusion.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates known physics from rough estimates, states assumptions, flags practical unknowns, and keeps all claims mutually consistent throughout the counterfactual analysis.

items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane with helium tanks and a giant balloon, the outcome would depend on when and how you deployed the balloon, but it would almost certainly not save you.

**The fundamental problem: buoyancy vs. terminal velocity**

A helium balloon generates lift through buoyancy—the difference between the weight of the helium inside and the weight of air it displaces. To lift a person (say, 70 kg or 154 lbs), you'd need to displace enough air to create that much upward force. At sea level, air weighs about 1.2 kg per cubic meter, so you'd need roughly 58 cubic meters (about 2,000 cubic feet) of helium just to achieve neutral buoyancy—and even more to actually slow your fall significantly.

**What would actually happen:**

1. **Inflation time**: Inflating a balloon large enough mid-fall would take time—likely many seconds, even with high-pressure tanks. Meanwhile, you'd be accelerating toward terminal velocity (around 120 mph or 195 km/h in a belly-down position, faster if head-down).

2. **Drag vs. buoyancy**: Even if you managed to inflate a large balloon, its primary effect wouldn't be buoyancy but *drag*. A big balloon increases your surface area dramatically, which increases air resistance. This could slow your fall somewhat, similar to a drogue parachute, but nowhere near enough to survive impact.

3. **Structural failure**: The forces involved would likely tear the balloon or rip it from your grasp. At high speeds, the balloon would experience enormous drag forces. Balloon materials aren't designed for these conditions—they'd likely burst or tear away.

4. **Insufficient lift**: Even a very large balloon wouldn't provide enough buoyancy to counteract your weight at altitude where air is thinner. As you descended into denser air, buoyancy would increase slightly, but you'd still be falling far too fast.

**The bottom line**: You would still hit the ground at lethal speed. The balloon might slow you from 120 mph to perhaps 80-100 mph if it stayed intact, but that's still absolutely fatal. A proper parachute works because it creates massive drag with a large, stable surface area—something a balloon cannot replicate while also carrying your weight.

This is why parachutes, not balloons, are used for safe descents.

edus.text: If you jumped from a plane with helium tanks and a giant balloon,
the outcome would depend on when and how you deployed the balloon,
but it would almost certainly not save you.
The fundamental problem is buoyancy vs. terminal velocity.
A helium balloon generates lift through buoyancy—the difference between the weight of the helium inside and the weight of air it displaces.
To lift a person (say, 70 kg or 154 lbs), you'd need to displace enough air to create that much upward force.
At sea level, air weighs about 1.2 kg per cubic meter,
so you'd need roughly 58 cubic meters (about 2,000 cubic feet) of helium just to achieve neutral buoyancy—
and even more to actually slow your fall significantly.
Inflating a balloon large enough mid-fall would take time—likely many seconds, even with high-pressure tanks.
Meanwhile, you'd be accelerating toward terminal velocity (around 120 mph or 195 km/h in a belly-down position, faster if head-down).
Even if you managed to inflate a large balloon,
its primary effect wouldn't be buoyancy but drag.
A big balloon increases your surface area dramatically,
which increases air resistance.
This could slow your fall somewhat, similar to a drogue parachute,
but nowhere near enough to survive impact.
The forces involved would likely tear the balloon or rip it from your grasp.
At high speeds, the balloon would experience enormous drag forces.
Balloon materials aren't designed for these conditions—
they'd likely burst or tear away.
Even a very large balloon wouldn't provide enough buoyancy to counteract your weight at altitude
where air is thinner.
As you descended into denser air, buoyancy would increase slightly,
but you'd still be falling far too fast.
The bottom line is that you would still hit the ground at lethal speed.
The balloon might slow you from 120 mph to perhaps 80-100 mph
if it stayed intact,
but that's still absolutely fatal.
A proper parachute works because it creates massive drag with a large, stable surface area—
something a balloon cannot replicate while also carrying your weight.
This is why parachutes, not balloons, are used for safe descents.

items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure. There are only a handful of organizations who might plausibly have more storage capacity or a larger server infrastructure. Here's my short list of the top contenders: NSA (http://www.nsa.gov/) NRO (http://www.nro.gov/) NGIP (https://www1.nga.mil/Pages/default.aspx) CIA (https://www.cia.gov/index.html) Schlumberger (http://www.slb.com/) Tencent (http://www.tencent.com/en-us/index.shtml) Chevron (http://www.chevron.com/) Honorable mentions: Amazon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River) (They're huge, but probably not as big as Google.) Facebook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_book) (They're on the right scale and growing fast, but still playing catch-up.) Microsoft (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Bob) (They have a million servers,[1]Data Center Knowledge: [Ballmer: Microsoft has 1 Million Servers although no one seems sure why.) Let's take a closer look at Google's computing platform. Follow the money We'll start by following the money. Google's aggregate capital expenditures–spending on building stuff[2]I'm excluding the cost of an extremely expensive building they bought in New York.—adds up to somewhere over $12 billion dollars.[3]Data Center Knowledge: Google’s Data Center Building Boom Continues: $1.6 Billion Investment in 3 Months (http://www.datacenterknowledge.com/archives/2013/07/19/google-data-center-spending-continues-to-soar-1-6-billion-in-3-months/) Their biggest data centers cost half a billion to a billion dollars, so they can't have more than 20 or so of those. On their website,[4]Data center locations (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/inside/locations/index.html) Google acknowledges that they have datacenters in the following locations: Berkeley County, South Carolina Council Bluffs, Iowa Atlanta, Georgia Mayes County, Oklahoma Lenoir, North Carolina The Dalles, Oregon Hong Kong Singapore Taiwan Hamina, Finland St Ghislain, Belgium Dublin, Ireland Quilicura, Chile In addition, they appear to operate a number of other large datacenters (sometimes through subsidiary corporations), including: Eemshaven, Netherlands Groningen, Netherlands Budapest, Hungary Wrocław, Poland Reston, Virginia Additional sites near Atlanta, Georgia They also operate equipment at dozens to hundreds of smaller locations around the world. Follow the power To figure out how many servers Google is running, we can look at their electricity consumption. Unfortunately, we can't just sneak up to a datacenter and read the meter.[5]Actually, wait, can we? Somebody should try that. Instead, we have to do some digging. The company disclosed that in 2010 they consumed an average of 258 megawatts of power.[6]Google used 2,259,998 MWh of electricity in 2010 (http://www.environmentalleader.com/2011/09/09/google-reveals-electricity-use-breaking-its-silence/), which translates to an average of 258 megawatts. How many computers can they run with that? We know that their datacenters are quite efficient, only spending 10-20% of their power on cooling and other overhead.[7]Google: Efficiency: How we do it (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/efficiency/internal/) To get an idea of how much power each server uses, we can look at their "container data center" concept from 2005. It's not clear whether they actually use these containers in practice—it may just have been a now-outdated experiment—but it gives an idea of what they consider(ed) reasonable power consumption. The answer: 215 watts per server. Judging from that number, in 2010, they were operating around a million servers. They've grown a lot since then. By the end of 2013, the total amount of money they've pumped into their datacenters will be three or four times what it was as of 2010. They've contracted to buy over three hundred megawatts of power at just three sites,[8]Google: Purchasing clean energy (http://www.google.com/green/energy/use/#purchasing) which is more than they used for all their operations in 2010. Based on datacenter power usage and spending estimates, my guess would be that Google is currently running—or will soon be running—between 1.8 and 2.4 million servers. But what do these "servers" actually represent? Google could be experimenting in all kinds of wild ways, running boards with 100 cores or 100 attached disks. If we assume that each server has a couple[9]Anywhere from 2 to 5 (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of 2 TB disks attached, we come up with close to 10 exabytes[10]As a refresher, the order is: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta. An exabyte is a million terabytes. of active storage attached to running clusters. 10 Exabytes The commercial hard disk industry ships about 8 exabytes worth of drives annually.[12]IDC: Worldwide External Disk Storage Systems Factory Revenue Declines for the Second Consecutive Quarter (http://www.idc.com/getdoc.jsp?containerId=prUS24302513) Those numbers don't necessarily include companies like Google, but in any case, it seems likely that Google is a large piece of the global hard drive market. To make things worse, given the huge number of drives they manage, Google has a hard drive die every few minutes.[11]Eduardo Pinheiro, Wolf-Dietrich Weber and Luiz Andre Barroso, [Failure Trends in a Large Disk Drive Population This isn't actually all that expensive a problem, in the grand scheme of things—they just get good at replacing drives—but it's weird to think that when a Googler runs a piece of code, they know that by the time it finishes executing, one of the machines it was running on will probably have suffered a drive failure. Google tape storage Of course, that only covers storage attached to running servers. What about "cold" storage? Who knows how much data Google—or anyone else—has stored in basement archives? In a 2011 phone interview with Paul Mah of SMB Tech, Simon Anderson of Tandberg Data let slip[13]SMB Tech: Is Tape Still Relevant for SMBs? (http://www.itbusinessedge.com/cm/blogs/mah/is-tape-still-relevant-for-smbs/?cs=45557) that Google is the world's biggest single consumer of magnetic tape cartridges, purchasing 200,000 per year. Assuming they've stepped up their purchasing since then as they've expanded, this could add up to another few exabytes of tape archives. Putting it all together Let's assume Google has a storage capacity of 15 exabytes, or 15,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes. A punch card can hold about 80 characters, and a box of cards holds 2000 cards: [Image: image] 15 exabytes of punch cards would be enough to cover my home region, New England, to a depth of about 4.5 kilometers. That's three times deeper than the ice sheets that covered the region during the last advance of the glaciers: [Image: image] That seems like a lot. However, it's nothing compared to the ridiculous claims by some news reports about the NSA datacenter in Utah. NSA datacenter The NSA is building a datacenter in Utah. Media reports claimed that it could hold up to a yottabyte of data,[14]CNET: NSA to store yottabytes in Utah data centre (http://crave.cnet.co.uk/gadgets/nsa-to-store-yottabytes-in-utah-data-centre-49304118/) which is patently absurd. Later reports changed their minds, suggesting that the facility could only hold on the order of 3-12 exabytes.[15]Forbes: Blueprints Of NSA's Ridiculously Expensive Data Center In Utah Suggest It Holds Less Info Than Thought (http://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2013/07/24/blueprints-of-nsa-data-center-in-utah-suggest-its-storage-capacity-is-less-impressive-than-thought/) We also know the facility uses about 65 megawatts of power,[16]Salt-Lake City Tribune: NSA Bluffdale Center won’t gobble up Utah’s power supply (http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/news/56493868-78/power-center-electricity-utah.html.csp) which is about what a large Google datacenter consumes. A few headlines, rather than going with one estimate or the other, announced that the facility could hold "between an exabyte and a yottabyte" of data[17]Dailykos: Utah Data Center stores data between 1 exabyte and 1 yottabyte (http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/08/05/1228923/-Utah-Data-Center-stores-data-between-1-exabyte-and-1-yottabyte) ... which is a little like saying "eyewitnesses report that the snake was between 1 millimeter and 1 kilometer long." Uncovering further Google secrets There are a lot of tricks for digging up information about Google's operations. Ironically, many of them involve using Google itself—from Googling for job postings in strange cities to using image search to find leaked cell camera photos of datacenter visits. However, the best trick for locating secret Google facilities might be the one revealed by ex-Googler talentlessclown (http://www.reddit.com/user/talentlessclown) on reddit:[18]reddit: Can r/Australia help find Google's Sydney data center? Seems like a bit of a mystery... (http://www.reddit.com/r/australia/comments/1hctj4/can_raustralia_help_find_googles_sydney_data/catef4f) The easiest way to find manned Google data centres is to ask taxi drivers and pizza delivery people. There's something pleasing about that. Google has created what might be the most sophisticated information-gathering apparatus in the history of the Earth ... and the only people with information about them are the pizza delivery drivers. Who watches the watchers? [Image: image] Apparently, Domino's.

items.model_answer:
If all the world's digital data were stored on punch cards, the consequences would be staggering in terms of physical scale, energy, and logistics.

A standard IBM punch card holds about 80 columns × 12 rows of possible hole positions, which corresponds to roughly 80 bytes of usable data (less in practice, since cards were typically used for text encoded one character per column). Each card weighs about 2.5 grams and is about 0.18 mm thick.

As of the mid-2020s, humanity generates and stores on the order of 150–200 zettabytes (1 ZB = 10²¹ bytes) of digital data globally. Converting just 100 zettabytes to punch cards at 80 bytes per card would require about 1.25 × 10²¹ cards. Stacked, that column of cards would be roughly 2.25 × 10¹⁷ meters tall — about 24,000 light-years, or a quarter of the way across the Milky Way galaxy. Their combined mass would be over 3 × 10¹⁸ kilograms, comparable to a small moon, and would consume the entire annual paper output of Earth many billions of times over. The forests required to produce this paper vastly exceed all the trees on the planet.

Beyond the physical absurdity, performance would collapse. Reading a punch card mechanically takes tens of milliseconds at best, compared to nanoseconds for RAM or microseconds for SSDs — a slowdown of roughly a million- to a billion-fold. Streaming a single high-definition movie (say 5 GB) would require about 62 million cards weighing 150 tonnes, and reading it linearly at vintage card-reader speeds (around 1,000 cards per minute) would take over 100 years. The internet as we know it — real-time search, video, cloud services — would be impossible; data access would resemble 1950s batch processing, with queries taking days or weeks.

Other ripple effects: storage facilities would need to be the size of continents; humidity, fire, and insect damage would become existential threats to information; encryption and compression would be largely pointless because the bottleneck is mechanical I/O, not computation; and modern fields like machine learning, genomics, and climate modeling — which depend on petabyte-scale datasets — simply could not exist. Civilization would effectively be frozen at a pre-1970s level of information technology, even if processors themselves were modern, because the storage medium would be the binding constraint on everything.

In short, punch cards are a beautifully tangible medium, but the exponential growth of digital data has long since outrun any physical, paper-based representation by many orders of magnitude.

As of the mid-2020s, humanity generates and stores on the order of 150–200 zettabytes of digital data globally.
1 ZB = 10²¹ bytes.
Converting just 100 zettabytes to punch cards at 80 bytes per card would require about 1.25 × 10²¹ cards.
Stacked, that column of cards would be roughly 2.25 × 10¹⁷ meters tall
about 24,000 light-years, or a quarter of the way across the Milky Way galaxy.
Their combined mass would be over 3 × 10¹⁸ kilograms,
comparable to a small moon,
and would consume the entire annual paper output of Earth many billions of times over.
The forests required to produce this paper vastly exceed all the trees on the planet.
Beyond the physical absurdity, performance would collapse.
Reading a punch card mechanically takes tens of milliseconds at best,
compared to nanoseconds for RAM or microseconds for SSDs
a slowdown of roughly a million- to a billion-fold.
Streaming a single high-definition movie (say 5 GB) would require about 62 million cards weighing 150 tonnes,
and reading it linearly at vintage card-reader speeds (around 1,000 cards per minute) would take over 100 years.
The internet as we know it — real-time search, video, cloud services — would be impossible;
data access would resemble 1950s batch processing,
with queries taking days or weeks.
Other ripple effects: storage facilities would need to be the size of continents;
humidity, fire, and insect damage would become existential threats to information;
encryption and compression would be largely pointless
because the bottleneck is mechanical I/O, not computation;
and modern fields like machine learning, genomics, and climate modeling — which depend on petabyte-scale datasets — simply could not exist.
Civilization would effectively be frozen at a pre-1970s level of information technology,
even if processors themselves were modern,
because the storage medium would be the binding constraint on everything.
In short,
punch cards are a beautifully tangible medium,
but the exponential growth of digital data has long since outrun any physical, paper-based representation by many orders of magnitude.

items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how tall your friends are. [Image: image] After 30 seconds, you'd be 30 feet—9 meters—off the ground. Judging from What-If #44 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/44/), this is getting close to your last chance for a friend to throw you a sandwich or water bottle or something.[2]Not that it will help, ultimately. [Image: image] After a minute or two you would be above the trees. You'd still be about as comfortable as you were on the ground. If it's a breezy day, it will probably get chillier thanks to the steadier wind above the treeline.[3]For this article, I'm going to assume a typical atmosphere temperature profile. It can, of course, vary quite a bit. After 10 minutes you would be above all but the tallest skyscrapers, and after 25 minutes you'd pass the spire of the Empire State Building. [Image: image] The air at these heights is about 3% thinner than it is at the surface. Fortunately, your body handles air pressure changes like that all the time. Your ears may pop, but you wouldn't really notice anything else. Air pressure changes quickly with height. Surprisingly, when you're standing on the ground, air pressure is even measurably lower at your head than at your feet. If your phone has a barometer in it, as a lot of new Android phones do, you can download an app and actually see the pressure difference between your head and your feet. A foot per second is pretty close to a kilometer per hour, so after an hour, you'll be about a kilometer off the ground. At this point, you definitely start to get chilly. If you have a coat, you'll still be ok, though you might also notice the wind picking up. At about two hours and two kilometers, the temperature would drop below freezing. The wind would also, most likely, be picking up. If you have any exposed skin, this is where frostbite starts to become a concern.[4]National Weather Service: Wind Chill Temperature Index (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/windchill/images/wind-chill-brochure.pdf) Starting at this point, the air pressure would drop below what you'd experience in an airliner cabin,[5]... which are typically kept pressurized at about 70%-80% of sea level pressure, judging from the barometer in my phone. and the effects would start to become more significant, but unless you had a warm coat, the temperature would be a bigger problem. Over the next two hours, the air would drop to below-zero[6]Either unit.​[7]Not Kelvin, though. temperatures. Assuming for a moment that you survived the oxygen deprivation, at some point you'd freeze to death. But when? The scholarly authorities on freezing to death seem to be, unsurprisingly, Canadians. The most widely-used model for human survival in cold air was developed by Peter Tikuisis and John Frim for the Defence and Civil Institute of Environmental Medicine in Ontario.[8]Prediction of Survival Time in Cold Air (http://cradpdf.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/PDFS/zba6/p144967.pdf)—see page 24 for the relevant tables. According to their model, the main factor in the cause of death would be your clothes. If you were nude, you'd probably succumb to hypothermia somewhere around the five hour mark, before your oxygen ran out.[9]And frankly, this really raises more questions than it answers. If you were bundled up, you may be frostbitten, but you would probably survive ... ... long enough to reach the Death Zone. [Image: image] Above 8,000 meters—above the tops of all but the highest mountains—the oxygen content in the air is too low to support human life. Near this zone, you would experience a range of symptoms, possibly including confusion, dizziness, clumsiness, impaired vision, and nausea. As you approach the Death Zone, your blood oxygen content would plummet. Your veins are supposed to bring low-oxygen blood back to your lungs to be refilled with oxygen. But in the Death Zone, there's so little oxygen in the air that your veins lose oxygen to the air instead of gaining it.[10]Linda D. Pendleton, When Humans Fly High: What Pilots Should Know About High-Altitude Physiology, Hypoxia, and Rapid Decompression (http://www.avweb.com/news/aeromed/181893-1.html) The result would be a rapid loss of consciousness and death. This would happen around the seven hour mark; the chances are very slim that you would make it to eight. [Image: image] And two million years later, your frozen body, still moving along steadily at a foot per second, would pass through the heliopause into interstellar space—the same boundary that Voyager just crossed.[11]Again. Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto, died in 1997. A portion of his remains were placed on New Horizons spacecraft, which will fly past Pluto and then continue out of the Solar System. It's true that your hypothetical foot-per-second trip would be cold, unpleasant, and rapidly fatal. But when the Sun becomes a red giant in four billion years and consumes the Earth, you and Clyde would be the only ones to escape. So there's that. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you suddenly began rising straight up at a constant one foot per second (about 0.30 m/s, or roughly the speed of a slow escalator), the experience would start out almost unremarkable and then become increasingly dangerous as you climbed.

For the first minute or so, almost nothing would feel wrong. You'd rise about 60 feet — roughly the height of a six-story building. People on the ground might assume you were on a lift. After ten minutes you'd be at 600 feet, higher than most buildings, and the wind would start to matter: even a light breeze would push you sideways, since you have no way to anchor yourself.

Temperature drops about 3.5°F per 1,000 feet of altitude. After an hour you'd be at 3,600 feet, noticeably colder, and after two hours at over 7,000 feet you'd be feeling the chill sharply, dressed (presumably) for ordinary surface weather.

The serious trouble begins around 8,000 feet, which you'd reach in about two and a quarter hours. Above this altitude the air pressure is low enough to cause altitude sickness — headache, nausea, shortness of breath. By 15,000 feet (just over four hours in) hypoxia becomes severe; most unacclimatized people cannot think clearly. By 18,000 feet, atmospheric pressure is half that at sea level. Around 22,000 feet (about six hours), unconsciousness from oxygen deprivation is essentially certain without supplemental oxygen, and you would almost certainly die in your sleep from hypoxia, exposure, or both before reaching higher altitudes.

If somehow you survived (with oxygen and a pressure suit), the journey continues. The stratosphere begins around 33,000 feet (about 9 hours). Above about 62,000 feet — the Armstrong limit, reached in roughly 17 hours — water in your body, including in your eyes and lungs, would boil at body temperature without a pressure suit. You'd reach the conventional edge of space (the Kármán line, 100 km or 328,000 feet) after about 91 hours, just under four days.

After that you'd keep drifting up at a foot per second indefinitely — but you'd never reach orbit, because orbiting isn't about altitude, it's about sideways speed. Earth would rotate beneath you, and as you climbed higher than geostationary altitude (about 22,000 miles, which you'd reach in roughly 3,700 years), you'd eventually fall behind Earth's rotation entirely.

In short: the first minute is boring, the first hour is cold and lonely, and by the third hour you're dying of hypoxia. A foot per second sounds gentle, but constant vertical motion through the atmosphere is unforgiving.

edus.text: If you suddenly began rising straight up at a constant one foot per second
(about 0.30 m/s, or roughly the speed of a slow escalator)
the experience would start out almost unremarkable
and then become increasingly dangerous as you climbed.
For the first minute or so, almost nothing would feel wrong.
You'd rise about 60 feet
roughly the height of a six-story building.
People on the ground might assume you were on a lift.
After ten minutes you'd be at 600 feet, higher than most buildings
and the wind would start to matter:
even a light breeze would push you sideways
since you have no way to anchor yourself.
Temperature drops about 3.5°F per 1,000 feet of altitude.
After an hour you'd be at 3,600 feet, noticeably colder
and after two hours at over 7,000 feet you'd be feeling the chill sharply
dressed (presumably) for ordinary surface weather.
The serious trouble begins around 8,000 feet
which you'd reach in about two and a quarter hours.
Above this altitude the air pressure is low enough to cause altitude sickness
headache, nausea, shortness of breath.
By 15,000 feet (just over four hours in) hypoxia becomes severe;
most unacclimatized people cannot think clearly.
By 18,000 feet, atmospheric pressure is half that at sea level.
Around 22,000 feet (about six hours), unconsciousness from oxygen deprivation is essentially certain without supplemental oxygen
and you would almost certainly die in your sleep from hypoxia, exposure, or both before reaching higher altitudes.
If somehow you survived
(with oxygen and a pressure suit)
the journey continues.
The stratosphere begins around 33,000 feet
(about 9 hours).
Above about 62,000 feet — the Armstrong limit, reached in roughly 17 hours —
water in your body, including in your eyes and lungs, would boil at body temperature without a pressure suit.
You'd reach the conventional edge of space
(the Kármán line, 100 km or 328,000 feet)
after about 91 hours, just under four days.
After that you'd keep drifting up at a foot per second indefinitely
but you'd never reach orbit
because orbiting isn't about altitude
it's about sideways speed.
Earth would rotate beneath you
and as you climbed higher than geostationary altitude
(about 22,000 miles, which you'd reach in roughly 3,700 years)
you'd eventually fall behind Earth's rotation entirely.
In short:
the first minute is boring,
the first hour is cold and lonely,
and by the third hour you're dying of hypoxia.
A foot per second sounds gentle,
but constant vertical motion through the atmosphere is unforgiving.

It does not invent arbitrary rescue or escape routes, and it preserves the long-range consequence that the ascent continues indefinitely and does not become orbit. However, it has some boundary-handling gaps: it says wind would push you sideways without clarifying whether that alters the core vertical-motion premise, it does not discuss what happens after death despite the criterion explicitly highlighting continued postmortem ascent, and some survival phrasing is overconfident or slightly awkward ('die in your sleep') given the scenario. Strong overall, but not rigorous enough for 9-10.
