items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV. The number of copies of the virus carried in someone's blood can vary dramatically,[1]Data on viral load—the number of copies of the virus per mL of blood—can be found in this paper (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23196933). but across all the people in the world, there probably exists about a spoonful worth of HIV. [Image: image] The typical healthy human body contains about \(3 \times 10^{12}\) viruses. This is actually not as many as you might expect; by volume, humans are apparently a less friendly environment for viruses than, say, soil.[2]An area of wetlands in Delaware (http://www.rcn.montana.edu/pubs/pdf/2008/Srinivasiah%20Res%20%20Micro%202008.pdf) contains something like four billion viruses per mL of soil, in case you were looking for a fun vacation destination. If you gathered together all the viruses in all the humans in the world, they would fill about ten oil drums: [Image: image] These 10 barrels only represent a tiny portion of the global virus community. Most of the world's viruses aren't found in humans. They're found in the sea. Seawater is full of microorganisms, and we've recently learned that those microorganisms are preyed on by viruses in a big way. Every day, about one in five living cells in the ocean is killed by a virus.[3]Marine viruses—major players in the global ecosystem (https://www.uni-due.de/imperia/md/content/water-science/ws0910/2031b_02z_ws0910_suttle_marine_viruses.pdf) These viruses are found from the surface of the ocean down to the depths.[4]Oddly, as you go further offshore and further down, the concentration of viruses doesn't decrease as much as the concentration of bacteria, so the virus-to-bacteria ratio is higher in the deep oceans than near the shore. Because the sea is so big,[5]Citation: Go and look at the sea. It's big. it contains a staggering number of viruses. If you piled up all these viruses—more than 1030 of them—in one place, they would be the size of a small mountain. [Image: image] It's hard to say exactly what the virus mountain would look like, but it would probably resemble something in between pus and meat slurry.[6]Blame Dave—he's the one who asked. Regardless of its exact appearance, it would almost certainly be disgusting. [Image: image] The pile wouldn't stay mountain-shaped for long, any more than a mountain of any organic secretion would.[7]If you don't believe me, try building a mountain of earwax or snot. You'll find you can't make it higher than a few inches before your friends and family show up and sit you down for a talk. To avoid a gigantic flood, it might be better to collect them into some kind of container. MetLife Stadium, host of Super Bowl XLVIII, has a volume of about 1.5 million cubic meters. Earth's viruses could fill the stadium about 150 times over. So if you watch the Super Bowl, take a moment to picture all the players floating, suspended, in a sea of yellowish-white secretions. [Image: image] Enjoy the game!

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth. This an illusion, of course; it's not possible to catch a bullet like that.[1]This was confirmed (http://www.discovery.com/tv-shows/mythbusters/mythbusters-database/catch-bullet-teeth.htm) by Mythbusters in episode 4 of Season 4. But under the right conditions, you could catch a bullet. It would just take a lot of patience.[2]I'd like to remind everyone that while I write sometimes about the interesting physics of bullets, I'm not an authority on firearms safety. I was raised Quaker (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers); I've never held a gun, much less fired one. A bullet fired straight up would eventually reach a maximum height.[3]Don't do this. In neighborhoods where people fire guns upward in celebration, bystanders are routinely killed (http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/PDF/wk/mm5350.pdf) by falling bullets. It probably wouldn't stop completely; more likely, it would be drifting sideways at a couple meters per second. At that speed, as long as you were in the right place at the right time, you could snatch it out of the air. If someone fired a bullet upward ... [Image: image] ... and you were hanging out in a hot-air balloon directly above the firing range ... [Image: image] ... it's possible that you could reach out and snag the bullet at the apex of its flight. If you succeeded, you might notice something odd: In addition to being hot, the bullet would be spinning. It would have lost its upward momentum, but not its rotational momentum; it would still have the spin given to it by the barrel of the gun. [Image: image] This effect can be seen, dramatically, when a bullet is fired at ice.[4]Floor water. As confirmed by dozens of YouTube videos (https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=bullet%20spinning%20ice) (and Mythbusters), bullets fired into ice are often found still spinning rapidly. You'd have to grab the bullet firmly; otherwise, it might jump out of your hand. If you don't have a balloon, you could potentially make this work from a mountain peak. Mount Thor, which you may remember from question #51 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/51/), features a vertical drop of 1,250 meters. According to ballistics lab Close Focus Research, this is almost exactly how high a .22 Long Rifle bullet will fly if fired directly upward.[5]Close Focus Research, Maximum Altitude For Bullets Fired Vertically (http://www.closefocusresearch.com/maximum-altitude-bullets-fired-vertically) [Image: image] If you want to use larger bullets, you'll need a much larger drop; an AK-47's bullet can go over two kilometers upward. There are no purely vertical cliffs that are that tall, so you'd need to fire the bullet at an angle, and it would have significant sideways speed at the top of its arc. However, a suitably tough baseball glove might be able to snag it.[6]In fact, according to Rifle Magazine, a gun writer once claimed (https://www.riflemagazine.com/magazine/article.cfm?magid=78&tocid=1094) that at a thousand yards, he could catch ordinary rifle bullets with a baseball glove. Of course, he was being figurative—you wouldn't see the bullet coming, so you'd be just as likely to catch it with your face as with your glove. In any of these scenarios, you'd have to get extraordinarily lucky. Given the uncertainty in the bullet's exact arc, you'd probably have to fire thousands of shots before catching one at exactly the right spot. And by that point, you may find you've attracted some attention. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Boundary Conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the only plausible versions of 'catching a slowed bullet': near the apex of a vertical shot, after substantial drag-induced deceleration, or with protective equipment, rather than treating a normally fired bullet as hand-catchable.
criteria.1-2: Treats an ordinary fired bullet as catchable by hand with little or no slowing; ignores speed, impact energy, and setup.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that the bullet must slow down but gives vague or physically implausible conditions for catching it.
criteria.5-6: Identifies a plausible slowing scenario, such as a vertical shot near its apex, but leaves key conditions underspecified.
criteria.7-8: Clearly describes realistic boundary conditions: low translational speed, precise positioning, timing, and safety constraints.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames multiple viable setups and explains why ordinary magic-style bullet catching is impossible while rare slowed-bullet capture could be possible.

criteria.name: Physics Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the relevant physical mechanisms: kinetic energy, gravity, air resistance, terminal/falling speeds, horizontal drift, spin from rifling, heat, and transfer of momentum to the catcher or glove.
criteria.1-2: Provides little or no physics, or relies on incorrect claims such as bullets simply stopping harmlessly in air.
criteria.3-4: Mentions speed or force but omits most mechanisms and contains major simplifications.
criteria.5-6: Covers basic deceleration and impact energy but misses important effects such as spin, drag, drift, or heat.
criteria.7-8: Explains most relevant mechanisms accurately and connects them to whether catching is feasible.
criteria.9-10: Gives a rich, causally linked account of translational slowing, residual spin, heat, drift, altitude, and catching dynamics.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows downstream consequences over the full chain from firing to slowing to attempted interception, including practical requirements and hazards over time and distance.
criteria.1-2: Stops at a yes/no answer without tracing what happens to the bullet or catcher.
criteria.3-4: Gives a short causal chain but skips major stages such as trajectory, apex behavior, or interception difficulty.
criteria.5-6: Follows the main sequence but only superficially discusses downstream risks or logistics.
criteria.7-8: Coherently traces firing angle, altitude, drift, falling/catching phase, and practical hazards.
criteria.9-10: Provides a complete long-range chain including trajectory uncertainty, repeated attempts, environmental effects, bystander danger, and equipment/location constraints.

criteria.name: Uncertainty, Probability, and Safety Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer appropriately calibrates feasibility: possible only under rare controlled conditions, extremely dangerous in practice, and not something to attempt.
criteria.1-2: Encourages or normalizes trying it; presents the outcome as easy or safe.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges danger but understates the improbability or practical difficulty.
criteria.5-6: States that it is dangerous and unlikely, but gives limited explanation of why.
criteria.7-8: Clearly emphasizes extreme risk, low probability, need for precise timing/location, and firearm safety concerns.
criteria.9-10: Strongly distinguishes theoretical possibility from practical recklessness, with well-calibrated uncertainty about trajectory, wind, bullet type, and human reaction limits.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Answer Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer avoids internal contradictions and maintains consistency with known ballistics, especially distinguishing slowed upward bullets from high-speed incoming bullets.
criteria.1-2: Contains severe contradictions, such as saying bullets cannot slow yet can be safely caught barehanded.
criteria.3-4: Has multiple inconsistencies about speed, direction, energy, or injury risk.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent but includes some ambiguous or conflicting statements about feasibility or danger.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent distinction between impossible normal bullet catching and possible slowed-bullet interception.
criteria.9-10: Is fully consistent, resolves apparent paradoxes, and carefully avoids overclaiming beyond the specified slowed-bullet scenario.

items.model_answer:
Catching a bullet after it has slowed down is far more plausible than catching one at muzzle velocity, but whether it's safe depends entirely on how much it has slowed.

A typical handgun bullet leaves the barrel at around 300–400 m/s (1,000–1,300 ft/s) and carries roughly 300–600 joules of kinetic energy. At those speeds, catching it with a bare hand is essentially equivalent to being shot — the bullet would punch right through your palm. Even an "underpowered" .22 still carries enough energy to penetrate skin, muscle, and small bones at close range.

However, bullets lose energy quickly through air drag, and especially dramatically when fired upward or at long range. A bullet fired straight up will rise until gravity stops it, then fall back down. On the way down, it's no longer being driven by propellant — it's only being pulled by gravity and slowed by air resistance. Most bullets reach a terminal velocity of roughly 50–100 m/s (about 100–200 mph) when falling, depending on their shape, mass, and orientation. That's still fast enough to break skin and crack a skull in many cases — falling bullets from celebratory gunfire kill people every year — but it's an order of magnitude less energetic than a fired bullet.

If a bullet had slowed even further — say, to 30 m/s or less, perhaps after passing through dense material, traveling at extreme range, or being fired from a very weak load — catching it could become comparable to catching a hard-thrown baseball (which travels around 40 m/s). A baseball delivers around 100–150 J, painful but survivable in a gloved hand. A bullet has much less surface area, though, so the same energy is concentrated on a tiny contact point. That means the practical threshold for "catchable" is lower for a bullet than for a ball: you'd want it traveling under perhaps 20–30 m/s, and you'd want a thick glove.

There's also a famous historical anecdote: a WWI pilot reportedly plucked a German bullet out of the air near the apex of its trajectory, when its forward velocity matched the plane's. So in principle, if you could match a bullet's velocity in its own reference frame, "catching" it becomes trivial — it's effectively standing still relative to you.

Bottom line: a freshly fired bullet cannot be safely caught by any human; a falling spent bullet might still wound or kill you; and only a heavily slowed bullet — well below 30 m/s — approaches the realm of something a person could realistically catch, and even then a bare hand is a bad idea.

nodes.text: Catching a bullet after it has slowed down is far more plausible than catching one at muzzle velocity,
but whether it's safe depends entirely on how much it has slowed.
A typical handgun bullet leaves the barrel at around 300–400 m/s (1,000–1,300 ft/s)
and carries roughly 300–600 joules of kinetic energy.
At those speeds, catching it with a bare hand is essentially equivalent to being shot —
the bullet would punch right through your palm.
Even an "underpowered" .22 still carries enough energy to penetrate skin, muscle, and small bones at close range.
However, bullets lose energy quickly through air drag,
and especially dramatically when fired upward or at long range.
A bullet fired straight up will rise until gravity stops it,
then fall back down.
On the way down, it's no longer being driven by propellant —
it's only being pulled by gravity and slowed by air resistance.
Most bullets reach a terminal velocity of roughly 50–100 m/s (about 100–200 mph) when falling,
depending on their shape, mass, and orientation.
That's still fast enough to break skin and crack a skull in many cases —
falling bullets from celebratory gunfire kill people every year —
but it's an order of magnitude less energetic than a fired bullet.
If a bullet had slowed even further — say, to 30 m/s or less,
perhaps after passing through dense material, traveling at extreme range, or being fired from a very weak load —
catching it could become comparable to catching a hard-thrown baseball
(which travels around 40 m/s).
A baseball delivers around 100–150 J,
painful but survivable in a gloved hand.
A bullet has much less surface area, though,
so the same energy is concentrated on a tiny contact point.
That means the practical threshold for "catchable" is lower for a bullet than for a ball:
you'd want it traveling under perhaps 20–30 m/s,
and you'd want a thick glove.
There's also a famous historical anecdote:
a WWI pilot reportedly plucked a German bullet out of the air near the apex of its trajectory,
when its forward velocity matched the plane's.
So in principle, if you could match a bullet's velocity in its own reference frame,
"catching" it becomes trivial —
it's effectively standing still relative to you.
Bottom line:
a freshly fired bullet cannot be safely caught by any human;
a falling spent bullet might still wound or kill you;
and only a heavily slowed bullet — well below 30 m/s — approaches the realm of something a person could realistically catch,
and even then a bare hand is a bad idea.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true. The answer to this question hinges on exactly how fast you can hit a golf ball. Sometimes, exact numbers don't matter that much. If my baseball, car, dog, or Zamboni goes a little faster than yours,[1]$20 says they will! it will go a little farther. But that's not how it works in rocket golf. The design of our spaceship turns out to involve an equation where the speed of the golf ball is in the exponent. That means a small change in speed can make a big difference. The equation in question—which might be my favorite in all of physics—the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: \[ \Delta v = v_\text{exhaust} \ln \frac{m_\text{initial}}{m_\text{final}} \] This equation comes up a lot in What If calculations. I like it both because it says something fundamental about our ability to explore the universe, and because you can use it to get really good at Kerbal Space Program. With some rearranging, the equation can help us figure out how much of our ship's weight has to be golf balls: \[ \frac{\text{Mass of ship plus golf balls}}{\text{Mass of ship alone}} = e ^ \left ( \frac{\text{Ship's change in speed}}{\text{Speed of golf ball}} \right ) \] Someone who, like me, has never been golfing before, might—after swinging and missing a few times—manage to hit the ball at 120 mph (50 m/s).[2]See Trackman's page on ball speed (http://mytrackman.com/explore/trackman-data/trackman-ball-data/ball-speed) To get to the Moon from low Earth orbit, you would need enough fuel to add 5,300 m/s to your ship's speed. By putting those numbers into the rocket equation, we can find out how large a sack of golf balls would have to be for the average golfer to reach the Moon. If we plug it in to Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=please+calculate+2*%28%283%2F%284*pi%29%29*%28%28e%5E%285300+m%2Fs+%2F+120mph%29%29*200+kg%29+%2F+%2865%25*1.15+kg%2FL%29%29%5E%281%2F3%29+thank+you) ... [Image: image] ... we find that the bag of golf balls will have to be just about exactly 100 billion miles in diameter. That's much, much bigger than our Solar System.[3]As a Fermi rule of thumb, planets in the inner Solar System are 100 million kilometers away and planets in the outer Solar System are a billion kilometers away. Or miles; either one works. [Image: image] It would also promptly and violently collapse into a black hole. Fortunately, we should be able to avert that disaster by making relatively small changes to the "120" in that equation. If we increase the golf ball's speed from 120 mph to 150, it shrinks the answer dramatically, and the required number of golf balls would fit snugly between the Sun and Mars. Still too big to avoid a catastrophic collapse, but we're getting somewhere. [Image: image] Tiger Woods can hit a golf ball at about 180 mph, which means that if he were powering our spaceship, the bag of golf balls would be only twice the diameter of the Sun! [Image: image] According (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/records-10000/fastest-golf-drive/) to the Guinness Book of World Records, the record for fastest golf drive is 211 mph, set by Maurice Allen in 2012. This corresponds to a bag of golf balls only 100,000 kilometers across—smaller than Jupiter, but still (obviously) not practical. However, golfer Ryan Winther claims (http://www.ryanwinther.com/about_records.htm) to have beaten this record, though without Guinness observers there.[4]And, obviously, it doesn't count unless it's overseen by people from a beer company. If you want to set a world record, hit a golf ball at a radar gun and get it certified by the Mike's Hard Lemonade people. His ball speed was measured by something called the "Titleist Performance Institute" to be 226.7 mph, and he claims a personal best of 237 mph. If he could consistently hit 237 mph, we could shrink our fuel container down to the size of Earth[5]Although it would still be large enough to partially collapse under its own gravity, similar to what happened to the mole of moles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/4/). [Image: image] This still wouldn't work; even in a high orbit, the massive tides from your ship—which is much more massive than the Moon—would be highly disruptive. We could probably shrink the fuel tank further by using "illegal" equipment. There are Superball-style balls and "trampoline face" clubs which can hit much farther, and which would not be permitted in tournament play.[6]On the other hand, we're talking about a sport that brought whites-only clubs with it into the 21st century (http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/01/AR2010060103918.html), and Agusta, host of the Masters, admitted its first woman in 2012 (http://www.reuters.com/article/2012/08/20/us-golf-augusta-idUSBRE87J0IE20120820). So maybe we shouldn't worry too much about their traditional rules. A hypothetical 270 mph drive would allow a fuel tank the size of the Moon. At this point, why are we even using a club? According (http://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0966) to research from the US Air Force Academy and BTG Research,[7]Oddly, both researchers have the name "Courtney". There are probably about 200,000 people in the US named Courtney (first or last); maybe we should recruit them to all build potato cannons. a potato cannon fueled by acetylene can launch a potato at 140 m/s (310 mph). If it were capable of launching golf balls at that speed,[8]We're not factoring in the weight of the acetylene—but then again, we also weren't factoring in the weight of the hamburgers the golfer would need to eat to keep hitting those drives. our ship would have a diameter of only 150 miles! [Image: image] There's the small problem that manufacturing that many golf balls would cost quintillions of dollars. You could bring the size down further by making the potato cannon more and more powerful and efficient, but at that point you're simply building a rocket. And the potato cannon scenario has an extra perk. If you somehow made the balls durable enough to survive atmospheric entry, and you set up your maneuver so the ejected golf balls covered the middle latitudes evenly, then over the course of this maneuver you would be statistically likely to hit a hole-in-one ... at every golf course in the world. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
This is a fun physics thought experiment! Let me work through what would actually happen.

**The short answer:** It wouldn't work. Golf balls hit from orbit would either stay in orbit, fall back to Earth, or escape into space—but they wouldn't "reach" the Moon in any useful sense.

**Why not:**

When you're already in orbit around Earth, you're moving at about 7.8 km/s (17,500 mph) just to maintain that orbit. Hitting a golf ball adds velocity relative to you, but the ball still inherits your orbital motion.

A professional golfer's swing might add roughly 70-90 m/s to the ball. This changes the ball's orbit slightly:

- **Hit in the direction of orbital motion:** The ball moves to a higher, more elliptical orbit. To actually reach the Moon (384,400 km away), you'd need to add about 3.1 km/s—roughly 35 times faster than any golf swing. The ball would just end up in a slightly higher Earth orbit.

- **Hit against orbital motion:** The ball slows down and drops to a lower orbit, potentially reentering the atmosphere and burning up.

- **Hit perpendicular to motion:** The orbital plane tilts slightly, but the ball still orbits Earth.

**Additional problems:**

- No air resistance in space means the ball travels farther than on Earth, but orbital mechanics still dominate
- The Moon is moving at 1 km/s in its own orbit, so timing and trajectory matter enormously
- Even if you somehow gave the ball enough velocity, you'd need incredibly precise aim—the Moon is a small target in the vastness of space

**What you'd actually need:** A velocity boost of about 3,100 m/s beyond orbital speed to reach the Moon—essentially a rocket, not a golf club.

So while astronaut Alan Shepard famously hit golf balls on the Moon's surface in 1971, hitting them *to* the Moon from orbit remains firmly in the realm of impossibility.

edus.text: This is a fun physics thought experiment!
Let me work through what would actually happen.
The short answer:
It wouldn't work.
Golf balls hit from orbit would either stay in orbit, fall back to Earth, or escape into space—
but they wouldn't "reach" the Moon in any useful sense.
Why not:
When you're already in orbit around Earth, you're moving at about 7.8 km/s (17,500 mph)
just to maintain that orbit.
Hitting a golf ball adds velocity relative to you,
but the ball still inherits your orbital motion.
A professional golfer's swing might add roughly 70-90 m/s to the ball.
This changes the ball's orbit slightly:
Hit in the direction of orbital motion:
The ball moves to a higher, more elliptical orbit.
To actually reach the Moon (384,400 km away), you'd need to add about 3.1 km/s—
roughly 35 times faster than any golf swing.
The ball would just end up in a slightly higher Earth orbit.
Hit against orbital motion:
The ball slows down and drops to a lower orbit,
potentially reentering the atmosphere and burning up.
Hit perpendicular to motion:
The orbital plane tilts slightly,
but the ball still orbits Earth.
Additional problems:
No air resistance in space means the ball travels farther than on Earth,
but orbital mechanics still dominate
The Moon is moving at 1 km/s in its own orbit,
so timing and trajectory matter enormously
Even if you somehow gave the ball enough velocity,
you'd need incredibly precise aim—
the Moon is a small target in the vastness of space
What you'd actually need:
A velocity boost of about 3,100 m/s beyond orbital speed to reach the Moon—
essentially a rocket, not a golf club.
So while astronaut Alan Shepard famously hit golf balls on the Moon's surface in 1971,
hitting them to the Moon from orbit remains firmly in the realm of impossibility.

items.question: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?
human_answers: Radio waves exert force on things. Not a lot of force. The average cell phone transmitter exerts about a billionth of a newton of pressure on its surroundings. That means that it would take several trillion cell phones to collectively levitate a snowflake; the pressure from one phone wouldn't even measurably slow it down. [Image: image] If the phone did put out enough energy to levitate a snowflake by radiation pressure, the power flowing through the snowflake (a few kilowatts) would quickly cause the snowflake to become a raindrop, which would quickly become water vapor, which would quickly become the least of your problems. [Image: image] The fate of the snowflake hints at what kinds of problems our car will encounter. If you want to slow down a one-ton car by radiation pressure, your radar gun would need to deliver about two trillion joules worth of radiation—the energy of a small nuclear weapon.[1]The formula for figuring out that amount out is simple: The energy required is equal to the desired change in speed (say, 20 mph) times the mass of the car times the speed of light. The radar gun would need to emit even more energy than that, since not all of the radiation will be absorbed (or reflected) by the car.[2]The fact that some of it is reflected makes things easier, since that doubles the momentum delivered by the radiation. This is why simple solar sails are white and not black. For more on radar reflectivity of materials, you can check out one of the worst scanned PDFs I've ever seen (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/601365.pdf). Your radar gun would also vaporize the car. This is a problem, in one sense, but it's also a solution. Even if most of the energy is reflected, the portion that was absorbed would convert the materials in the car into gas or plasma. The expanding cloud would exert a lot more pressure on the car than the radiation itself.[3]This process, called ablation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_ablation), is also what got rid of the Moon in the What If #13 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/). This is convenient—it means that we wouldn't need nearly as much energy to stop the car as we would using radiation pressure alone. There are even simpler ways to slow down a car with radiation. For example, you could aim a radiation beam at the tires and melt them, or use the electromagnetic radiation to knock out the car's electrical systems. Or just use a laser pointer to blind the driver and hope they reflexively slow down. Of course, you don't need any of those things. If your goal is to slow down the car—rather than to catch speeders—your radar gun doesn't need any power. You can just stand by the side of the road next to a police car holding a fake radar gun. [Image: image] In the end, a radar gun capable of slowing cars through radiation pressure would be roughly equivalent to a nuclear weapon, and using nuclear strikes in response to traffic violations is probably overkill. It would work, in the literal sense, but it would also destroy the offender, car, police officer, road, and all other traffic for miles around.[4]It would also cause fragments of the driver to violate the speed limit in all directions at once. Of course, maybe using the apocalyptic radar gun wouldn't be necessary; just the threat of a nuclear strike against drivers would probably deter speeding. Come to think of it, maybe that's what those other signs you sometimes see are hinting at. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
To "stop" a speeding car using radar, you'd essentially need to transfer enough momentum (or deposit enough energy) via electromagnetic radiation to overcome the car's kinetic energy and forward momentum. Let's work through what that would take.

**Approach 1: Radiation pressure (momentum transfer)**

Radar waves carry momentum p = E/c. To decelerate a 1500 kg car traveling at 30 m/s (about 67 mph) to a stop in, say, 5 seconds, you'd need to apply a force of:

F = ma = 1500 × 6 = 9000 N

The radiation pressure force from a perfectly absorbed beam is F = P/c, so:

P = F × c = 9000 × 3×10⁸ ≈ **2.7 × 10¹² watts (2.7 terawatts)**

That's roughly 1000 times the output of a large nuclear power plant, focused entirely into a single radar beam aimed at the car for five seconds straight. If the car is a perfect reflector rather than absorber, you'd need half that — still over a terawatt.

**Approach 2: Energy deposition (vaporization/destruction)**

A more "practical" way to stop a car with radar would be to deposit enough energy to destroy it. Vaporizing a car (~1500 kg of mostly steel and aluminum) requires roughly 10¹⁰ joules. Doing that in one second requires about **10 gigawatts**, comparable to a directed-energy weapon vastly beyond any speed-gun radar.

**For comparison**, a police traffic radar gun emits about 10–100 milliwatts. So you'd need to scale up the power by a factor of roughly **10¹³ to 10¹⁴** to physically halt a car with radiation pressure — clearly unphysical for any handheld device, and well beyond even the most powerful military radars (which top out around 10s of megawatts peak).

**Bottom line:** A radar beam capable of stopping a speeding car through momentum transfer alone would need to deliver power on the order of a terawatt — comparable to a significant fraction of total global electricity generation — concentrated into a single beam. Long before reaching that level, the beam would simply incinerate the car (and everything else nearby) rather than gently decelerating it.

items.question: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?
human_answers: For most of the history of civilization, there were about 270 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. In the last hundred years, industrial activity has pushed that number up (http://www.skepticalscience.com/print.php?r=45) to 400 parts per million. One "part per million" of CO2 weighs about 7.8 billion tons. A can of soda contains in the neighborhood of 2.2 grams of CO2, so you would need about 450 quadrillion cans of soda. That's enough to cover the Earth's land with ten layers of cans. [Image: image] There's clearly not enough room to do this. Even if we stacked the cans up to the edge of space,[1]I don't have any hard numbers, but my guess would be that you could probably stack supermarket soda six-pack crates a few hundred meters high before the bottom layer ruptures. they'd still take up an area the size of Rhode Island.[2]We shouldn't actually try it, given what happened last time (http://what-if.xkcd.com/8/). We'd need to add even more cans to keep up with ongoing emissions. We're currently increasing the atmosphere's CO2 concentration by an average of 2 parts per million each year: [Image: image] At that rate, we'd need to add one can of soda per person every 30 seconds, which is about 10,000 times the current consumption rate.[3]The global average (http://what-if.xkcd.com/74/) is one can per person every 5 days. In the US, the average is one every 18 hours. That would add a new layer of cans to the ground every 6[4]I originally had the wrong number here; thank you to Paulina for catching it! years or so. This layer of cans would get pretty annoying. [Image: image] Are there any ways out of this predicament? In some areas, you can turn in soda cans for recycling and receive a small amount of money; in Massachusetts, where I live, it's 5 cents. If you collected one year's worth of soda cans—instead of layering them across the Earth's surface—and emptied them out, you could redeem them for $372 trillion. With that much money, you could simply buy the world's current reserves[5]Source: xkcd.com/980 (http://xkcd.com/980), bottom right. of coal, oil, and natural gas—the source of the whole problem. Then, you put it all back in the ground and leave it there. [Image: image] Problem solved.

items.model_answer:
If every bottle and can of carbonated soda on Earth were suddenly opened and all the dissolved CO₂ escaped into the atmosphere, the effect on the climate would be utterly negligible. Here's why.

A typical 2-liter soda bottle contains roughly 5–6 grams of dissolved CO₂ (carbonation runs about 3–4 volumes of gas per volume of liquid). Global soft drink production is on the order of 200 billion liters per year, which corresponds to perhaps 500,000 to 1 million metric tons of CO₂ dissolved in soda annually. The standing inventory of soda actually sitting in bottles, cans, warehouses, and store shelves at any given moment is much smaller than the annual production—probably a few hundred thousand tons of CO₂ at most.

For comparison, human activities emit about 37 billion metric tons of CO₂ per year. So all the CO₂ in the world's bottled soda represents less than one hundred-thousandth of annual emissions—equivalent to just a few minutes of normal human output. The atmospheric CO₂ concentration (currently around 420 ppm) would rise by something on the order of 0.00005 ppm, far below any detectable level.

There's another important point: the CO₂ in soda isn't "new" carbon being added to the system. It's typically captured as a byproduct of industrial processes like ethanol fermentation, ammonia production, or natural gas processing. That CO₂ would have been released to the atmosphere anyway; bottling it in soda just delays its release by weeks or months. So releasing it all at once doesn't actually change the long-term carbon balance—it merely shifts the timing slightly.

The more noticeable consequences would be local and immediate: a tremendous amount of foam and sticky liquid everywhere, and a brief, very localized rise in CO₂ near concentrated stockpiles (potentially suffocating in an enclosed warehouse, since CO₂ is denser than air). But globally, the climate would not notice.

edus.text: If every bottle and can of carbonated soda on Earth were suddenly opened and all the dissolved CO₂ escaped into the atmosphere,
the effect on the climate would be utterly negligible.
Here's why.
A typical 2-liter soda bottle contains roughly 5–6 grams of dissolved CO₂
carbonation runs about 3–4 volumes of gas per volume of liquid.
Global soft drink production is on the order of 200 billion liters per year,
which corresponds to perhaps 500,000 to 1 million metric tons of CO₂ dissolved in soda annually.

The standing inventory of soda actually sitting in bottles, cans, warehouses, and store shelves at any given moment is much smaller than the annual production—probably a few hundred thousand tons of CO₂ at most.
For comparison, human activities emit about 37 billion metric tons of CO₂ per year.
So all the CO₂ in the world's bottled soda represents less than one hundred-thousandth of annual emissions—equivalent to just a few minutes of normal human output.
The atmospheric CO₂ concentration (currently around 420 ppm) would rise by something on the order of 0.00005 ppm,
far below any detectable level.
There's another important point:
the CO₂ in soda isn't "new" carbon being added to the system.
It's typically captured as a byproduct of industrial processes like ethanol fermentation, ammonia production, or natural gas processing.
That CO₂ would have been released to the atmosphere anyway;
bottling it in soda just delays its release by weeks or months.
So releasing it all at once doesn't actually change the long-term carbon balance—
it merely shifts the timing slightly.
The more noticeable consequences would be local and immediate:
a tremendous amount of foam and sticky liquid everywhere,
and a brief, very localized rise in CO₂ near concentrated stockpiles
potentially suffocating in an enclosed warehouse,
since CO₂ is denser than air.
But globally, the climate would not notice.

items.question: What If I Threw a Tungsten Countertop into the Sun?
human_answers: Not very far. With its high melting point, tungsten is a good[1]Except that the word "good" implies that you have some kind of goal you're working toward, which—given how strange the thing you're doing is—I'm not sure about. choice for a sundiving countertop. The first problem would be sunlight. As the countertop approached the Sun, it would heat up. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, but the Sun is one of the meltiest things in the Solar System. When the countertop got within a couple of solar radii, it would liquify. [Image: image] If you protected it with a heat shield of some kind, or dropped it from a sundiving spaceship, it could enter the Sun's atmosphere relatively intact. In this case, some interesting physical effects would destroy it.[2]"Some interesting physical effects would destroy it" summarizes the answers to a large percentage of the questions submitted to this blog. Because the Sun is so heavy, anything that falls to its surface will be accelerated to a tremendous speed by its gravity. A falling countertop would reach speeds of over 600 km/s—0.2% of the speed of light. (Our rockets can only accelerate spacecraft to 10-20 km/s.) From the countertop's point of view, particles from the Sun's atmosphere would be slamming into it at 600 km/s. These particles would pack quite a punch.[3]From a particle physics point of view, the individual protons would have energy of about 2 keV. When the countertop got within about a few thousand kilometers[4]I don't want another unit-related word to mentally keep track of, but it's always seemed a little weird that we don't call thousands of kilometers "megameters". of the Sun's surface, these collisions would start delivering more energy to the countertop than the sunlight. The collisions would fling individual tungsten atoms away from the surface—a process called sputtering (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputtering). Between the sputtering and ordinary heating from the impacts, the countertop would start to absorb a lot of energy very quickly. If the countertop were larger, it could penetrate into the Sun's photosphere—the first layer beneath the "surface"—and potentially trigger a solar flare.[5]For a scientific discussion of this, see the article Impacts of comets onto the Sun and coronal mass ejections (http://meetings.copernicus.org/www.cosis.net/abstracts/EGU05/04384/EGU05-J-04384.pdf). For a science fiction discussion of this, see Stephen Baxter and Arthur C. Clarke's 2005 novel Sunstorm. But as it is, it wouldn't even make it through the Sun's atmosphere—it would be vaporized somewhere in the Sun's chromosphere. [Image: image] This brings us around to a key question: Who the hell has tungsten countertops? Sure, it has good heat tolerance. But I'd be nervous about using tungsten as a food-preparation surface. In September of 1994 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8874460), a French soldier drank wine from a rifle barrel. Fifteen minutes later, he started having seizures. He was rushed to the hospital and treated for "acute tungsten intoxication"—the first known case in medical history. He reportedly made a full recovery, although concentrations of tungsten were present in all his body tissues for weeks. The lesson here is to use normal materials. Michael, just make your countertops out of granite and don't drop them in the Sun. And if you're a French soldier, please just drink wine like a normal person. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Throwing a tungsten countertop into the Sun would be a spectacularly anticlimactic event from the Sun's perspective, but an interesting journey for the countertop itself.

A typical kitchen countertop made of solid tungsten would be enormously heavy. Tungsten has a density of about 19.3 g/cm³, so a countertop measuring roughly 2.5 meters by 0.65 meters by 4 cm thick would weigh around 1,250 kilograms—well over a ton. Tungsten is, in fact, one of the densest and most refractory metals known, with the highest melting point of any pure metal at 3,422 °C (6,192 °F) and a boiling point near 5,930 °C (10,706 °F).

As the countertop fell toward the Sun, it would first heat up gradually from solar radiation. By the time it crossed inside Mercury's orbit, surface temperatures would climb past 400 °C, but tungsten would shrug this off easily—it's used in rocket nozzles and incandescent filaments precisely because it tolerates extreme heat. Even at the Sun's "surface" (the photosphere), where temperatures hit about 5,500 °C, the countertop would finally melt and then begin to boil and vaporize. Tungsten's boiling point is actually slightly above the photospheric temperature, so it would linger as a glowing molten blob a bit longer than most materials before evaporating into tungsten vapor.

Once inside the Sun proper, the temperature climbs rapidly—millions of degrees in the convective zone and core. The vaporized tungsten atoms would be ionized, stripped of their electrons, and dispersed into the solar plasma. The atoms themselves wouldn't be destroyed; they'd simply join the swirling mix of mostly hydrogen and helium that makes up the Sun.

As for the Sun, it wouldn't notice at all. The Sun has a mass of about 2 × 10³⁰ kilograms, so adding 1,250 kg is like adding a single grain of sand to the entire Sahara Desert—it's about 10⁻²⁷ of the Sun's mass. There would be no measurable change in brightness, temperature, or behavior. The tungsten atoms would slowly diffuse and circulate, eventually mixing throughout the convective zone over thousands of years, but they'd just be a few extra heavy nuclei lost among the roughly 10⁵⁷ particles already there.

So in short: the countertop would be utterly destroyed, and the Sun wouldn't even burp.

edus.text: Throwing a tungsten countertop into the Sun would be a spectacularly anticlimactic event from the Sun's perspective,
but an interesting journey for the countertop itself.
A typical kitchen countertop made of solid tungsten would be enormously heavy.
Tungsten has a density of about 19.3 g/cm³,
so a countertop measuring roughly 2.5 meters by 0.65 meters by 4 cm thick would weigh around 1,250 kilograms—well over a ton.
Tungsten is, in fact, one of the densest and most refractory metals known,
with the highest melting point of any pure metal at 3,422 °C (6,192 °F)
and a boiling point near 5,930 °C (10,706 °F).
As the countertop fell toward the Sun,
it would first heat up gradually from solar radiation.
By the time it crossed inside Mercury's orbit,
surface temperatures would climb past 400 °C,
but tungsten would shrug this off easily—
it's used in rocket nozzles and incandescent filaments precisely because it tolerates extreme heat.
Even at the Sun's "surface" (the photosphere),
where temperatures hit about 5,500 °C,
the countertop would finally melt
and then begin to boil and vaporize.
Tungsten's boiling point is actually slightly above the photospheric temperature,
so it would linger as a glowing molten blob a bit longer than most materials
before evaporating into tungsten vapor.
Once inside the Sun proper,
the temperature climbs rapidly—millions of degrees in the convective zone and core.
The vaporized tungsten atoms would be ionized,
stripped of their electrons,
and dispersed into the solar plasma.
The atoms themselves wouldn't be destroyed;
they'd simply join the swirling mix of mostly hydrogen and helium
that makes up the Sun.
As for the Sun,
it wouldn't notice at all.
The Sun has a mass of about 2 × 10³⁰ kilograms,
so adding 1,250 kg is like adding a single grain of sand to the entire Sahara Desert—
it's about 10⁻²⁷ of the Sun's mass.
There would be no measurable change in brightness, temperature, or behavior.
The tungsten atoms would slowly diffuse and circulate,
eventually mixing throughout the convective zone over thousands of years,
but they'd just be a few extra heavy nuclei lost among the roughly 10⁵⁷ particles already there.
So in short:
the countertop would be utterly destroyed,
and the Sun wouldn't even burp.

items.question: What If Earth Spun Fast Enough for a Day to Last One Second?
human_answers: If this is going to happen, I hope it doesn't happen late in the afternoon next Friday. The Earth rotates,[citation needed (https://web.archive.org/web/20151210155028/http://www.timecube.com/)] which means its midsection is being flung outward by centrifugal force.[1]Which is still a real thing (http://xkcd.com/123/). This centrifugal force isn't strong enough to overcome gravity and tear the Earth apart, but it's enough to flatten the Earth slightly and make it so you weigh almost a pound less at the Equator than you do at the poles.[2]This is due to several effects, including centrifugal force, the flattened shape of the Earth, and the fact that if you go far enough toward the pole in North America people start offering you poutine. If the Earth (and everything on it) were suddenly sped up so that a day only lasted one second, the Earth wouldn't even last a single day.[3]Either kind. The Equator would be moving at over 10% of the speed of light. Centrifugal force would become much stronger than gravity, and the material that makes up the Earth would be flung outward. [Image: image] You wouldn't die instantly—you might survive for a few milliseconds or even seconds. That might not seem like much, but compared to the speed at which you'd die in other What If articles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/1/) involving relativistic speeds, it's pretty long. The Earth's crust and mantle would break apart into building-sized chunks. By the time a second[4]I mean, a day. had passed, the atmosphere would have spread out too thin to breathe—although even at the relatively stationary poles, you probably wouldn't survive long enough to asphyxiate. [Image: image] In the first few seconds, the expansion would shatter the crust into spinning fragments and kill just about everyone on the planet, but that's relatively peaceful compared to what would happen next. Everything would be moving at relativistic speeds, but each piece of the crust would be moving at close to the same speed at its neighbors. This means things would be relatively calm ... until the disk hit something. The first obstacle would be the belt of satellites around the Earth. After 40 milliseconds, the ISS would be struck by the edge of the expanding atmosphere and would be vaporized instantly. More satellites would follow. After a second and a half, the disc would reach the belt of geostationary satellites orbiting above the Equator. Each one would release a violent burst of gamma rays as the Earth consumed it. [Image: image] The debris from the Earth would slice outward like an expanding buzzsaw. The disk would take about ten seconds to pass the Moon, another hour to spread past the Sun, and would span the Solar System within a day or two. Each time the disc engulfed an asteroid, it would spray a flood of energy in all directions, eventually sterilizing every surface in the Solar System. Since the Earth is tilted, the Sun and the planets aren't usually lined up with the plane of the Earth's equator. They'd have a good chance of avoiding the buzzsaw[5]I keep reading this as "Buzzfeed". directly. However, Next Friday, April 25th, the Moon will cross the plane of the Earth's equator (as it does every two weeks). If Dylan sped up the Earth at this moment, the Moon would be right in the path of the resulting planetary buzzsaw. The impact would turn the moon into a comet, sending it rocketing from the Solar System in a spray of debris. The flash of light and heat would be so bright that if you were standing at the surface of the Sun, it would be brighter above you than below. Every surface in the Solar System—Europa's ice, Saturn's rings, and Mercury's rocky crust—would be scoured clean ... [Image: image] ... by moonlight.

items.model_answer:
If Earth spun fast enough for a day to last one second, the consequences would be catastrophic and immediately fatal to all life.

**Rotational velocity at the equator:**
Currently, Earth's equator moves at about 1,670 km/h. For a one-second day, the equator would need to spin at approximately 40,075 km/s (Earth's circumference divided by one second) — roughly 86,400 times faster than now. This is about 13% the speed of light.

**Immediate physical consequences:**

*Centrifugal force:* The outward acceleration at the equator would be approximately 4 million m/s², or about 400,000 times Earth's gravity. Everything not firmly anchored — atmosphere, oceans, soil, buildings, and all living things — would be instantly flung into space. Even solid rock would experience stresses far exceeding its structural strength.

*Planetary deformation:* Earth would no longer be spherical. The centrifugal force would overcome gravitational binding, causing the planet to flatten dramatically into an oblate shape, potentially disintegrating entirely. The equatorial bulge would be extreme, and material would stream off into space.

*Atmospheric loss:* The atmosphere would be stripped away instantly, as gas molecules at the equator would exceed escape velocity many times over.

*Gravitational effects:* Effective gravity at the equator would become strongly negative (outward), while polar regions would retain some inward pull, creating bizarre and lethal gravitational gradients.

*Tidal and orbital effects:* The Moon would experience extreme tidal forces from Earth's rapidly changing gravitational field, and Earth-Moon dynamics would be severely disrupted.

In summary, Earth would essentially tear itself apart, ejecting its atmosphere, oceans, and surface material into space while potentially fragmenting into a debris field. No life could survive even a fraction of a second under these conditions.

items.question: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?
human_answers: Fast. [Image: image] Raindrops are tiny. Even in the heaviest rainstorms, the water in the air weighs less than the air itself (which is one of several reasons you can't swim upward in a rainstorm). Even at very high speeds, they can't break a windshield via their momentum alone. Under ordinary circumstances, raindrops don't damage car windshields at all. However, they can destroy the windows of supersonic aircraft. Here's what happens when a raindrop hits a glass surface at high speed: When the droplet makes contact with the surface, a shockwave travels back up through the droplet. [Image: image] Normally, this shockwave would move at the speed of sound within the liquid—about 1300 m/s, four times faster than in air. However, at high impact speeds, this shockwave actually moves substantially faster than the speed of sound in water. The water is squeezed between the incoming drop and the glass surface, which makes it squirt sideways in all directions. These jets of water can move even faster than the original (already supersonic) droplet, and even faster than the shockwaves we mentioned. [Image: image] One paper (http://e-collection.library.ethz.ch/eserv/eth:26251/eth-26251-02.pdf) ran a simulation of water droplets hitting a surface at 500 m/s (about Mach 1.5), and found that the water sprayed out from the point of contact at over 6000 m/s—Mach 18.[1]That's a pretty simple way to expel material at 6 km/s. I wonder if anyone's ever tried to come up with a spacecraft propulsion system using it ... The sharp pulse from the shockwave can crack glass. The highest pressures are found in the ring around the edge of the droplet, and only exist for a tiny fraction of the impact. [Image: image] In addition to the direct downward pressure, the water jetting sideways can cause damage, too. If the material has any microscopic holes, cracks, or bumps, those jets can strike them and create new cracks or widen existing ones. Even at high speeds, a raindrop won't create a bullet hole on its own—but a long series of supersonic droplets would start to eat away at the glass, cracking and pitting it like sand.[2]This type of "erosion" can also cause damage to steam turbine blades (http://www.technicaljournalsonline.com/ijeat/VOL%20II/IJAET%20VOL%20II%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL%20JUNE%202011/ARTICLE%2014%20IJAET%20VOLII%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL-%20JUNE%202011.pdf). Eventually, the windshield could fail catastrophically. Luckily, cars can't drive at Mach 1 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/61/) without lifting off, so your windshield is safe from ordinary rain. On the other hand, if you're driving under a thunderstorm with strong updrafts ... [Image: image] ... the precipitation can smash your windshield at any speed.

items.model_answer:
If raindrops became the dominant cause of windshield failure before aerodynamic or impact-related speed effects, the entire design philosophy of vehicle glazing—and a good deal of materials science—would shift in interesting ways.

Today, windshields are engineered primarily against three threats: stone impacts, aerodynamic pressure at high speeds, and structural loads in a rollover. Rain is treated as a minor surface phenomenon, handled by wipers, hydrophobic coatings, and good drainage. The kinetic energy of a raindrop hitting a windshield at highway speeds is tiny compared to a pebble or a bird strike, because water deforms and disperses on contact. That dispersal—governed by the Weber number and droplet breakup dynamics—is why rain feels harmless even at 120 km/h.

For rain to break a windshield before speed-related forces did, one of several physical conditions would have to change. The droplets would need to be much larger (cloudburst-sized drops can exceed 6 mm and approach terminal velocities near 10 m/s), the vehicle would need to move fast enough that cumulative droplet impacts caused erosion rather than instantaneous fracture, or the glass would need to be unusually brittle or thin. In fact, this regime already exists in aerospace: supersonic aircraft and helicopter rotor blades suffer **rain erosion**, where repeated droplet impacts at high Mach numbers cause pitting, stress waves, and eventual cracking long before any single drop "breaks" the surface. The mechanism is water-hammer pressure—when a droplet strikes a rigid surface faster than the speed of sound in water, it briefly behaves like a solid, generating pressures of hundreds of MPa.

So in a counterfactual world where rain damages windshields first, automotive glass would be designed more like leading edges on jet aircraft: laminated with elastomeric or polyurethane erosion-resistant coatings, possibly using sacrificial outer layers replaced periodically. Drivers might avoid heavy rain at speed the way pilots avoid hail. Insurance categories would change, weather forecasting would become safety-critical for driving, and hydrophobic nano-coatings—currently a convenience—would become structural.

The deeper lesson is that "what breaks first" depends on the ratio of impact energy to material strength and on the timescale of loading. Speed normally wins because solid debris concentrates energy in a point; rain loses because water spreads it. Reverse that balance and you reverse the engineering priorities.

nodes.text: If raindrops became the dominant cause of windshield failure before aerodynamic or impact-related speed effects,
the entire design philosophy of vehicle glazing—and a good deal of materials science—would shift in interesting ways.
Today, windshields are engineered primarily against three threats: stone impacts, aerodynamic pressure at high speeds, and structural loads in a rollover.
Rain is treated as a minor surface phenomenon, handled by wipers, hydrophobic coatings, and good drainage.
The kinetic energy of a raindrop hitting a windshield at highway speeds is tiny compared to a pebble or a bird strike,
because water deforms and disperses on contact.
That dispersal—governed by the Weber number and droplet breakup dynamics—is why rain feels harmless even at 120 km/h.
For rain to break a windshield before speed-related forces did, one of several physical conditions would have to change.
The droplets would need to be much larger
(cloudburst-sized drops can exceed 6 mm and approach terminal velocities near 10 m/s),
the vehicle would need to move fast enough that cumulative droplet impacts caused erosion rather than instantaneous fracture,
or the glass would need to be unusually brittle or thin.
In fact, this regime already exists in aerospace:
supersonic aircraft and helicopter rotor blades suffer rain erosion,
where repeated droplet impacts at high Mach numbers cause pitting, stress waves, and eventual cracking
long before any single drop "breaks" the surface.
The mechanism is water-hammer pressure—
when a droplet strikes a rigid surface faster than the speed of sound in water,
it briefly behaves like a solid, generating pressures of hundreds of MPa.
So in a counterfactual world where rain damages windshields first,
automotive glass would be designed more like leading edges on jet aircraft:
laminated with elastomeric or polyurethane erosion-resistant coatings,
possibly using sacrificial outer layers replaced periodically.
Drivers might avoid heavy rain at speed the way pilots avoid hail.
Insurance categories would change,
weather forecasting would become safety-critical for driving,
and hydrophobic nano-coatings—currently a convenience—would become structural.
The deeper lesson is that "what breaks first" depends on the ratio of impact energy to material strength and on the timescale of loading.
Speed normally wins because solid debris concentrates energy in a point;
rain loses because water spreads it.

and you reverse the engineering priorities.

items.question: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?
human_answers: You would have to drink a lot of blood. A person contains about 5 liters of blood, or 14 glasses. [Image: image] If your blood is more than about half a percent alcohol, you stand a pretty good chance of dying. There have been a handful of cases of people surviving with a blood alcohol level of above 1%, but the LD50—the level at which 50% of people will die—is 0.40 (http://www.nellis.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-110211-015.pdf) (0.4%). If someone had a BAC of 0.40, and you drank all 14 glasses of their blood in a short amount of time,[1]Hey, there's a 50% chance they were going to die anyway. you would throw up: [Image: image] You wouldn't throw up because because of the alcohol; you'd just throw up because you're drinking blood. If you somehow avoided vomiting, you would have ingested a total of 20[2]Thank you to Conor Braman, among others, for correcting a missing zero in the original version of this calculation. grams of ethanol, which is the amount you'd get from a pint of beer. [Image: image] Depending on your weight, drinking that much blood could raise your own blood alcohol level to about 0.05. This is low enough that you could legally drive in many jurisdictions, but high enough to double your risk of an accident if you did. If your BAC is 0.05, it means only 1/8th of the alcohol from the other person's blood made it into yours. Supposing that after you drank all this blood, someone killed you and drank your blood,[3]It's only fair. they would then have a BAC of 0.006. If this process were repeated about 25 times, there would be fewer than 8 molecules of ethanol left in the last person's blood. After a few more cycles, there would likely be none;[4]By homeopathic standards, this is still quite concentrated. they'd just be drinking regular blood.[5]Like a loser. Whether there's any alcohol in it or not, drinking 14 glasses of blood wouldn't be fun. There's not a huge amount of medical literature on the subject, but anecdotal evidence from online forum posts suggests that any normal person who tries to drink more than about a pint of blood will vomit: [Image: image] If you drink blood regularly, over a long period of time the buildup of iron in your system can cause iron overload (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_overload). This syndrome, which sometimes affects people who have repeated blood transfusions, is one of the few conditions for which the correct treatment is bloodletting (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodletting).[6]Others include PCV (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycythemia_vera) and PCT (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyria_cutanea_tarda). Drinking one person's blood probably wouldn't cause iron overload. What it could give you is a blood-borne disease. Most such diseases are caused by viruses that can't survive in the stomach, but they could easily get into your blood through scratches in your mouth or throat as you drank. Diseases you could get from drinking an infected person's blood include hepatitis B and C, HIV, Hantaviruses, and Ebola. I'm not a doctor, and I try not to give medical advice in these articles. However, I will confidently say that you shouldn't drink the blood of someone with Ebola. That said, drinking or eating blood is not unheard of. It's a taboo in many cultures, but the British eat "black pudding", which is largely blood, and there are similar dishes all around the world. Maasai pastoralists in east Africa once lived mainly on milk, but also sometimes drank blood (http://digitalcommons.calpoly.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1005&context=honors), drawing it from their cattle and mixing it with the milk to form a sort of extreme protein shake. So the bottom line is that drinking enough of someone's blood to get drunk would be very difficult, probably quite unpleasant, and might give you some serious diseases. In the end, the blood itself would do awful things to your body long before the booze ever could. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Ethanol Dose and BAC Transfer Accuracy
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons from the drunk person's BAC, total blood volume, and ethanol concentration to the drinker's likely alcohol dose and resulting BAC.
criteria.1-2: Claims the drinker would easily get drunk or die from alcohol with little or no quantitative support.
criteria.3-4: Mentions BAC or alcohol transfer but gives substantially wrong amounts or ignores blood volume.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that blood contains relatively little ethanol, but uses rough or incomplete calculations.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates that even all the blood from a severely intoxicated person contains only about a drink or two of ethanol.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects BAC, roughly 5 L of blood, grams of ethanol, and the drinker's diluted BAC, showing why alcohol is not the main danger.

criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer realistically handles the practical and biological consequences of drinking large amounts of human blood.

criteria.3-4: Notes it would be unpleasant but gives little physiological explanation.
criteria.5-6: Mentions vomiting or stomach distress from consuming blood, but lacks detail about quantity or limits.
criteria.7-8: Explains that drinking enough blood to matter alcohol-wise would require liters and would likely cause vomiting before intoxication.
criteria.9-10: Clearly separates alcohol effects from blood-consumption effects, including volume burden, nausea, vomiting, digestion, and practical inability to retain enough blood.

criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of non-alcohol hazards from drinking another person's blood, especially pathogens and repeated-exposure risks.

criteria.3-4: Vaguely mentions disease or contamination without specifying mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Identifies blood-borne infection risk but omits transmission caveats or other toxicological issues.
criteria.7-8: Discusses blood-borne pathogens such as hepatitis, HIV, or Ebola and notes entry through mouth/throat lesions.
criteria.9-10: Covers pathogen risks, stomach survivability limits, mucosal cuts, and distinguishes one-time exposure from chronic issues such as iron overload.

criteria.name: Long-Range Counterfactual Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a coherent causal chain under extensions of the premise, such as repeated blood-drinking or secondary drinkers.
criteria.1-2: Introduces impossible or contradictory downstream effects without causal connection.
criteria.3-4: Gives a short answer with little downstream reasoning beyond the first sip.
criteria.5-6: Follows the main outcome but does not address dilution, metabolism, or repeated-transfer implications.
criteria.7-8: Correctly reasons that ethanol becomes highly diluted in the drinker's bloodstream and would diminish further in repeated transfers.
criteria.9-10: Provides a clear multi-step chain from donor intoxication to ingestion, absorption, dilution, possible secondary transfer, and eventual negligible ethanol.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer states conclusions with appropriate confidence, avoids overclaiming, and remains internally consistent about alcohol, blood, and health effects.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, false certainties, or sensational claims unsupported by the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct points but mixes them with conflicting statements or exaggerated certainty.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible but imprecise about thresholds, variability, or medical risk probabilities.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language about body size, BAC, pathogen exposure, vomiting likelihood, and donor intoxication level.
criteria.9-10: Consistently distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes while avoiding contradictions and preserving the central conclusion: the blood is more dangerous and unpleasant than the alcohol.

items.model_answer:
If you drank the blood of a drunk person, you would consume a very small amount of alcohol, but not enough to make you intoxicated.

Here's why:

**Alcohol concentration in blood**: When someone drinks alcohol, it enters their bloodstream. Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is typically measured as a percentage. A legally drunk person might have a BAC of 0.08% to 0.15%, meaning 0.08-0.15 grams of alcohol per 100 milliliters of blood.

**The math**: The human body contains roughly 5 liters of blood. If you drank, say, 100 ml of blood from someone with a BAC of 0.10%, you'd consume only about 0.1 grams of alcohol—roughly equivalent to a few drops of beer.

**Comparison**: A standard drink contains about 14 grams of alcohol. You'd need to drink several liters of blood to get the equivalent of one alcoholic beverage, which is obviously impractical and dangerous for other reasons.

**Other risks**: Drinking human blood poses serious health risks including bloodborne diseases (HIV, hepatitis B and C), iron overload, and potential immune reactions. These dangers far outweigh any minimal alcohol content.

In short, you wouldn't get drunk from drinking a drunk person's blood—the alcohol concentration is far too diluted. But you would expose yourself to significant medical risks from consuming blood itself.

edus.text: If you drank the blood of a drunk person,
you would consume a very small amount of alcohol,
but not enough to make you intoxicated.
Here's why:
When someone drinks alcohol,
it enters their bloodstream.
Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is typically measured as a percentage.
A legally drunk person might have a BAC of 0.08% to 0.15%,
meaning 0.08-0.15 grams of alcohol per 100 milliliters of blood.
The human body contains roughly 5 liters of blood.
If you drank, say, 100 ml of blood from someone with a BAC of 0.10%,
you'd consume only about 0.1 grams of alcohol
roughly equivalent to a few drops of beer.
A standard drink contains about 14 grams of alcohol.
You'd need to drink several liters of blood to get the equivalent of one alcoholic beverage,
which is obviously impractical and dangerous for other reasons.
Drinking human blood poses serious health risks including bloodborne diseases (HIV, hepatitis B and C), iron overload, and potential immune reactions.
These dangers far outweigh any minimal alcohol content.
In short,
you wouldn't get drunk from drinking a drunk person's blood—
the alcohol concentration is far too diluted.
But you would expose yourself to significant medical risks from consuming blood itself.

items.question: How Many Birds Would It Take to Collapse into a Giant Bird Ball?
human_answers: The video shows starlings, birds which ... • gather in giant flocks of sometimes more than a million animals • can talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VZYG00_qvE) • sound like R2-D2, though not as much as bobolinks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ABjBldAtPQ#t=9) do The gravitational force between adjacent starlings is small. If two birds were flying half a meter apart and tried to go perfectly straight, they would fly for over a thousand kilometers before the gravitational force between them finally steered them into colliding. [Image: image] Side note: The following is the first sentence from a journal article (http://jeb.biologists.org/content/204/19/3311) on starling metabolism:We trained two starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) to fly in a wind tunnel whilst wearing respirometry masks. I really think the paper should have stopped there; no matter what their results were, they can't possibly improve on the achievement they opened with. [Image: image] Anyway, back to gravity. To calculate the gravitational force from a whole flock of starlings, we need to know the flock's density. Conveniently, a 2008 paper (http://arxiv.org/abs/0802.1667) in Animal Behavior gathered some detailed statistics on starling flocks. The highest density they saw was about half a starling per cubic meter.[1]0.54 (•)>m-3 If the birds weigh about 85 grams each, that means the air in a starling flock weighs 25 times more than the starlings themselves.[2]This makes a certain intuitive sense. If they were that much heavier than the air between them, it's hard to imagine how they'd be able to stay airborne by pushing off of it with their wings. This means that the air's gravity is 25 times stronger than the starling cloud's gravity, and it's the air's gravity that will dominate the collapse. The collapse of giant clouds of gas or birds is governed by the equation for the Jeans instability (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeans_instability). It suggests that in order to undergo collapse, a cloud of uniform room-temperature air full of starlings would have to be much larger than the Earth to collapse. [Image: image] The gas cloud's gravity would be very weak, so the starlings would probably have a hard time flying until they got used to it. (Birds can fly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w4sZ3qe6PiI&feature=kp) in zero g—or, at least, they flap around in confusion. But, to be fair, that's how I'd react if I were abruptly and without warning yanked from my bed and tossed into the air in a zero g airplane cabin.) Such a cloud wouldn't form in the first place without some extra compression. To collapse naturally under its own gravity, the starling cloud would need to be so large that it would engulf the Solar System. When it did collapse, it would heat up, and the starlings ... [Image: image] ... would become a star.

items.model_answer:
This is a fascinating physics question about gravitational collapse! Let me work through this systematically.

For a collection of birds to gravitationally collapse into a "giant bird ball," we need the gravitational binding energy to overcome the structural integrity and thermal energy of the system.

**Key considerations:**

1. **Gravitational collapse threshold**: An object will collapse under its own gravity when its mass exceeds the point where gravitational pressure overcomes internal pressure. For a rough sphere of birds, we need the escape velocity from the surface to exceed the typical velocities of particles (birds) in the system.

2. **Critical mass estimate**: Using dimensional analysis, a self-gravitating sphere needs radius R where:
   - Gravitational binding energy: ~GM²/R
   - This must exceed thermal/kinetic energy: ~NkT (where N is number of birds)

3. **Practical calculation**: 
   - Average bird mass: ~1 kg (using medium-sized birds)
   - Bird density when packed: ~300 kg/m³ (mostly air between birds)
   - For gravitational binding to dominate, we need a sphere massive enough that surface gravity is significant

Using the Jeans mass criterion (the minimum mass for gravitational collapse):

M_Jeans ≈ (kT/Gm)^(3/2) × (1/ρ^(1/2))

For bird-like conditions (room temperature, low density packing):

**Answer: Approximately 10^25 to 10^26 birds**

This would create a sphere roughly 10,000 km in radius—about the size of Earth! At this scale, the outer birds would experience enough gravitational attraction to overcome any tendency to fly away, and the mass would begin collapsing inward.

Below this number, the birds' structural strength, thermal motion, and ability to flap would prevent gravitational collapse. The exact number depends on bird species, packing density, and whether the birds are alive (and struggling) or treated as passive matter.

edus.text: This is a fascinating physics question about gravitational collapse!
Let me work through this systematically.
For a collection of birds to gravitationally collapse into a "giant bird ball,"
we need the gravitational binding energy to overcome the structural integrity and thermal energy of the system.
Key considerations:
Gravitational collapse threshold:
An object will collapse under its own gravity when its mass exceeds the point where gravitational pressure overcomes internal pressure.
For a rough sphere of birds, we need the escape velocity from the surface to exceed the typical velocities of particles (birds) in the system.
Critical mass estimate:
Using dimensional analysis, a self-gravitating sphere needs radius R where:
Gravitational binding energy: ~GM²/R
This must exceed thermal/kinetic energy: ~NkT
where N is number of birds
Practical calculation:
Average bird mass: ~1 kg
using medium-sized birds
Bird density when packed: ~300 kg/m³
mostly air between birds
For gravitational binding to dominate, we need a sphere massive enough that surface gravity is significant.
Using the Jeans mass criterion
the minimum mass for gravitational collapse
For bird-like conditions
room temperature, low density packing
Answer: Approximately 10^25 to 10^26 birds
This would create a sphere roughly 10,000 km in radius
about the size of Earth!
At this scale, the outer birds would experience enough gravitational attraction to overcome any tendency to fly away,
and the mass would begin collapsing inward.
Below this number, the birds' structural strength, thermal motion, and ability to flap would prevent gravitational collapse.
The exact number depends on bird species, packing density, and whether the birds are alive
and struggling
or treated as passive matter.
