items.question: What If You Dropped a 7-Kilogram Bowling Ball into the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: It is a good thing you mentioned the weight, because of a very surprising fact: Most bowling balls float. It's true. Bowling balls all have about the same volume, so they all displace the same weight in seawater—12.13 lbs, or about 5.5 kg. But their weights vary substantially, from as little as 6 lbs to a max of 16. Only the balls that weigh more than 12.13 lbs will sink. [Image: image] "Hang on a moment," the serious bowlers reading this are saying, "most bowling balls are at the heavy end of that range. The usual range is more like 14-16 lbs for men and 10-14 lbs for women. Maybe the average women's ball floats, but the overall average ball surely sinks." This is definitely true for serious bowlers, but for casual bowlers, it might be better to define the "average" ball using the distribution on the rack of balls at the local bowling alley. These house balls often list the weight on them, so rather than go to a bowling alley, I just sifted through all the Flickr photos of bowling balls and tallied up all the visible weights. The average was 10½ lbs. [Image: image] So at the very least, for most people, the average bowling ball they've picked up in their lives probably floats. If nothing else, this makes the popular simile "sank like a bowling ball"—which appears in a number of books (https://www.google.com/search?q=%22sank+like+a+bowling+ball%22&btnG=Search+Books&tbm=bks&tbo=1)—seem a little poorly chosen.[1]In defense of the authors of Volume 53 of North Dakota Quarterly, the simile they used is, "sank like a bowling ball in whipped cream," which is perfectly reasonable. On the other hand, How To Hook a Man (And a Baby) and The Year's Work in Lebowski Studies are on their own. But Doug's bowling ball is 7 kg (15.5 lbs), making it plenty heavy enough to sink in the ocean. How fast will it fall? Small falling spheres in viscous (goopy) liquids (like hair gel (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1108.3427.pdf)) exhibit weird behaviors and sometimes complex oscillation, but bowling balls falling through water are pretty straightforward. Their falling speed is determined by the drag equation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_equation) and their weight (accounting for buoyancy). For Doug's bowling ball, that terminal velocity will be roughly 1.3 meters per second, which means it will take two hours and 20 minutes to reach the bottom. That's plenty of time to enjoy a two-hour movie (http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0118715/). A 13-pound bowling ball, which is much closer to neutrally buoyant in seawater, would take four and a half hours to reach the bottom. On the other hand, a bowling ball made of solid iron would reach the bottom in half an hour. A bowling ball made of lead would reach the bottom in 23 minutes, and a bowling ball made of solid gold would make it in 17. However, a bowling ball made of solid gold would also weigh more than the average bowler.[2]At least, I think it would, but I can't think of a way to sample the weight of the average bowler without getting punched. A bowling ball made of solid osmium, the heaviest naturally-occurring element, would weigh 120 kilograms, and could sink to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in just 16 minutes. But what if you got the weight wrong? What if the bowling ball you were using turned out to be 7 pounds, not 7 kilograms? Or maybe it's 10.5 pounds—the "average" bowling ball, at least according to a dubious Flickr sample. In that case, the ball would never reach the bottom. Instead, it would drift sideways with the currents. We can track what course it would take using the Adrift.org.au ocean plastic tracking tool (http://www.adrift.org.au/map?lat=11.3&lng=142.6&center=-180&startmon=Jan). The bowling ball would first drift west, past Luzon in the Philippines, then probably north along the coast of China, turning right at Japan and heading out over the Pacific. Sometime in the summer of 2018, it would approach the coast of California. Most likely, it would follow the coast for a little while, then become swept up in the great Pacific garbage patch (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch). However, it's possible that it would be swept up on shore instead. If, during those three years, Doug took his boat from the Mariana islands to Los Angeles, found a nice, sheltered cove, and set up ten carefully weighted bowling pins just below the surface, then there is a tiny, tiny chance ... [Image: image] ... that he could succeed in bowling the single most improbable strike of all time.

If you dropped a 7-kilogram bowling ball into the Mariana Trench, here's what would happen:

**The descent:**
The ball would initially accelerate downward due to gravity, but quickly reach a terminal velocity as water resistance balances gravitational force. In water, terminal velocity for a bowling ball is much lower than in air—roughly 2-3 meters per second depending on the ball's exact size and surface properties. At this speed, it would take approximately 3-4 hours to reach the bottom of Challenger Deep (about 11,000 meters down).

**Pressure effects:**
As the ball descends, it experiences increasing hydrostatic pressure—reaching about 1,100 atmospheres (roughly 16,000 psi or 110 megapascals) at the bottom. A standard bowling ball is typically made of polyurethane, reactive resin, or polyester plastic around a dense core. These materials are relatively incompressible, so the ball would likely survive intact. However, if there were any air pockets or voids in the manufacturing, those would be compressed significantly, potentially causing cracks or structural damage.

**What happens at the bottom:**
The ball would simply settle into the sediment on the ocean floor. The Mariana Trench bottom is covered in soft, muddy sediment, so the ball would likely sink partially into it and remain there indefinitely. The extreme pressure, near-freezing temperatures (1-4°C), and lack of light mean very little would happen to it afterward—deep-sea decomposition is extremely slow, and the synthetic materials in bowling balls are highly resistant to degradation.

The ball would essentially become a permanent fixture of the trench floor unless retrieved.

items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle. A tower to space would be very different from a space elevator. A space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator) would be about 100,000 kilometers tall, while a tower "to space" would only need to be 100 kilometers. As Ethan mentions, it would need to be pressurized, with an airlock every few miles. [Image: image] A stairway to space[1]If there's a bustle in your hedgerow, well, uh, boy, I don't know what to tell you. I guess ask it to leave? would have about half a million steps. World-champion stair-climbers[2]or "towerrunners" like Christian Riedl (http://stairsport.com/12h-stair-climbing-world-record-attempt-by-christian-riedl/) or Kristin Frey (http://www.kristinfrey.com/) can travel roughly a Mount Everest's height in a day; Riedl set the half-day record last October by climbing 13,145.65 meters (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/stair-climbing-vertical-height-%2812-hours%29) in 12 hours. At that pace—taking the other twelve hours to rest, eat, and sleep each day—it would take him a little over a week to reach the top. Climbing all those stairs would burn calories, which would mean you'd need to carry food. It turns out that the most efficient food you can carry, in terms of calories per pound, is butter—which is why Arctic explorers carry so much of it (http://abcnews.go.com/Technology/GlobalWarming/story?id=4853093). Suppose your backpack (http://www.amazon.co.uk/Disney-Frozen-Childrens-Multicoloured-FROZEN001018/dp/B00O2EO8XU) holds 9 liters. Climbing 10 stairs (http://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/pages/articleviewer.aspx?year=2002&issue=04000&article=00021&type=abstract) burns about a calorie, which means climbing all the way up to space will burn about 72,000 calories. If you fill your backpack with butter, it would hold almost enough calories (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=9+liters+of+butter) to get you to the top. However, since it would take you weeks to climb all those stairs, you'd also need your normal dietary allowance of 2,000 calories (three sticks of butter) per day. Combining that with the 72,000 calories just from climbing the stairs, and you'd probably need to upgrade to a more serious 16-liter backpack (http://www.disneystore.com/anna-and-elsa-backpack-for-girls-personalizable/mp/1367267/1000290/). If you fill that backpack with butter, it will let you carry around 110,000 calories,[3]Coincidentally, about the amount you get (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Product_Code=QW-PERSON) from eating a human body. which should be enough to get you to the top if you're really dedicated. If you didn't want to eat 35 pounds of butter,[4]For whatever weird reason. you could try getting to the top by motorcycle. Based on how quickly this rider (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8CZiqEjQDk) ascends 45 stairs, a motorcycle could conceivably make it to the top in a day. [Image: image] Ok, so you got to the top. Now what? Getting up to space isn't that hard, after all—the hard part is getting into orbit (http://what-if.xkcd.com/58/), and the tower doesn't help you very much with that. So what else could you do? Michael Longuet-Higgins (http://noc.ac.uk/about-us/history/national-oceanography-centre-southampton/influential-scientists/professor-michael-s) was a research professor at the University of Cambridge and an expert in fluid dynamics, bubbles, and unusual types of waves.[5]Given his apparent research interests, this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p70s1BNvBXI) would blow his mind.​[6]Or this one (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=711bZ_pLusQ), or this gadget (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/creatableslabs/project-nesm-never-ending-slinky-machine), or this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JwohMl9Toww). In 1953, Dr. Longuet-Higgins was shown, by a colleague, an "interesting toy" which had recently appeared on the market. This toy, "Slinky," had some unusual properties. The professor immediately set to work analyzing it, and wrote up his results in a paper (http://www2.eng.cam.ac.uk/~hemh/TV/On_Slinky_the_dynamics_of_a_loose_heavy_spring.pdf). Dr. Longuet-Higgins first determined through mathematical modeling that the rate at which the Slinky descends steps should depend only on the properties of the spring itself, and not the size or shape of the stairs. He and his colleague conducted a series of experiments "on five different flights of stairs, of various dimensions, in Trinity College, Cambridge." Their conclusion: The Slinky descended a constant rate of about 0.8 seconds per step.[7]Except on some wide, flat stairs, where the Slinky "came to rest after three or four steps at most," which gives me a wonderful mental image of two disappointed British professors at the bottom of a staircase.​[8]Sadly, this was before the invention of the StairMaster. Fun fact: After a surprise StairMaster management shakeup in 2011, for some reason not a single newspaper ran the headline "StairMaster CEO steps down". Dr. Longuet-Higgins determined that the Slinky quickly reached a constant descent rate after first few steps. This tells us that if you placed a Slinky (similar to his) at top of the stairway to space, and gave it just the right nudge ... [Image: image] ... it would make it back to the bottom in just over five days. Or, to put that in more appetizing units: [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup fidelity: elevator vs stairway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly preserves the key physical distinction in the prompt: a space elevator and a stairway/tower to 'space' are not equivalent structures and imply very different scales, endpoints, and engineering constraints.
criteria.1-2: Treats the stairway and space elevator as the same thing, or assumes both simply reach orbit with no distinction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a difference between them but gives major wrong scales or endpoints, such as a 100 km elevator or a stairway reaching geostationary orbit.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that the stairway only needs to reach near-space while the elevator must extend vastly farther, but gives limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains the approximate scale contrast, such as ~100 km for a stairway/tower to space versus tens of thousands to ~100,000 km for an elevator, and distinguishes reaching space from reaching orbit.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the counterfactual around both structures coexisting, clearly separating the stairway's atmospheric/altitude role from the elevator's orbital transport role and using that distinction consistently throughout.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for human ascent on the stairway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly reasons through what climbing or riding up a stairway to space would require, including atmosphere, pressure, food/energy, time, fatigue, and access infrastructure.
criteria.1-2: Ignores human survival and ascent mechanics, or says people can simply walk up into space unaided.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one issue such as oxygen or fatigue but leaves most survival and logistics mechanisms unexplained.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant constraints, such as pressurization, airlocks, time to climb, food, and rest, but with shallow or partially inconsistent reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent account of a pressurized stairway, repeated airlocks or stations, ascent times on the order of days to weeks for climbers, and energy/food requirements.
criteria.9-10: Integrates the stairway mechanics quantitatively and causally, including approximate step counts or altitude, climb-rate limits, calories, rest cycles, pressure management, and why vehicles might change the timescale.

items.model_answer:
If both a space elevator and a literal stairway to space existed, we'd have two fundamentally different approaches to reaching orbit, each with distinct engineering challenges and uses.

**The Space Elevator**

A space elevator would be a tethered structure extending from Earth's surface to geostationary orbit (about 36,000 km up) or beyond. It would use a counterweight and the balance between gravitational pull and centrifugal force to remain taut. Climbers would ascend the cable using electric motors, taking days or weeks to reach orbit but using far less energy than rockets. The main challenge is finding a material strong enough—carbon nanotubes are theoretically capable, but manufacturing kilometers-long cables remains beyond current technology.

**The Stairway to Space**

A physical stairway would be an even more audacious structure. To reach just the Kármán line (100 km, the boundary of space), you'd need roughly 200 million steps. The engineering would be nightmarish: the structure would need to withstand extreme winds, temperature variations, and its own enormous weight. Unlike the space elevator, which uses orbital mechanics for support, a stairway would require massive compression strength from the ground up. No known material could support such a freestanding tower.

**Practical Comparison**

If both somehow existed:

- **Energy efficiency**: The space elevator wins dramatically. Climbing stairs to 100 km would burn roughly 100,000 calories per person—and that's just to the edge of space, not orbit. The elevator uses external power.

- **Speed**: The elevator would be faster for reaching orbital altitudes. Even a slow climber at 200 km/h reaches geostationary orbit in a week. Walking stairs at 5 km/h would take 20 hours just to reach 100 km.

- **Capacity**: The elevator could carry massive payloads. The stairway would be limited to what people or robots could carry.

- **Destination**: The elevator naturally reaches orbital velocity at geostationary altitude. The stairway would just get you high—you'd still need horizontal velocity to orbit.

In reality, both face enormous materials science challenges, but the space elevator is at least theoretically possible with advanced materials, while a freestanding stairway to orbital heights violates practical engineering limits.

items.question: What If Tug-of-War Teams Pulled on an Iron Rod Instead of a Rope?
human_answers: A couple dozen people could pull a half-inch iron rod apart. Tug-of-war, a simple game in which two teams try to pull a rope in opposite directions, has a surprisingly bloody history. I don't mean that there's some kind of gruesome historical forerunner of modern tug-of-war.[1]Although it's definitely an ancient sport (http://www.usatowa.com/history.html), so I'm sure people have come up with all kinds of horrific variations over the centuries that I don't really want to spend hours reading about. Humans seem to be creative when it comes to that kind of thing. I mean that modern tug-of-war involves a lot more death and mutilation than you might expect—precisely because people underestimate how few people it takes to break "strong" things like heavy rope. As detailed in a riveting article (http://priceonomics.com/a-history-of-tug-of-war-fatalities/) in Priceonomics, recent games of tug-of-war have resulted in hundreds of serious injuries and numerous deaths—all caused, one way or another, by ropes snapping. In particular, this seems to happen when large groups of students try to set a world record for largest tug-of-war game. When a rope under many tons of tension suddenly snaps, the recoiling ends can—and do—cause a terrifying variety of injuries. [Image: image] Before we answer Markus's question, it's worth noting that the physics of tug-of-war can be a little tricky (https://www.lhup.edu/~dsimanek/scenario/insight.htm#mechanics). It seems like common sense that the "stronger" team has an advantage, but that's not quite right. To win, you need to resist sliding forward better than the other team. If you can't resist sliding, then increasing your arm strength means you'll just pull yourself forward. Since sliding friction is often proportional to weight, tug-of-war on many surfaces is simply a contest over who's heavier.[2]Champion tug-of-war teams focus on body angle, footwork, digging into the ground, and timing pulls to throw off the other team. The strongest team in the world would lose a tug-of-war with a six-year-old and a sack of bricks, as long as the sack had a firm grip. [Image: image] So, how much force can tug-of-war players exert? A 2011 paper (http://web.nchu.edu.tw/~biosimulation/journal/pdf/vol-3-no01/vol-3-no-1-b-0003.pdf) analyzing the immune systems of several "elite tug-of-war players"[3]The paper notes that "Few studies have been done to examine the effects of [the] tug-of-war sport on physiological responses," which seems likely enough to me. measured their average pull force (on a school gym floor) to be about 102.5 kilograms-force, or about 1.5x their body weight. The ultimate tensile strength (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_tensile_strength) of cast iron is about 200 megapascals (MPa), so we can use a simple formula to figure out how many players would be needed to break one. \[ \text{People required}=\frac{\pi\times\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\text{ inch} \right )^2\times200\text{ MPa}}{102.5\text{ kg}/\text{person}}\approx25\text{ people} \] Two teams of 25 people[4]I originally wrote 25 people total, forgetting that two people pulling with 100 units of force each will produce 100 units of tension on the rope, not 200! Thank you for Gordon McDonough for pointing this out. could probably pull a half-inch iron bar apart. An inch-thick iron bar could be torn in half by teams of 101 people,[5]People often play tug-of-war with their dogs. Going by weight alone, 30 humans would probably be about evenly matched against 101 dalmatians. and a 2-inch-diameter bar would need over 400. It's hard to have a tug-of-war with something thicker than about 2 inches. Since you're not allowed to install handles on the rope,[6]Or wrap it around your hand, for reasons which will become clear if you read some of the articles on tug-of-war injuries. it has to be narrow enough to grip easily. While "400 people" may be the limit for plain iron bars, there are much stronger substances out there. Common types of steel, for example, have a tensile strength about 10 times that of cast iron. Common half-inch rebar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar), for example, would in theory take teams of over 200 people to pull apart, compared to 25 for cast iron. Other substances are even stronger; a half-inch shaft made from high-grade steel or a polymer like Kevlar (or, theoretically, a solid silicon crystal) could handle the pulling force from teams of anywhere between 500 and 800 competitive tug-of-war players. If we limit ourselves to a two-inch diameter rope, which seems to be about the maximum size for tug-of-wars,[7](William Safire (http://www.theonion.com/articles/william-safire-orders-two-whoppers-junior,3351/) returns from the grave to point out that it should really be tugs-of-war.) then the maximum number of tug-of-war players given a super-strong rope like Kevlar is in the neighborhood of 10,000.[8]Or several times that many, if they're not very athletic. If we figured out how to manufacture large ropes out of graphene ribbons, which have tensile strengths over 10 times higher (http://arxiv.org/pdf/0709.0992.pdf) than existing materials, we could theoretically support a tug-of-war between teams of up to 100,000 players each. Such a rope would be over 200 miles long, and could stretch from New York to Washington. [Image: image] If our experience with nylon ropes failing is any indication, when the graphene finally snapped, the death toll could be enormous among both players and bystanders. Lengths of graphene would crack across the landscape like bullwhips, slicing down forests and demolishing buildings. In the end, trying to develop stronger ropes leads only to greater danger to everyone, both participants and bystanders. In the ultimate game of tug-of-war ... [Image: image] ... the only winning move is not to pull.

items.model_answer:
If tug-of-war teams pulled on an iron rod instead of a rope, several important differences would emerge:

**Mechanical behavior**: An iron rod is essentially rigid and doesn't stretch under typical human pulling forces. Unlike a rope that can elongate slightly and store elastic energy, the rod would transmit forces almost instantaneously from one end to the other. This means there would be no "give" in the system—any imbalance in force would immediately translate to motion.

**Failure mode**: The contest would likely end differently. Instead of one team gradually pulling the other across a line, the rod might fail catastrophically. If teams pulled hard enough, the rod could buckle (bend suddenly) under compressive forces, especially if it's long and slender. Buckling occurs when a long column under compression becomes unstable and bends sideways. Alternatively, if the rod is short and thick enough to resist buckling, it might fail at weak points through fracture, though this would require enormous force.

**Grip and safety**: Gripping a smooth metal rod is much harder than gripping a rope, especially with sweaty hands. Teams would need different techniques—perhaps wrapping the rod or using mechanical grips. The rigid nature also makes it more dangerous; if someone loses grip or the rod fails, there's risk of injury from the hard, unyielding material swinging or falling.

**Compression vs. tension**: Here's the key physics difference: in a rope tug-of-war, the rope is always in tension (being stretched). With a rigid rod, the side that's winning puts their end in tension while the losing side's end experiences compression. The middle of the rod experiences complex stress states. Ropes can only pull; rods can both pull and push, which fundamentally changes the mechanics.

**Practical outcome**: Most likely, the contest would be shorter and less dynamic, ending either when one team's grip fails or when the rod buckles if it's sufficiently long and thin.

items.question: What If the Moon Were Replaced by a Black Hole of the Same Mass?
human_answers: "Not much" and "not much." [Image: image] A black hole the mass of the Moon would have an event horizon about the size of a sand grain. Specifically, according to one of my favorite charts (http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2003/of03-001/htmldocs/images/chart.pdf), a black hole moon would be a grain of fine to medium-fine sand, and could pass through a sieve of size ASTM No. 70 or larger. I mean, I guess a black hole with the mass of the Moon would pass right through any sieve, destroying it in the process, but that's neither here nor there.[1]The expression "that's neither here nor there" can be kind of confusing and ambiguous, but I guess that's neither here nor there. Since the Moon's mass and position wouldn't change, the tides on Earth wouldn't change, either. When you're floating outside a spherical mass, its pull on you is the same regardless of whether the mass is concentrated at the center of the sphere or spread out throughout it. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth's orbit wouldn't change, although life on Earth might (http://what-if.xkcd.com/49/). With the Moon gathered into a point, there'd be no moonlight, which would affect the life cycles of all kinds of nocturnal animals. But compared to a lot of the other (http://xkcd.com/1338/) things we've done, that would be fairly minor. The Earth's orbit is stabilized by the Moon (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v361/n6413/abs/361615a0.html), but the lunar-mass black hole would probably serve the same role. This black hole Moon (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mbBbFH9fAg) would be pretty low-profile. If it were much smaller, it would evaporate through Hawking radiation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation), but a black hole the size of the Moon actually absorbs more energy from the cosmic background radiation than it emits through the Hawking mechanism. Our black hole would really be black. [Image: image] At least, if it didn't eat anything. If the black hole devoured any objects, it would let off a tremendous blast of radiation. Black holes burn brightly as they devour things; the whirlpool of matter heats up as it falls inward (http://www.gothosenterprises.com/black_holes/outside_black_holes.html), causing it to glow brightly.[2]A black hole can't devour matter too fast, though, because at some point it would be producing so much radiation that it would blast its own "food" away. This is called the Eddington limit (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). If our black hole were devouring matter at the Eddington limit, it would be hot enough to sterilize the Earth. Fortunately, there's not a lot out there for it to eat, so it wouldn't glow very brightly for now. It would spend most of its time drastically altering the orbits of nearby dust particles—one sand grain pushing other sand grains around.[3]Even if it sucked in matter at the rate the Earth—with its much larger "collecting area"—sucks in interplanetary dust, it wouldn't necessarily be a problem for us. But there would be one interesting effect: In addition to getting darker, Earth would get colder, because moonlight warms the Earth. It's a very tiny contributor to our global energy balance; the Moon is five or six orders of magnitude dimmer than the Sun. But it's there. Measurements show that global temperature varies with a 28-day cycle (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2000GL011651/abstract); all else being equal, the Earth is hottest during the full moon. It's a tiny difference—small fractions of a degree—but it's there. But it turns out most of this effect is not due to moonlight. The largest contributor is the fact that the Earth is slightly closer to the Sun during a full Moon: [Image: image] Calculating the amount of energy radiated back to Earth by the Moon is deceptively tricky. The Moon reflects sunlight, but with some surprising twists. When the Moon is half-illuminated, you might think it would be half as bright as when full—but it's much less bright than that (http://home.earthlink.net/~kitathome/LunarLight/moonlight_gallery/technique/moonbright.htm). And once you account for that, there are even trickier effects to deal with, because science is the worst.[4]Like the fact that the waxing Moon is 20% brighter (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2402251?sid=21105340972791&uid=2&uid=4&uid=3739808&uid=3739256) than the waning Moon, or that the Moon is a mild retroreflector (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_surge). Then, on top of all the weird visible-light effects, the Moon also heats up under the Sun, then radiates that heat as infrared light. There's a great discussion of the Moon's effect on the Earth's energy budget in this article (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/67/12/10.1119/1.19109?ver=pdfcov) by Robert Knox. The upshot is that the Moon's infrared heat radiation turns out to affect Earth's temperature about 10 times more than the visible moonlight, but still about 10 times less than the effect from gravity moving Earth closer and farther from the Sun. Knox even quantifies the effect this has on Earth's radiation balance—the presence of infrared moonlight warms the planet by 1.2 milli-degrees Fahrenheit (m°F). [Image: image] Without moonlight, the planet would cool down slightly. But given the accelerating rate at which we're adding (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keeling_Curve) CO2 to the atmosphere—which changes the Earth's energy balance—we'd make up the difference in a couple of weeks. So all in all, the conversion of the Moon to a black hole might not even be that big of a deal. Unless, of course, it happened on certain days between 1969 and 1972, in which case Nixon (http://www.archives.gov/presidential-libraries/events/centennials/nixon/images/exhibit/rn100-6-1-2.pdf) would've needed yet another one of those speeches (http://xkcd.com/1484/). [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If the Moon were replaced by a black hole of the same mass (about 7.35 × 10²² kg), the orbital dynamics would remain unchanged, but nearly everything else would be dramatically different.

**Orbital mechanics:** Since gravitational force depends only on mass and distance, Earth would continue orbiting this black hole exactly as it currently orbits the Moon. The tides would persist with the same strength and timing, as tidal forces are also mass-dependent.

**The black hole itself:** A black hole with the Moon's mass would have a Schwarzschild radius of only about 0.1 millimeters—roughly the width of a human hair. This tiny event horizon would be invisible to the naked eye, appearing as an absolutely black point in space.

**Visibility and light:** The most immediate change would be the loss of moonlight. The Moon reflects sunlight, providing illumination at night, but a black hole would absorb all light that crosses its event horizon. The night sky would be significantly darker. You might observe gravitational lensing effects—background starlight bending around the black hole—but given its small size and distance, this would be subtle and require telescopes to detect clearly.

**Accretion and radiation:** The black hole would gradually accrete matter from the solar wind, cosmic dust, and any stray particles. However, given the extremely low density of material in cislunar space, the accretion rate would be minuscule. Any accretion disk would be faint, likely not visible without instruments. There would be no dangerous radiation threatening Earth.

**Long-term stability:** The system would be stable. The black hole wouldn't "suck in" Earth or anything else—gravity doesn't work that way. Objects in stable orbits remain in stable orbits regardless of whether the central mass is a moon, a black hole, or a bowling ball of equivalent mass.

The primary consequence would be cultural and biological: the loss of moonlight would affect nocturnal ecosystems, human culture, and our historical relationship with the night sky.

edus.text: If the Moon were replaced by a black hole of the same mass (about 7.35 × 10²² kg),
the orbital dynamics would remain unchanged,
but nearly everything else would be dramatically different.
Since gravitational force depends only on mass and distance,
Earth would continue orbiting this black hole exactly as it currently orbits the Moon.
The tides would persist with the same strength and timing,
as tidal forces are also mass-dependent.
A black hole with the Moon's mass would have a Schwarzschild radius of only about 0.1 millimeters—roughly the width of a human hair.
This tiny event horizon would be invisible to the naked eye,
appearing as an absolutely black point in space.
The most immediate change would be the loss of moonlight.
The Moon reflects sunlight, providing illumination at night,
but a black hole would absorb all light that crosses its event horizon.
The night sky would be significantly darker.
You might observe gravitational lensing effects—background starlight bending around the black hole—
but given its small size and distance,
this would be subtle
and require telescopes to detect clearly.
The black hole would gradually accrete matter from the solar wind, cosmic dust, and any stray particles.
However, given the extremely low density of material in cislunar space,
the accretion rate would be minuscule.
Any accretion disk would be faint,
likely not visible without instruments.
There would be no dangerous radiation threatening Earth.
The system would be stable.
The black hole wouldn't "suck in" Earth or anything else—
gravity doesn't work that way.
Objects in stable orbits remain in stable orbits
regardless of whether the central mass is a moon, a black hole, or a bowling ball of equivalent mass.
The primary consequence would be cultural and biological:
the loss of moonlight would affect nocturnal ecosystems, human culture, and our historical relationship with the night sky.

items.question: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?
human_answers: Believe it or not, your flamethrower idea is actually the more practical of the two. The flamethrower also has the advantage that, unlike the microwave, it won't interfere with wifi (unless you aim it directly at the router). [Image: image] I'm writing this article from Boston, which is currently buried under a truly ridiculous amount of snow (http://www.buzzfeed.com/mjs538/please-stop-snowing). We've had more snow in the past 30 days (http://weather.ou.edu/~splillo/misc.html) than Anchorage, Alaska usually gets in an entire winter.[1]Meanwhile, Anchorage is on Twitter wondering (https://twitter.com/NWSBoston/status/567172928593485824) where their snow went and threatening revenge (https://twitter.com/NWSAnchorage/status/567566488517619712). Here's (https://twitter.com/EricHolthaus/status/567350490912931840) a neat visualization of the atmospheric pattern during these polar vortexes. Vortices. Whatever. Our transit system has broken down (http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/02/14/transportation/U7vNqP861gKQFRly2jmjdL/story.html) and our roofs[2]Tolkien prefers rooves. are collapsing (http://www.whdh.com/story/28133433/dozens-of-roof-collapses-reported-across-new-england). The mayor gave a press conference (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2015/02/15/boston-mayor-seems-pretty-tired-all-this-dang-snow/OYtAnLLNQ2iMBMRaxTJYzJ/story.html?s_campaign=bcom%3Asocialflow%3Atwitter) in which he announced, "I don't know what to say to anybody anymore. Hopefully it will stop eventually." So snow removal is on all our minds. But snow is hard to melt. (And we've been trying (https://twitter.com/NotifyBoston/status/564524089017401347)[3]I love that tweet because it sort of sounds like it comes from an alternate fairy-tale universe where cities farm snow and snow-melters form the base of the economy.) Your microwave idea certainly sounds like it should be more practical than a flamethrower. Microwaves seem clean and efficient; after all, we don't use flamethrowers in our kitchens. [Image: image] But there's a big problem: Microwaves heat water very well, but they don't really work on ice (http://www.thenakedscientists.com/HTML/content/kitchenscience/exp/-324719c1f8/). Fortunately, there are other ways to get energy into the ice. In addition to your flamethrower suggestion, you could, for example, use infrared heat lamps or lasers.[4]Pick a frequency where snow has a low albedo; otherwise, the FBI may hunt you down for lasering aircraft (http://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/why-its-terrible-idea-point-lasers-airplanes-n28841). But whatever you use, you'll run into another problem: It takes an awful lot of energy to melt snow. Melting a gram of snow takes about 335 joules of energy. To put that another way, a 60-watt lightbulb is capable of melting about a pound of snow an hour. A foot of snow contains roughly the same amount of water as an inch of rain, give or take (http://www.theweatherprediction.com/habyhints/346/). Let's assume you've had a decent snowstorm of about a foot[5]For the record, by this standard, Boston has had a "decent snowstorm" every few days for the past month.—meaning an inch worth of water—and that you want to melt a 9-foot-wide swath while driving along at 55 mph. Luckily, this happens to be one of those happy physics situations where we can just multiply together every number we're looking at, and the answer (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=55+mph+*+water+density+*+1+inch+*+9+feet+*+335+J%2Fgram) turns out to be the measurement we want: \[55\text{ mph}\times1\text{ inch}\times9\text{ feet}\times\text{water density}\times335\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{gram}}=574\text{ megawatts}\] Unfortunately, it's not the answer we'd like. The nuclear reactor on an aircraft carrier, for example, produces less than 200 megawatts. To melt snow in front of your car, you'd need three of those. [Image: image] What about your your original flamethrower idea? Gasoline may have a phenomenally high energy density (http://what-if.xkcd.com/128/), but it's not high enough. No matter how big the tank on your flamethrower was, you'd run out of fuel constantly. Gas mileage in the US is often measured in "miles per gallon" of gasoline. With your flamethrower guzzling fuel, your mileage would be about 17 feet per gallon. You might be better off dropping the flamethrower entirely. Instead, take a cue from the rail agencies, who use jet-engine-powered snowblowers (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/23/mbtas_mattapan_line_relies_on_snowzilla_in_worst_weather/) to clear train tracks. In the end, it's easier to just move the snow out of your way. [Image: image]

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures the dominant constraint: the enormous energy and power needed to melt road snow at driving speeds.
criteria.1-2: Ignores energy requirements or treats melting as easy with a powerful enough microwave.
criteria.3-4: States it would take a lot of power but provides no meaningful scale or uses implausible numbers.
criteria.5-6: Uses latent heat or rough snow volume reasoning to show the requirement is very large.
criteria.7-8: Estimates road width, snow water equivalent, vehicle speed, and latent heat to reach hundreds of megawatts scale.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent quantitative chain comparable to about 574 MW for a 9-foot swath, 1 inch water equivalent, at 55 mph, and explains assumptions.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows downstream effects beyond initial melting, including road conditions, vehicle operation, infrastructure, and environment.
criteria.1-2: Only answers whether the microwave melts ice, with no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few hazards but without causal connection to the counterfactual setup.
criteria.5-6: Connects melting to runoff, refreezing, vehicle power needs, and limited usefulness.
criteria.7-8: Traces consequences such as slush formation, black ice, drainage load, visibility/steam, thermal damage, and vehicle impracticality.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain from energy delivery to meltwater management, traffic safety, refreezing, infrastructure effects, regulatory concerns, and operational failure modes.

criteria.name: Comparison to Alternatives and Practical Endpoint
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a plausible practical conclusion and compares microwave melting with more realistic snow-removal methods.
criteria.1-2: Concludes the device is practical or superior without justification.
criteria.3-4: Says it is impractical but gives weak or unrelated reasons.
criteria.5-6: Correctly concludes it is impractical mainly due to power/efficiency limits.
criteria.7-8: Explains why mechanical removal, plows, snowblowers, heat lamps, lasers, or flamethrowers may be more plausible yet still energy-limited.
criteria.9-10: Clearly concludes that moving snow is generally easier than melting it, while fairly comparing microwaves, combustion heating, infrared/lasers, and plows under the same constraints.

criteria.name: Safety, Interference, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles hazards and uncertainties without contradicting established physics or the premise.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible claims, or ignores obvious microwave hazards.
criteria.3-4: Mentions safety vaguely but includes questionable claims about radiation, power, or legality.
criteria.5-6: Identifies plausible hazards such as electromagnetic interference, burns, arcing, shielding needs, and bystander exposure.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes ionizing from non-ionizing radiation, notes shielding/beam-control issues, and avoids overstating certainty.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainties while consistently addressing RF exposure, electronics/wifi interference, vehicle shielding, reflections, regulatory limits, and thermal/mechanical hazards without internal contradictions.

items.model_answer:
Mounting a high-power microwave emitter on a car to melt road ice sounds clever in principle, but in practice it would be inefficient, dangerous, and largely impractical. Here's why.

Microwaves heat water by exciting its dipolar molecules, but ice is actually a poor microwave absorber. In solid ice, the water molecules are locked into a crystal lattice and can't rotate freely, so their dielectric loss factor is roughly two orders of magnitude lower than that of liquid water. This means a microwave beam aimed at a frozen road surface would mostly pass through or reflect off the ice rather than depositing energy into it. Only once a thin film of liquid water formed (perhaps from surface melting by sunlight or friction) would absorption ramp up — and then runaway heating could occur, since liquid water absorbs microwaves very efficiently.

To melt a meaningful layer of ice on a roadway, you'd need enormous power. Melting just 1 mm of ice across a 2-meter-wide lane at 30 km/h requires on the order of 100–200 kilowatts of delivered thermal energy, and that's assuming perfect coupling. Real coupling efficiency to ice might be 10% or less, pushing required emitter power into the megawatt range. That far exceeds what a vehicle's engine or generator could supply; military-grade high-power microwave sources of that magnitude require dedicated power plants or large pulsed-power systems.

The safety problems are severe. Stray microwaves at those power levels would cook biological tissue — pedestrians, pets, the driver, and other motorists would be at risk of deep thermal burns and cataracts. Microwaves also couple strongly into metal: nearby cars, guardrails, manhole covers, and rebar in concrete would heat unevenly, induce arcing, and potentially damage embedded sensors and electronics. Vehicle key fobs, pacemakers, GPS units, and cell phones in the vicinity would be disrupted or destroyed. Asphalt itself contains moisture and would heat, crack, and possibly catch fire as binders degrade.

There are also engineering issues with the antenna: producing a focused beam concentrated on a road surface a meter or two away is awkward at typical microwave wavelengths (12 cm at 2.45 GHz), since near-field focusing requires an aperture comparable to the beam spot. A higher frequency (e.g., 24 or 95 GHz) would focus better and couple slightly better to thin water films, but high-power sources at those frequencies are exotic and expensive.

In short, microwaves are the wrong tool. Infrared lamps, hot air, brine spraying, or simple mechanical scraping all deliver more joules of useful heat per dollar and per watt, with vastly less collateral hazard. The microwave-car idea is a fun thought experiment that mainly illustrates why we don't already do it.

edus.text: Mounting a high-power microwave emitter on a car to melt road ice sounds clever in principle,
but in practice it would be inefficient, dangerous, and largely impractical.
Here's why.
Microwaves heat water by exciting its dipolar molecules,
but ice is actually a poor microwave absorber.
In solid ice, the water molecules are locked into a crystal lattice and can't rotate freely,
so their dielectric loss factor is roughly two orders of magnitude lower than that of liquid water.
This means a microwave beam aimed at a frozen road surface would mostly pass through or reflect off the ice rather than depositing energy into it.
Only once a thin film of liquid water formed
would absorption ramp up
and then runaway heating could occur,
since liquid water absorbs microwaves very efficiently.
To melt a meaningful layer of ice on a roadway, you'd need enormous power.
Melting just 1 mm of ice across a 2-meter-wide lane at 30 km/h requires on the order of 100–200 kilowatts of delivered thermal energy,
and that's assuming perfect coupling.
Real coupling efficiency to ice might be 10% or less,
pushing required emitter power into the megawatt range.
That far exceeds what a vehicle's engine or generator could supply;
military-grade high-power microwave sources of that magnitude require dedicated power plants or large pulsed-power systems.
The safety problems are severe.
Stray microwaves at those power levels would cook biological tissue
pedestrians, pets, the driver, and other motorists would be at risk of deep thermal burns and cataracts.
Microwaves also couple strongly into metal:
nearby cars, guardrails, manhole covers, and rebar in concrete would heat unevenly, induce arcing, and potentially damage embedded sensors and electronics.
Vehicle key fobs, pacemakers, GPS units, and cell phones in the vicinity would be disrupted or destroyed.
Asphalt itself contains moisture and would heat, crack, and possibly catch fire as binders degrade.
There are also engineering issues with the antenna:
producing a focused beam concentrated on a road surface a meter or two away is awkward at typical microwave wavelengths (12 cm at 2.45 GHz),
since near-field focusing requires an aperture comparable to the beam spot.
A higher frequency (e.g., 24 or 95 GHz) would focus better and couple slightly better to thin water films,
but high-power sources at those frequencies are exotic and expensive.
In short, microwaves are the wrong tool.
Infrared lamps, hot air, brine spraying, or simple mechanical scraping all deliver more joules of useful heat per dollar and per watt,
with vastly less collateral hazard.
The microwave-car idea is a fun thought experiment
that mainly illustrates why we don't already do it.

items.question: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?
human_answers: If you're like me, your first thought on hearing this question was, "That's ridiculous; there's no way that could work." Your first thought is right. But just to be sure, let's take a closer look. Grip strength depends on a lot of factors, like hand slickness and surface material. But for the moment, let's assume Rex's hands are able to grab the pole tightly. What happens to the rest of his body? [Image: image] It's hard to find good numbers on how much force it takes to tear off a person's arm.[1]Which is probably a good thing, to be honest. There are threads on the question on MetaFilter (http://ask.metafilter.com/133821/How-much-force-to-tear-off-a-limb) and the Straight Dope message boards (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=515612), and frequent discussion of the death of Robert-François Damiens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert-Fran%C3%A7ois_Damiens),[2]Damiens was tortured to death for attempting to assassinate Louis XV, but a team of horses had trouble tearing him limb from limb. but not too much hard data. For the record, there are lots (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/20/3552/11014/Tendon-material-properties-vary-and-are) of studies (http://www.udel.edu/PT/PT%20Clinical%20Services/journalclub/sojc/95_96/apr96/itoi.pdf) and lectures (http://wings.buffalo.edu/eng/mae/courses/417-517/Orthopaedic%20Biomechanics/Lecture%203u.pdf) on the breaking strength of tendons, which tend to give values of around 50-150 MPa. That's stronger than skin (27 MPa (http://www.ircobi.org/downloads/irc12/pdf_files/59.pdf)) but weaker than bone (120 MPa (http://www.robmech.co.za/proceed/ROBMECH2011_Unene%20N.%20MAnganyi_Biological%20considerations%20in%20the%20structural%20design%20of%20smart%20prosthetics.pdf)). However, to figure out the overall strength of the arm, we need to tally up all the tendons, muscles, and tissues in the wrist, arm, and shoulder, their cross-sectional area, and figure out which parts would be put under strain in what order. Instead, it might be easier to consider people who try to pull off this maneuver in real life: Gymnasts. A gymnast on the uneven parallel bars pushes the human body to its limits while performing maneuvers very similar to Rex's flagpole stunt.[3]In some ways, at least. A 2009 study (http://www.jbiomech.com/article/S0021-9290(09)00609-5/fulltext) used 3D motion capture to measure the forces involved in an elite gymnast's routine. They found that the athlete's hands exerted a force of over 3 kN on the bar at the bottom of a swing. In other words, the gymnast was briefly supporting almost 700 lbs of weight. Let's be generous and assume that Rex is even better than the elite gymnast in the study. (After all, the gymnast has to worry about long-term injury, while Rex's concerns are a lot more short-term). Suppose Rex's arms can handle a swing force of over 10 kN, three times more than the gymnast (and twice as much as these (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1JBx2Mm9e8) guys (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJYOs5VFjwk)!). How will he do? Let's see how much force Rex needs to withstand. The "tallest building in town" here in Boston is the 240-meter-tall Hancock Tower (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Tower); if he jumped off the top, he'd be going nearly 100 mph by the time he was halfway down. At that speed, the force on his arms (speed squared over the radius of his turn[4]Which is effectively somewhere between 1 and 2 meters here.) would be around ... 100 kN (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=100+lbs+*+(100+mph)%5E2+%2F+(1.5+meters)). [Image: image] Really, the numbers are just telling us what common sense told us from the start: You can't grab hold of something while going 100 mph, much less swing around it. If you want get a more vivid intuitive sense of the forces involved, consider this: In 2006, GQ put baseball star Albert Pujols in a lab and measured his swing. They clocked the speed of his bat at 87 mph, similar to the speed of the flagpole relative to our falling person. So if you want to pull off Rex's stunt, first go find Albert Pujols, have him swing his bat as hard as you can ... and try to grab it. [Image: image] And remember: You're just trying to stop the momentum of a 31-ounce piece of wood. When you're falling past the flagpole, you're going to be catching your whole body, so it's going to be up to 100 times worse. Good luck! [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
This is a classic physics scenario, and the answer depends on the height of the fall, the position of the flagpole, and—critically—whether the person's arms could withstand the forces involved.

When a person falls from a rooftop and grabs a horizontal flagpole sticking out from the building below, their downward motion gets converted into rotational motion around the flagpole. If we assume the flagpole is rigid and the grip holds, the person's kinetic energy at the moment of the grab determines how high they can swing back up. By conservation of energy, if friction and grip slippage are ignored, they could swing up to approximately the same height from which they fell—meaning if the flagpole is, say, 3 meters below the roof, they could in principle swing back up to roof level on the other side of the pole.

However, the real problem is the forces on the arms at the bottom of the swing. When you fall and suddenly catch yourself, your body must decelerate from its falling velocity to zero vertical velocity almost instantaneously, then be redirected into a circular arc. The centripetal force required is F = mv²/r, where v is the falling speed at the moment of the catch and r is the length of the arms (roughly 0.7 m). For a fall of just 3 meters, v ≈ 7.7 m/s, giving a centripetal acceleration of about 85 m/s², or roughly 8.5 g's. Add the 1 g of gravity, and the arms must support nearly 10 times body weight—around 700 to 800 kg of force for an average adult. This is at the upper limit of what trained gymnasts can briefly tolerate; for an untrained person, the shoulders would likely dislocate and the grip would fail.

For longer falls, the situation rapidly becomes impossible. A fall from 10 meters produces speeds around 14 m/s, yielding forces exceeding 30 g's—well beyond what any human body can absorb through the arms. The person would either rip their arms off, tear their hands from the pole, or, more realistically, the sudden jolt would cause them to lose grip immediately and continue falling, perhaps now spinning.

There's also the issue of timing: grabbing a thin pole while falling at 8+ m/s requires reflexes and precision that exceed normal human ability. Even if you saw the pole coming, your hands would need to close around it in a fraction of a second with exactly the right grip strength.

So while the energy argument allows the swing back to the roof in principle, in practice this maneuver only works in cartoons and action movies. A real person attempting this from any significant height would suffer severe shoulder and arm injuries and almost certainly lose their grip before completing the swing.

edus.text: This is a classic physics scenario,
and the answer depends on the height of the fall, the position of the flagpole, and—critically—whether the person's arms could withstand the forces involved.
When a person falls from a rooftop and grabs a horizontal flagpole sticking out from the building below,
their downward motion gets converted into rotational motion around the flagpole.
If we assume the flagpole is rigid and the grip holds,
the person's kinetic energy at the moment of the grab determines how high they can swing back up.
By conservation of energy,
if friction and grip slippage are ignored,
they could swing up to approximately the same height from which they fell—
meaning if the flagpole is, say, 3 meters below the roof,
they could in principle swing back up to roof level on the other side of the pole.
However, the real problem is the forces on the arms at the bottom of the swing.
When you fall and suddenly catch yourself,
your body must decelerate from its falling velocity to zero vertical velocity almost instantaneously,
then be redirected into a circular arc.
The centripetal force required is F = mv²/r,
where v is the falling speed at the moment of the catch and r is the length of the arms (roughly 0.7 m).
For a fall of just 3 meters, v ≈ 7.7 m/s,
giving a centripetal acceleration of about 85 m/s², or roughly 8.5 g's.
Add the 1 g of gravity,
and the arms must support nearly 10 times body weight—
around 700 to 800 kg of force for an average adult.
This is at the upper limit of what trained gymnasts can briefly tolerate;
for an untrained person, the shoulders would likely dislocate and the grip would fail.
For longer falls, the situation rapidly becomes impossible.
A fall from 10 meters produces speeds around 14 m/s,
yielding forces exceeding 30 g's—
well beyond what any human body can absorb through the arms.
The person would either rip their arms off, tear their hands from the pole, or, more realistically, the sudden jolt would cause them to lose grip immediately and continue falling,
perhaps now spinning.
There's also the issue of timing:
grabbing a thin pole while falling at 8+ m/s requires reflexes and precision that exceed normal human ability.
Even if you saw the pole coming,
your hands would need to close around it in a fraction of a second
with exactly the right grip strength.
So while the energy argument allows the swing back to the roof in principle,
in practice this maneuver only works in cartoons and action movies.
A real person attempting this from any significant height would suffer severe shoulder and arm injuries
and almost certainly lose their grip before completing the swing.

items.question: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?
human_answers: This isn't really relevant, but I have to ask: Is there a reason you specifically wanted your corpse to be naked? Just making things extra weird for the technicians loading up the capsule and/or throwing you out of the airlock? [Image: image] If you tried this, the first thing that would happen to your corpse would be that it would dry out. This would probably start before you made it to space; the dry, climate-controlled air in the pre-launch waiting area would help draw moisture from your body. In the Manual of Forensic Taphonomy, Franklin Damann and David Carter outline the process of human decomposition. According to them, it takes a lot of effort to keep corpses from drying out during the embalming process.[1]The citation they give for that fact is "(C. A. Wacker, pers. comm.)," which I like to think means it was shared in a conversation that totally broke up the dinner party they were both at. In extremely dry environments like the Atacama Desert in Chile, "spontaneous mummification" can occur—and space is even drier than Chile.[2]The space tourism industry has not adopted this as a slogan. Also, "Chile: Not as Dry as Space!" was probably nixed by the Chilean tourism board. Once your body made it to space, this process would ramp up quickly. Most of the "ecology" responsible for decomposing your corpse would be killed off quickly by the drying process (along with the lack of oxygen, temperature swings, and solar radiation levels), so your body wouldn't decay very much. Instead, you'd become a freeze-dried mummy, after losing about 80% of your body weight in water.[3]This is how much liquid you can remove from fresh animal tissue, according to lab experiments reported in Arthur C. Aufderheide's book The Scientific Study of Mummies. That makes sense; after all, according to that commonly-repeated piece of trivia, human bodies are around 70% water. Or is it 65%? Or 80%? The exact number is a little vague, and seems to depend on who you ask. In a footnote in her wonderful book, Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers, writer Mary Roach mentioned that she had methodically Googled the phrase "human body is <X> percent water", for X from 0 to 100. She reported a wide range of claims, including several pages asserting that we're 98% water. It's really gratifying to know I'm not the only person who spends a lot of time carefully cataloging weird stuff like that. What happens next depends on exactly where in space you are. If you're in an orbit that passes near the Earth, your orbit will quickly decay, and before long you'll re-enter the atmosphere and burn up. If you're in a slightly higher orbit, you'll last longer, but you'd also be in the zone where space debris (http://commons.erau.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=stm) was thickest. Impacts with small bits of debris would start to leave pits and scars on your surface; they would often find these on Space Shuttle windows after a flight. Eventually, probably after a few decades, you'd probably have a violent collision with something. Higher orbits are safer. If you were some distance away from the Earth, near where geosynchronous satellites orbit, there would be less debris to run into. Furthermore, for large, dense objects, orbits out there are stable (http://www.readcube.com/articles/10.1029%2F92JE00032?show_checkout=1) for a very long time. You could spend centuries drifting among TV broadcast satellites. [Image: image] If you wanted to last even longer, you could launch yourself away from Earth completely, finding a quiet and stable orbit somewhere in interplanetary space. There, over the course of millennia, you'd be slowly baked by the Sun's radiation and pitted and powdered by micrometeorites. But if your goal is to weird out future space travelers, that might not be the best plan. Space is big; if someone randomly stumbles on your corpse, it suggests that there must be a lot of people zipping around the solar system. And if space travel has become that common, there will be lots of corpses floating around;[4]Weird that "lots of corpses floating around" is somehow an optimistic prediction about the future of space travel. discovering yours will be more archaeologically exciting than anything. You'll be stuck in a lab or museum somewhere and contribute to someone's research paper—a bland end to your exciting prank. Unless, of course, you happen to be found by the only people in space even weirder than you. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我经常开玩笑说我希望将我的遗体送入轨道。不是“撒我的骨灰”的意思，而是“把我赤裸的尸体扔出气闸”的意思。老实说，我的主要动机是让遥远的未来的某人感到困惑，但这是一个有趣的科学问题：在几年、几十年或几个世纪的过程中，我在轨道上的身体会发生什么？

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately explains the body's early physical and biological changes in orbit, especially dehydration, freezing/thermal cycling, oxygen loss, radiation, and suppression of normal decomposition.
criteria.1-2: Claims ordinary Earth-like rotting, instant explosion, or other false dramatic effects with little mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some vacuum or freezing effects but misses dehydration/mummification or misstates decomposition substantially.
criteria.5-6: Describes drying/freezing and reduced decay, with some correct causes but limited detail or minor misconceptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains rapid desiccation/freeze-drying, microbial shutdown, oxygen absence, temperature extremes, and radiation effects.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced, mechanistic account of mummification-like preservation, water loss, tissue changes, and why normal decomposition largely stops.

criteria.name: Orbit-dependent long-term fate
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes different orbital regimes and traces how altitude and environment affect the corpse over time.
criteria.1-2: Gives one fixed outcome for all orbits, ignoring altitude, drag, and orbital stability.
criteria.3-4: Vaguely says it may fall or drift forever but does not connect outcomes to orbital conditions.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes low orbit decay versus higher orbit persistence, but with weak timing or incomplete distinctions.
criteria.7-8: Explains low-Earth reentry, longer survival in higher orbits, debris-rich regions, and more stable high/geosynchronous orbits.
criteria.9-10: Accurately compares LEO, higher Earth orbit, GEO-like regions, and escape/interplanetary trajectories with plausible timescales and causal drivers.

criteria.name: External space environment impacts over decades to millennia
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects from debris, micrometeorites, solar radiation, thermal stress, and possible atmospheric reentry.
criteria.1-2: Omits long-term environmental interactions or invents implausible effects unrelated to orbit.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one long-term hazard, such as burning up or radiation, without explaining cumulative effects.
criteria.5-6: Covers several hazards but treats them shallowly or with unclear sequencing.
criteria.7-8: Connects debris pitting, micrometeorite erosion, radiation damage, heating/cooling cycles, and reentry where applicable.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent long-range degradation pathway from initial preservation to eventual collision, erosion, reentry, or prolonged drifting depending on location.

criteria.name: Causal chain coherence and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent cause-effect chain under the counterfactual premise of a human body left in orbit.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, such as simultaneous rapid decay and permanent perfect preservation, or impossible orbital behavior.
criteria.3-4: Has a recognizable chain but frequent inconsistencies or unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, though some steps are underexplained or mildly contradictory.
criteria.7-8: Sequences events logically from exposure to preservation to orbital/environmental fate with few inconsistencies.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a tightly reasoned, physically consistent chain across immediate, medium-term, and long-term consequences.

criteria.name: Uncertainty, assumptions, and plausibility calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain details such as exact orbit, body condition, clothing/container status, timescales, and probability of collisions.
criteria.1-2: Presents precise but unsupported claims or ignores critical assumptions entirely.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty superficially while still overcommitting to specific outcomes.
criteria.5-6: States some assumptions and gives broadly plausible but imprecise estimates.
criteria.7-8: Clearly conditions conclusions on orbit, exposure, and timescale, using cautious probability language.
criteria.9-10: Expertly calibrates uncertainty, avoids false precision, and separates robust mechanisms from scenario-dependent outcomes.

items.model_answer:
When a human body is left in orbit, several processes occur, though they differ significantly from decomposition on Earth:

**Immediate effects:**
The body would undergo rapid decompression if exposed to vacuum without a spacesuit. Fluids would vaporize, gases would expand, and the body would swell. However, contrary to popular depiction, the body wouldn't explode—skin is strong enough to contain internal pressure.

**Preservation through mummification:**
In the vacuum of space, there's no oxygen, moisture, or microorganisms—the primary agents of decomposition on Earth. Instead, the body would undergo a form of freeze-drying or mummification. Water would sublimate directly from solid to gas, gradually desiccating the tissues.

**Temperature effects:**
In sunlight, the body could heat to around 120°C (250°F). In shadow, it would cool to approximately -100°C (-150°F). This cycling would continue with each orbit, though the lack of atmosphere means heat transfer occurs only through radiation, making the process relatively slow.

**Long-term fate:**
The mummified remains would persist for an extremely long time—potentially millions of years if in a stable orbit far from Earth. Eventually, the orbit would decay due to residual atmospheric drag (if in low Earth orbit) or perturbations from gravitational forces, causing the body to either re-enter Earth's atmosphere and burn up, or drift into deep space.

**Radiation exposure:**
Without Earth's protective atmosphere and magnetosphere, the body would be exposed to cosmic radiation and solar radiation, which would gradually break down organic molecules over extended periods.

The body would essentially become a preserved, mummified artifact rather than decomposing in the traditional sense.

items.question: What If You Dug Straight Down at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: This question is the reverse of question #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/), which asked how you'd die if you rose steadily at a foot per second. Digging at the same rate would kill you more quickly. [Image: image] After you get through the surface layers,[1]See question #132 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/132/) for more on that. temperatures rise pretty steadily as you go deeper, a trend that continues all the way to the core. In some areas, where the hot magma[2](Lava (http://xkcd.com/1405/).) is closer to the surface, the ground gets hotter more quickly. The Southern Methodist University Geothermal Lab has produced some superb maps (http://www.smu.edu/Dedman/Academics/Programs/GeothermalLab/DataMaps/TemperatureMaps) showing the temperature of deep rocks in different parts of the United States. If you look at the map of the 3.5 km layer (http://www.smu.edu/~/media/Site/Dedman/Academics/Programs/Geothermal%20Lab/Graphics/TemperatureMaps/SMU_2011_35kmTemperature.ashx?la=en), you see that at that depth, most of the US is colored greenish-yellow, representing temperatures somewhere around 100°C—with one glaring exception. In northwest Wyoming, there's a circle of ground colored bright red, where the rock is much hotter than normal. That circle is the Yellowstone supervolcano (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera). [Image: image] The SMU maps show that even if you avoided digging in Yellowstone, you'd quickly encounter temperatures too hot for an unprotected human. The ground typically gets hotter at an average of about 35°C per kilometer, so at a rate of a foot per second, you'd encounter lethal heat within an hour or two. But wait a moment. Let's say your hole is about a meter wide. At the rate you're digging, you have to remove roughly half a ton of material every second. No human would be capable of lifting that first foot of material out of the hole so quickly, and it only gets worse after that. After a minute of digging, you'd be 60 feet down, and would have to lift all that rock and dirt a huge distance vertically to get it out of the hole. The power required to do that lifting—just after the first minute—would be roughly 150 horsepower. [Image: image] Even if you're not doing the lifting yourself, the way your question is worded makes it pretty clear that you are in this hole. Whatever process you're using is going to require huge amounts of energy to lift all that rock, and that energy is inevitably going to result in the hole being heated somehow. Even if the layer you're digging through wasn't hot when you started, it will be. What if we assume you're protected against the heat from the ground (and the digging mechanism)? Well, in that case, the pressure would become a problem. As you go deeper, air pressure increases. Below about 5 km, the pressure is high enough that oxygen (http://www.scuba-doc.com/oxygentox.html) becomes toxic (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LOZuxwVk7TU). So what if you're protected against the heat, pressure, and the digging process? Well, at that point, we've redefined the rules so much that I'm not sure it makes sense to try to calculate an answer. The question—"what would kill you if you kept digging downward"—has left the realm of physics and become fantasy. Which, come to think of it, makes the answer perfectly clear. [Image: image]

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the scenario as a person or process descending straight downward at one foot per second and uses appropriate order-of-magnitude quantities for depth, time, tunnel size, and material removal.

criteria.9-10: Precisely grounds the scenario with consistent rate, depth, time, shaft-size, and mass-flow reasoning while keeping estimates appropriately approximate.

criteria.name: Excavation mechanics and energy consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the immediate practical problem that digging a human-sized vertical hole at one foot per second requires removing enormous amounts of rock and lifting it increasingly far, demanding extreme power and producing heat.
criteria.1-2: Does not mention spoil removal, mechanical work, or the impossibility of digging at the required rate.
criteria.3-4: States that digging would be hard or impossible but gives no mechanism or scale.
criteria.5-6: Identifies large material removal as a major barrier but only roughly explains lifting or power demands.
criteria.7-8: Explains that hundreds of kilograms per second may need removal and that lifting spoil from increasing depth requires rapidly growing power.
criteria.9-10: Clearly develops the excavation chain: mass flow, vertical lifting distance, power on the order of many horsepower or more, machinery limits, and added heat in the shaft.

criteria.name: Thermal and geothermal hazard reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately explains that Earth’s temperature rises with depth and that lethal heat would arrive within hours or sooner depending on geology, with special cases such as volcanically active regions.
criteria.1-2: Ignores temperature or claims the interior remains survivable for a long time without justification.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heat vaguely but gives no depth, timing, or geothermal mechanism.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes geothermal heating and likely lethal temperatures within kilometers but with limited quantitative support.
criteria.7-8: Uses a plausible geothermal gradient, such as tens of degrees Celsius per kilometer, to estimate lethal heat within about one to a few hours.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects descent rate, geothermal gradient, local variation, and machine-generated heat to show heat is one of the earliest fatal mechanisms.

criteria.name: Pressure, atmosphere, and human survivability mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of deeper downstream hazards beyond heat, especially increasing air pressure, oxygen toxicity, ventilation limits, structural instability, and the need for extraordinary protection.
criteria.1-2: Discusses only generic death or fantasy outcomes with no physiological or environmental mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions suffocation or pressure in vague terms but with major inaccuracies.
criteria.5-6: Identifies at least one deeper hazard such as air pressure, oxygen toxicity, ventilation, or cave-in risk but lacks a connected explanation.
criteria.7-8: Explains that pressure rises with depth and can make ordinary air dangerous, while also noting ventilation and shaft stability concerns.
criteria.9-10: Integrates pressure, oxygen toxicity at multi-kilometer depths, heat, ventilation, and structural hazards into a coherent survivability analysis.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer presents a plausible causal sequence from initial digging to failure or death, distinguishes dominant hazards by timescale, states assumptions, and avoids self-contradictory or overconfident claims.
criteria.1-2: Gives an incoherent chain with contradictions, impossible claims, or unsupported certainty.
criteria.3-4: Provides a loose list of hazards but no clear ordering, assumptions, or causal dependencies.
criteria.5-6: Has a mostly plausible sequence but misses key caveats or treats speculative assumptions as certain.
criteria.7-8: Orders hazards sensibly, notes that changing protections changes the answer, and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a tightly reasoned counterfactual chain, calibrates uncertainty and local variation, explains when the scenario leaves ordinary physics for fantasy, and maintains internal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If you somehow managed to dig straight down at a steady one foot per second, your journey would be both surprisingly fast and astonishingly brutal. Let's trace what would happen.

In the first minute, you'd descend 60 feet, already past the foundations of most buildings and into the realm of basements, sewers, and subway tunnels. Within about two minutes, you'd be deeper than the deepest subway systems. After roughly 15 minutes, you'd pass the depth of the deepest mines on Earth, like South Africa's Mponeng gold mine (about 13,000 feet, or 4 km). Already, the temperature around you would be around 60°C (140°F), hot enough to be lethal without cooling.

After about an hour, you'd be roughly 3,600 feet… wait, let me recompute: at one foot per second, an hour gives you 3,600 feet, only about 1.1 km. So actually the deepest mine takes about 3.6 hours to reach. By around 10 hours, you'd be 36,000 feet down—deeper than the Mariana Trench is below sea level, and roughly the depth of the deepest borehole ever drilled (the Kola Superdeep Borehole, about 40,230 feet). At that depth, the rock is roughly 180°C (356°F), and the pressure would crush any unreinforced cavity shut.

Continuing down, after about a day and a half (around 130,000 feet, or 40 km), you'd punch through the Earth's crust into the mantle. Here things become physically absurd: temperatures climb past 1,000°C, and the rock behaves as a slow-flowing plastic solid. Without magical protection, you'd be vaporized.

If we assume you're invincible and the hole stays open, you'd keep going. The mantle is about 2,900 km thick. At one foot per second (roughly 0.3 m/s), crossing it takes about 110 days. Temperatures rise to around 3,700°C at the core-mantle boundary.

Then comes the outer core—liquid iron and nickel at around 4,000–5,000°C. About 2,300 km thick, it would take you another 88 days to traverse. The inner core, solid iron under crushing pressure, is about 1,200 km in radius and would take roughly 46 more days.

In total, reaching Earth's center (about 6,371 km down) at one foot per second would take roughly 243 days, or about eight months. Reaching the other side would take about 16 months.

Along the way, gravity would gradually weaken. At the center, you'd be weightless, pulled equally in all directions. If you kept going past the center, "down" would reverse—you'd suddenly be digging "up" toward the opposite surface, which would be psychologically disorienting even for an invincible digger.

The real answer, of course, is that no one and nothing could survive this. The heat alone would kill you within hours, the pressure within a day, and the molten iron of the core is not something flesh, steel, or any known material can withstand. But as a thought experiment, it's a reminder that Earth is both smaller than it feels—traversable in under two years at a slow walking pace—and far more hostile beneath our feet than the thin, cool crust suggests.
