edus.text: If you somehow managed to dig straight down at a steady one foot per second,
your journey would be both surprisingly fast and astonishingly brutal.
Let's trace what would happen.
In the first minute, you'd descend 60 feet,
already past the foundations of most buildings and into the realm of basements, sewers, and subway tunnels.
Within about two minutes, you'd be deeper than the deepest subway systems.
After roughly 15 minutes, you'd pass the depth of the deepest mines on Earth,
like South Africa's Mponeng gold mine (about 13,000 feet, or 4 km).
Already, the temperature around you would be around 60°C (140°F),
hot enough to be lethal without cooling.
After about an hour, you'd be roughly 3,600 feet…
wait, let me recompute:
at one foot per second, an hour gives you 3,600 feet,
only about 1.1 km.
So actually the deepest mine takes about 3.6 hours to reach.
By around 10 hours, you'd be 36,000 feet down—
deeper than the Mariana Trench is below sea level,
and roughly the depth of the deepest borehole ever drilled
(the Kola Superdeep Borehole, about 40,230 feet).
At that depth, the rock is roughly 180°C (356°F),
and the pressure would crush any unreinforced cavity shut.
Continuing down, after about a day and a half (around 130,000 feet, or 40 km),
you'd punch through the Earth's crust into the mantle.
Here things become physically absurd:
temperatures climb past 1,000°C,
and the rock behaves as a slow-flowing plastic solid.
Without magical protection, you'd be vaporized.
If we assume you're invincible and the hole stays open,
you'd keep going.
The mantle is about 2,900 km thick.
At one foot per second (roughly 0.3 m/s),
crossing it takes about 110 days.
Temperatures rise to around 3,700°C at the core-mantle boundary.
Then comes the outer core—
liquid iron and nickel at around 4,000–5,000°C.
About 2,300 km thick,
it would take you another 88 days to traverse.
The inner core,
solid iron under crushing pressure,
is about 1,200 km in radius
and would take roughly 46 more days.
In total, reaching Earth's center (about 6,371 km down) at one foot per second would take roughly 243 days, or about eight months.
Reaching the other side would take about 16 months.
Along the way, gravity would gradually weaken.
At the center, you'd be weightless,
pulled equally in all directions.
If you kept going past the center,
"down" would reverse—
you'd suddenly be digging "up" toward the opposite surface,
which would be psychologically disorienting even for an invincible digger.
The real answer, of course, is that no one and nothing could survive this.
The heat alone would kill you within hours,
the pressure within a day,
and the molten iron of the core is not something flesh, steel, or any known material can withstand.
But as a thought experiment,
it's a reminder that Earth is both smaller than it feels—
traversable in under two years at a slow walking pace—
and far more hostile beneath our feet than the thin, cool crust suggests.

items.question: What If You Dropped a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: Nope! Jupiter's pressure, density, and temperature curves are different from ours. At the point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the density is high enough for a submarine to float, the pressure is high enough to crush the submarine,[1]Which makes it more dense. and the temperature is high enough to melt it.[2]Which makes it harder to drive. [Image: image] But there's another problem: Jupiter is a gas giant, but submarines—as you can figure out from etymology—go under water. [Image: image] Air and water are different. This seems straightforward enough, but they're also the same in a lot of ways. They're both "fluids," and some of the same rules apply to each. In some sense, when you look up at the sky (http://xkcd.com/1556/), you're looking up from the bottom of a deep sea of air. Things float when they're less dense than the fluid around them. This works the same for balloons in air and boats in water. The late Terry Pratchett wrote a truly beautiful passage about this, in the prologue to his book Going Postal. He says that since water is in many respects a wetter form of air,[3]Sounds reasonable enough to me. as ships sink, eventually they reach a point where the water was too dense to sink any further. This layer forms an underwater surface on which shipwrecks collect, drifting around beneath the waves but far above the sea floor:It’s calm there. Dead calm.Some stricken ships have rigging; some even have sails. Many still have crew, tangled in the rigging or lashed to the wheel.But the voyages still continue, aimlessly, with no harbour in sight, because there are currents under the ocean and so the dead ships with their skeleton crews sail on around the world, over sunken cities and between drowned mountains, until rot and shipworms eat them away and they disintegrate.Sometimes an anchor drops, all the way to the dark, cold calmness of the abyssal plain, and disturbs the stillness of centuries by throwing up a cloud of silt. I love that passage. It's also completely wrong. Ships sink all the way to the bottom. (Sir Terry knew this, as the rest of the passage makes clear, but he's describing how ships work on Discworld, not Earth.) Air follows the ideal gas law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law). The more pressure you put on it, the smaller (and denser) it gets. Water, on the other hand, is pretty much incompressible. When you dive into the ocean, the pressure increases as you go deeper (rising by one atmosphere every 10 meters or so) but the water's density barely changes all the way down to the sea floor. Buoyancy depends on density, not pressure. There's a point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the pressure is equal to a little more than an Earth atmosphere—which is the pressure a submarine is used to—but the air there is barely a tenth as dense as ours. A submarine in that layer would fall even faster than it would in the air on Earth. [Image: image] To reach a depth where it could "float" in Jupiter, the submarine would have to go halfway to the center of the planet, where the intense pressure turns the air into a metallic soup (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_hydrogen) that's hotter than the surface of the Sun. The pressure there would be so high that not only would the submarine be crushed, the substances that make it up would probably be converted into new and exciting forms. It's hard to create those kinds of conditions in a lab, so we don't know a lot about how materials behave with that much pressure pushing down on them. [Image: image] In the sea, on the other hand, the density of the fluid stays relatively constant. That means the submarine can find its appropriate pressure range and float there. In other words, submarines only work because water doesn't follow the ideal gas law. But there's one more twist: Water sort of does obey the ideal gas law. The equations governing water under normal pressure are similar to (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.0534.pdf) the equation for a gas under about twenty thousand atmospheres of pressure. In a sense, this is why water seems incompressible to us—it behaves as if it's already compressed so much that an extra atmosphere or two hardly makes a difference. So, in some ways, water and air are more similar than they seem, but in the ways that matter for a submarine, they really are different. Which, of course, brings us back to why it's called a submarine—it operates under a "mare". A vehicle designed to operate beneath a sea of air would be called a subaerine.[5]The "gas" in "gas giant" is from the Greek word for void (χάος, kháos), so maybe a vessel (σκάφη, skáphē) that travels through a gas giant's atmosphere would be a khaoskaphe. Which, come to think of it, is a perfectly good description of a car. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence and Endpoint Plausibility

items.model_answer:
Dropping a submarine into Jupiter would be a spectacularly violent affair, and the vessel would never reach anything resembling a stable "ocean" to explore. Here's what would happen as it fell.

Jupiter has no solid surface. Instead, it's a giant ball of hydrogen and helium that gradually transitions from gas to supercritical fluid to liquid metallic hydrogen as you go deeper. So the submarine would simply fall into the atmosphere rather than splashing down.

In the upper atmosphere, the submarine would be hit by Jupiter's brutal winds, which can exceed 400 mph in jet streams, and tossed through ammonia ice clouds at temperatures around -145°C (-234°F). Jupiter's gravity is about 2.5 times Earth's, so the sub would accelerate downward rapidly. Within minutes it would plunge into thicker layers of ammonium hydrosulfide and water clouds, where it might encounter lightning storms vastly more powerful than anything on Earth.

As the submarine descended further, the pressure would skyrocket. A typical military submarine is built to withstand maybe 50–80 atmospheres of pressure. On Jupiter, you reach that pressure only a few hundred kilometers down, well within what's still considered the atmosphere. The hull would implode, crushing the submarine like a soda can. The Galileo probe, which was specifically engineered for this descent in 1995, survived only to about 22 atmospheres (about 150 km below the cloud tops) before being destroyed.

If somehow you had an indestructible submarine, the journey would only get stranger. About 5,000 km down, hydrogen becomes a supercritical fluid—neither gas nor liquid—at temperatures of thousands of degrees. Around 20,000 km down, hydrogen transitions into liquid metallic hydrogen, an electrically conductive exotic state of matter at pressures of millions of atmospheres and temperatures hotter than the surface of the Sun. The submarine, even if it could resist crushing, would be vaporized by the heat long before reaching this depth.

So in short: the submarine would be torn apart by winds, frozen, struck by lightning, then crushed by pressure within minutes, and any imagined deeper journey would end in melting and vaporization. Jupiter is not a place that rewards naval engineering.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Ride a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: We don't know! We've only flown spacecraft into a gas planet's atmosphere twice (both Jupiter). One had no cameras, and one went in at night (and was being disposed of, so wasn't taking pictures anyway). If you took a submarine to Jupiter, it would burn up. Jupiter has a deep gravity well; after falling down toward it from space, you're going very fast. There's no easy way to shed that speed other than slamming into the atmosphere and letting it slow you down, but the entry is about four times faster than the Space Shuttle or Apollo Earth reentries. Only the Galileo probe has survived a Jupiter atmospheric entry. [Image: image] The Galileo probe survived by being a bullet with a big heat shield, and several inches of the shield were burned away before it finished slowing down and started falling vertically by parachute. The probe only sent back about half a megabyte of data to the Galileo orbiter, and had no camera, so we don't know what it saw. We could, I guess, try to do the same thing with a submarine—by mounting a giant heat shield on the front—but it would probably qualify as the most Kerbal (https://youtu.be/vwrLR2kv5KA?t=1119) vehicle ever built. [Image: image] If our submarine survived, what would we see?[1]I mean, submarines don't usually have a lot of windows, but we at least have a periscope, right? The best pictures we have of Jupiter's atmosphere are probably these carefully processed mosaics (http://www.planetary.org/blogs/emily-lakdawalla/2010/2644.html) of the Great Red Spot, but they're still taken from very far away. At those resolutions, a huge Earth thunderstorm would appear as roughly one pixel. Trying to figure out what Jupiter's clouds would look like from those pictures is like using this (http://visibleearth.nasa.gov/view.php?id=78314) to reconstruct these (http://stormandsky.smugmug.com/Thumbnail-Galleries). By combining the pictures with other science data, we've been able to put together a pretty good idea of what Jupiter's atmosphere is like, but there are some pretty big questions still unanswered which make it hard to be too confident about what it would actually look like. For example, you know the Great Red Spot? We don't know what all that red stuff is. [Image: image] Author Michael Carroll has done a lot of thinking about planetary atmospheres, and his book Drifting on Alien Winds (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160) vividly describes of what it would be like to descend through Jupiter's clouds. He was also kind enough to answer some of my questions about Jupiter. Here's a rough sketch of what you'd see as you descended through the clouds; for more, definitely check out his book (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160). [Image: image] Jupiter's upper atmosphere (the part we would see before we died (http://what-if.xkcd.com/138/)) has three main layers—an upper layer of haze and ammonia clouds, similar to cirrostratus (https://www.google.com/search?q=cirrostratus&tbm=isch) clouds on Earth. Below that is a thick, reddish-brown ammonium hydrosulfide cloud layer. The lowest layer consists of white water clouds, which occasionally rise into towering thunderstorms that occasionally push through the middle layer. Between these cloud layers, the air is probably pretty clear. At those levels, it would be less dense than the air on Earth, so you could see a long way. Thanks to Rayleigh scattering (https://xkcd.com/1145/), the sky would be blue, and objects far off in the distance would fade to blue just like they do on Earth (http://thehelpfulartteacher.blogspot.com/2010/11/landscapes-continuedatmospheric.html). But since Jupiter is so huge, we might not see the clouds disappear over the horizon; the towers might just fade off into the distance. We don't really know how accurate these pictures are, though, until we send a camera to fly down into Jupiter's atmosphere and send pictures back. Juno, scheduled to reach Jupiter next year, carries a pretty nice camera (http://www.msss.com/all_projects/junocam.php),[2]Thank you to Emily Lakdawalla for her helpful background about various spacecraft cameras, including her many thorough spreadsheets. which should give us slightly better-resolution pictures, but it still won't really give us a sense of what the cloud decks look like from within them. For that, we need to send in a probe with a camera—and there's nothing like that on the horizon. There's certainly more science value in visiting Europa than in satisfying our curiosity about the Jovian sky. But with interplanetary cubesats (http://www.nasa.gov/directorates/spacetech/niac/staehle_interplanetary_cubesats.html) soon to make their debut, who knows—maybe someone out there will put together a camera, heat shield, and parachute, and hitch a ride on the next outer planets mission. And then, finally, we'll get to look at Jupiter's clouds from both sides (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v9j_j-cUwKc). [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Riding a submarine into Jupiter would be an extraordinarily hostile and ultimately fatal journey, quite different from underwater exploration on Earth.

**Initial descent through the atmosphere:**
As you enter Jupiter's upper atmosphere, you'd encounter hydrogen and helium gas at extremely high velocities due to Jupiter's rapid rotation and powerful winds exceeding 400 mph. The "submarine" would experience intense buffeting and heating from atmospheric friction. Unlike Earth's oceans where pressure increases gradually, Jupiter's atmospheric pressure rises dramatically with depth.

**The crushing pressure problem:**
Jupiter has no solid surface or liquid ocean in the traditional sense. As you descend, the hydrogen atmosphere becomes progressively denser and hotter. Around 1,000 kilometers down, pressures reach about 1 million times Earth's atmospheric pressure, and temperatures soar to thousands of degrees. At these conditions, hydrogen transitions into a liquid metallic state—electrically conductive and nothing like water. No submarine hull could withstand these pressures; even the strongest materials would be crushed and vaporized long before reaching this depth.

**Radiation and magnetic fields:**
Jupiter's intense magnetic field and radiation belts would bombard your craft with lethal radiation doses within minutes, frying any electronics and biological matter.

**The experience:**
If somehow protected, you'd see the sky darken from pale tan to deep red and eventually black as you descend. Lightning storms far more powerful than Earth's would flash around you. The "ocean" you'd eventually reach wouldn't be water but a strange, hot, metallic hydrogen fluid under unimaginable pressure, glowing from its own heat.

In reality, any vessel would be destroyed within the first few hundred kilometers of descent—compressed, melted, and torn apart by forces no engineering could overcome.

nodes.text: Riding a submarine into Jupiter would be an extraordinarily hostile and ultimately fatal journey,
quite different from underwater exploration on Earth.
As you enter Jupiter's upper atmosphere,
you'd encounter hydrogen and helium gas at extremely high velocities due to Jupiter's rapid rotation and powerful winds exceeding 400 mph.
The "submarine" would experience intense buffeting and heating from atmospheric friction.
Unlike Earth's oceans where pressure increases gradually,
Jupiter's atmospheric pressure rises dramatically with depth.
Jupiter has no solid surface or liquid ocean in the traditional sense.
As you descend,
the hydrogen atmosphere becomes progressively denser and hotter.
Around 1,000 kilometers down, pressures reach about 1 million times Earth's atmospheric pressure,
and temperatures soar to thousands of degrees.
At these conditions, hydrogen transitions into a liquid metallic state—electrically conductive and nothing like water.
No submarine hull could withstand these pressures;
even the strongest materials would be crushed and vaporized long before reaching this depth.
Jupiter's intense magnetic field and radiation belts would bombard your craft with lethal radiation doses within minutes,
frying any electronics and biological matter.
If somehow protected,
you'd see the sky darken from pale tan to deep red and eventually black as you descend.
Lightning storms far more powerful than Earth's would flash around you.
The "ocean" you'd eventually reach wouldn't be water but a strange, hot, metallic hydrogen fluid under unimaginable pressure,
glowing from its own heat.
In reality, any vessel would be destroyed within the first few hundred kilometers of descent—compressed, melted, and torn apart by forces no engineering could overcome.

items.question: What If Earth Were Made Entirely of Protons and the Moon of Electrons?
human_answers: This is, by far, the most destructive What-If scenario to date. You might imagine an electron Moon orbiting a proton Earth, sort of like a gigantic hydrogen atom. On one level, it makes a kind of sense; after all, electrons orbit protons, and moons orbit planets. In fact, a planetary model of the atom (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr_model) was briefly popular (although it turned out not to be very useful for understanding atoms.[1]This model was (mostly (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/81/2/10.1119/1.4769785)) obsolete by the 1920s, but lived on in an elaborate foam-and-pipe-cleaner diorama I made in 6th grade science class.) [Image: image] If you put two electrons together, they try to fly apart. Electrons are negatively charged, and the force of repulsion from this charge is about 20 orders of magnitude stronger than the force of gravity pulling them together. If you put 1052 electrons together—to build a Moon—they push each other apart really hard. In fact, they push each other apart so hard, each electron would be shoved away with an unbelievable amount of energy. It turns out that, for the proton Earth and electron Moon in Noah's scenario, the planetary model is even more wrong than usual. The Moon wouldn't orbit the Earth because they'd barely have a chance to influence each other;[2]I interpreted the question to mean that the Moon was replaced with a sphere of electrons the size and mass of the Moon, and ditto for the Earth. There are other interpretations, but practically speaking the end result is the same. the forces trying to blow each one apart would be far more powerful than any attractive force between the two. If we ignore general relativity for a moment—we'll come back to it—we can calculate that the energy from these electrons all pushing on each other would be enough to accelerate all of them outward at near the speed of light.[3]But not past it; we're ignoring general relativity, but not special relativity. Accelerating particles to those speeds isn't unusual; a desktop particle accelerator (http://www.amazon.com/s/?field-keywords=crt+monitor) can accelerate electrons to a reasonable fraction of the speed of light. But the electrons in Noah's Moon would each be carrying much, much more energy than those in a normal accelerator—orders of magnitude more than the Planck energy, which is itself many orders of magnitude larger than the energies we can reach in our largest accelerators. In other words, Noah's question takes us pretty far outside normal physics, into the highly theoretical realm of things like quantum gravity and string theory. So I contacted Dr. Cindy Keeler, a string theorist with the Niels Bohr Institute. I explained Noah's scenario, and she was kind enough to offer some thoughts. [Image: image] Dr. Keeler agreed that we shouldn't rely on any calculations that involve putting that much energy in each electron, since it's so far beyond what we're able to test in our accelerators. "I don't trust anything with energy per particle over the Planck scale. The most energy we've really observed is in cosmic rays; more than LHC by circa 106, I think, but still not close to the Planck energy. Being a string theorist, I'm tempted to say something stringy would happen—but the truth is we just don't know." Luckily, that's not the end of the story. Remember how we're ignoring general relativity? Well, this is one of the very, very rare situations where bringing in general relativity makes a problem easier to solve. [Image: image] There's a huge amount of potential energy in this scenario—the energy that we imagined would blast all these electrons apart. That energy warps space and time just like mass does.[4]If we let the energy blast the electrons apart at near the speed of light, we'd see that energy actually take the form of mass, as the electrons gained mass relativistically. That is, until something stringy happened. The amount of energy in our electron Moon, it turns out, is about equal to the total mass and energy of the entire visible universe. An entire universe worth of mass-energy—concentrated into the space of our (relatively small) Moon—would warp space-time so strongly that it would overpower even the repulsion of those 1052 electrons. Dr. Keeler's diagnosis: "Yup, black hole." But this is no an ordinary black hole; it's a black hole with a lot of electric charge.[5]The proton Earth, which would also be part of this black hole, would reduce the charge, but since an Earth-mass of protons has much less charge than a Moon-mass of electrons, it doesn't affect the result much. And for that, you need a different set of equations—rather than the standard Schwarzschild equations (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_radius), you need the Reissner–Nordström ones (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reissner%E2%80%93Nordstr%C3%B6m_metric). In a sense, the Reissner-Nordström equations compare the outward force of the charge to the inward pull of gravity. If the outward push from the charge is large enough, it's possible the event horizon surrounding the black hole can disappear completely. That would leave behind an infinitely-dense object (http://www.amazon.com/s/?url=search-alias%3Dindustrial&field-keywords=infinitely+dense+object) from which light can escape—a naked singularity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked_singularity). Once you have a naked singularity, physics starts breaking down in very big ways. Quantum mechanics and general relativity give absurd answers, and they're not even the same absurd answers. Some people have argued (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_censorship_hypothesis) that the laws of physics don't allow that kind of situation to arise. As Dr. Keeler put it, "Nobody likes a naked singularity." In the case of an electron Moon, the energy from all those electrons pushing on each other is so large that the gravitational pull wins, and our singularity would form a normal black hole. At least, "normal" in some sense; it would be a black hole as massive as the observable universe.[6]A black hole with the mass of the observable universe would have a radius of 13.8 billion light-years, and the universe is 13.8 billion years old, which has led some people to say "the Universe is a black hole!" (It's not (http://www.preposterousuniverse.com/blog/2010/04/28/the-universe-is-not-a-black-hole/).) Would this black hole cause the universe to collapse? Hard to say. The answer depends on what the deal with dark energy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy) is, and nobody knows what the deal with dark energy is. But for now, at least, nearby galaxies would be safe. Since the gravitational influence of the black hole can only expand outward at the speed of light, much of the universe around us would remain blissfully unaware of our ridiculous electron experiment. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If Earth were made entirely of protons and the Moon entirely of electrons, the consequences would be catastrophic on a scale that dwarfs almost any other "what if" scenario in physics. The reason is that the electrostatic (Coulomb) force between charged particles is roughly 10^36 times stronger than gravity, and you'd be replacing Earth's neutral matter with about 3.6 × 10^51 protons and the Moon's matter with a comparable number of electrons.

First, consider what happens to Earth itself. Every proton repels every other proton with enormous force. Earth's gravity, which currently holds it together, would be utterly negligible compared to this mutual repulsion. The planet would not merely fly apart—it would explode with energy vastly exceeding anything in astrophysics short of a supernova. A rough calculation of the electrostatic self-energy of a uniformly charged sphere the size of Earth, carrying ~5.4 × 10^32 coulombs of charge, gives something on the order of 10^48 joules. For comparison, the Sun radiates about 4 × 10^26 watts, so Earth's disassembly energy would equal millions of years of total solar output, released essentially instantaneously. The same fate awaits the Moon, whose electrons would repel one another just as fiercely.

Second, consider the Earth–Moon interaction. The two bodies carry opposite charges of roughly equal magnitude, so they attract. Plugging into Coulomb's law with a separation of about 384,000 km, the attractive force comes out to roughly 10^33 newtons—about 10^33 times stronger than the gravitational attraction that currently keeps the Moon in orbit. The Moon would not orbit; it would be yanked toward Earth at a substantial fraction of the speed of light. But of course neither body would survive long enough for that collision, because each is already blowing itself apart on a much shorter timescale.

Third, the surrounding universe would feel it too. A net charge of 5 × 10^32 C produces an electric field that, even at the distance of the Sun, would be astronomically strong, ionizing and accelerating everything in its path. Long before any of this matters, though, the protons and electrons released into space would recombine in a colossal burst of gamma rays as they form neutral hydrogen, releasing roughly 13.6 eV per recombination times ~10^51 particles—again on the order of 10^39 joules just from recombination, on top of the kinetic energy from the explosions.

In short, the scenario can't really play out as a stable "Earth and Moon" at all. The instant such a configuration existed, both bodies would explode with supernova-level violence, the debris would be hurled together and apart by titanic electric forces, and what remained would eventually recombine into a vast, hot cloud of hydrogen gas. It's a vivid illustration of why bulk matter in the universe is electrically neutral to extraordinary precision: even tiny charge imbalances on astronomical scales would produce forces that overwhelm gravity completely.

edus.text: If Earth were made entirely of protons and the Moon entirely of electrons,
the consequences would be catastrophic on a scale that dwarfs almost any other "what if" scenario in physics.
The reason is that the electrostatic (Coulomb) force between charged particles is roughly 10^36 times stronger than gravity,
and you'd be replacing Earth's neutral matter with about 3.6 × 10^51 protons and the Moon's matter with a comparable number of electrons.
First, consider what happens to Earth itself.
Every proton repels every other proton with enormous force.
Earth's gravity, which currently holds it together, would be utterly negligible compared to this mutual repulsion.
The planet would not merely fly apart—it would explode with energy vastly exceeding anything in astrophysics short of a supernova.
A rough calculation of the electrostatic self-energy of a uniformly charged sphere the size of Earth, carrying ~5.4 × 10^32 coulombs of charge, gives something on the order of 10^48 joules.
For comparison, the Sun radiates about 4 × 10^26 watts,
so Earth's disassembly energy would equal millions of years of total solar output, released essentially instantaneously.
The same fate awaits the Moon, whose electrons would repel one another just as fiercely.
Second, consider the Earth–Moon interaction.
The two bodies carry opposite charges of roughly equal magnitude,
so they attract.
Plugging into Coulomb's law with a separation of about 384,000 km, the attractive force comes out to roughly 10^33 newtons
—about 10^33 times stronger than the gravitational attraction that currently keeps the Moon in orbit.
The Moon would not orbit;
it would be yanked toward Earth at a substantial fraction of the speed of light.
But of course neither body would survive long enough for that collision,
because each is already blowing itself apart on a much shorter timescale.
Third, the surrounding universe would feel it too.
A net charge of 5 × 10^32 C produces an electric field that, even at the distance of the Sun, would be astronomically strong,
ionizing and accelerating everything in its path.
Long before any of this matters, though,
the protons and electrons released into space would recombine in a colossal burst of gamma rays as they form neutral hydrogen,
releasing roughly 13.6 eV per recombination times ~10^51 particles
—again on the order of 10^39 joules just from recombination, on top of the kinetic energy from the explosions.
In short, the scenario can't really play out as a stable "Earth and Moon" at all.
The instant such a configuration existed, both bodies would explode with supernova-level violence,
the debris would be hurled together and apart by titanic electric forces,
and what remained would eventually recombine into a vast, hot cloud of hydrogen gas.
It's a vivid illustration of why bulk matter in the universe is electrically neutral to extraordinary precision:
even tiny charge imbalances on astronomical scales would produce forces that overwhelm gravity completely.

items.question: What If All Sunlight Reaching Earth Were Bundled into a 1-Meter Beam?
human_answers: Here's the situation Max is describing: [Image: image] If you were standing in the path of the beam, you would obviously die pretty quickly. You wouldn't really die of anything, in the traditional sense. You would just stop being biology and start being physics. When the beam of light hit the atmosphere, it would heat a pocket of air to millions of degrees[1]Fahrenheit, Celsius, Rankine, or Kelvin—it doesn't really matter. in a fraction of a second. That air would turn to plasma and start dumping its heat as a flood of x-rays in all directions. Those x-rays would heat up the air around them, which would turn to plasma itself and start emitting infrared light. It would be like a hydrogen bomb going off, only much more violent. [Image: image] This radiation would vaporize everything in sight, turn the surrounding atmosphere to plasma, and start stripping away the Earth's surface. But let's imagine you were standing on the far side of the Earth. You're still definitely not going to make it—things don't turn out well for the Earth in this scenario—but what, exactly, would you die from? The Earth is big enough to protect people on the other side—at least for a little bit—from Max's sunbeam, and the seismic waves from the destruction would take a while to propogate through the planet. But the Earth isn't a perfect shield. Those wouldn't be what killed you. Instead, you would die from twilight. [Image: image] The sky is dark at night[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flunixin)] because the Sun is on the other side of the Earth.[citation needed (http://library.williams.edu/citing/game/)] But the night sky isn't always completely dark. There's a glow in the sky before sunrise and after sunset because, even with the Sun hidden, some of the light is bent around the surface by the atmosphere. If the sunbeam hit the Earth, x-rays, thermal radiation, and everything in between would flood into the atmosphere, so we need to learn a little about how different kinds of light interact with air. Normal light interacts with the atmosphere through Rayleigh scattering. You may have heard of Rayleigh scattering as the answer to "why is the sky blue." This is sort of true, but honestly, a better answer to this question might be "because air is blue." Sure, it appears blue for a bunch of physics reasons, but everything appears the color it is for a bunch of physics reasons.[2]When you ask, "Why is the statue of liberty green?" the answer is something like, "The outside of the statue is copper, so it used to be copper-colored. Over time, a layer of copper carbonate formed (through oxidation), and copper carbonate is green." You don't say "The statue is green because of frequency-specific absorption and scattering by surface molecules." When air heats up, the electrons are stripped away from their atoms, turning it to plasma. The ongoing flood of radiation from the beam has to pass through this plasma, so we need to know how transparent plasma is to different kinds of light. At this point, I'd like to mention the 1964 paper Opacity Calculations: Past and Future (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022407364900202), by Harris L. Mayer, which contains the single best opening paragraph to a physics paper I've ever seen:Initial steps for this symposium began a few billion years ago. As soon as the stars were formed, opacities became one of the basic subjects determining the structure of the physical world in which we live. And more recently with the development of nuclear weapons operating at temperatures of stellar interiors, opacities become as well one of the basic subjects determining the processes by which we may all die. Compared to air, the plasma is relatively transparent to x-rays. The x-rays would pass through the plasma, heating it through effects called Compton scattering (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton_scattering) and pair production (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanical_scattering_of_photon_and_nucleus), but would be stopped quickly when they reached the non-plasma air outside the bubble. However, the steady flow of x-rays from the growing pocket of superhot air closer to the beam would turn a steadily-growing bubble of air to plasma. The fresh plasma at the edge of the bubble would give off infrared radiation, which would head out toward the horizon (along with the infrared already on the way), heating whatever it finds there. [Image: image] This bubble of heat and light would wrap around the Earth, heating the air and land as it went. As the air heated up, the scattering and emission from the plasma would cause the effects to propogate farther and farther around the horizon. Furthermore, the atmosphere around the beam's contact point would be blasted into space, where it would reflect the light back down around the horizon. Exactly how quickly the radiation makes it around the Earth depends on many details of atmospheric scattering, but if the Moon happened to be half-full at the time, it might not even matter. When Max's device kicked in, the Moon would go out, since the sunlight illuminating it would be captured and funneled into a beam. Slightly after the beam made contact with the atmosphere, the quarter moon would blink out. [Image: image] When the beam from Max's device hit the Earth's atmosphere, the light from the contact point would illuminate the Moon. Depending on the Moon's position and where you were on the Earth, this reflected moonlight alone could be enough to burn you to death ... [Image: image] ... just as the twilight wrapped around the planet, bringing on one final sunrise.[3]Here's an image which is great for annoying a few specific groups of people: [Image: image] [Image: image] There's one thing that might prevent the Earth's total destruction. Can Max's mechanism actually track a target? If not, the Earth could be saved by its own orbital motion. If the beam was restricted to aiming at a fixed point in the sky, it would only take the Earth about three minutes to move out of the way. Everyone on the surface would still be cooked, and much of the atmosphere and surface would be lost, but the bulk of the Earth's mass would probably remain as a charred husk. The Sun's death ray would continue out into space. Years later, if it reached another planetary system, it would be too spread out to vaporize anything outright, but it would likely be bright enough to heat up the surfaces of the planets. [Image: image] Max's scenario may have doomed Earth, but if it's any consolation, we wouldn't necessarily die alone.

items.model_answer:
# What If All Sunlight Reaching Earth Were Bundled into a 1-Meter Beam?

To explore this, let's start with the actual numbers. Earth intercepts sunlight across its cross-sectional area, a disk with radius ~6,371 km, giving an area of roughly 1.28 × 10¹⁴ m². The solar constant at Earth's distance is about 1,361 W/m², so Earth intercepts a total power of approximately **1.74 × 10¹⁷ watts** (174 petawatts).

If we compressed all of that into a beam with a cross-section of 1 m² (a disk roughly 1.13 m across), the intensity would be about **1.74 × 10¹⁷ W/m²**—roughly 128 million times more intense than normal sunlight.

### What that intensity actually means

Such a beam would be vastly more powerful than anything we encounter in nature on Earth's surface. For comparison:

- Industrial laser cutters operate at intensities around 10⁶–10⁹ W/m².
- The intensity at the surface of the Sun itself is only about 6.3 × 10⁷ W/m².
- Our beam would be roughly **2.7 billion times more intense than sunlight at the Sun's surface**.

The radiation pressure alone (P = I/c for absorption) would be on the order of 6 × 10⁸ Pa, or about 6,000 atmospheres of pressure—enough to mechanically blast through most materials.

### Effects on matter

Anything the beam struck would not simply "burn." At these intensities, ordinary thermal physics breaks down:

1. **Instant vaporization and ionization.** Solid matter would be converted to plasma in nanoseconds. The beam would drill through steel, rock, or water effectively instantaneously, limited mostly by the speed at which vaporized material could clear the path.

2. **Plasma blooming.** The vaporized material would itself become opaque plasma, absorbing more energy and re-radiating it as a blinding fireball. The air column the beam traveled through would ionize, producing a luminous channel similar to a lightning bolt but sustained.

3. **Atmospheric shockwave.** Heating a 1-meter-wide column of atmosphere to plasma temperatures would create an enormous, continuous explosion along the beam's path—a sustained pressure wave radiating outward, devastating the surroundings for kilometers.

4. **Effective black-body temperature.** Treating the beam's intensity as σT⁴, the equivalent radiative temperature is around 41,000 K—hotter than the photospheres of most stars and well into the regime where matter only exists as plasma.

### The bigger-picture absurdity

A 1-meter beam carrying 174 PW would deposit, in one second, roughly 1.74 × 10¹⁷ joules—equivalent to about 40 megatons of TNT, or roughly 2,500 Hiroshima bombs every second. Aimed at the ground, it would carve a continuously deepening crater while vaporizing surrounding terrain. Aimed at the ocean, it would flash-boil massive volumes of water and inject enormous amounts of steam into the atmosphere. Pointed into space, it would be a planet-scale directed-energy weapon visible across the solar system.

Meanwhile, the rest of Earth, deprived of sunlight, would plunge into darkness and begin freezing rapidly—surface temperatures would fall below 0 °C within days and continue dropping toward radiative equilibrium with deep space (modulated by residual geothermal heat).

### Why this can't physically happen

Beyond the practical impossibility of the "bundling," there's a fundamental optical limit: the **brightness theorem** (conservation of étendue). You cannot focus light from an extended source to an intensity greater than the source itself produces, because doing so would imply heating a target hotter than the source—violating the second law of thermodynamics. The Sun's surface puts out ~6.3 × 10⁷ W/m², and no passive optical system can exceed that at the focal spot. Our hypothetical beam would be billions of times brighter than the Sun's surface, which is why it requires magic rather than mirrors.

So the thought experiment is really a way of appreciating just how *diffuse* sunlight is when spread across Earth's hemisphere—and how staggering the total energy budget becomes once you imagine concentrating it.

hotter than the photospheres of most stars
and well into the regime where matter only exists as plasma.
The bigger-picture absurdity.
A 1-meter beam carrying 174 PW would deposit, in one second, roughly 1.74 × 10¹⁷ joules—
equivalent to about 40 megatons of TNT, or roughly 2,500 Hiroshima bombs every second.
Aimed at the ground, it would carve a continuously deepening crater while vaporizing surrounding terrain.
Aimed at the ocean, it would flash-boil massive volumes of water and inject enormous amounts of steam into the atmosphere.
Pointed into space, it would be a planet-scale directed-energy weapon visible across the solar system.
Meanwhile, the rest of Earth, deprived of sunlight, would plunge into darkness and begin freezing rapidly—
surface temperatures would fall below 0 °C within days
and continue dropping toward radiative equilibrium with deep space (modulated by residual geothermal heat).
Why this can't physically happen.
Beyond the practical impossibility of the "bundling," there's a fundamental optical limit: the brightness theorem (conservation of étendue).
You cannot focus light from an extended source to an intensity greater than the source itself produces,
because doing so would imply heating a target hotter than the source—
violating the second law of thermodynamics.
The Sun's surface puts out ~6.3 × 10⁷ W/m²,
and no passive optical system can exceed that at the focal spot.
Our hypothetical beam would be billions of times brighter than the Sun's surface,
which is why it requires magic rather than mirrors.

and how staggering the total energy budget becomes once you imagine concentrating it.

items.question: What If You Built a Siphon from Europa's Ocean to Earth?
human_answers: No, but I like where you're going with this. [Image: image] Siphons are neat—they let you pump water up and over a barrier using just a tube and gravity. You can use siphoning to empty swimming pools, fill awkwardly-shaped containers, or get up to all kinds of trouble.[1]I asked some friends to suggest which thing in their house they'd be most upset to find someone siphoning water into. Answers included: Spice drawer, gumball machine, tea collection, bottle of vitamins, watercolor paint set, bag of rice with a cell phone in it, mint-condition instant oatmeal collection, carefully tuned musical glasses, ice hotel, prizewinning sand castle, sodium action figure collection, gremlin cage, Martian soil sample, dehydrated astronaut ice cream, and rack of those water-sensing self-inflating lifeboats. [Image: image] It's not necessarily obvious at first glance, but siphoning works because of air pressure. Before we answer the Europa question, it may help to go over how siphons work. If you take a tube full of water and point the ends down, gravity will try to pull the water down, making it fall out of both sides. If the water did start to fall out, a vacuum would form in the middle, since there's no way for air to get in to fill the gap. Each column of water would then have a vacuum on one side and air on the other, which means it would be pushed back up into the tube. [Image: image] In reality, this doesn't happen; the air pressure stops the vacuum from opening up in the first place, and the water just sits there in the tube. Or, at least, it would if it were perfectly balanced. If the water in one end is slightly lower than the other, then the column of water on that side pushes down harder against the air than the column on the other side. This imbalance causes the water to "tip" and run out of the heavier end. [Image: image] To siphon something, you can just keep feeding more water into the tube on the higher side. As long as the surface of that water is higher up than the place where the water is coming out, the siphon will keep running. [Image: image] If the column of water is more than about 34 feet[2]10 meters​[3]2 giraffes high, the pressure from the weight of the water becomes too strong for Earth's air pressure to counteract, and the water does fall out from both sides and briefly create a vacuum.[4]Although as the pressure drops, the water boils away to fill it, so you can't actually get too close to a pure vacuum this way. However, if you use something like olive oil (or mercury), you can get much closer. This means that on Earth's surface, you can't siphon water over a barrier that's more than 34 feet high. In Denver, where the air pressure is lower, the limit is 28 feet (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%28air+pressure+at+altitude+of+denver%29+%2F+%28water+density+*+earth+gravity%29). In a vacuum—in theory—you can't siphon at all.[5]In practice, it turns out siphons do work in a vacuum, at least a little bit (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8F4i9M3y0ew), because the "stickiness" of the water keeps it from pulling apart in the middle. Europa has barely any atmosphere, so you won't be able to do much siphoning. But you also can't siphon water out of the atmosphere from a planet in general. A column of atmosphere, which is miles high, pushes down only as hard as a column of water 34 feet high. The water column is smaller because water is much denser than air. As long as the stuff on top is less dense than the liquid below it, you can't use the pressure from the stuff on top to siphon the liquid up above the stuff on top.[6]Most of the time, things sort themselves into layers, with the denser ones on the bottom. Occasionally, in the Earth, layers of dense rock will end up above layers of less-dense oil. This is why—when oil wellheads break—oil can sometimes come spurting out without any help from the pumps. Even if you could generate a lot of pressure, pumping water from Europa's surface would take some work. Europa's gravity is weaker than Earth's, which means lifting something up from the surface of Europa takes less energy, but it's still not easy. The energy required to "climb out of Europa's gravity well" is the same as the energy required to climb up 209 kilometers (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=Newton%27s+constant+*+europa+mass+%2F+%28earth+gravity+*+europa+radius%29) against Earth's surface gravity. (Earth's gravity well, by comparison, is about 6,379 kilometers "deep"—click on this comic (http://xkcd.com/681/) for an illustration.) Once you've lifted the water out of Europa's gravity well, you then have to lift it the rest of the way out of Jupiter's, which is a lot deeper. Then, you have to do more work to push the water on a trajectory where it intercepts Earth. In terms of energy, the whole task is roughly equivalent to lifting the water about 2,500 kilometers in Earth gravity: [Image: image] You could send the water to Earth by launching it from the surface of Europa at about 7 km/s. Conveniently, since Europa has no atmosphere, you don't need to use inefficient (http://what-if.xkcd.com/38/) rockets to climb up to space. You can launch the water directly from the surface using something simpler, like a coilgun (http://www.coilgun.info/theorymath/ieee/induction_1995.pdf). When the water reaches Earth, it can use atmospheric braking to slow down, and the individual bottles could be steered directly to their targets. Timing the deliveries would be tricky, sure, but it sure would be impressive if you got it right. Plus, you could totally one-up Amazon's drone delivery scheme. [Image: image] At current electricity prices, the launch would cost a minimum of 50 cents (US) per bottle. Of course, getting electricity on Europa is probably a bit more expensive than getting it on Earth,[7]Or would need an awfully long cord. and setting up the purification plant and bottling operation on Europa wouldn't be cheap, to put it mildly. All in all, you're going to have to charge an awful lot per bottle to break even on this whole operation. And if it turns out Europa's water has some weird alien pathogen in it, you might accidentally kill all your customers.[8]And, possibly, everyone else. This may sound like your plan is pretty impractical and unrealistic, especially since there's no point to it all. Water is water. Once you've purified the water on Europa to make it drinkable, it won't be much different from water here on Earth. On the other hand, we ship water around the world from Fiji (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji_Water) for no reason, so who knows. Maybe, with the right marketing, this idea could work. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Siphon physics and feasibility under Europa-to-Earth conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons about whether a siphon could operate from Europa's ocean to Earth, including the roles of pressure, gravity, vacuum, water-column height, and continuity of the liquid column.
criteria.1-2: Claims the siphon would straightforwardly work or fail for irrelevant reasons, with major misunderstandings of siphons, pressure, or gravity.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes some siphon limitation but gives incomplete or confused reasoning, such as mentioning distance only without pressure/vacuum constraints.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that an ordinary siphon would not work, with partial explanation involving atmosphere, pressure limits, or vacuum.
criteria.7-8: Explains the failure using relevant mechanisms: insufficient atmospheric pressure, enormous height/distance, vacuum/boiling/cavitation, and lack of a continuous supported water column.
criteria.9-10: Gives a precise causal account of siphon operation and why Europa-to-Earth siphoning is impossible, including pressure-head limits, Europa's near-vacuum, gravity wells, and the impossibility of using Earth's atmosphere to pull water across space.

criteria.name: Long-range transport and energy-chain reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the downstream causal chain after siphoning fails: extracting water, escaping Europa and Jupiter, transferring to Earth, and safely delivering it.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the transport chain or treats interplanetary water movement as trivial.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that moving water through space is hard but lacks a coherent sequence of required steps.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several major stages, such as extraction, launch, transfer orbit, and Earth capture, but with rough or missing causal links.
criteria.7-8: Coherently traces the energy and engineering requirements from Europa's ocean through Jupiter escape and Earth arrival, with plausible qualitative comparisons.
criteria.9-10: Provides a well-ordered, quantitatively informed chain covering ice/ocean access, launch velocity or equivalent energy, Jupiter's gravity well, trajectory targeting, Earth reentry/braking, and delivery constraints.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling and mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explores the counterfactual setup without collapsing into a simple dismissal, while covering key physical, engineering, and planetary-science mechanisms specific to Europa.
criteria.1-2: Rejects the premise with little reasoning or substitutes an unrelated scenario.
criteria.3-4: Addresses only one mechanism, such as tube length or freezing, while missing most relevant consequences.
criteria.5-6: Covers multiple relevant mechanisms but unevenly, such as siphon failure plus some launch or contamination issues.
criteria.7-8: Balances the direct answer with a broader counterfactual analysis of atmosphere, ice shell/ocean access, freezing, vacuum exposure, energy, orbital mechanics, and delivery.
criteria.9-10: Fully exploits the premise by distinguishing impossible siphoning from alternative transport methods and tracing major physical, operational, biological, and economic consequences.

criteria.name: Plausibility, quantitative calibration, and uncertainty management
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether claims are scaled appropriately and uncertainties are acknowledged, especially for distances, pressures, velocities, energy costs, Europa's environment, and speculative biological risks.
criteria.1-2: Uses wildly implausible numbers or confident false claims, with no uncertainty awareness.
criteria.3-4: Includes a few plausible facts but exaggerates, invents unsupported figures, or treats speculative outcomes as certain.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible qualitatively, with limited numerical grounding or weak distinction between known physics and uncertain details.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable orders of magnitude or comparisons and clearly flags uncertainties such as ocean access, power supply, contamination, and trajectory logistics.

# A Siphon from Europa to Earth

This is a wonderfully absurd thought experiment, but it's instructive because it breaks every assumption that makes a siphon work in the first place. Let's walk through why.

**Siphons need gravity and continuous fluid.** A working siphon relies on a continuous column of liquid in a tube, with gravity pulling the down-leg harder than the up-leg, and atmospheric pressure pushing the fluid up over the hump. The maximum height a siphon can lift water on Earth is only about 10 meters, because that's the height of water column that atmospheric pressure (about 101 kPa) can support before the liquid cavitates and the column breaks.

**Europa is roughly 600 million kilometers away.** Even ignoring the engineering impossibility of a tube that long, you'd need to lift the water out of Europa's gravity well (escape velocity ~2 km/s), then across interplanetary space, then down into Earth's gravity well. A siphon can't do that. There's no continuous "downhill" from Europa to Earth — Europa orbits Jupiter, which orbits the Sun, and Earth orbits the Sun at a smaller radius. In terms of gravitational potential, Earth is actually *deeper* in the Sun's well than Europa, so naively you might think water would "fall" toward us. But the path isn't a straight gravitational gradient; it loops through Jupiter's enormous potential well.

**Space is a vacuum.** A siphon's hump can't exceed the height that ambient pressure can support. With zero pressure in space, the water column would immediately cavitate — it would boil into vapor at any point above a tiny height in Europa's weak gravity (about 1.3 m/s²). The "siphon" would simply outgas at the top and stop flowing.

**The water would freeze and boil simultaneously.** In the vacuum of space, exposed water flash-boils from low pressure while radiating heat away, and the resulting vapor freezes into ice crystals. Your tube would need to be pressurized and heated along its entire 600-million-km length, at which point it's not a siphon — it's a pipeline with pumps.

**If you did somehow pump it:** Europa's subsurface ocean is estimated to contain roughly 2–3 times the volume of all Earth's oceans (~3 × 10¹⁸ m³). Dumping that onto Earth would raise sea levels catastrophically — by hundreds of meters — drowning every coastal city and most continental lowlands. It would also be salty, possibly laced with sulfur compounds from Europa's chemistry, and would arrive at temperatures near freezing.

**The bottom line:** "Siphon" is the wrong concept entirely. No passive fluid-dynamic device can move water between worlds. What you're really describing is an interplanetary aqueduct, which would require active pumping, thermal management, pressurization, and structural support against tidal forces, orbital mechanics, and the relative motion of Europa and Earth (which changes by hundreds of millions of kilometers as they orbit). And if you succeeded, you'd flood the planet.

nodes.text: This is a wonderfully absurd thought experiment,
but it's instructive
because it breaks every assumption that makes a siphon work in the first place.
Let's walk through why.
Siphons need gravity and continuous fluid.
A working siphon relies on a continuous column of liquid in a tube,
with gravity pulling the down-leg harder than the up-leg,
and atmospheric pressure pushing the fluid up over the hump.
The maximum height a siphon can lift water on Earth is only about 10 meters,
because that's the height of water column that atmospheric pressure (about 101 kPa) can support
before the liquid cavitates and the column breaks.
Europa is roughly 600 million kilometers away.
Even ignoring the engineering impossibility of a tube that long,
you'd need to lift the water out of Europa's gravity well (escape velocity ~2 km/s),
then across interplanetary space,
then down into Earth's gravity well.
A siphon can't do that.
There's no continuous "downhill" from Europa to Earth —
Europa orbits Jupiter,
which orbits the Sun,
and Earth orbits the Sun at a smaller radius.
In terms of gravitational potential, Earth is actually deeper in the Sun's well than Europa,
so naively you might think water would "fall" toward us.
But the path isn't a straight gravitational gradient;
it loops through Jupiter's enormous potential well.
Space is a vacuum.
A siphon's hump can't exceed the height that ambient pressure can support.
With zero pressure in space,
the water column would immediately cavitate —
it would boil into vapor at any point above a tiny height in Europa's weak gravity (about 1.3 m/s²).
The "siphon" would simply outgas at the top
and stop flowing.
The water would freeze and boil simultaneously.
In the vacuum of space,
exposed water flash-boils from low pressure
while radiating heat away,
and the resulting vapor freezes into ice crystals.
Your tube would need to be pressurized and heated along its entire 600-million-km length,
at which point it's not a siphon —
it's a pipeline with pumps.
If you did somehow pump it:
Europa's subsurface ocean is estimated to contain roughly 2–3 times the volume of all Earth's oceans (~3 × 10¹⁸ m³).
Dumping that onto Earth would raise sea levels catastrophically —
by hundreds of meters —
drowning every coastal city and most continental lowlands.
It would also be salty,
possibly laced with sulfur compounds from Europa's chemistry,
and would arrive at temperatures near freezing.
The bottom line:
"Siphon" is the wrong concept entirely.
No passive fluid-dynamic device can move water between worlds.
What you're really describing is an interplanetary aqueduct,
which would require active pumping, thermal management, pressurization, and structural support against tidal forces, orbital mechanics, and the relative motion of Europa and Earth
which changes by hundreds of millions of kilometers as they orbit.
And if you succeeded,
you'd flood the planet.

items.question: What If You Tried to Start a Fire with Moonlight and a Magnifying Glass?
human_answers: At first, this sounds like a pretty easy question. A magnifying glass concentrates light on a small spot. As many mischevious kids can tell you, a magnifying glass as small as a square inch in size can collect enough light to start a fire. A little Googling (http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2012/08/27/bafact-math-the-sun-is-400000-times-brighter-than-the-full-moon/) will tell you that the Sun is 400,000 times brighter than the Moon, so all we need is a 400,000-square-inch magnifying glass. Right? [Image: image] Wrong. Here's the real answer: You can't start a fire with moonlight[1]Pretty sure this is a Bon Jovi song. no matter how big your magnifying glass is. The reason is kind of subtle. It involves a lot of arguments that sound wrong but aren't, and generally takes you down a rabbit hole of optics. [Image: image] First, here's a general rule of thumb: You can't use lenses and mirrors to make something hotter than the surface of the light source itself. In other words, you can't use sunlight to make something hotter than the surface of the Sun. There are lots of ways to show why this is true using optics, but a simpler—if perhaps less satisfying—argument comes from thermodynamics: Lenses and mirrors work for free; they don't take any energy to operate.[2]And, more specifically, everything they do is fully reversible—which means you can add them in without increasing the entropy of the system. If you could use lenses and mirrors to make heat flow from the Sun to a spot on the ground that's hotter than the Sun, you'd be making heat flow from a colder place to a hotter place without expending energy. The second law of thermodynamics says you can't do that. If you could, you could make a perpetual motion machine. [Image: image] The Sun is about 5,000°C, so our rule says you can't focus sunlight with lenses and mirrors to get something any hotter than 5,000°C. The Moon's sunlit surface is a little over 100°C, so you can't focus moonlight to make something hotter than about 100°C. That's too cold to set most things on fire. "But wait," you might say. "The Moon's light isn't like the Sun's! The Sun is a blackbody—its light output is related to its high temperature. The Moon shines with reflected sunlight, which has a "temperature" of thousands of degrees—that argument doesn't work!" It turns out it does work, for reasons we'll get to later. But first, hang on—is that rule even correct for the Sun? Sure, the thermodynamics argument seems hard to argue with,[3]Because it's correct. but to someone with a physics background who's used to thinking of energy flow, it may seem hard to swallow. Why can't you concentrate lots of sunlight onto a point to make it hot? Lenses can concentrate light down to a tiny point, right? Why can't you just concentrate more and more of the Sun's energy down onto the same point? With over 1026 watts available, you should be able to get a point as hot as you want, right? Except lenses don't concentrate light down onto a point—not unless the light source is also a point. They concentrate light down onto an area—a tiny image of the Sun.[4]Or a big one (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=sunspotter+solar+telescope)! This difference turns out to be important. To see why, let's look at an example: [Image: image] This lens directs all the light from point A to point C. If the lens were to concentrate light from the Sun down to a point, it would need to direct all the light from point B to point C, too: [Image: image] But now we have a problem. What happens if light goes back from point C toward the lens? Optical systems are reversible, so the light should be able to go back to where it came from—but how does the lens know whether the light came from B or to A? In general, there's no way to "overlay" light beams on each other, because the whole system has to be reversible. This keeps you from squeezing more light in from a given direction, which puts a limit on how much light you can direct from a source to a target. Maybe you can't overlay light rays, but can't you, you know, sort of smoosh them closer together, so you can fit more of them side-by-side? Then you could gather lots of smooshed beams and aim them at a target from slightly different angles. [Image: image] Nope, you can't do this.[5]We already know this, of course, since earlier we said that it would let you violate the second law of thermodynamics. It turns out that any optical system follows a law called conservation of étendue. This law says that if you have light coming into a system from a bunch of different angles and over a large "input" area, then the input area times the input angle[6]Note to nitpickers: In 3D systems, this is technically the solid angle, the 2D equivalent of the regular angle, but whatever. equals the output area times the output angle. If your light is concentrated to a smaller output area, then it must be "spread out" over a larger output angle. [Image: image] In other words, you can't smoosh light beams together without also making them less parallel, which means you can't aim them at a faraway spot. There's another way to think about this property of lenses: They only make light sources take up more of the sky; they can't make the light from any single spot brighter,[7]A popular demonstration of this: Try holding up a magnifying glass to a wall. The magnifying glass collects light from many parts of the wall and sends them to your eye, but it doesn't make the wall look brighter. because it can be shown[8]This is left as an exercise for the reader. that making the light from a given direction brighter would violate the rules of étendue.[9]My résumé says étendue is my forté. In other words, all a lens system can do is make every line of sight end on the surface of a light source, which is equivalent to making the light source surround the target. [Image: image] If you're "surrounded" by the Sun's surface material, then you're effectively floating within the Sun, and will quickly reach the temperature of your surroundings.[10](Very hot) If you're surrounded by the bright surface of the Moon, what temperature will you reach? Well, rocks on the Moon's surface are nearly surrounded by the surface of the Moon, and they reach the temperature of the surface of the Moon (since they are the surface of the Moon.) So a lens system focusing moonlight can't really make something hotter than a well-placed rock sitting on the Moon's surface. Which gives us one last way to prove that you can't start a fire with moonlight: Buzz Aldrin is still alive. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
You cannot start a fire with moonlight and a magnifying glass, no matter how large the lens or how perfectly you focus it.

The fundamental reason is thermodynamic: a magnifying glass works by concentrating light from a source onto a smaller area, but it cannot make that focused spot hotter than the surface of the light source itself. This is a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics and the principle of étendue conservation in optics.

The Sun's surface temperature is about 5,500°C, which is why focusing sunlight can easily ignite materials. The Moon, however, doesn't produce its own light—it merely reflects sunlight. The Moon's surface temperature ranges from about -173°C in shadow to 127°C in direct sunlight. When you focus moonlight, you're concentrating reflected sunlight that has already been scattered and diminished, and the effective temperature of this focused light cannot exceed the Moon's surface temperature.

Additionally, moonlight is roughly 400,000 times dimmer than direct sunlight. Even if you used an enormous lens to collect moonlight from a large area and focus it to a point, you still couldn't raise the temperature of that point above the Moon's surface temperature—far too cool to ignite anything.

So while the magnifying glass would concentrate the moonlight into a brighter spot, that spot would remain cold, and no fire would start.

edus.text: You cannot start a fire with moonlight and a magnifying glass,
no matter how large the lens or how perfectly you focus it.
The fundamental reason is thermodynamic:
a magnifying glass works by concentrating light from a source onto a smaller area,
but it cannot make that focused spot hotter than the surface of the light source itself.
This is a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics and the principle of étendue conservation in optics.
The Sun's surface temperature is about 5,500°C,
which is why focusing sunlight can easily ignite materials.
The Moon, however, doesn't produce its own light—
it merely reflects sunlight.
The Moon's surface temperature ranges from about -173°C in shadow to 127°C in direct sunlight.
When you focus moonlight, you're concentrating reflected sunlight that has already been scattered and diminished,
and the effective temperature of this focused light cannot exceed the Moon's surface temperature.
Additionally, moonlight is roughly 400,000 times dimmer than direct sunlight.
Even if you used an enormous lens to collect moonlight from a large area and focus it to a point,
you still couldn't raise the temperature of that point above the Moon's surface temperature—
far too cool to ignite anything.
So while the magnifying glass would concentrate the moonlight into a brighter spot,
that spot would remain cold,
and no fire would start.

items.question: How Many Gravity Assists Would It Take to Stop Jupiter?
human_answers: More than we can afford. Spacecraft sometimes perform close flybys of heavy, fast-moving planets, which can let them gain speed without using fuel.[1]It may sound strange that you could gain speed by flying toward a planet and then away from it, since intuitively it seems like any speed you gain from flying toward it, you should lose flying away. But it's not really about gravity at all; gravity assists could work just as well with ropes or springs, if you could make them big enough. When you you fly toward a planet, swing around it, and fly back in the direction you came, it's as if you "bounced off" the planet. If the planet is moving, this bounce can give you an extra kick—like a tennis ball thrown at the windshield of a passing truck. You can check out What If #38 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/38/) for details—or, at least, a drawing of the tennis ball thing. Due to conservation of momentum, the maneuver also slows the planet down very slightly, but no one really worries about that. [Image: image] Planets don't slow down much during a flyby because they're so much heavier than spacecraft. When New Horizons flew by Jupiter, it gained about 4,000 m/s of velocity, while Jupiter lost about 10-21 m/s.[2]The geometry is a little complicated, since they were changing both speed and direction. If you want to learn more, look for a copy of this paper (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/71/5/10.1119/1.1539102); it's a great tutorial. 10-21 meters per second may not sound like much, but it very slightly changed Jupiter's orbit, shortening its year and bringing it slightly closer to the Sun. Thanks to that flyby, by the time the Sun goes supernova, Jupiter's calendar will be several dozen nanoseconds out of sync from where it would be otherwise! [Image: image] "Several dozen nanoseconds out of sync" isn't really satisfying, so we'll definitely need more than one flyby. How many can we pull off? The New Horizons mission cost the US government about \$700,000,000 over the full planned lifetime of the mission from 2001 to 2016. Over that same period, the government spent about \$47,879,840,000,000 on other things. If we cut all the spending on those other things[3]It's probably nothing important. and funneled it all into New Horizons probes, we could have launched 68,000 identical New Horizons probes. This would create some problems. For one, New Horizons carries a chunk of plutonium for power. This chunk—about 10 kg of it—was made from uranium in a reactor (http://www.nature.com/news/nuclear-power-desperately-seeking-plutonium-1.16411). To make enough plutonium for 68,000 New Horizons would require a substantial chunk of the world's uranium reserves. But it gets worse.[4]It always seems to, with plutonium. When NASA launches a spacecraft carrying plutonium, they estimate the odds of a launch accident which would release radioactive material into the atmosphere. Usually, these odds are around 1 in 300. With 68,000 launches, then, we can expect a little over 200 nuclear accidents, which probably isn't good. [Image: image] But it would all be worth it if we could slow down Jupiter! Sadly, 68,000 New Horizons probes aren't nearly enough. We'd still only rob Jupiter of a tiny fraction of its speed. Over the lifetime of the Solar System, the error in Jupiter's calendar would only add up to 2 milliseconds. If we made the spacecraft cheaper, we could send more of them, but sooner or later we'd start running out of materials. We'd definitely run out of fuel for all these rocket launches, but let's assume we've built some kind of space elevator to make launches cheap. We'd run out of uranium (to make the plutonium) pretty quickly, but we could replace the uranium with a chunk of lead—after all, this spacecraft doesn't really need to work. Eventually, though, we'd start running out of lead, too. If we replaced the lead with something else—say, rocks, or old garbage—we'd run out of that, too. At some point, in our desperate attempts to reduce Jupiter's forward speed, we'd be reduced to stuffing handfuls of rocks and dirt into a burlap sack with a NASA logo on the side. [Image: image] Then, believe it or not, we would run out of rocks. The Earth's crust only has so much stuff[5]This is the technical term. in it. Even if we peeled up the upper few dozen kilometers of crust and flung it at Jupiter—and for the record, I do not recommend we do this—it would trim less than a single mile per hour off Jupiter's speed. Really, it makes sense that this plan doesn't work. Earth weighs a lot less than Jupiter,[6]Earth weighs almost exactly pi milliJupiters. so even if we throw the entire Earth at Jupiter, it would still only reduce Jupiter's speed by a fraction of a percent—on the order of a few dozen miles per hour. The situation is similar to the one in the tennis ball analogy from earlier: If you want to stop a truck with tennis balls, the tennis balls need more momentum than the truck, which means they need to be extremely heavy, fast, or both. And at the core, that's the problem with this idea. Gravity assists are just like throwing a tennis ball at a speeding truck, and to stop a truck ... [Image: image] ... you need an awfully big tennis ball.

items.model_answer:
This is a fascinating thought experiment that requires considering the physics of gravity assists and Jupiter's orbital mechanics.

**The short answer:** It's effectively impossible to stop Jupiter using gravity assists alone.

Here's why:

**Jupiter's orbital energy is enormous.** Jupiter has a mass of about 1.9 × 10²⁷ kg and orbits the Sun at roughly 13 km/s. Its orbital kinetic energy is approximately 1.4 × 10³⁵ joules—an almost incomprehensibly large amount.

**Gravity assists transfer momentum, not create it.** A gravity assist works by transferring orbital momentum between two bodies. To slow Jupiter down, you'd need to repeatedly send massive objects past it in configurations that steal Jupiter's orbital momentum. Each encounter would transfer only a tiny fraction of Jupiter's momentum to the assisting body.

**The practical constraints are prohibitive:**

1. **You'd need an enormous mass budget.** Even using large asteroids or small moons, you'd need to perform countless gravity assists. The assisting bodies would gain speed (potentially ejecting them from the solar system), while Jupiter would slow incrementally.

2. **The number would be astronomical.** If you used Earth-mass objects (already an absurd proposition), you'd need thousands to millions of precisely orchestrated encounters, depending on the geometry. Using realistic asteroid masses, the number would be in the billions or more.

3. **Orbital mechanics makes it worse.** As Jupiter slows, its orbit changes, making subsequent encounters harder to arrange. You'd need to constantly adjust trajectories.

**A rough estimate:** If you could somehow use Mars-mass objects (about 10% of Earth's mass) in optimal gravity assist configurations, each transferring perhaps 0.01% of Jupiter's orbital momentum, you'd need roughly **10,000 to 100,000 such encounters** just to significantly alter Jupiter's orbit—and far more to actually "stop" it (bring it to near-zero orbital velocity).

In reality, this is purely theoretical. The logistics, energy requirements, and time scales involved make it physically impossible with any conceivable technology.
